Jinavaṃsadīpaṃ [O 0.0001]

The Lamp of the Conqueror's Lineage

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

1.

1.

Mahādayo yo hadayo’dayo’dayo

Hitāya dukkhānubhave bhave bhave,

Akāsi sambodhipadaṃ padaṃ padaṃ

Tamābhivandāmi jinaṃ jinaṃ jinaṃ; (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

The Greatly Compassionate One, whose heart arose again and again for the welfare of those experiencing suffering in existence after existence, established the path to full enlightenment, step by step—Him, the Conqueror, I reverently salute again and again.

2. [O 0.0002]

2.

Pahāya yatthā’bhiratiṃ ratiṃ ratiṃ

Ramanti dhammeva munī munī munī,

Vimuttidaṃ sabbabhavā bhavā’bhavā

Tamābhivande mahitaṃ hitaṃ hitaṃ; (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

Having abandoned delight in pleasures again and again, the sages delight only in the Dhamma again and again. The giver of liberation from all becoming, from both becoming and non-becoming—Him, the greatly revered, the benefactor, I reverently salute again and again.

3. [O 0.0004]

3.

Nipītasaddhammarasā rasā’rasā

Supuññakhetto’rasataṃ sataṃ sataṃ,

Gatā vidhūtā vinayena yena ye

Tamābhivande’sigaṇaṅgaṇa’ṅgaṇaṃ; (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

Those who have drunk the essence of the True Dhamma, who are without craving, a supreme field of merit for the virtuous, again and again; who have gone forth, purified by the discipline—that host of sages, stainless again and again, I reverently salute.

4. [O 0.0005]

4.

Jinā’natambhoruha haṃsarājinī

Jinorasānaṃ mukhapañjarā’li nī,

Sadatthasāraṃ sarasaṃ visūda nī

Upetu me mānasameva vāṇi nī;

May the speech of the Conqueror, like a row of swans on his lotus-face, and the speech of his sons, like a swarm of bees from their cage-like mouths—speech full of the essence of true meaning, elegant, and most pure—come to my mind.

5.

5.

Kammāvasesā vicito’pajātyā

Ganthā’hisaṅkhāravibandhakā me,

Paṇāma puññātisayena’nena

Mā pākadānā’vasarā bhavantu;

May the remnants of my kamma, accumulated through births, my fetters and binding formations, by the surpassing merit of this homage, not find an opportunity to yield their fruit.

6.

6.

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa jinassa vaṇṇaṃ

Vaṇṇeyya kappampi kajito suvaṇṇo,

Kappassi’vosāna manattatāya

Na pāpuṇe buddhaguṇāna mantaṃ;

Even if an eloquent poet were to praise the qualities of the golden-hued Conqueror for an eon, at the very end of that eon, due to their endlessness, he would not reach the limit of the Buddha's virtues.

7. [O 0.0006]

7.

Niddhanta cāmīkara cāru rūpaṃ

Sarassatī bhūsaṇa bhāsanaṃca,

Anañña sādhāraṇa ñāṇamassa

Avāviyā’cintiya mapakpameyyaṃ;

His radiant beauty surpassing refined gold, his speech an ornament to Sarasvatī, and his incomparable, extraordinary wisdom—are unfathomable, inconceivable, and immeasurable.

8.

8.

Kuhiṃ asādhāraṇa rūpa līlā

Kuhiṃ asādhāraṇa vāṇi līlā,

Kuhiṃ asādhāraṇañāṇa līlā

Kuhiṃ nu me mandamatissa līlā;

Where is his matchless grace of form? Where is his matchless grace of speech? Where is his matchless grace of wisdom? Where, indeed, is the grace of my own dull mind?

9. [O 0.0007]

9.

Vibhāvimānī paravamhino ye

Issā’bhimānena vibhaññamānā,

Gavesayantī’dha parassa randhaṃ

Tesaṃ pasaṃsāgarahāhi kimme;

Those who are conceited, scorning others, afflicted by envy and pride, seeking faults in others here—what use to me is their praise or blame?

10.

10.

Pasattha satthāgama pāradassī

Ye sādhavo sādhu guṇappasantā,

Ganthassa nimmāṇaparissamaṃ no

Jānanti teyeva idhappamāṇā;

The wise, who see to the far shore of the Teacher's teaching, the virtuous, serene, delighting in good qualities—they alone are the measure here, they who know the effort of our composing this work.

11.

11.

Ādiccavaṃsappabhavassa tassa

Jinassa satthāgamakovidehi,

Vuttopi pubbācariyehi yesu

Ganthesu saṅkhepavasena vaṃso;

The lineage of that Conqueror, sprung from the Solar Race, was also related concisely in those texts by the ancient teachers skilled in the Teacher's scriptures.

12.

12.

Na tehi sakkā sugatassa vaṃsaṃ

Kiñcāpi viññātu masesayitvā,

Sampuṇṇavaṃsassa vibhāvanāya

Tasmā samussāhita mānasena;

Since it was not possible for them to know the lineage of the Well-Gone One in its entirety, therefore, with an inspired mind, for the sake of clarifying the complete lineage, this work is undertaken.

13. [O 0.0008]

13.

Abhippasanno ratanattayamhi

Pasatthavaṃsappabhavo pabhunaṃ,

Vibhusaṇo vissutakittighoso

Yo bhāti laṅkāya muḷārabhāgyo;

Deeply devoted to the Triple Gem, born of a praised lineage of lords, an ornament whose fame is widely proclaimed—he shines in Lanka, a possessor of immense good fortune.

14.

14.

Amandacāgā’bhiratassa

Punandu nāmassa dayādhanassa,

Buddhe pasādātisayassa tassa

Ajjhesanañcāpi paṭiggahetvā;

And having accepted the request of him named Punandu, who delights in unstinting generosity, is rich in compassion, and possesses surpassing faith in the Buddha,

15.

15.

Nassāya pubbācariyo’padesaṃ

Sotūna matthāya mayā hitāya,

Niruttiyā māgadhikāya sammā

Vidhīyate’daṃ jinavaṃsadīpaṃ;

Relying on the instruction of former teachers, for the benefit and welfare of the listeners, this "Lamp of the Conqueror's Lineage" is now correctly composed by me in the Magadhi language.

16. [O 0.0009]

16.

Saddhāsinehānugatāya paññā-

Dasāya sotūhi manovimāne,

Padīpito’yaṃ jinavaṃsadīpa-

Dīpoharepāpatamappabandhaṃ;

May this lamp, the Lamp of the Conqueror's Lineage, being lit in the mansion of the mind by listeners endowed with the affection of faith and the state of wisdom, dispel the darkness of misfortune without hindrance.

17.

17.

Puraṅgapuṇṇā sirijambudīpe

Sampattibhārena divā’vatiṇṇā,

Yā devarājassa’marāvatī’vā-

Marāvatīnāma purī pure’sī;

In glorious Jambudīpa there was a city of old named Amarāvatī, which, laden with prosperity, seemed to have descended from heaven, like Amarāvatī, the city of the king of the gods.

18.

18.

Vijjādharānañca vihaṅgamānaṃ

Vibandha vehāsagatiṃ bahāsa,

Yasmiṃ purasmiṃ jitaveri cakkaṃ

Pākāracakkaṃ viya cakkavāḷaṃ;

In which city the circle of ramparts, like the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, seemed to mock the unobstructed sky-path of the Vidyādharas and birds, and where the circle of enemies was conquered.

19. [O 0.0010]

19.

Sañcumbitamhoja rajo pabandha-

Supiñjarāpā parikhāhirāmā,

Puritthi pākāra nitambabhāge

Samubbahī kañcana mekhalā’bhaṃ;

The beautiful moats, with water made golden by the clinging pollen of the lotuses they kissed, bore the splendor of a golden girdle upon the hip-like region of the city's ramparts.

20.

20.

Rattindivā rattamaṇi’ndanīla-

Maṇippabhārañjita rājadhāni,

Babandha yā’mandasurindacāpa-

Samujjalākāsatalabbilāsaṃ;

That royal city, colored day and night by the radiance of ruby and sapphire gems, captured the splendor of the sky, which shone brightly like the great bow of the king of the gods.

21.

21.

Yahiṃvadhūnaṃ vadanambujehi

Katāvamānaṃ hariṇaṅkabimbaṃ,

Pabhāhi nīlopalatoraṇātaṃ

Sokābhībhūtaṃca vivaṇṇamāpa;

Where the moon's orb was scorned by the lotus-faces of the women, and, by the brilliance from the blue sapphire archways, became pale as if overcome with sorrow.

22. [O 0.0011]

22.

Saroruha’ntī maṇimandirābhā-

Sañcumbitaṃ puṇṇasasaṅkabimbaṃ;

Saṅkāya rāmājanatā’bhirāmā

Kare pasāresi puramhi yasmiṃ;

In which city, when the full moon's orb, kissed by the splendor of the jeweled mansions, created the illusion of being a lotus, the charming people would stretch out their hands in doubt.

23.

23.

Yattha’ṅganānaṃ paṭibimbitāni

Ādāsabhittīsu mukhambujāni,

Āsuṃ vighātāya madhubbatānaṃ

Vilocanālīna manuggahāya;

Where the lotus-faces of women reflected on mirror-like walls were a torment to the bees and a snare for the swarms of onlookers' eyes.

24.

24.

Sammatta mātaṅga dharādharehi

Yasmiṃ abhissanda madassavanti,

Turaṅga raṅgehī taraṅga mālā

Samākulevā’si vidhūta dhūlī;

Where intoxicated elephants, like mountains, poured forth streams of ichor, and the dust, stirred up by the ranks of horses, was like an ocean agitated with a garland of waves.

25. [O 0.0012]

25.

Nikkhittavīṇā maṇinupurānaṃ

Vilāsinīnaṃ mudupāṇi pāde,

Mattālimālā kalanādinī kiṃ

Nālaṅkaruṃ yattha katāvakāsā;

Where, on the soft hands and feet of playful women—hands that had set down their lutes, feet that wore jeweled anklets—what could sweetly humming garlands of intoxicated bees, finding an opportunity, not adorn?

26.

26.

Dhavatthinīnaṃ kucasārasehi

Nettālibhārā’nananīrajehi,

Yā hāsavīcīhi purī rajanyā

Rarāja samaphullasarojinī’va;

That city, by night, with the crane-like breasts of its amorous women, with their lotus-faces heavy with bee-like eyes, and with the waves of their laughter, shone like a fully blossomed lotus pond.

27.

27.

Candappabhā cumbita candakanta

Pāsāṇadhārā maṇicandikāsū,

Candānanānaṃ yahi maṅganāhaṃ

Parissamasso’pasamāya’hesuṃ;

Where cascades from moonstones, kissed by the moon's rays, on jeweled terraces were for the moon-faced women, to calm the weariness of their sport.

28. [O 0.0013]

28.

Yasmiṃ pūre uddhamadho vinaddha-

Jutippabandho maṇimandirānaṃ,

Samubbahī geruka paṅka diddha-

Vitāna paccattharaṇabbilāsaṃ

In which city, the continuous radiance of the jeweled mansions, bound above and below, bore the splendor of canopies and coverings smeared with red ochre paste.

29.

29.

Suvaṇṇa muttā maṇi vaṃsavaṇṇā-

Pavāḷa rūpī vajirehiñcā’pi,

Yā sattadhaññehi dhanehi phītā

Ahū puri dhaññavatī’va nārī; (Silesabandhanaṃ)

Golden, pearls, gems, bamboo-colored, coral-hued, and also with diamonds—that city was prosperous with the seven kinds of grain and with wealth, like the city named Dhannavatī.

30.

30.

Pasāritā’nekadisāmukhesu

Vicittavatthā’bharaṇādipūrā,

Yatthā’paṇā nijjitakapparukkhā

Kariṃsu lokābhimatatthasiddhiṃ;

Spread out in many directions, filled with various garments, ornaments, and so forth, where the shops surpassed the wish-fulfilling trees, they brought about the fulfillment of the world's desires.

31. [O 0.0014]

31.

Parāgarattā madhupātimattā

Samhinnavelā ghananīlavālā,

Haṃsāsayā pañcasarābhirāmā

Yasmiṃ taḷākā viya kāmabhogī; (Silesabandhanaṃ)

Reddened by pollen, intoxicated by honey-drinkers, with broken shores and dense, dark water-weeds, a dwelling for swans, delightful with the five arrows of love—therein the lakes were like enjoyers of sensual pleasures.

32.

32.

Purantarasmiṃ ratanagghikānaṃ

Raṃsippabandhehi hatandhakāre,

Kundāravindabbhudayenayasmiṃ

Rattindivābheda mavedi loko;

In the inner city, where darkness was dispelled by festoons of radiance from precious jewels, the world perceived no difference between night and day, owing to the blooming of jasmine and lotuses.

33. [O 0.0015]

33.

Mātaṅgajīmūtaghaṭāya ghaṇṭā-

Ṭaṅkāragambhīraravāya yasmiṃ,

Palambhītā mattasikhaṇḍimālā

Akā vikālepi akhaṇḍakīḷaṃ;

Therein, by the deep sound of the clanging of bells, like a host of elephants and thunderclouds, a flock of intoxicated peacocks, being deceived, performed an unbroken dance even at an untimely hour.

34.

34.

Puramhi yasmiṃ caraṇambujehi

Vadhūjato bandhitanūpurehi,

Vikāsa kokāsana sīsa baddha

Mattāli sesa’mbujinī ajesi;

In that city, the host of women, with their lotus-feet adorned with anklets, surpassed the lotus pond crowned with blooming red lotuses and intoxicated bees.

35.

35.

Rasātalaṃ nāgaphaṇāvanaddhaṃ

Nabhotalaṃ vijjulatāvanaddhaṃ,

Yā chāditā rūpiyajātarūpa-

Dhajāvalīhā’jini rājadhānī;

That royal capital, veiled by rows of silver and gold banners, surpassed the netherworld covered with serpent hoods and the vault of the sky entwined with flashes of lightning.

36. [O 0.0016]

36.

Nānatthasāraṃ mitadhātuvaṇṇaṃ

Chandārahaṃ pāṇagaṇā’bhirāmaṃ,

Kavippasatthaṃ sarasaṃ silesā-

Laṅkārapajjaṃ’va puraṃ yamāsi; (Silesabandhanaṃ)

That city was rich in various essences, harmonious in its elements and colors, worthy of desire, delightful to the host of beings, praised by poets, full of sentiment, like a poem embellished with clever wordplay.

37.

37.

Puramhi tasmiṃ karuṇānidhāno

Buddhaṅkuro brāhmaṇasāravaṃse,

Asaṅkhakappāna mito catunnaṃ

Lakkhādikānaṃ udapādi pubbe;

In that city, a repository of compassion, the Buddha-sprout, was born into a pre-eminent Brahmin lineage, four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons ago.

38.

38.

Bhovādivaṃse’kadivākarassa

Puññānubhāvo’dayamaṅgalehi,

Jātassa kho sampati jambudīpo

Vilumpayī maṅgalavāsalīlaṃ;

When he, the one sun of the Bhovādi lineage, was born, through the auspicious signs of the arising of the power of his merit, Jambudīpa was at once stripped of its auspicious charm and beauty.

39. [O 0.0017]

39.

Jātakkhaṇe tassa sarīrajena

Gandhena vaṇṇena sake nikete,

Hatappabhā candanateladīpā

Saṇṭhānamattehi vijāniyāsuṃ;

At the moment of his birth, by the fragrance and radiance born of his body in his own abode, the sandalwood and oil lamps, their light extinguished, were known only by their shapes.

40.

40.

Vimuttadosāhi sukhedhitāhi

Dhātīhi kumbhorupayodharāhi,

Bhato kumāro sukumārakāyo

Khepesi so kānici vāsarāni;

Nourished by faultless, well-tended nurses with pitcher-like breasts, the tender-bodied prince passed some days.

41.

41.

Mahāmahecā’tha pavattamāne

Saveda vedaṅga vidū vidūhi,

Kārāpayuṃ te pitaro’rasassa

Nāmaṃ sumedho’ti padatthasāraṃ;

Then, while a great festival was taking place, his parents had the wise ones, skilled in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, bestow upon their own son the name Sumedha, a name of profound meaning.

42. [O 0.0018]

42.

Uḷārabhāgyena samaṃ kumāre

Saṃvaddhamāne jananī na tittiṃ,

Pāyāsi nīlāmakalalocanāliṃ

Mukhambujaṃ tassa’bhicumbamānā;

As the prince grew, together with his great fortune, his mother, kissing his lotus-face, could not get her fill of gazing with her line of spotless, dark eyes.

43.

43.

Sukhedhita’ṅgāvayavo kumāro

Vimānabhumyā maṇinimmitāya,

Parodi mātāpitaro’bhiyācaṃ

Bimbaṃ kanijaṃ jānuyugena gacchaṃ;

The prince, whose limbs and members were nurtured in happiness, crawling on his pair of knees upon a jeweled palace floor, cried, asking his parents for his own reflection.

44.

44.

Suvaṇṇabimbo’pamacārurūpo

Samācaraṃ dhātibhujā’valambaṃ,

Viññāsapāda’ṅgulimañjarīhi

Salīlamāvāsamalaṅkarittha;

Of beautiful form like a golden image, moving about while supported by the nurses' arms, he playfully adorned the dwelling with the placing of his spray-like toes.

45. [O 0.0019]

45.

Nijena tejena ca jivalokaṃ

Yasena’pubbācarimaṃ phusanto,

Tirokaritvā ravicandasobhaṃ

Saṃvaḍḍhi dhīro ubhato sujato;

Pervading the world of beings with his own splendor and unprecedented glory, and obscuring the radiance of the sun and moon, the wise one, well-born on both sides, grew up.

46.

46.

So sattamā yāva pitāmahassa

Yugā sagabbhāsayasuddhiko’si,

Nihīnajacco’ti na jātivādā

Khitto’pakuṭṭho bhavi vippaseṭṭho;

He was pure from the womb up to the seventh generation of his paternal ancestors. He was not scorned or reviled with talk of birth as 'one of inferior caste,' but became a chief among the wise.

47.

47.

Vedantayaṃ so sanighaṇṭu satthaṃ

Sakeṭubhaṃ sākkharabheda satthaṃ,

Sādhabbatabbedi’tihāsa satthaṃ

Avedi vedaṅgayutaṃ pa satthaṃ;

He mastered the three Vedas with the Nighaṇṭu (glossaries) and Keṭubha (rituals), the texts on phonetics, the treatises on etymology and history, and the Vedāṅgas together with their associated texts.

48.

48.

Ajjhāyako mantadharo pavīṇo

Kalāsu lokāyatalakkhaṇesu,

Papūrakāri padako kavīnaṃ

Tetā’si veyyākaraṇo gaṇiso;

He was a reciter, a bearer of mantras, skilled in the arts, in the Lokāyata, and in the science of signs, a provider of verses for poets, a grammarian, and an accountant.

49. [O 0.0020]

49.

Kandappadappā’naladhumarāji-

Līlāvalambi nijamassurāji,

Na kevalaṃ komalagaṇḍabhāgaṃ

Manampi thīnaṃ malinīkarittha;

His own row of mustaches, hanging gracefully like a wreath of smoke from the fire of Kāma's pride, not only darkened the soft part of his cheeks but also sullied the minds of women.

50.

50.

Tandebhavaṇṇāyatana’ṇṇavamhi

Narūpataṇhātaraṇi narānaṃ,

Pāyāsi cakkhāyatanappiyāhi

Tīrantaraṃ cittaniyāmakaṭṭhā;

In the ocean of craving, striving, becoming, and sense-bases, he who was for men a vessel of desire for human form, dear to the eye, reached the further shore, the state of a pilot for the mind.

51.

51.

Dvijo sumedho suvisuddhamedho

Mātāpitunnaṃ nidhanāvasāne,

Puññānubhāvappabhavaṃ agāra-

Majjhāvasaṃ kāmasukhaṃ’nubhuñjī;

The twice-born Sumedha, of most pure wisdom, after the death of his parents, dwelling in his house, enjoyed sensual pleasures arising from the power of merit.

52. [O 0.0021]

52.

Nisajja pāsādatale’kadā so

Pallaṅkamādhāya rahogatova,

Punabbhavuppatti sarīrabhedo

Dukkho’ti cintesi sabhāvacintī;

Sitting one day on the palace terrace, having assumed the cross-legged posture and gone into solitude, he, a contemplator of reality, reflected: 'The arising of renewed existence and the breaking up of the body are suffering.'

53.

53.

Jāto sa’haṃ jātijarārujādi-

Dhammo’mhi tasmā bhavadukkhasuññaṃ,

Niccaṃ ajātiṃ ajaraṃ arogaṃ

Gavesituṃ vaṭṭati nibbuti’nti;

'Being born, I am subject to the nature of birth, aging, disease, and so forth. Therefore, it is proper to seek Nibbāna, which is eternal, unborn, ageless, and free from sickness, devoid of the suffering of existence.'

54.

54.

Yathāpidukkhe sati ca’tthisātaṃ

Tadaññamuṇhe sati sītamatthi,

Bhavamhi sante vibhavo’pi evaṃ

Nibbāṇamatthī tividhaggisante;

Just as when suffering exists, there is also pleasure, and when heat exists, there is cold; likewise, when existence is present, there is also cessation of existence. Nibbāna exists when the three fires are quenched.

55. [O 0.0022]

55.

Sāvajjadhamme ihavijjamāne

Saṃvijjate bho niravajjadhammo,

Ajāti hoti sati jātiyā’ti

Evaṃ vicintesi sadatthavintī;

'When blameworthy phenomena are found here, a blameless phenomenon is also found; when birth exists, there is also non-birth.' Thus reflected he, the seeker of true meaning.

56.

56.

Disvā yathā guthagato taḷākaṃ

Na tassa doso na tamotareyya,

Kilesadhove amatamhi sante

Tathā na sevetha na tassa doso;

Just as, seeing a pond full of filth, it is not the pond's fault, and one should not enter it; likewise, when the deathless exists for washing away defilements, if one does not resort to it, it is not the fault of the deathless.

57.

57.

Pāpāriruddho sati khemamagge

Na tassa doso na sukhaṃ vajeyya,

Pāpāriruddho sati khemamagge

Tathā nagaccheyya na tassa doso; (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

Just as, when a safe path exists, one who is obstructed by enemies does not reach the safe destination, and it is not his fault; likewise, if one does not go to the deathless, it is not the fault of the deathless.

58. [O 0.0023]

58.

Yathāpi vejje sati ghorarogī

Na tassa doso ta labhe tikicchaṃ,

Rāgādirogī sati buddhavejje

Dhammosadhaṃ ne’cchati kassa doso;

Just as, when a doctor is available, it is not the doctor's fault if a grievously ill patient does not receive treatment; so too, when the Buddha-doctor is present, if a patient with the disease of lust and so forth does not desire the medicine of the Dhamma, whose fault is it?

59.

59.

Yo kaṇṭhabaddhaṃ kuṇapaṃ pahāya

Yathāsukhaṃ gacchati sericārī,

Tathevi’maṃ kucchita pūtikāyaṃ

Yaṃnūna gaccheyyamahaṃ jahitvā;

As one who abandons a corpse bound to his neck and goes freely as he pleases, so too this despised, putrid body—indeed, I should abandon it and go.

60.

60.

Uccāraṭhānamhi janā’napekkhā

Katvā karīsāni kayathā vajanti,

Tathā sarīraṃ kuṇapehi pūraṃ

Yaṃnūna gaccheyyamahaṃ jahitvā;

As people, indifferent to a latrine, having deposited their excrement, go as they please; so too this body, filled with filth—indeed, I should abandon it and go.

61. [O 0.0024]

61.

Nāvaṃ yathā jajjaramāpagāhiṃ

Vajeyya netā atapekkhakova,

Tathā navadvārasavaṃ sarīraṃ

Yaṃnūna gaccheyyamahaṃ jahitvā;

Just as a leader would abandon a decrepit ship in a river without concern, so too, this body with its nine flowing openings—indeed, I should abandon it and go.

62.

62.

Corehi gacchaṃ avahārabhītyā

Khemaṃ sumedho puramotareyya,

Tathā sarīraṃ kusalāvahāraṃ

Yaṃnūna gaccheyyamahaṃ jahitvā;

As a wise man, traveling with robbers and fearing plunder, would enter a safe city; so too, this body, which plunders what is wholesome—indeed, I should abandon it and go.

63.

63.

Nekkhamma saṅkappa paro’pamāhi

Anussaritve’vamuḷāravīro,

Hato’rapāre tibhave asāre

Vihāsi ukkaṇṭhitamānaso so;

Thus reflecting with similes on renunciation and other lofty matters, that noble hero dwelt with a yearning mind, afflicted by this shore and the far in the worthless threefold existence.

64. [O 0.0025]

64.

Suvaṇṇa muttā maṇi rūpiyādi-

Dhanehi dhaññehi ca pūritāni,

Avāpuritvāna,tha kosakoṭṭhā-

Gārāni taṃ dassayi rāsivaḍḍho;

Then the treasurer, having opened them, showed him the treasuries and granaries, filled with gold, pearls, gems, silver, and other wealth, and with grain.

65.

65.

Pitāmahānaṃ pakapitāmahānaṃ

Mātāpitunnaṃ vibhavā panettha,

Anappakāthāvarajaṅgamāte

Saṃdissare dhīra sumedhavippa;

‘Herein is the wealth of our grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and parents. O wise and discerning brahmin, these vast possessions, both movable and immovable, are to be seen.’

66.

66.

So sattamā yāva paveṇivaṭṭā

Vibhāvayitvā vibhavassarāsiṃ,

Dhanāgamassāpi dhanabbayassa

Pamāṇa’mācīkkhipamāṇadassiṃ;

Having displayed the heaps of wealth from the lineage up to the seventh generation, he also explained the measure of income and expenditure to the discerning one.

67.

67.

Kuṭumbametaṃ paṭipajjamāno

Kāmesu devoviya indriyāni,

Icchānurūpaṃ paricārayassu

Icceva mārocayi rāsivaḍḍho;

‘While managing this household, indulge your senses in sensual pleasures like a god, according to your wish.’ Thus spoke the treasurer.

68. [O 0.0026]

68.

Amuṃ mahantaṃ dhanadhaññarāsiṃ

Samāvinitve’ka kahāpaṇampi,

Nā’dāya mātāpitaropya’ho to

Gatā yathākamma mito parattha;

‘Alas, though they amassed this great heap of wealth and grain, my parents went from here to the next world according to their deeds, unable to take even a single coin with them.’

69.

69.

Tabbatthusāraggahaṇātisūro

Vossaggasanto atha sattasāro,

Rañño samārociya etamatthaṃ

Bheriṃ carāpesi sake puramhi;

Exceedingly heroic in grasping the essence of that matter, then, peaceful in relinquishment, with truth as his essence, having informed the king of this matter, he had a drum beaten in his own city.

70.

70.

Santappayi bherivirāvagandha-

Māghāya sampattajātā’lijātaṃ,

Bhovādi nānāratanādibhoga-

Madhūhi sattāha’manāthanātho;

For seven days, the protector of the helpless satisfied the assembled multitude of beings who had arrived, with the sound of drums, perfumes, garlands, and with various enjoyments such as jewels and sweet things.

71. [O 0.0027]

71.

Tadagga yaññālaya vārivāha-

Dhārānipātaddhanavuṭṭhihetu,

Mahā janassā’dhikavatthutaṇhā-

Taṭāni bhinnāni manodahesu;

Because of that supreme sacrificial offering, a rain of wealth like a downpour from rain clouds, the banks of the great populace's excessive craving for possessions were broken in the lakes of their minds.

72.

72.

Sukhedhito kāmasukhaṃ pahāya

Gharā’bhīnikkhamma tato sumedho,

Ajjhogahetvā himavanta’māpa

Dhammesako dhammakapakabbata’ntaṃ;

Brought up in comfort, the wise Sumedha, abandoning sensual pleasures, then went forth from home. Having entered the Himalayas, he, a seeker of Dhamma, reached the vicinity of the Dhammaka mountain.

73.

73.

Vitakkamaññāya’tha devaraññā

Vyāpārito māpayi vissakammo,

Tahiṃ vivekakkhamaka massamañca

Manoramaṃ caṅkamabhumibhāgaṃ;

Then, understanding his thought, the king of devas employed Vissakamma, who constructed there a hermitage suitable for seclusion and a delightful walking area.

74. [O 0.0028]

74.

Tamassamaṃ pabbajitehi suññaṃ

Upecca soñcāramavāpuritvā,

Ñatvā tadantolikhita’kkharāni

Khāriṃparikkhārabharaṃavekkhi;

Having approached that hermitage, empty of ascetics, he opened the door, and reading the letters inscribed inside, he observed the carrying-pole with its load of requisites.

75.

75.

Nivatthavatthaṃnavavadosupetaṃ

Vivajjiyāvajjiyavajjadassi,

Dhāresitaṃbārasadhānisaṃsa-

Manojapupphattharavākacīraṃ;

Seeing the fault in what is blameworthy, he discarded the worn cloth endowed with nine faults, and put on the bark-fibre garment, which had twelve advantages and was as delightful as a spread of flowers.

76.

76.

Punnāgapupphattharakā’bhirāmaṃ

Aṃse vidhāyā’jinacammakhaṇḍaṃ,

Katvā jaṭāmaṇḍala mittamaṅge

Tivaṅka mādāya’tha khārikājaṃ;

Having placed on his shoulder a piece of antelope skin, delightful as a spread of punnāga flowers, and having made a circle of matted hair on his head, he then took up the triple-bent staff and the carrying-pole.

77.

77.

Bhujaṅgabhogo’rubhujena dhīro

Ādāya cālambanadaṇḍakoṭiṃ,

Samaggahī tāpasavesamevaṃ

Virattacittoka vibhaveva bhave’pi;

Thus the wise one, with his mighty arm like a serpent's coil, taking hold of the tip of his supporting staff, took up the ascetic's garb, his mind detached from both worldly possessions and continued existence.

78. [O 0.0029]

78.

So caṅkamī caṅkamamotaritvā

Silātalasmiñca divā nisajji,

Sāyaṃ paviṭṭho vasi paṇṇasālaṃ

Nipajji kaṭṭhattharasesamañce;

He walked on the path and, descending from it, sat on a stone slab by day. In the evening, he entered and dwelt in the leaf-hut, lying down on a couch strewn with wood.

79.

79.

Pacacūsakālamhi pabujjhito so

Āvajjayitvā’gamanappavattiṃ,

Vivekakāmassa mame’ttha vāso

Kāmaṃ gharāvāsasamo siyā’ti;

Awakening at dawn, he reflected on his situation: ‘For me, who desires solitude, living here would indeed be like living at home.’

80.

80.

Aduñhi paṇṇacchadanaṃ kapota-

Pādāruṇaṃ beluvapakkavaṇṇā,

Bhūmīpi bhittī rajatāvadātā

Mañco’pi cittattharavārurūpo;

‘Indeed, this leaf-hut is reddish like a pigeon's foot, the color of a ripe beluva fruit. The floor and walls are also white as silver, and the couch is of a beautiful form with variegated coverings.’

81. [O 0.0030]

81.

Subhāka manāpā mama pakaṇṇasālā

Sādīnavā dupparibhāriyā’yaṃ,

Paṇītabhikkhā pariyeṭṭhi mūla-

Dukkhassa natthi’ti pamāṇa manto;

‘My beautiful and pleasant leaf-hut is full of danger and hard to maintain. The search for fine alms is a root of suffering.’ Thus the wise one reflected.

82.

82.

Agārasaññāya paṭikkhapitvā

Tañca’ṭṭhadosā kulapaṇṇasālaṃ,

Dasaṅga sādhāraṇa rukkhamūlaṃ

Phalāphakhalāhāra mupecca bhojī;

Having rejected the perception of it as a house and that family leaf-hut with its eight faults, he resorted to the root of a tree, common to the ten ascetic practices, and ate food of various fruits.

83.

83.

Sumedhaso so divasāni satta

Mahāpadhānaṃ padahaṃ sumedho,

Patto abhiññāsu vasisu pāraṃ

Sabbaṃka samāpattisukhaṃ avindi;

That wise Sumedha, for seven days applying himself to the great striving, reached the further shore of mastery in the higher knowledges and experienced all the bliss of meditative attainments.

84. [O 0.0031]

84.

Tasmiṃkhaṇe kānana devatāhi

Sādhū’ti nigghositapītighoso,

Abbhuggato tassa yasena saddhiṃ

Visuddhavijjācaraṇu’bbhavena;

At that moment, a joyous cry of ‘Well done!’ was proclaimed by the forest deities, and this sound arose together with his fame, born of his pure knowledge and conduct.

85.

85.

Vijjādharā tagguṇadīpakāni

Mutiṅgavīṇādhanibandhavāni,

Gāyiṃsu gītāni’va naccamāno

Himācalo sampati sampavedhi;

The Vidyādharas sang songs that proclaimed his virtues, interwoven with the sounds of drums and lutes. At that time, the Himalaya mountain, as if dancing, trembled greatly.

86.

86.

Muddhaṅkuraṃ bhudharakuṭabāhu-

Satehi tannijjhara cāmarehi,

Vidhūyamānehi vidhūtapāpaṃ

Katopahāreva mahāsarā’pī;

With its peaks like hundreds of arms and its waterfalls like yak-tail fans being waved, the mountain, like a crest-jewel, seemed to make an offering to him whose evil was scattered away; and the great lakes did likewise.

87. [O 0.0032]

87.

Akālameghaddhani bherirāva-

Vyāpāritā mattasikhaṇḍisaṇḍā;

Ajjhāvasantaṃ vanasaṇḍamajjhaṃ

Mahiṃsucā’khaṇḍanataṇḍavena;

Spurred on by the drum-like sound of unseasonal thunder, flocks of intoxicated peacocks performed an unbroken, wild dance upon the earth around him who was dwelling in the midst of the forest grove.

88.

88.

Mandā’nilā’mandabhujā’valamba-

Sunīlasākhāmaṇivijanīhi,

Lataṅganā’liṅgitasālasāmī

Saṃvijayuṃ vitadarampi dhīraṃ;

Gentle breezes fanned even the fearless wise one with the dark blue, jeweled fans of the branches of the lordly Sāla trees, which, embraced by creeper-women, hung down like mighty arms.

90. [O 0.0033]

90.

Kapītanā’soka tamāla nīpā

Kapītanā’soka tamāla nīpā, (samattapādabhyāsa mahā yamakaṃ)

Kapītanā’soka tamāla nīpā

Kapītanā’soka tamāla nīpā;

Kapittana, Asoka, Tamāla, Nīpa; Kapittana, Asoka, Tamāla, Nīpa; Kapittana, Asoka, Tamāla, Nīpa; Kapittana, Asoka, Tamāla, Nīpa.

91.

91.

Na velalitā kiṃ pasavakā’vataṃsā

Latāvitānā madhupālisālī,

Latāvitānā madhupā’lisālī

Na vellitā kiṃ pakasavā’vataṃsā;(Samuggabheda yamakaṃ)

Are not the garlands of pasavaka flowers swaying? The vine canopies are resplendent with rows of bees. The vine canopies are resplendent with rows of bees; are not the garlands of pakasa flowers trembling?

92. [O 0.0034]

92.

Pupphāvalī kandala pāṭalaggā

Kalāpinī sā vanarājinīlā,

Pupphākulī kandana pāṭalakkhī

Kalāpanīlā vara rājinīva; (Addhagomuttikā bandhanaṃ)

A garland of flowers with prominent Kandala and Pāṭala; that forest-line, dark blue and peacock-like. Filled with flowers, causing lamentation, with red eyes; like an excellent queen, dark blue and beautifully adorned.

93. [O 0.0035]

93.

Natāsiro mañjarikāsuramhā

Natāsiro pañjalikāva ramme,

Vane nibaddhaṃ ramito vibhāsi

Vineyya bandhūracīto pahāro; (Pādagomuttikā bandhanaṃ)

With bowed head, like a divine sprout; with bowed head, charming like one with folded hands. Bound in the forest, you shine, delighted; having removed the beautifully arranged assault.

94.

94.

Rajokirantā’vanatā latāsuṃ

Lājokirantā vanitā natāva,

Dvijoaraññaṃ vasitā pitāgho

Gajotarantova latā vitānaṃ; (Silokagomuttikā bandhanaṃ ākulajālamitipi)

The pollen-scattering vines are bowed down; the parched-rice-scattering women are bowed down like them. The twice-born dwelt in the forest, a parricide, like an elephant crossing a vine canopy.

95. [O 0.0036]

95.

Mataṅgajindā na masakkariṃsu

Pādāni natvāna padipadhāmaṃ,

Paññādhavaṃ pīna tapaṃ phalehi

Himaddipāde parisuttamañhi; (Kabbanāma gabbha cakkaṃ)

The lordly elephants did not fail to show respect, having bowed at the feet of that beacon of light, the lord of wisdom, rich in austerity and its fruits, who was supremely pure at the foot of the snowy mountain.

96. [O 0.0037]

96.

Mettāya chattaṃ’va phaṇaṃ phaṇindo

Dhāresi sīse vasino cacāra,

Nathāmavā’kāva’balesu kiñci

Medhāya nando thiravāci kheme; (Kavināma gabbha cakkaṃ)

The serpent king held his hood over the master's head like an umbrella of loving-kindness as he walked. He did nothing forceful among the weak. Rejoicing in wisdom, firm of speech, he was secure.

97. [O 0.0038]

97.

No’sitehi’ssa santāsa’nū’na tosa vato do,

Dāyato vasato na’nusantāsassa hitesino; (Gāthaddhavisaya paṭiloma yamakaṃ)

From the cold, no fear arose in him, the vow-holder; his joy was undiminished, giving satisfaction. Dwelling and giving, he caused no distress to the well-wisher.

98.

98.

Yokā’sā’vāsa kāyo kāma’kāma’makāma’kā,

Sakāyanā’nāya’kāsa vāma nā ga ganā’mavā; (Sabbato bhadda bandhanaṃ)

This body is a dwelling for craving, desiring sense-pleasures, yet free from desire. It is one's own, leading to security, vast as the sky, not crooked, a noble being, unmoving, and faultless.

99. [O 0.0039]

99.

Dayāya vasito dāye yāpajāsiva māsadā,

Yajārahaṃ rañjamāno vasihaṃso ciraṃvasi; (Addhabbhama bandhanaṃ)

Mastered by compassion, in giving; ever auspiciously sustaining the people; delighting in what is worthy of offerings, the master-swan dwelt for a long time.

100.

100.

Madhumada madhukara virute virute

Malayaja surahīta pavane pavane

Himavati vikasita padume padume

Adhisukha manubhavi savasi savakasi; (Pādanta yamakaṃ)

In the resounding hum of bees intoxicated with honey; in each breeze made fragrant with sandalwood; on the Himalaya, in each blooming lotus; he experienced supreme bliss, dwelling in his own abode.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānandadānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe dūrenidāne sumedhabrāhmaṇāpadānaparidīpo.

Thus, in the Jinavaṃsadīpa, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, a source of joy for the hearts of all poets, ends the elucidation of the story of the brahmin Sumedha in the Dūrenidāna.

Paṭhamo saggo.

The First Canto.

1. [O 0.0040]

1.

(Mandā’kkantā) marapurasiriṃ sabbasampattisāraṃ

Jambuddīpā’sama sarasije kaṇṇikā sannikāsaṃ,

Rammaṃ rammavhaya puravaraṃ pāramīpāradassī

Buddho dīpaṅkara dasabalo sabbalokekadī; ()

Tasmiṃ kāle vipulakaruṇā nārisañcodita’tto

Nānā khīṇāsava parivuto cārikaṃ sañcaranto,

Saṃvattento sunipuṇatayaṃ dhammacakkaṃ kamena

Patvā tasmiṃ paṭivasati sodassanavhe vihāre; ()

In the delightful, excellent city called Ramma, which possessed the splendor of a celestial city, the essence of all prosperity, like the pericarp of a peerless lotus in Jambudīpa—there the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, seer of the far shore of the perfections, the Ten-Powered One, the sole lamp for all the world, was residing. At that time, his mind stirred by immense compassion, surrounded by many whose cankers were destroyed, he wandered on tour, skillfully setting in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma. Arriving there in due course, he dwelt in the monastery named Sodassana.

3. [O 0.0041]

3.

Sutvā dipaṅkara bhagavato nāgarā kittisaddaṃ

Sambuddho so itipi arahaṃ tyādinā’bbhuggataṃ taṃ,

Gāhāpetvā tuvaṭatuvaṭaṃ vatthabhesajja pānaṃ

Tannittā’suṃ pamuditamatā gandhamakālādihatthā; ()

The citizens, hearing the sound of the Blessed Dīpaṅkara's fame, which had arisen as, 'He is a Perfectly Enlightened One, an Arahant,' and so forth, had robes, medicine, and drink quickly procured. With joyful minds and with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in hand, they went forth.

4.

4.

Patvā dīpaṅkaratarihariṃ gandhamālādikehi

Pūjetvāta’ñajalimukulikā ekamantaṃ nisinnā,

Dhammaṃ sutvā savaṇasubhagaṃ buddhapāmokkhasaṅghaṃ

Saṃyācitvā muditahadayā svāttayā’pagañjuṃ; ()

Having approached Dīpaṅkara, the lion who has crossed over, and having worshipped him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they then sat to one side with their hands folded like lotus buds. After hearing the Dhamma, which is pleasant to the ear, they invited the Sangha with the Buddha at its head and, with joyful hearts, departed to their own abodes.

5. [O 0.0042]

5.

Sajjetvā te dutiyadivase sajjanā dānasālaṃ

Ussāpattā dhajakadaliyo puṇṇakumbhe ṭhapennā,

Kubbantā’pi dhavalasuḷinu’kkhepa lājopahāraṃ

Evaṃ tassā’gamana mayanaṃ laṅkarontā vihāsuṃ; ()

On the second day, those virtuous people, having prepared the alms-hall, raised banners and plantain trees and placed full water pots. They also made offerings of scattered white powder and parched grain. Thus they remained, decorating the path for his arrival.

6.

6.

Abbhuggantvā atha himavatā so sumedho tapassi

Gacchaṃ tesaṃ upari nabhasā vākacīraṃ dhunanno,

Disvā pītippamuditajate añjasaṃ sodhayante

Sañjhāmegho riva parilasaṃ dhataritthe’kamantaṃ; ()

Then that ascetic Sumedha, having risen up from the Himalaya, was traveling through the sky above them, shaking his bark-cloth garment. Seeing the people, filled with joy and delight, clearing the path, he descended to one side, gleaming like an evening cloud.

7.

7.

Saṃsodhentā kalalavisamaṭṭhāna saṅkāradhānaṃ

Kasmā tumhe paṭipathamimaṃ’laṅkarothā’ti pucchi,

Bhante dīpaṅkaratarahari’dāni nissāya rammaṃ

Buddho hutvā viharati mahādhammasaṅkhaṃ dhamanto; ()

As they were clearing a muddy, uneven place that was a receptacle for rubbish, he asked, 'Why do you adorn this path?' They replied, 'Venerable sir, the lion-like Dīpaṅkara, who has crossed over, having now become a Buddha, dwells in the city of Ramma, blowing the great conch of the Dhamma.'

8. [O 0.0043]

8.

So sambuddho parivutamahābhikkhusaṅgho yato no

Gāmakkhettaṃ pavisati tato’laṅkaromā’bruviṃsu,

Buddhūppādo kimuta sutaraṃ dullabho buddhasaddo

Iccevaṃso sumariya alaṅkattukāmo’si maggaṃ; ()

They said: 'Because that Perfectly Enlightened One, surrounded by a great Sangha of bhikkhus, is entering our village domain, we are therefore adorning it.' He then reflected thus: 'The arising of a Buddha is rare; how much rarer still is the sound of the word "Buddha"!' Reflecting in this way, he became desirous of adorning the path.

9.

9.

Jhānā’bhiññā ratatakavacu’jjotamāna’ttabhāvo

Saddhāye’so acalasadiso iddhimā tāpaso’ti,

Sallakkhetvā kalalavisamaṃ duggamaggappadesaṃ

Sajjetuṃ te sapadi muditā sādhavo tassa’daṃsu; ()

'This ascetic, endowed with jhānas and higher knowledges, his being radiant like golden armor, steadfast in faith like a mountain, is powerful indeed!' Having thus observed, those virtuous people, delighted, quickly gave him a muddy, uneven, and difficult section of the path to prepare.

10. [O 0.0044]

10.

Nānāpupphaṃ jalajathalajaṃ ocinitvā vanamhā

Tetvā devāsurabhavanato koviḷārādipupphe,

Ānetvā’haṃ bhujagabhavatā phullakaṇḍuppalāni

Chekosmī’ti vithariya pathaṃ iddhiyā saṃvidhātuṃ; ()

'Having gathered various aquatic and terrestrial flowers from the forest, having brought koviḷāra and other flowers from the realms of devas and asuras, and having fetched blooming kaṇḍuppala lotuses from the realm of the nāgas, I could, by my psychic power, prepare the path, for I am skilled in this.' Thus he thought.

11.

11.

Katve’vaṃ me hadayamakuḷaṃ tovikāseyya tasmā

Veyyāvaccaṃ visadamatino kāyikaṃ saṃvidhāya,

Ajjevā’haṃ vipulakusalaṃ sañcinissa’ntī dhīro

Saṃsodhetuṃ kalalakalusaṃ añjasaṃ ārabhittha; ()

'If I were to prepare the path thus with psychic power, my heart-bud would not blossom. Therefore, by performing physical service with a clear mind, I shall today accumulate vast merit.' Thinking thus, the wise one began to cleanse the muddy defilement from the path.

12.

12.

Passantānaṃ vimalanayano’bhāsa jimūtagabbhe

Buddhobuddho’tya’bhihitavaco vijjurājīva cārī,

Tasmiṃ paṅke nijakaratala’mebhājapacchihi dhīmā

Paṃsuṃ datvā rajatadhavalaṃ vālukaṃ vokiranto; ()

As he worked, the sound 'Buddho, Buddho!' was heard, like a streak of lightning moving through the heart of a storm cloud for those who watched with clear eyes. The wise one, placing soil and scattering silver-white sand, worked in that mire with his own hands and with baskets.

13. [O 0.0045]

13.

Tasmi ṭhāne kallalulite suṭṭhu nā’laṅkateva

Saddhiṃ dīpaṅkara’nadhivaro’nekakhīṇāsavehi,

Patto brahmā’maranaraphaṇisiddhavijjādharānaṃ

Saṃvattante suvipulamahe pāṭihīre uḷāre; ()

While that muddy place was still not yet fully adorned, the unsurpassed Dīpaṅkara arrived, together with numerous arahants. As a sublime miracle and a vast festival for the Brahmās, devas, humans, nāgas, siddhas, and vidyādharas unfolded, he drew near.

14.

14.

Hema’mbhojo’pamasuvadanaṃ maṇḍitaṃ lakkhaṇho-

Sītyā’nubyañjanavilasitaṃ ketumālāvilāsaṃ,

Satthāraṃ taṃ disidisi pabhāniccharanta’ñjasambhi

Āgacchantaṃ viya maṇitale mattamātaṅgarājā; ()

He saw that Teacher, his beautiful face like a golden lotus, adorned with the major marks, resplendent with the eighty minor characteristics, and glorious with the flame-like radiance. Emitting light in every direction, he came along the path like a majestic elephant king upon a jeweled surface.

15. [O 0.0046]

15.

Oloketvā vimalanayanañcandaniluppalāni

Ummiletvā ratanaphalakaṃ akkamantova piṭṭhiṃ,

Nānākhīṇāsavaparicuto kaddamaṃ nā’kkamitvā

Sambuddhoyaṃ vajatu iti me dīgharattaṃ hitāya; ()

Opening his pure eyes, which were like blue lotuses, he looked upon him and thought: 'May this Perfectly Enlightened One, attended by many whose cankers are destroyed, proceed without stepping on the mud. May this be for my welfare and happiness for a long time!' Then, making his back like a jeweled plank to be trod upon, he lay down.

16.

16.

Sallakkhetvā khara’jinajaṭāvākacīrāni kese

Omuñcitvā visamakalale pattharitvā’ttabhāvaṃ,

Setuṃ katvā paramapaṇidhī kominī codita’tto

Pañcā’bhiññāratanamaṇimā svā’cakujjo nipajji; ()

Spreading out his rough antelope skin, matted hair, and bark-cloth garments, he laid his own body across the uneven mud, making of it a bridge. With supreme resolve, his mind urged on, he lay down straight and unmoving, like a jewel endowed with the five higher knowledges.

17.

17.

Sutvā gāthāpadampi na me bhāriyaṃ saṃkilese

Viddhaṃsetvā varasivuraṃ pattumicche sacā’haṃ,

Saṃvijjante tibhavabhavane dukkhitā’nantasatte

So’bhaṃ eko kathamadhigame dhamma maññātaveso;()

'If I so wished, by destroying the defilements, I could attain the supreme city of peace; for me, this would not be difficult, even by hearing but a single verse. But since infinite beings exist, suffering in the three realms of existence, how could I, for myself alone, realize this Dhamma?'

18. [O 0.0047]

18.

Yannūnā’haṃ parahitarato sammadaññāya bodhiṃ

Āropetvā nikhilajanataṃ’nuttaraṃ dhammanāvaṃ,

Uttāretvā varasivapuraṃ vaṭṭadukkhodadhimhā

Pacchā dīpaṅkaramuni yathā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇissaṃ; ()

What if I, delighting in the welfare of others, should perfectly awaken to enlightenment, and place all people upon the supreme ship of the Dhamma? Having ferried them across the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra to the excellent city of peace, then, afterwards, like the sage Dīpaṅkara, I too shall attain Nibbāna.

19.

19.

Iccevaṃ so pumariya samodhānayitvā’ṭṭhadhamme

Saṃsāramhā’vataraṇamahāseturūpo pajānaṃ,

Muddhābaddha’ñjalipuṭajaṭo paṅkapiṭṭhe nipanno

Sambodhatthaṃ paṇidhimakari tāva tappādamūle; ()

Thus that man, having combined the eight qualities, being like a great bridge for beings to descend from Saṃsāra, with matted hair and hands joined in reverence upon his head, lying upon the muddy ground, made his aspiration for enlightenment at the feet of that very one.

20. [O 0.0048]

20.

Ussisaṭho sapadi bhagavā pañcavaṇṇappasādaṃ

Ummīletvā nayanayugalaṃ phullanīluppalābhaṃ,

Disvā nīlopalamaṇimayaṃ vātapānañcayaṃ’va

Ugghāṭento isivaramhāpaṅkajaṃ paṅkapiṭṭhe; ()

Suddenly, the Blessed One, standing at the head of the path, opening his pair of eyes—like blooming blue lotuses and possessed of a five-colored radiance—as if opening a window made of blue lotus jewels, saw the great ascetic, a lotus upon the muddy ground.

21.

21.

Etassi’jajhissati iti ayaṃ patthanā’nāgataṃsa-

Ñāṇaṃ sammā patiniya ito kappalakkhādhikānaṃ,

Āvajjento upari caturāsaṅkhiyānantya’vedi

Patvā bodhiṃ ahamiva siyā gotamo nāma buddho; ()

'This one's aspiration will be fulfilled.' Thus, by means of his knowledge of the future, duly reflecting back from here over more than a hundred thousand aeons beyond the four incalculables, he knew: 'Having attained enlightenment, like me, this one will be a Buddha named Gotama.'

22.

22.

Tumhe sampassatha iti imaṃ tāpasaṃ saṅghamajjhe

Vatve’vaṃ so padamasadisaṃ dhammarājā dadanto,

Samhinditthā’dharakisalayā’lattakaṃ nāgataṃya-

Paññāmuddā’ṅkitapadasataṃ vattasandesagabbhaṃ; ()

Having spoken thus, 'Behold this ascetic in the midst of the Sangha!', the King of Dhamma, bestowing an incomparable prophecy, proclaimed a hundred verses marked with the seal of wisdom, containing a message for the future.

23. [O 0.0049]

23.

Vāsaṭṭhānaṃ kapilanagaraṃ nāma māsāmahesi

Mātā suddhodananarapati te pitā’diccavaṃse,

Bimbā bimbā dharavati piyā hema bimbā bhirāmā

Tasmiṃkāle tanujaratanaṃ rāhulo hessate te; ()

Your dwelling place will be the city named Kapila; your mother, the great queen Māyā; your father, King Suddhodana of the solar lineage. Your beloved wife will be Bimbā, beautiful as a golden image. At that time, your jewel of a son, Rāhula, will be born to you.

24.

24.

Hessante te paṭhamadutiyassāvakā sāriputta-

Moggallānā dvijakulabhavā bhuripaññiddhimanto,

Ānandākhyo yati pati rupaṭṭhāyakosāvikānaṃ

Khemātheri parama yugalaṃ uppalabbaṇṇatheri; ()

Your foremost disciples will be Sāriputta and Moggallāna, born into brahmin families, endowed with great wisdom and psychic power. The monk named Ānanda will be your personal attendant. Among the female disciples, the foremost pair will be Khemātherī and Uppalavaṇṇātherī.

25. [O 0.0050]

25.

Assattho te vijayaviṭapī tvañca kho gotamavho

Chabbassānī padahiya gharā nikkhamitvā sakamhā,

Pāyāsaggaṃ parivisiya bho tvaṃ sujātāya dinnaṃ

Bodhiṃ bujjhissasi iti dhuvaṃ bodhimūle nisajja; ()

Your Bodhi tree will be the Assattha, the tree of victory, and you will be known as Gotama. Having gone forth from your home and striven for six years, and having partaken of the excellent milk-rice given by Sujātā, you will surely awaken to enlightenment, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

26.

26.

Satthā sañjhāghanapaṭalato muttavijjullate,va

Sandassetvā nijabhujalataṃ cīvarabbhantaramhā,

Pakhyākāsi jaladhararavā’kāragambhīraghoyaṃ

Nicchāretvā suradhanurivo’bhāsa chabbaṇṇaraṃsi; ()

The Teacher, like a streak of lightning freed from a mass of evening clouds, displayed his vine-like arm from within his robe and proclaimed with a voice as deep as the sound of thunder, sending forth six-colored rays that shone like a celestial bow.

27.

27.

Amhe dīpaṅkarabhagavato sāsane nā’vabuddhā

Lacchāmā’ti tava parimukhe’vā’yatiṃ mokkhadhammaṃ,

Tasmiṃ pattā’khīla suranarāpatthayuṃ taṅkhaṇevaṃ

Pūjetvā’tañjalisarasije pādapīṭhamhi tassa; ()

'We did not awaken in the dispensation of the Blessed Dīpaṅkara, but we shall obtain the deathless Dhamma in your presence in the future.' At that very moment, all gods and humans, filled with faith, made this aspiration, worshipping at his feet with hands folded like lotus buds.

28. [O 0.0051]

28.

Buddho brahmāmaranarasiro cumbitaṅghī sarojo

Sampūjetvā’ṭṭhahi jaṭilakaṃ pupphamuṭṭhīhi tamhā,

Pakkāmi so kanakasikharīhāri kiñjakkhabhāre

Ubbhūta’mhoruhavanasire appayanto padāni; ()

The Buddha, whose lotus-like feet were kissed by the heads of Brahmās, gods, and humans, having been worshipped there by the matted-haired ascetic with eight handfuls of flowers, then departed, placing his feet upon the heads of the lotuses that had sprung up, his form as captivating as a golden mountain peak.

29.

29.

Rammaṃ rammaṃ mahīya jaṭilaṃ pupphamuṭṭhīhi katvā

Khīṇā khīṇāsavavasigaṇā dakkhiṇaṃ pakkamiṃsu,

Devā’devā pavuramakaruṃ vandanāmānapūjaṃ

Dīpaṃ dīpaṅkaradasabalañcā’nugantvā nivattā; ()

The assembly of Arahants, masters with taints destroyed, making the earth delightful with handfuls of flowers for the matted-haired ascetic, departed to the right. Gods and asuras made a great sound of homage, respect, and veneration; and having followed the Island, Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, they turned back.

30. [O 0.0052]

30.

Tamhā ṭhānā gatasati jane sannisinnassa tassa

Pallaṅkenā’maranara pariccanta pupphāsanamhi,

Jātikkhettā tahimupagatā devatā etamatthaṃ

Ārocesuṃ mahitavaraṇā añjalimañjarīhiṃ; ()

When the people had departed from that place, and he was seated cross-legged upon the flower-seat abandoned by gods and humans, deities from his birth-realm who had gathered there announced this matter to him with great reverence, with hands folded like blossom clusters:

31.

31.

Pubbe pupphāsanupari samārūḷhabuddhaṅkurānaṃ

Addhāne’ve’tarahi bhavatocā’sanārohaṇamhi,

Ekālokā dasahi guṇitā lokadhātu sahassī

Saṃvattante tvamanavarataṃ hessase tena buddho; ()

'Just as in the past, at the time of Buddha-sprouts who ascended the flower-seat, so now at this moment of your ascent, ten thousand world-systems become a single light. Therefore, you will without fail become a Buddha.'

32.

32.

Tāsaṃ vācaṃ savaṇamadhuraṃ devatānaṃ nisamma

Bhiyyo cittappabhavavīriyo pītivipphāritatto,

Pubbe sattuttamaparicitā bodhisambhāradhammā

Āvajjesi kati iti sudhī dhammadhātuṃ sahetuṃ; ()

Hearing the ear-sweet words of those deities, with vigor born of mind greatly increased and his body expanded with joy, the wise one reflected upon the qualities that are the requisites for enlightenment, familiar to the supreme beings of the past, investigating the nature of phenomena with its cause.

33. [O 0.0053]

33.

Okujjitvā dharaṇiṭhapito puṇṇa kumbho sumedha

Vissandetvā salilamakhilaṃ kintupaccāharetha,

Evaṃ datvā dhanasutakalatta’ṅgapaccaṅgajīve

Nibbinno mā bhavi’ti paṭhamaṃ pāramiṃ’dhiṭṭhahi so; ()

Just as a full pot placed upon the ground and overturned, having poured out all its water, would not draw it back in, so too, having given away wealth, sons, wives, limbs great and small, and even life, he resolved upon the first perfection, thinking: 'May I not be regretful.'

34.

34.

Nā’pekkhitvā yathariva nijaṃ jīvitaṃ jīvitaṃ’va

Rakkhanto sañcarati camari cāmara candikābhaṃ,

Evaṃ sīlaṃ varasivapuradvāramārakkha dhīra

Ajjhiṭṭhāsi iti sadutiyaṃ pāramiṃ suddhasīlo; ()

Just as the camari deer, not caring for its own life, wanders guarding its moon-bright tail as if it were its very life, so he, of pure virtue, resolved on the second perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, O wise one, I shall guard my virtue, the gate to the excellent city of bliss.'

35. [O 0.0054]

35.

Saṃviggo yo ciraparivasaṃ ghorakārāgharamhi

Muttīṃ tamhā’gamayati yathā hohi nekkhammanitto

Nibbinno tvaṃ tathariva bhave bandhanāgārarūpe

Ajjhiṭṭhāsi tatiyampi so pāramintye’kacārī; ()

Just as one, agitated by long dwelling in a dreadful prison, seeks release from it, so he, the solitary wanderer, resolved on the third perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, being disgusted with existence, which is like a prison-house, be intent on renunciation!'

36.

36.

Hīnukkaṭṭhaṃ kulamanugharaṃ bhikkhako bhikkhu bhikkhaṃ

Aṇvāhiṇḍaṃ labhati naciraṃ saṃvaraṭṭho yathe’vaṃ,

Sambodhattha bhaja paṭibale paṇḍite puṭṭhapañho

Ajjhiṭṭhāsi tvamiti matimā pāramiṃ so catutthiṃ; ()

Just as a monk on his alms round, going from house to house among families high and low, obtains his sustenance, so he, the intelligent one, resolved on the fourth perfection, thinking: 'For the sake of enlightenment, you must seek out the able and the wise and question them.'

37.

37.

Niccussāho vicarati yathā kesarī sericārī

Evaṃ ṭhāne gamanasayanecā’sane tvaṃ sumedha,

Ussoḷhī tyāsithilavīriyo hoti sambodhanatthaṃ

Ajjhīṭṭhāsi thiravīriyavā pañcamiṃ pāramiṃ so; ()

Just as a lion, wandering at will, moves about with constant energy, so he, firm in energy, resolved on the fifth perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, Sumedha, in standing, walking, sitting, and reclining, be resolute and of unflagging energy for the sake of awakening.'

38. [O 0.0055]

38.

Iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ pathaviriva bho sabbamānāvamānaṃ

Nāpajjitvā manasiviktiṃ tvaṃ sahanto khamanto,

Sambodhatthaṃ paravadhakhamo hohi’tī khantivādī

Ajjhiṭṭhāsi parahitarato chaṭṭhamiṃ pāramiṃ so; ()

Just as the earth endures all things, pleasant and unpleasant, honor and dishonor, without its mind being affected, so he, an exponent of patience, delighting in the welfare of others, resolved on the sixth perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, you must be patient and forbearing; for the sake of awakening, be tolerant of harm from others!'

39.

39.

Vīthiṃ nātikkamati niyamaṃ osadhītārakā’yaṃ

Evaṃ santuttama paricitaṃ saccavācaṃ sumedha,

Tvaṃ māvitikkami karahaci boddhukāmo subodhiṃ

Ajjhiṭṭhāsi’tya’vitathakathi sattamiṃ pāramiṃ so; ()

Just as the morning star does not transgress its fixed path, so he, a speaker of truth, resolved on the seventh perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, Sumedha, desiring to awaken to supreme enlightenment, you must never transgress truthful speech, practiced by the supreme peaceful ones.'

40. [O 0.0056]

40.

Tamhāṭhānā balavapavane vāyamāne’pi thokaṃ

Kappaṭṭhāsi tacalati yathā pabbato suppataṭṭho,

Tvaṃ tiṭṭhāhi tathariva adhiṭṭhānadhammesu daḷhaṃ

Ajjhiṭṭhāsī’tyavalasadiso ca’ṭṭhamiṃ pāramiṃ so; ()

Just as a well-established mountain, standing for an aeon, does not move in the slightest even when a strong wind blows, so he, like an unmoving mountain, resolved on the eighth perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, you must stand firm in your resolutions.'

41.

41.

Otiṇṇesu udakarahado bho nihīnuttamesu

Sītattaṃ sampharati hi samaṃ vārinā bhāvayeni,

Mettāyevaṃ tibhavabhavane sabbasattesu tulyaṃ

Ajjhiṭṭhāsi samuti navamiṃ pāramiṃ metta citto; ()

Just as a lake of water, O sir, imparts coolness equally with its water to all who enter it, whether high or low, so he, with a mind of loving-kindness, resolved on the ninth perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, I must develop loving-kindness equally toward all beings in the three realms of existence.'

42.

42.

Iṭṭhāniṭṭhe sati paṭihate vatthujāte yathāhi

Majjhattā’yaṃ vasumativadhū hoti dukkhe sukheka vā,

Evaṃ bho tvaṃ bhava samatulāsantibho’pekkha ko’ti

Ajjhiṭṭhāsi savasi dasamiṃ pāramiṃ bhurimedho; ()

Just as this earth remains neutral in the face of sorrow and happiness, when encountering things both liked and disliked, so he, of great wisdom and self-mastery, resolved on the tenth perfection, thinking: 'Likewise, O sir, you must be balanced, peaceful, and equanimous.'

43. [O 0.0057]

43.

Ālolento tidasapamitaṃ pāramisāgaraṃ so

Sattādhiso nisitamatimā ñāṇamatthā’calena,

Āvajjesi vasumatavadhu sādhukāraṃ’va denti

Saṃkampi sampati satimato dhammatejena tena; ()

That Master of beings, with sharp intellect, investigating the ocean of the thirty perfections with the unshakeable churning-stick of his knowledge, reflected. And the earth, as if giving a cry of approval, trembled at that moment through the Dhamma-power of that mindful one.

44.

44.

Bhīrūcchamhī ghaṇapathaviyā kampamātāyi’māya

Patvā dīpaṅkarabhagavato rammavāsī samīpaṃ,

Sampucchiṃsu vasumati bhusaṃ kampi taṃkissahetu

Āvajjetvā samuti munino tampavattiṃ kathesi; ()

The people, both fearful and fearless, were amazed by this solid earth quaking. Having approached the Blessed Dīpaṅkara, who was residing in Ramma, they asked, 'The earth has quaked violently; for what reason is this?' The sage, reflecting, then declared the cause of that event.

45.

45.

Nikkaṅkhā te punapi nagarā nāgarā taṃ upecca

Sampūjesuṃ caraṇayugalaṃ gandhamālādikehi,

Katvā tena’ñjalisarasije yena dīpaṅkare’ṇo

Uṭṭhāsi so purisatisaho sannīsinnāsanamhā; ()

Those city-dwellers, now free from doubt, again approached him and honored his pair of feet with perfumes, garlands, and the like. Having made a lotus-like añjali in the direction of Dīpaṅkara, that bull among men then rose from the seat where he had been sitting.

46. [O 0.0058]

46.

Mā te rogo bhavi paṭibhayaṃ mā bhavi chambhitattaṃ

Saṅkappo te paramapaṇidhi sijjhataṃ khippameva,

Itthañcā’sithutipadasataṃ jātikhettā gatā taṃ

Pupphādīhi mahīya jaṭilaṃ nijjarā byāhariṃsu; ()

'May no disease befall you, may no fear or trembling come upon you. May your supreme aspiration be swiftly fulfilled.' Thus, the deathless ones spoke hundreds of verses of praise, honoring the ascetic with flowers and other offerings from the birthplace.

47.

47.

Abbhuggantvā pavanapadaviṃ devatānaṃ manāni

Bodhātvo himavati sakaṃ assamaṃ tāpaso so,

Patto atthācalamupagamī taṅkhaṇe raṃsimālī

Saṅkocetvā sarasijavanaṃ saṃharitvā’ṃsujālaṃ; ()

Having ascended into the path of the wind, delighting the minds of the deities, that ascetic in the Himalayas reached his own hermitage. At that moment, the radiant sun, having approached the setting mountain, caused the lotus grove to close, withdrawing his net of rays.

48. [O 0.0059]

48.

Rammaṃ dīpaṅkarabhagavato rammavatyā’bhidhānaṃ

Vāsaṭṭhānaṃ janakajananī dve sudevassumedhā,

Niccopaṭṭhāyakayativaro sāgatomaṅgaloca

Tissocā’suṃ paṭhamadutiyassāvakā theranāgā; ()

The delightful dwelling place of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was named Rammavatī. His father was Sudeva and his mother was Sumedhā. The constant attendant, the excellent sage, was Sāgata. Maṅgala and Tissa were the first and second disciples, great elders.

49.

49.

Nānākhīṇāsavaparivuto cā’si nandā sunandā

Tassā’hesuṃ paṭhamadutiyassāvikā aggabhūtā,

Kāyo’sitiratanapamito pipphalināmabodhi

Aṭṭhāsi so pacurajanataṃ tārayaṃ vassalakkhaṃ; ()

He was surrounded by various ones whose taints were destroyed. Nandā and Sunandā were his first and second female disciples, the foremost ones. His body was eighty ratanas in measure, and the Bodhi tree was named Pipphalī. He stood for a hundred thousand years, saving many people.

50.

50.

Satthā dīpaṅkaravho suranarasaraṇodīpadīpocirassaṃ

Dīpevo dhammadīpaṃ tibhuvanabhavane vīta’vijjandhakāraṃ

Aggikkhandho’vabhāsaṃ vihariya parinibbāyi khīṇāsavā’pi

Khīṇasnehāpadīpāyathariva ariyā sāvakā nibbutā’suṃ; ()

The Teacher named Dīpaṅkara, a lamp and refuge for gods and men, for a long time lit the lamp of the Dhamma in the three-world existence, dispelling the darkness of ignorance. Having dwelt shining like a mass of fire, he attained final Nibbāna. And the noble disciples, their taints destroyed, were extinguished, just as lamps are when their fuel is exhausted.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānandadānanidāne jitavaṃsadīpe dūrenidāne sumedha tāpasassa mūlapaṇiṭhānaṭṭhapanapavatti paridīpo dutiyo saggo.

Thus, in the Jitavaṃsadīpa—the source of delight for the hearts of all poets—composed by the sage named Medhānanda, this is the second chapter, the exposition on the account of the establishment of the original aspiration of Sumedha the ascetic in the Distant Epoch.

1. [O 0.0060]

1.

Lokaṃ (’vasantatilako) kumudākaraṃ mā

Koṇḍaññanāmabhagavā’tha pabodhayatto,

Jāto tadā varamatī vijitāvi rājā

Sampanna cakkaratano’bhavi cakkamatti; ()

Then the Blessed One named Koṇḍañña, intent on awakening the world, which was like a pond of water-lilies, arose. At that time, the wise King Vijitāvi was born; endowed with the wheel-jewel, he became a wheel-turning monarch.

2.

2.

Saṅghassa buddhapamukhassa uḷāradānaṃ

Datvā vidhāya paṇidhiṃ varabodhiyā so,

Rajjaṃ pahāya jinasāsanamotaritvā

Jhānānya’lattha paṭilaṅvarappadāno; ()

Having given a great gift to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head, he made an aspiration for supreme enlightenment. Having abandoned his kingdom and entered the Dispensation of the Conqueror, he attained the meditative absorptions, having received the supreme gift.

3. [O 0.0061]

3.

Tassā’si rammavatināma puraṃ sunando

Rājā ahosi janako jananī sujātā,

Bhaddassubhaddasamaṇā varasāvakā’suṃ

Tisso’patissa’samaṇi varasāvikāyo; ()

His city was named Rammavatī. King Sunanda was his father, and his mother was Sujātā. The monks Bhadda and Subhadda were the excellent disciples, and the nuns Tissā and Upatissā were the excellent female disciples.

4.

4.

Lakkhāyuko vijayabodhi visālasāla-

Kalyāṇi nāma tadupaṭṭhahi cā’nuruddho,

Tassā’ṭṭha sītiratanappamitaṃ sarīraṃ

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

His lifespan was a hundred thousand years. His victory-Bodhi was a great Sāla tree named Kalyāṇī, and Anuruddha was his attendant. His body was eighty-eight ratanas in measure, and there were three gatherings of noble disciples.

5.

5.

Tassā’parena samayeni’ha’naṅgabhaṅgo

Uppajji maṅgalajino janamaṅgalāya,

Buddhaṅkuro’tiruciro surucī samañño

Āsi tadā’vatisuro dvijavaṃsaketu; ()

At a time after that, the Victor Maṅgala, the destroyer of desire, arose here for the welfare of the people. At that time, the Buddha-embryo, known as Suruci, was exceedingly handsome, a great being and the banner of the twice-born lineage.

6. [O 0.0062]

6.

Datvā sasāvakajitassa dināni satta

Patthesi bodhimasamaṃ gavapānadānaṃ,

Pabyākato bhagavatā bhavanā’hīgantvā

Pabbajjito sukhamavindi samādhijaṃ so; ()

Having given a gift of cattle and drink to the Victor with his disciples for seven days, he aspired for unsurpassed enlightenment. Having received the prophecy from the Blessed One, he went forth from home, and having become an ascetic, he found the bliss born of concentration.

7.

7.

Tassu’ntaraṃ puravaraṃ pitaro’ttara’vhā

Āsuṃ sudevasamaṇo vasi dhammaseno,

Tassā’ggasāvakayugaṃ sakasāvikānaṃ

Bhaddaṃyugaṃ abhavi sivalicā’pya’sokā; ()

His excellent city was Uttara, and his parents were named Uttara. His pair of chief disciples were the monks Sudeva and Dhammasena. The excellent pair among his female disciples were Sīvalī and Asokā.

8. [O 0.0063]

8.

Taṃ pālito jinamupaṭṭhahi aṭṭha’sīti

Hattho’si tassa vajirūpamarūpakāyo,

Bodhī’pi nāgataru sāvakasantipātā

Āsuṃ tayo navutivassasahassamāyu; ()

Pālita attended upon that Victor. His body was eighty-eight cubits tall, of incomparable form, like a diamond. The Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree. There were three gatherings of disciples, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

9.

9.

Tassā’parena sumano karuṇānidhāno

Nātho manojamathano udapādi loke,

Buddhaṅkuro’bhavi tadā’tulanāgarājā

Teja’ggijālajalito atuliddhimā so; ()

After him, Sumana, a treasury of compassion, the Protector, the crusher of desire, arose in the world. At that time, the Buddha-embryo became an incomparable Nāga king, blazing with a fiery net of glory, possessing incomparable psychic power.

10.

10.

Nāgo’pi nāgabhavanamhi sasāvakassa

Buddhassa dibbaturiyehi katupahāro,

Datvāna dānamatulaṃ paṇidhiṃ akāsi

Buddho bhavissasi tuvanti ahāsi buddho; ()

The Nāga, in his Nāga abode, made an offering to the Buddha and his disciples with divine musical instruments. Having given an incomparable gift, he made an aspiration. The Buddha then declared: 'You will become a Buddha.'

11. [O 0.0064]

11.

Khemavhayaṃ puramahū janako sudanto

Rājā janetti sirimā nijasāvakānaṃ;

Aggā bhaviṃsu saraṇo vasi bhāvitatto

Soṇā tadaggasamaṇi’si tathu’pasoṇā; ()

His city was named Khema. His father was King Sudanta, and his mother was Sirimā. Among his own disciples, the foremost were Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta. The foremost nuns were Soṇā and also Upasoṇā.

12.

12.

Tassā’si nāgataru bodhi udenatero-

Paṭṭhāyako navutivassasahassamāyu,

Ubbedhato navutihatthamitaṃ sarīraṃ

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

His Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree, and the elder Udena was his attendant. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. His body was ninety cubits in height, and there were three gatherings of noble disciples.

13.

13.

Tassā’parena udapādi’ha revatākhyo

Devādivanditapado bhuvi devadevo,

Sattuttamo bhavi tadā atidevanāmo

Bhovādivaṃsatilako catuvedavedī; ()

After him, one named Revata arose here, the god of gods on earth, whose feet were venerated by deities and others. At that time, the highest of beings, named Atideva, was a crest-jewel of the brahmin lineage and a master of the four Vedas.

14. [O 0.0065]

14.

Baddhañjalī sirasi dhammakathaṃ nisamma

Gantvāna taṃ saraṇamuttaramuttariyaṃ;

Datvā’hipatthayi sukhodhimatho mahesi

Buddho bhavissasi tuvantī visākarittha; ()

With hands clasped respectfully on his head, having heard the Dhamma discourse, he went to that supreme, unsurpassed refuge. Then, having made an offering, he aspired for blissful enlightenment. The Great Seer made the declaration: 'You will become a Buddha.'

15.

15.

Tassā’si dhaññavatināma puraṃ jinassa

Mātā mahesi vipulā vipulo pitā’si,

Sabrahmadevavaruṇo bhavi saṅghamajjhe

Bhaddā ca bhaddayugalaṃ duvidhaṃ subhaddā; ()

The Victor's city was named Dhaññavatī. His father was Vipula and his mother was Vipulā. His chief disciples were Varuṇa and Brahmadeva. The excellent pair of female disciples were Bhaddā and Subhaddā.

16.

16.

Taṃ sambhavo vasi upaṭṭhahi nāgabodhi

Rukkhopya’sitiratanaṃ bhavi attabhāvo,

Āyuppamāṇampi saṭṭhisahassavassaṃ

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātāta;

Sambhava was his attendant. His Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree, and his body was eighty ratanas in height. His lifespan was sixty thousand years, and there were three gatherings of noble disciples.

17. [O 0.0066]

17.

Tassā’paramhi samaye janapārijāto

Uppajji sobhitajino jitapañcamāro,

Ajjhāyako sakalaveda muḷārabhogī

Buddhaṅkuro bhavi tadā’jitanāmavappo;

In a time after him, the Victor Sobhita arose, a celestial tree for the people, conqueror of the five Māras. At that time, the Buddha-embryo was a brahmin named Ajita, a master of all the Vedas, enjoying great wealth.

18.

18.

Dhammaṃ nisamma saraṇesu patiṭṭhahitvā

Saṅghassa buddhapamukhassa uḷāradānaṃ,

Datvā padhānapaṇidhāna makāsi dhīro

Tvaṃ lacchasi’ti varabodhi mahāsi satthā; ()

Having heard the Dhamma and become established in the refuges, and having given a great gift to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head, the wise one made the chief aspiration. The Teacher declared: 'You will attain supreme enlightenment.'

19.

19.

Rammaṃ sudhammamahu tassa puraṃ sudhammo

Rājā ahosi janako janikā sudhammā

Tassā’ggasāvakayugaṃ asamo sunetto

Tassāvikā’ggayugalaṃ nakulā sujātā; ()

His delightful city was Sudhamma. His father was King Sudhamma, and his mother was Sudhammā. His foremost pair of disciples were Asama and Sunetta, and the foremost pair of his female disciples were Nakulā and Sujātā.

20. [O 0.0067]

20.

Nāgassa nāgataru bodhi sarīramaṭṭha-

Paṇṇāsahatthapamitaṃ tamatomathero,

Sopaṭṭhahī navutivassasahassamāyu

Āsuṃ tayo ariya sāvaka sannipātā; ()

His Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in measure. The elder Anoma attended upon him. His lifespan was ninety thousand years, and there were three gatherings of noble disciples.

21.

21.

Uppajji tassa aparena anomadassi

Buddho pabuddhakamalāmalanīlanetto,

Buddhaṅkuro jitasurāri tadāni yakkha-

Senāpatī bhavi mahiddhimahānubhāvo; ()

After him arose the Buddha Anomadassi, with blue eyes like pure, opened lotuses. At that time, the Buddha-embryo was a conqueror of the asuras, and became a general of the yakkhas, of great psychic power and majesty.

22.

22.

Sambodhi maggapuriso paṇidhānayaṃ so

Saṅghassa buddhapamukhassa uḷāradānaṃ,

Pādāsi tisu saraṇesu patiṭṭhahitvā

Buddho bhavissasi tuvanti jino’bruvitaṃ; ()

That person on the path to full enlightenment, having been established in the three refuges, gave a great gift to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head and made his aspiration. The Conqueror declared to him: 'You will become a Buddha.'

23. [O 0.0068]

23.

Ṭhānañhi candavatināma yasodharākhyā

Mātā mahesi yasavā janako janindo,

Tassa’ggasāvakayugaṃ nisabho atomo

Dve sundarī ca sumanā carasāvikā’suṃ; ()

His city was named Candavatī. His mother was the queen named Yasodharā, and his father was the king Yasavā. His foremost pair of disciples were Nisabha and Atoma, and his two foremost female disciples were Sundarī and Sumanā.

24.

24.

Bodhī’pi tassa kakudho munidehamaṭṭha-

Paṇṇāsahatthapamitaṃ varuṇābhidhāno,

Thero upaṭṭhahi ca lakkhapamāṇamāyu

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

His Bodhi tree was the Kakudha tree. The sage's body was fifty-eight cubits in measure. The elder named Varuṇa attended upon him. His lifespan was a hundred thousand years, and there were three gatherings of noble disciples.

25.

25.

Tassā’parena padumo dipadānamindo

Jāto pabujjhitamanopadumo pajānaṃ,

Dhīro babhūva varavāraṇakumbhabhedī

Sīho tadā rucirakesarabhāragīvo; ()

After him arose Paduma, lord of bipeds, born, awakening the mind-lotus of the people. At that time, I, the wise one, became a lion that breaks the temples of choice elephants, with a neck bearing a beautiful mane.

26. [O 0.0069]

26.

Buddhaṃ nirodhasukhavediyanaṃ vatamhi

Sattāhamakkhipadūmehi tamaccayitvā,

Cittaṃ pasādiya punā’gatasāvakesu

Sīho vibhāsi paṭiladdhavarappadāno; ()

While the Buddha was experiencing the bliss of cessation, for seven days I honored him with unblinking lotus-eyes. Then, having gladdened my mind, I returned to my disciples. As a lion, I shone forth, having received an excellent boon.

27.

27.

Tassā’si campakapuraṃ padumābhidhāno

Rājā ahosi janako asamā janettī,

Sālopasālayatayo varasāvakā’suṃ

Rāmā’pi tassa paramāsamaṇi surāmā; ()

His city was Campaka. His father was the king named Paduma, and his mother was Asamā. His excellent disciples were the ascetics Sāla and Upasāla, and his foremost female ascetics were Rāmā and Surāmā.

28.

28.

Nāmenu’paṭṭhahi vasi varuṇo tamaṭṭha-

Paṇṇāsahatthamita massa sarīramā’si,

Bodhi’pi soṇataru lakkhapamāṇamāyu

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

The sage Varuṇa by name attended upon him. His body was fifty-eight cubits in measure. His Bodhi tree was the Soṇa tree, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years. There were three assemblies of noble disciples.

29. [O 0.0070]

29.

Tassā’parena varado muni nāradavho

Pāpandhakāranikaraṃ bhīduro’dapādi,

Buddhaṅkuro bhavi tadā’khilajhātabhiññā-

Lābhī pavattaphalabhoji tapodhanīso; ()

After him arose the sage Nārada, the bestower of boons, a destroyer of the massed darkness of evil. At that time, I, a Buddha-sprout, became an obtainer of all jhānas and higher knowledges, one who enjoyed the resultant fruits, a lord of ascetics rich in austerity.

30.

30.

Katvānu’ḷārapaṇidhāna muḷāraviro

Datvā sasāvakajinassa uḷāradānaṃ,

Pūjesi taṃ surabhinā haricandanena

Satthāpi sampati viyākaraṇaṃ adāsi; ()

Having made a great aspiration, the great hero gave a great gift to the Conqueror together with his disciples. He honored him with fragrant sandalwood, and the Teacher then gave a prediction.

31.

31.

Tassā’si dhaññavatināma puraṃ sumedho

Rājā ahosi janako jananī anomā,

Dve bhaddasālajitamittavasi vasina-

Maggo’ntarā samaṇi phagguṇi bhikkhunītaṃ; ()

His city was named Dhaññavatī. His father was King Sumedha, and his mother was Anomā. His two foremost disciples, masters of self-control, were Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta. Among the female ascetics, the bhikkhunī Phagguṇī was foremost.

32. [O 0.0071]

32.

Vāseṭṭhabhikkhu tadupaṭṭhahi rūpakāyo

Tassā’ṭṭhasitiratanaṃ mahasoṇasākhī,

Bodhiddumo navutivassasahassamāyu

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasantipātā; ()

The monk Vāseṭṭha attended upon him. His physical body was eighty-eight ratanas tall. His Bodhi tree was the great Soṇa tree. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. There were three assemblies of noble disciples.

33.

33.

Tassā’parena padumuttara dhammarājā

Jāto tilokapadumo padumappitaṅghī,

Aḍḍho uḷāravibhavo maharaṭṭhiyo so

Buddhaṅkuro bhavi tadā jaṭilābhidhāno;()

After him was born Padumuttara, the king of Dhamma, the lotus of the three worlds, with feet like lotuses. He was wealthy, of great splendor, a great ruler. At that time, I, a Buddha-sprout, was known by the name Jaṭila.

34.

34.

Sambodhiyā’dhigama paccayapatthanaṃ so

Virovidhāya padumuttarapādamūle,

Saṅghassa buddhapamukhassa ticivarāni

Pādāsi tīsuratanesu abhippasanno; ()

That hero, at the feet of Padumuttara, made an aspiration to fulfill the conditions for attaining perfect enlightenment. Greatly pleased with the Three Jewels, he gave the three robes to the Sangha headed by the Buddha.

35. [O 0.0072]

35.

Tassā’si haṃsavatināma puraṃ jinassa

Ānandabhupati pitā janikā sujātā,

Dve tassa devalasujātavasi vasinaṃ

Aggā bhaviṃsu samaṇisvāmitāsamā’ggā; ()

The Conqueror's city was named Haṃsavatī. His father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Sujātā. His two foremost disciples, masters of self-control, were Devala and Sujāta. Among the female ascetics, Amitā and Asamā were foremost.

36.

36.

Lakkhāyuko sajayabodhika visālasāla

Rukkho upaṭṭhahi muniṃ sumanābhidhāno,

Tassa’ṭṭha’sitiratanappamitaṃ sarīraṃ

Āsuṃ tayo bhagavato gaṇasannipātā; ()

The sage named Sumana attended upon him. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years, and his tree of victorious enlightenment was the broad Sāla tree. His body was eighty-eight ratanas in measure. There were three assemblies of the Blessed One's followers.

37.

37.

Tassā’parena samayena sumedhanāmo

Lokamhi pātubhavi lokahitāya satthā,

Buddhaṅkuro kira tadānyu’bhato sujāto

Svā’sitikoṭivibhavo’ttara māṇavo’si; ()

In a later time, the Teacher named Sumedha appeared in the world for the welfare of the world. At that time, I, a Buddha-sprout, was a noble youth, well-born on both sides, possessing a fortune of eighty crores.

38. [O 0.0073]

38.

Vissajjiyāna vibhavaṃ tiṃsatikoṭiṃ

Datvāna dānamasmaṃ sugate sasaṅghe,

Pabbajjito paramabodhi mapatthayittha

Byākāsi somuni ta’mijjhanabhāva’maddhā; ()

Having given away a fortune of thirty crores and having offered gifts to the Well-Farer together with the Sangha, he went forth and aspired for supreme enlightenment. That Sage then proclaimed the certain fulfillment of his aspiration.

39.

39.

Rammaṃ sudassanamahū nagaraṃ sudanto

Tassā’si bhūpati pitā jananī sudattā,

Saṅghesu’hosu saraṇo vasi sabbakāmo

Rāmā yamāni paramānya’bhavuṃka surāmā; ()

His delightful city was Sudassana. His father was King Sudanta, and his mother was Sudattā. In his Sangha, the masters Saraṇa and Sabbakāma were foremost. Among the female disciples, Rāmā and Surāmā were foremost.

40. [O 0.0074]

40.

Bodhī’pi nīpataru sāgaranāmathero

’Paṭṭhāsi taṃ navutivassasahassamāyu,

Tassā’ḍhasitiratanu’ggatamāsi gattaṃ

Āsuṃ tayo satimato gaṇasantipātā; ()

His Bodhi tree was the Nīpa tree. The elder named Sāgara attended upon him. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. His body rose to a height of eighty-eight ratanas. There were three assemblies of the mindful one's disciples.

41.

41.

Tassā’parena samayena janappadīpo

Jāto sujātabhagavā jitapañcamāro,

Sampannasattaratato varacakkavatti

Rājā babhūvi’ha mahāpuriso tadāso; ()

In a later time, the Lamp of the People was born, the Blessed One Sujāta, conqueror of the five Māras. At that time, I, a great being, became a noble universal monarch, endowed with the seven treasures.

42.

42.

Dhammā’matena mudito ratanadvayassa

Datvā sasattaratanaṃ catudīparajjaṃ,

Pabbajji bodhipaṇidhiṃ paṇidhāya dhīmā

Ñatvā mahāmuni tamijjhanabhāvamāha;

Delighted by the deathless Dhamma, he gave away his kingdom over the four continents with its seven treasures to the Two Jewels. The wise one then went forth, making an aspiration for enlightenment. The Great Sage, knowing this, spoke of its certain fulfillment.

43. [O 0.0075]

43.

Rammaṃ sumaṅgalamahū puramuggatākhyo

Rājā pitābhavi pabhāvatināma mātā,

Aggābhaviṃsu ca sudassanadevatherā

Nāgā gaṇassadasi nāgasamālatheri; ()

His delightful city was Sumaṅgala. His father was the king named Uggata, and his mother was named Pabhāvatī. The elders Sudassana and Deva were his foremost disciples. Among the female disciples, the elderīs Nāgā and Nāgasamālā were foremost.

44.

44.

Taṃ nāradomuniru’paṭṭhahi ca’ttabhāvo

Paṇṇāsahatthapamito bhaviveṇubodhi,

Tassā’bhavī navutivassasahassamāyu

Āsuṃ tayo dhītimato gaṇasannipātā; ()

The sage Nārada attended upon him. His physical form was fifty cubits in measure, and his Bodhi tree was the Veṇu tree. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. There were three assemblies of the resolute one's disciples.

45.

45.

Tassā’pareni’ha nirūpamarūpasāro

Jātobabhūva piyadassisamantadassi,

Dhīro tadanya’bhavi kassapamāṇavo so

Vedesu tīsu kusalo kusalaṃ gavesi; ()

After him, Piyadassī was born here, of matchless form, the essence of beauty, the all-seeing one. At that time, I was the wise youth Kassapa, skilled in the three Vedas, a seeker of the good.

46. [O 0.0076]

46.

So koṭilakkhaparimāṇadhatabbayena

Saṅgassa buddhapamukhassa mahāvihāraṃ,

Katvā padāsi abhipatthitabuddhabhāvo

Buddho’pi tappaṇidhisiddhi siyā’tya’bhāsi; ()

With an expense of a lakh of crores, he built a great monastery and gave it to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Aspiring to the state of Buddhahood, he made this offering, and the Buddha declared: 'May this aspiration of yours succeed!'

47.

47.

Candāmahesi jananī janako pudinno

Rājā babhūva puramassa anomanāmaṃ,

Āsuṃ tadaggayugalāni sujātadhamma-

Dinnā gaṇassadasi pakālitasabbadassi; ()

His city was named Anoma. His mother was Queen Candā, and his father was King Sudinna. His foremost pair of disciples were Sujāta and Dhammadinna. Among the female disciples, Pālita and Sabbadassī were foremost.

48.

48.

Taṃ sotavhasamaṇo samupaṭṭhahittha

Bodhī piyaṅgu bhagavā’si asitihattho,

Aṭṭhāsika so navutivassasahassama’ssa

Āsuṃ tayo matimato gaṇasannipātā; ()

The monk named Sota attended upon him. His Bodhi tree was the Piyaṅgu tree. The Blessed One was eighty cubits tall. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. There were three assemblies of the wise one's disciples.

49. [O 0.0077]

49.

Tassā’parena samayenu’dapādi loke

Lokatthasādhanarato munira’tthadassī,

Sattuntamo’pi niratikkamadhammasimo

Tejiddhimā isi tadā’si susimanāmo; ()

In a later time, there arose in the world the sage Atthadassī, delighting in accomplishing the world's welfare. He was the highest of beings, whose righteous domain could not be surpassed. At that time, I was a seer of great spiritual power named Susima.

50.

50.

Ānīya dibbabhavanā kusumāni tassa

Mandāravāni supatiṭṭhitapādapīṭhe,

Sampūjiyāna paṇidhānamakāsi satthā

Tvaṃ mādiso’bruvi bhavissasi cā’yatinti; ()

Having brought divine Mandārava flowers from the celestial abode and honored the Buddha's well-established footstool with them, he made an aspiration. The Teacher then declared: 'In the future, you too shall become one like me.'

51.

51.

Tassā’si sobhitapuraṃ bhavisāgaravho

Rājā pitā janatidevi sudassanākhyā,

Santopasantasamaṇā varasāvakā’suṃ

Dhammā tadaggasamaṇipya’bhavuṃ sudhammā; ()

His city was Sobhita. His father was the king named Sāgara, and his mother was the queen named Sudassanā. His excellent disciples were the monks Santo and Pasanta. Among the female ascetics, Dhammā and Sudhammā were foremost.

52. [O 0.0078]

52.

Tañcā’bhayo munirūpaṭṭhahi sopya’sīti-

Hatthuggato satasahassapamāṇamāyu,

Campeyyasākhi bhavi bodhi subodhihetu

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasavakasannitā; ()

The sage Abhaya attended upon him. He was eighty cubits in height, with a lifespan of one hundred thousand years. His Bodhi tree, for the sake of perfect enlightenment, was the Campaka tree. There were three assemblies of his noble disciples.

53.

53.

Tassā’parena udapādi’ha dhammadassī

Nissīmadhī’nadhivaro bhavapāradassi,

So tāvatiṃsabhavatamhi mahānubhāvo

Buddhaṅkuro bhavi tadā kira devarājā;()

After him, Dhammadassī arose here, of boundless wisdom, unsurpassed, a seer of the further shore of existence. At that time, I, a Buddha-sprout, was indeed the king of gods, of great power in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

54.

54.

Dibbāni gandhakusumāni kathāgatassa

Cakkaṅkitorucaraṇamburuhāsanamhi,

Pūjesi dibbaturiyehi ca buddhabhāvaṃ

So patthayaṃ munitamijjha nabhāvamāha; ()

He offered divine fragrant flowers and divine music at the lotus-seat of the Tathāgata's great, wheel-marked feet. Aspiring to the state of Buddhahood, he made this offering, and the Sage declared that his aspiration would be fulfilled.

55. [O 0.0079]

55.

Ṭhāniyamāsi saraṇaṃ sugatassa tassa

Rājā pitā’si saraṇo janani sunandā,

Aggābhaviṃsu padumovasi phussadevo

Khemā ca bhikkhusamaṇisva’pi sabbanāmā; ()

His city was Saraṇa. His father was King Saraṇa, and his mother was Sunandā. His foremost disciples were Paduma and Phussadeva. Among the female monastics, the foremost were Khemā and Sabbanāmā.

56.

56.

Thero sunettavisuto tadupaṭṭhahi so

Lakkhāyuko’si jayabodhi ñca bimbijālo,

Tassā’pya’sitiratanappamitaṃ sarīraṃ

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

The renowned elder Sunetta attended upon him. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years, and his Bodhi tree was the Jayabodhi-Bimbijāla. His body was eighty ratanas in measure. There were three assemblies of noble disciples.

57.

57.

Tassā’parena samayeni’ga siddhabodhi

Siddhatthanāmavidito udapādi satthā,

Buddhaṅkuro bhavi tadā’khīlaṅajhānalābhī

Bhoji pavattitaphalaṃ vasi maṅgalākhyo; ()
