After him, at another time, the Teacher named Siddhattha, of accomplished enlightenment, arose here. At that time, the Buddha-to-be was an ascetic named Maṅgala, who had attained all the jhānas and was enjoying the fruit thereof.

58. [O 0.0080]

58.

Sampannagandharasikaṃ paripakkamekaṃ

Ānīya so vipakulajambubhalaṃ vanamhā,

Pādāsi tassa paṇidhīkatabuddhabhāvo

Tañcānubhuya bhagavāpi viyākarittha; ()

Bringing from the forest a single, large, fully ripened rose-apple fruit, endowed with fragrance and taste, he offered it, having made an aspiration for Buddhahood. And the Blessed One, having partaken of it, made a prediction.

59.

59.

Vehāramāsi nagaraṃ jayasenanāmo

Rājā ahosi janako jananī suphassā

Bhikkhūsu tassa vasi sambahulo sumitto

Dve sīvali ñca samaṇīsu varā surāmā; ()

His city was Vehāra. His father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Suphassā. Among the monks, his foremost were Sambahula and Sumitta. Among the female monastics, the two excellent ones were Sīvalī and Surāmā.

60.

60.

Taṃ revatomuni munindamuṭṭhahittha

Bodhī’pi tassa kaṇikāramabhīruho’si,

Lakkhāyuko sa’narasārathi saṭṭhihattho

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

That sage Revata, the lord of sages, arose. His Bodhi tree was a kaṇikāra tree. That charioteer of men had a lifespan of one hundred thousand years and was sixty cubits tall. There were three assemblies of noble disciples.

61. [O 0.0081]

61.

Tassā’pareni’ha samubbhavi nissanāmo

Satthā pasatthacaraṇo caturo’ghatiṇṇo,

Buddhaṅkuro bhavi tadāni sujātarājā

Rājaññamoḷimaṇilaṅkatapādapīṭho; ()

After him, here arose the Teacher named Sobhita, praised for his conduct, who had crossed the four floods. At that time, the Buddha-to-be was King Sujāta, whose footstool was adorned with the crest-jewels of kings.

62.

62.

Hitvā sa’rajjamisiveyadharo sudhīro

Dibbehi’nekakusumehi jinaṃ vajantaṃ,

Pūjesi muddhani tamāpavitānasobhaṃ

Satthā’pi tappaṇidhisiddhi siyā’tya’bhāsi; ()

Having renounced his kingdom, that wise sage, a bearer of sacred lore, honored the Conqueror as he was going with many divine flowers, which formed a beautiful canopy over his head. The Teacher then declared, 'May your aspiration be fulfilled!'

63.

63.

Khemaṃ purañhi janako janasandhanāmo

Rājā janetti padumā nijasaṅghamajjhe,

Dve brahmadevudaya vissutatheranāgā

Phussā ca aggayugalānya’bhavuṃ sudattā; ()

His city was Khemā. His father was King Janasandha, and his mother was Padumā. In his assembly, the two renowned great elders were Brahmadeva and Udaya, and the chief pair of female disciples were Phussā and Sudattā.

64. [O 0.0082]

64.

Taṃ sambhavovasi vasindamupaṭṭhahittha

Tassā’sanavhataru bodhi sa’saṭṭhitattho,

Aṭṭhāsi vassagaṇanāya mahesi lakkhaṃ

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

The attendant Sambhava attended upon him, the lord of the earth. His Bodhi tree was the tree called Asana. He was sixty cubits tall. The great sage lived for one hundred thousand years, and there were three assemblies of noble disciples.

65.

65.

Tassā’parena bhavasāgarapādassi

Phusso mahāmuniri’hakabbhudapādi loke,

Dhīro tadāni vijitāvi jitārivaggo

Rājā babhūva surarājanibho’rutejo; ()

After him, the great sage Phussa, who had seen the further shore of the ocean of existence, arose here in this world. At that time, the wise King Vijitāvī, conqueror of the host of enemies, arose, of great splendor, like the king of the gods.

66.

66.

Sambodhi maggapuriso paṇīdhāya phītaṃ

Rajjaṃ vivajjiya sa’pabbajito janassa,

Aññāya tīṇipiṭakāni kathesi dhammaṃ

Vyākāsi phussabhagavā’pi’va pubbabuddhā; ()

That person on the path to full enlightenment, having made his aspiration, renounced his prosperous kingdom and went forth for the sake of the people. Having mastered the three Piṭakas, he taught the Dhamma. Then the Blessed Phussa, like the Buddhas of the past, made a prediction concerning him.

67. [O 0.0083]

67.

Tassā’si kāsinagaraṃ jayasenanāmo

Rājā pitā’si janati sirimā mahesi,

Saṅghesu’bhosu’pi surakkhitadhammasetā

Cālā tadaggayugalāni tathū’pañcālā; ()

His city was Kāsī. His father was King Jayasena, and his mother was the illustrious Queen Sirimā. In both assemblies, his chief disciples were Surakkhita and Dhammasenā, and his chief female disciples were Cālā and Upacālā.

68.

68.

Bodhiddumā’malakasākhi sarīramaṭṭha-

Paṇṇāsahatthapamitaṃ sabhiyābhidhāno,

Sopaṭṭhahī navutivassasahassamāyu

Āsuṃ tayo bhakavato gaṇasannipātā; ()

His Bodhi tree was an āmalaka tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in measure. The one named Sabhiya attended upon him. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. There were three gatherings of the Blessed One's disciples.

69.

69.

Tassā’parena sanarāmarasattasāro

Satthā vipassi’ha samubbhavi sabbadassī,

Kammena kenaci mahiddhimahānubhāvo

Buddhaṅkuro’bhavi tadā’tulanāgarājā; ()

After him, the Teacher Vipassī, the all-seeing one, the essence of beings human and divine, arose here. At that time, through some kamma, the Buddha-to-be, of great psychic power and majesty, became the incomparable king of nāgas.

70. [O 0.0084]

70.

Aṅgīrasassa ghanakañcanahaddapīṭhaṃ

Pādāsi tassa khavitaṃ ratanehi nānā,

So buddhabhāvamahipatthiya bodhisatto

Vyākāsi tatthasunisajja jino vipassi; ()

He offered to that Aṅgīrasa a solid golden throne, inlaid with various jewels. The Bodhisatta having aspired to the state of Buddhahood, the Conqueror Vipassī, having sat down well upon it, then made a prediction concerning him.

71.

71.

Tassā’si bandhumatināmapuraṃ tadeva-

Nāmo pitā janani bandhumatī mahesi,

Dve khaṇḍatissavasino varasāvakā’suṃ

Candā ca bhaddayugalaṃ bhavi candamittā; ()

His city was named Bandhumatī. His father was King Bandhumā, and his mother was Queen Bandhumatī. The two excellent disciples were Khaṇḍa and Tissa. The noble pair of female disciples were Candā and Candamittā.

72.

72.

Dehaṃ asitiratataṃ tamasokathero-

Paṭṭhāsi bodhiviṭapī bhavi kaṇhavaṇṭā,

Vāsaṃakā munira’sītisahassavassaṃ

Āsuṃ tayo ariyasāvakasannipātā; ()

His body was eighty cubits high. The elder Asoka attended upon him. His Bodhi tree was the black-stalked one. The sage lived for eighty thousand years, and there were three assemblies of noble disciples.

73. [O 0.0085]

73.

Tassā’parena adhisīlasamādhipañño

Satthā samubbhavī sikhī janakappasākhī,

Dhīro tadā’bhavi arindamanāmarājā

Saddho pahūtaratato ratanattayamhi; ()

After him, the Teacher Sikhī arose, endowed with higher virtue, concentration, and wisdom, a branch from the tree of humanity. At that time, the wise King Arindama, faithful to the Triple Gem and possessed of abundant treasures, was the Buddha-to-be.

74.

74.

Bhikkhañca sattaratanābharaṇābhirāmaṃ

Ñatvāna hatthiratanaṃ sugate sasaṅghe,

So buddhabhāvamahipatthayi sattasāro

Vyākāsi lacchasi sukhodhipadanti satthā; ()

Having given alms, and the elephant-treasure, delightfully adorned with the seven kinds of jewels, to the Sugata and his Sangha, he, the essence of beings, aspired to the great state of Buddhahood. The Teacher declared, 'You will attain the state that is an ocean of bliss.'

75.

75.

Buddhassa cāriṇavatī nagaraṃ ahosi

Mātā pabhāvati pitā aruṇavha rājā,

Saṅghesu’bhosu abhibhuvasi sambhavo ca

Aggābhaviṃsu makhilāpadumābhidhānā; ()

The Buddha's city was Aruṇavatī. His mother was Pabhāvatī, and his father was the king named Aruṇa. In both assemblies, the chief disciples were Abhibhū and Sambhava, and the chief female disciples were Makhilā and Padumā.

76. [O 0.0086]

76.

Khemaṅkaro jinamupaṭṭhahi sattatiṃsa-

Hatthucchito vijayabodhi ca puṇḍariko,

So sattatiṃsatisahassa mitāyuko’si

Āsuṃ tayo tadiyasāvakasannipātā; ()

Khemaṅkara attended upon the Conqueror. He was thirty-seven cubits high, and his victorious Bodhi tree was the Puṇḍarīka. He had a lifespan of thirty-seven thousand years. There were three gatherings of his disciples.

77.

77.

Tassā’pareni’ha samubbhavi ketumālā-

Byāmappabhāparilasaṃ munivessabhū’ti,

Buddhaṅkuro kira tadāni sudassanavha-

Rājā babhūva pararājagajindasīho; ()

After him, here arose the sage Vessabhū, shining with a fathom-long halo of rays. At that time, the Buddha-to-be was indeed the king named Sudassana, a lion to the elephant-like opposing kings.

78.

78.

Saṅghassa buddhapamukhassa sacīvaraṃ so

Datvāna dānamatulaṃ jinasāsanamhi,

Sabbaññubodhimabhipatthiya pabbajittha

Buddho bhavissasi dhuvanti tamāhasatthā; ()

Having given an incomparable gift, including robes, to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, in the Victor's Dispensation, and aspiring to All-Knowing Enlightenment, he went forth. The Teacher declared to him, 'You shall surely become a Buddha.'

79. [O 0.0087]

79.

Tassā’pya’nopamapuraṃ bhavi suppatīto

Rājā pitā yasavatī janikā mahesī,

Soṇuttarā ca nijasāvakasāvikānaṃ

Dāmā matiddhiparamā paramā samālā; ()

His city was also Anopama. His father was King Suppatīta, and his mother was Queen Yasavatī. Among his disciples, the chief were Soṇa and Uttara. The chief female disciples were Dāmā and Samālā, supreme in wisdom and psychic power.

80.

80.

Bodhī’pi tassa bhavi sālamahīrūho’pa-

Sampannabhikkhu tadupaṭṭhahi saṭṭhihattho,

Satthā vihāsi samasaṭṭhisahassavassaṃ

Āsuṃ tayo tadiyasāvakasattipātā; ()

His Bodhi tree was a great Sāla tree. The monk Upasampanna attended upon him. The Teacher was sixty cubits tall and lived for sixty thousand years. There were three gatherings of his disciples.

81.

81.

Tassā’pareni’kaha samubbhavi saccasando

Veneyyabandhu bhagavā kakusandhanāmo,

Buddhaṅkuro bhuvi tadā’bhavi khemarājā

Dānappabandhajalasekasudhotahattho; ()

After him, here arose the Blessed One Kakusandha, truthful, a kinsman to the teachable. At that time, the Buddha-to-be was King Khema on earth, his hands well-washed by the water of continuous giving.

82. [O 0.0088]

82.

So pattacīvarapabhūtikamannapānaṃ

Datvā sasāvakajinassa gharā’bhigantvā,

Pabbajji bodhipaṇidhiṃ paṇidhāya rājā

Satthāsayā’tya’vaca tappaṇidhānasiddhi; ()

Having gone to the Conqueror's dwelling and given food, drink, bowls, robes, and other requisites to him and his disciples, the king made the aspiration for enlightenment and went forth. The Teacher declared, 'Your aspiration will be fulfilled.'

83.

83.

Khemavahayaṃ nagaramassa pitā’ggidatto

Vippo vibhāvi abhavi janikā visākhā,

Sañjivatheradutiyo vidhuro ca thero

Sāmā tadaggayugalaṃ bhavi campakākhyā; ()

His city was named Khemavatī. His father was the renowned Brahmin Aggidatta, and his mother was Visākhā. The elder Vidhura and the elder Sañjīva were his chief disciples. The chief pair of female disciples were Sāmā and Campakā.

84. [O 0.0089]

84.

Taṃ buddhijo jinamupaṭṭhahi tassa gattaṃ

Tāḷisahatthamitamāsi sirisabodhi,

Tāḷisahāyanasahassapamāṇamāyu

Eko’va tassa bhavi sāvakasannipāto; ()

The Buddha's spiritual son attended upon the Conqueror. His body was forty cubits in measure, and his Bodhi tree was a Sirīsa. His lifespan was forty thousand years. There was only one gathering of his disciples.

85.

85.

Tassā’paramhi samaye karuṇānidhāno

Lokābhibhū kanakabhudharahārirūpo,

Uppajji koṇagamanomuni pabbatākhyo

Bhumissaro bhavi mahāpuriso tadāni; ()

At a later time, the Compassionate One, the Conqueror of the World, with a beautiful form like a golden mountain, the sage Koṇāgamana, arose. At that time, the Great Being, named Pabbata, became the Lord of the Earth.

86.

86.

Saṅghassa buddhapamukhassa uḷāradānaṃ

Datvā mahagghavaracivarasāṭake ca,

So pakabbajittha abhipatthita buddhabhāvo

Buddho bhavissasi tuvanti tamāhasatthā; ()

Having given a generous offering, including costly and superb robes, to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, he then went forth, aspiring for Buddhahood. The Teacher declared to him, 'You will become a Buddha.'

87. [O 0.0090]

87.

Nāmena sobhavati tampuramuttarākhyā

Mātā pitā’vanisuro bhavi yaññadatto,

Hīyosottaravasī samaṇi samuddā

Tasso’ttarā ca paramā parisāsu’bhosu; ()

His city was named Sobhavatī. His mother was named Uttarā, and his father was the king Yaññadatta. Among the two assemblies, his chief female disciples were Samuddā and Uttarā, who were supreme.

88.

88.

Taṃ sotthijo jinamupaṭṭhahi tiṃsahattho

Aṅgīraso bhavi udumbarasākhi bodhi,

So tiṃsahāyanasahassamitāyuko’si

Eko’va tassa bhavi sāvakasantipāto; ()

Sotthija attended upon that Victor. He was thirty cubits tall and of the Aṅgīrasa clan. His Bodhi tree was an Udumbara tree. His lifespan was thirty thousand years, and there was only one gathering of his disciples.

89.

89.

Tassā’pareni’ha mahāmuni kassapākhyo

Lokamhi pātubhavi khaggavisāṇakappo,

Buddhaṅkuro bhuvi tadā’bhavi jotipālo

Vedesu tīsu sakalāsu kalāsu cheko; ()

After him, the great sage named Kassapa, solitary as a rhinoceros horn, appeared here in the world. At that time, the Buddha-to-be on earth was Jotipāla, skilled in the three Vedas and in all the arts.

90. [O 0.0091]

90.

Kalyāṇamittadutiyo sugataṃ upecca

Sutvāna dhammamathasāsana motaritvā,

Sabbaññubhāvamhipatthayi māṇavo so

Vyākāsi kassapamunī’pi munī’ca pubbā; ()

Accompanied by a good friend, having approached the Sugata and heard the Dhamma, he entered the Dispensation. That young man then aspired to the state of omniscience. The sage Kassapa, as had the sages of the past, also made this prophecy.

91.

91.

Bārāṇasi nagaramāsi pitā ca mātā

Dve brahmadattadhanavatya’bhidhānavanto,

Bhikkhusu tassa samaṇisva’pi tissabhāra-

Dvājā ca bhaddayugalātya’nuloruvelā; ()

His city was Bārāṇasī. His father was Brahmadatta, and his mother was Dhanavatī. Among his monks, the chief disciples were Tissa and Bhāradvāja; and among his female disciples, the excellent pair were Anulā and Uruvelā.

92.

92.

Taṃ sabbamittasamaṇo samupaṭṭhahittha

Nigrodhasākhī jayabodhi sa’vīsahattho,

Tassā’si visatisahassa pamāṇamāyu

Eko’va’hū ariyasāvakasannīpāto; ()

The monk Sabbamitta attended upon him. His Bodhi tree of victory was a Nigrodha tree. He was twenty cubits tall. His lifespan was twenty thousand years. There was only one gathering of noble disciples.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatitā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānanda dānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe dūrenidāne bodhisattassa sesapaṇidhātaṭṭhapana pavatti paridīpo tatiyo saggo.

Thus, in the Jinavaṃsadīpa, composed by the striving monk named Medhānanda, which is a treasure that brings joy to the hearts of all poets, this is the third chapter, the Dūrenidāna, which illuminates the account of the Bodhisatta's establishment of the remaining aspirations.

1. [O 0.0092]

1.

Dīpaṅkarādicatuvīsati buddhapāda-

Mūlesu laṅapaṇidhāna mahānidhāno,

Lakkhādhikaṃ caturasaṅkhiyakappasaṅkhaṃ

Puññābhisandamabhisaṅkhari bodhisatto; ()

At the feet of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, having received the aspiration, the Bodhisatta, a great treasure, accumulated a stream of merit for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand kalpas more.

2.

2.

Etthantare vividhabāhiravatthujātaṃ

Sisa’kkhimaṃsarudhirāni ca puttadāre,

So jivitampi kapaṇaḍikayācakānaṃ

Vīro pariccaji pajāya hitatthameva; ()

During this period, the hero relinquished various external possessions—his own head, eyes, flesh, and blood, his children and wife, and even his life—to beggars and mendicants, solely for the welfare of all beings.

3. [O 0.0093]

3.

Dānādhimuttipariyesana vippaveso

Patvā tapovanamakitti tapodhanassa,

Tihaṃ alattha sakaṭāhamaloṇaḍākaṃ

Yassā’bhibhūtajaṭharassa jighacchitattā; () (Akitticariyaṃ)

Inclined to generosity and abandoning all seeking, he went to the hermitage of Akitti, who was rich in austerity. As his belly was overcome by hunger, he obtained for three days a cartload of unsalted gruel.

4.

4.

Kantāramagga paṭipanna manātapattaṃ

Pacceka buddhamahipassiya saṅakkhavippo,

Phuṭṭhaṃ sakiccapasuto sūriyātapena

Yo chattupāhaṇamadāsi sudhotapāṇi; () (Saṅkhacariyaṃ)

The Brahmin Saṅkha, seeing a Pacceka Buddha proceeding on a desert path without a parasol, afflicted by the sun's heat yet intent on his task, with purified hands gave him a parasol and sandals.

5.

5.

Dubbhikkhapīḷanabhayena kaliṅgaraṭṭhā

Saṃyācataṃ yadupagamma dhanañjayavho,

Soṇḍāya gayha nijamañjana nāgarājaṃ

Yo dakkhiṇodaka nisekamakāsi rājā; () (Kurudhammacariyaṃ)

King Dhanañjaya, fearing the affliction of famine, approached those who were begging from the Kaliṅga country. That king, taking his royal Nāga elephant named Añjana by the trunk, performed the libation of water for the gift.

6. [O 0.0094]

6.

Hutvāna yo mahasudassana cakkavattī

Rājā kusāvatipuramhi divā ca ratto,

Vatthattapānamupatesi carāpayitvā

Bheriṃka asesakapaṇḍikayācakānaṃ; () (Mahāsudassanacariyaṃ)

He who, having become the great wheel-turning monarch Mahāsudassana in the city of Kusāvatī, by day and by night, provided clothes, food, and drink, having the drum beaten for all beggars and mendicants without exception.

7.

7.

Yo sattabhumibhujasāsi purohito’pi

Rājūhi laddhamakhilaṃ dhanadhaññarāsiṃ,

Sampattayācakajanassa paricchajitvā

Puññappabandhamabhisañcini bodhihetu; () (Mahāgovindacariyaṃ)

Though he was the chief minister to the rulers of seven lands, having obtained all wealth and grain from the kings, he gave it away to the beggars who had gathered, accumulating a continuous stream of merit for the sake of enlightenment.

8.

8.

Dhammānusāsi nimināma mahībhujo’pi

Sālaṃ vidhāya mithilāya catummukhaṃ yo,

Acchinnamatthijanapakkhicatuppadānaṃ

Dānaṃ pavattayī purā dadataṃ variṭṭho; () (Nimirājacariyaṃ)

The righteous king named Nimi, having established a four-gated hall in Mithilā, maintained an unbroken flow of charity to those in need, birds, and quadrupeds, becoming the foremost of givers of old.

9. [O 0.0095]

9.

Yo ekarājasutacandakumārabhūto

Muddhābhiseka karaṇāya janehi gacchaṃ,

Saṃvejito savibhave tibhave’pi yaññā-

Vāṭaṃ vidhāya’bhipavattayi dānavaṭṭaṃ; () (Candakumāracariyaṃ)

He who was Prince Candakumāra, the only son of the king, while going with his people for his coronation, was stirred by a sense of urgency regarding the three worlds with all their glory, established a sacrificial ground and set in motion the wheel of generosity.

10.

10.

Yo vatthusāragahaṇena atittarūpo

Bhumissaro’pi sivināma surādhipassa,

Jaccandhavesagahitassa vilocanāni

Uppāṭayitva padadaṃ labhi dibbacakkhū; () (Sivirājacariyaṃ;)

The king named Sivi, lord of the earth, being unsatisfied with giving mere external possessions, tore out his eyes and gave them to the lord of the gods disguised as a man born blind, and thereby obtained the divine eye.

11.

11.

Dānādhimuttiparamo sasapaṇḍito yo

Mittenu sāsiya adhiṭṭhituposathaṅgo,

Aṅgāramuddhani papāta sajīvitāsaṃ

Hitvā dvijassa tanumaṃsapadātukāmo; () (Sasapaṇḍitacariyaṃ; Itidānapāramīṃ)

The wise hare, supremely devoted to generosity, having instructed his friends and undertaken the Uposatha observance, abandoned all hope for his life and jumped onto a heap of burning coals, desiring to give the brahmin the flesh of his own body.

12. [O 0.0096]

12.

Yo mātuposakakari bhisamuddharatto

Andhāya hatthidamakena kareṇukāya,

Soṇḍāya suṭṭhugahito’pya’vikaṇḍitassa

Sīlassa khaṇḍanabhayā najanesi kopaṃ; () (Mātuposakacariyaṃ)

He who was an elephant supporting his blind mother, fond of extracting lotus stalks, though firmly seized by the trunk by an elephant trainer, felt no anger, fearing the breaking of his unbroken virtue.

13.

13.

Yo bhuridattabhujago’parivammikaṭṭho,

Sīlabbataṃ visadharo samadhiṭṭhahitvā,

Peḷāya khittabhujage ahiguṇṭhikamhi

Sīlassa kuppanabhayena jahāsi kopaṃ; () (Bhuridattacariyaṃ;)

The serpent Bhūridatta, the venomous one, who dwelt upon an anthill, having firmly undertaken the observance of virtue, though thrown into a basket by a snake charmer, abandoned anger, fearing the violation of his virtue.

14.

14.

Sīlabbatādivibhavo jalitiddhimā yo

Campeyyanāmabhujago ahiguṇṭhikamhi,

Icchānurūpavicaro camarī’va vālaṃ

Sīlaṃ jugopa napi tabbadhake cukopa; () (Campeyyacariyaṃ;)

The serpent named Campeyya, possessed of the wealth of virtue and vows, radiant with psychic power, though caught by a snake charmer, guarded his virtue as a yak guards its tail and felt no anger toward his tormentor.

15. [O 0.0097]

15.

Yo cūlabodhivisuto samadiṭṭhahatvā

Sīlabbataṃ vanamupecca vasaṃ piyāya,

Tāyaṃ pasayha gahitāya’pi kāsiraññā

Sīlabbisodhanaparo pajahittha rosaṃ; () (Cūlabodhicariyaṃ)

Renowned as Cūlabodhi, having undertaken the rules and vows, he went to the forest to live with his beloved. Even when she was forcibly seized by the king of Kāsi, he, intent on purifying his virtue, abandoned anger.

16.

16.

Yo bhiṃsarūpi mahiso’pi valimukhassa

Āguṃ titikkhamakhīlaṃ parisuddhasilo,

Rukkhaṭṭhayakkhavacanāni paṭikkhipitvā

Taṃ sīlabhaṅgabhayato bhayato mumoca; ()

The buffalo, though terrifying in form, patient and of pure conduct, tolerated the offense of the monkey. He rejected the words of the tree-dwelling yakkha and, fearing the breaking of his virtue, freed the monkey from fear.

17.

17.

Yo vuyhamānamapanīya nadīpavāhā

Mittadduhiṃ putasajīvitadānahetu,

Raññā mumoca vadhiyaṃ avikopanena

Sīlassa rūruhariṇo’pi harissavaṇṇo, () (rūrumigarājacariyaṃ;)

The golden Ruru deer, having rescued one who was being swept away by the river's current—a betrayer of a friend—was released from execution by the king on account of his unangered virtue.

18. [O 0.0098]

18.

Yo dantakaṭṭhasakalehi jaṭākulehi

Kuddhena kuṭajaṭilena katāhisāpo,

Mātaṅganāmamuni sīladhanaṃ jugopa

Sampātasāparipumiddhibalena rakkhaṃ; () (Mātaṅgacariyaṃ;)

The sage named Mātaṅga, though cursed by an angry, crooked ascetic with tangled matted hair and pieces of tooth-sticks, guarded the treasure of his virtue, protecting it by the power of his perfect psychic abilities.

19.

19.

Maggāvatiṇṇamadhamaṃ kalhābhīlāsā-

Saṅghaṭṭitobhayarathaṅgamadhammayakkhaṃ,

Kopagginā naparijhāpayamiddhimā yo

Sīlaṃ rarakkha khalu dhammikayakkharājā; () (Dhammādhamma devaputtacariyaṃ;)

The righteous yakkha-king, though powerful, was not consumed by the fire of anger and protected his virtue when the unrighteous yakkha, who had descended onto the path, crashed both their chariot wheels due to strife and desire.

20.

20.

Yo porisādavasagassa jayaddisassa

Rañño paṭiññamadhikicca vijivitāso,

Khīttāyudho tadupagamma alīnasatto

Yakkhaṃ damesi nanu sīlavataṃ nidānā; () (Alīnasattacariyaṃ;)

He who, honoring his promise to King Jayaddisa who was under the power of the man-eater, having abandoned hope for his life and cast aside his weapons, approached that yakkha with an unshrinking spirit and tamed him—surely, this was from the foundation of his virtue.

21. [O 0.0099]

21.

Yo saṅkhapālabhujago nijabhogapūra-

Vyābhaṅgibhārataravāhiti bhojaputte,

Kāruññamāpa abhigantumapādatāya

Sīlassa bhaṅgabhayato’pi hutāsatejo; () (Saṅkhapālacariyaṃ; Iti sīlapāramiṃ;)

The serpent Saṅkhapāla, whose power was like fire, felt compassion for the Bhoja youths who carried him, a crushing and heavy burden with the fullness of his coils, and did not retaliate, fearing the breach of his virtue.

22.

22.

Saṅkhāradhammakhaṇabhaṅgasabhāvadassi

Ussāvabinduvilayaṃ’va yudhañjayo yo,

Rājā janassa rudato pavihāya rajjaṃ

Nekkhammapāramimapurayi pabbajitvā; () (Yudhañjaya cariyaṃ;)

Seeing the nature of conditioned things as liable to momentary dissolution, like the vanishing of a dewdrop, King Yudhañjaya, leaving his weeping people and his kingdom, perfected the pāramī of renunciation by going forth.

23.

23.

Yo somanassavisuto kururājaputto

Dussīlakuṭajaṭilabbacanaṃ paṭicca,

Raññā niyojitavadho vadhakāvakāsaṃ

Laddhānusāsiya’bhinikkhami cattarajjo; () (Somanassa cariyaṃ;)

The prince of the Kurus, renowned as Somanassa, heeding the words of a wicked, crooked ascetic, was sentenced to death by the king. Having obtained an opportunity from the executioner and instructed him, he abandoned the kingdom and went forth.

24. [O 0.0100]

24.

Yo kāsirājatanujo’pi ayogharākhyo

Īhaṃ bhato ciramayogharavāsahīrū,

Rajjaṃ pahāya paramaṃ pitarā padattaṃ

Nekkhammapāramiparo vanamotarittha; () (Ayogharacariyaṃ;)

The son of the king of Kāsi, called Ayoghara, born here, who was ashamed of dwelling long in the iron house, abandoned the supreme kingdom given by his father and descended to the forest, intent on the perfection of renunciation.

25.

25.

Yo pañcakāmaguṇadīpanato’padiṭṭha-

Sambhattamittavacanampi paṭikkhipitvā,

Niddhantakañcananibhacchavi kañcanākhyo

Patvā tapovanamapabbaji bandhavehi; () (Bhisacariyaṃ;)

Named Kañcana, whose skin had the luster of refined gold, though shown the five sensual pleasures, rejecting even the trustworthy advice of intimate friends, he went forth from his relatives, having reached the ascetic's grove.

26. [O 0.0101]

26.

Pakkhittadaddulanahārurivā’nalamhi

Saṅkhāradhammavisaye paṭivaṭṭitatto,

Yo soṇabhusurasudhī vibhavaṃ pahāya

Pabbajjituṃ sapariso pavanaṃ jagāma; () (Soṇapaṇḍitacariyaṃ; Iti nekkhamma pārami;)

Like a moth thrown into a flame, whose mind was turned away from the realm of conditioned things, the wise brahmin Soṇa, renouncing prosperity, went to the forest with his retinue to go forth.

27.

27.

Yo seṇako sudhi pasibbakagabbhasāyiṃ

Vippassi mohakalusikatamānasassa,

Sappaṃ sughoramupadassiya dīghadassī

Paññāsupāramimapūrayi bhurimedho; () (Seṇakapaṇḍita cariyaṃ;)

The wise Seṇaka, who lay in the womb of a basket, the far-sighted one of vast wisdom, showed the very dreadful snake to Vipassī, whose mind was defiled by the stain of delusion, and thus fulfilled the highest perfection of wisdom.

28.

28.

Yo yaṃ mahosadhasamākhyasudhī sudhīso

Ummaggasaṃvutanisaggavatisamo’pi,

Ummaggato’va sabalaṃ mithilādhināthaṃ

Paññāpajāpatipati riputo mumoca; () (Mahosadhacariyaṃ iti paññā pāramī;)

He, the wise one named Mahosadha, chief of the wise, equal to one possessing the innate wisdom contained in the Ummagga, this master of wisdom, from the Ummagga itself, freed the lord of Mithilā with his forces from the enemy.

29. [O 0.0102]

29.

Vālenu’ḷāravīriyo vīriyena ghoraṃ

Saṃsāradukkhamiva yo kisakālako’pi,

Gambhīrasāgarajalaṃ sapajānukampī

Ussiñcituṃ satatamārahi sattasāro; () (Kālaka cariyaṃ)

He, the tiny black one, whose energy was vast, by his energy, as if to overcome the dreadful suffering of saṃsāra, compassionate towards beings, constantly strove to bail out the deep ocean water, he who was the essence of beings.

30.

30.

Rājāmahādijanako janakundacando

Gambhīrabhurisalilaṃ salilākaraṃ yo,

Sūro’rubāhuvīriyo vīriyaṃ tatāra

Saṃsārasindhutaraṇe taraṇīsarūpo; () (Mahājanakacariyaṃ; Iti vīriyapārami;)

King Mahājanaka, a jasmine-moon to the people, a hero of mighty arm-strength, crossed with his energy the ocean of deep, abundant waters, becoming like a raft for crossing the ocean of existence.

31.

31.

Yo khantitintahadayo yatikhantivādī

Chedāpite’pi sakalaṃ sakalattabhāve,

Samapūtakhantijalamevabhūsaṃ siseca

Vyāpādapāvakapadittakalāburāje; () (Khantivādī cariyaṃ)

The ascetic who preached patience, whose heart was steeped in patience, even when his entire being was caused to be severed, abundantly sprinkled the pure and even water of patience upon the king of Kalābu, who was inflamed by the fire of ill-will.

32. [O 0.0103]

32.

Yo dhammapālanaparo susu dhammapālo

Kārāpite’pi vadhakeha’simālakammaṃ,

Āsannatāpanirayamhi patāparāje

Khantiṃ pavattayi manappitakhantimetto; () (Dhammapāla cariyaṃ; Iti khantipāramī;)

Truly a protector of the Dhamma, devoted to protecting the Dhamma, even when the executioners were ordered to perform the work of the sword-circle, he maintained forbearance toward the tormenting king, who was like a nearby hell of suffering, his mind devoted to patience and loving-kindness.

33.

33.

Yo antarīpagabhayaṃkarasuṃsumāra-

Muddhāsamappitapado kapirājabhūto,

Dinnaṃ paṭiññamanukubbamanaññalabbhaṃ

Najjā papāta paratīramasaccabhīrū; () (Kapirāja cariyaṃ)

The monkey king, having placed his foot on the head of the dreadful crocodile in the midst of the river, fulfilling his given promise, unattainable by another, leapt to the far bank of the river, fearing untruth.

34. [O 0.0104]

34.

Yo saccapāramiparo vasi paccanāmo

Saccena saccamahīsandhiya saccadassī,

Poriṃ samaggakaraṇiṃ sirijambudīpe

Sampālayaṃ sakalalokamavoca vācaṃ; () (Saccasavbhaya cariyaṃ;)

The master named Sacca, devoted to the perfection of truth, seeing the truth, having bound the great earth with truth, protecting glorious Jambudīpa by making the citizens united, spoke words to the whole world.

35.

35.

Yo vaṭṭapotakadijo avirūḷhapakkha-

Pādo’tikhuddakakulāvakagabbhasāyī,

Saccena soḷasakarisamitappadese

Dāvagginibbutimakā thiramāyugantaṃ; () (Vaṭṭapotaka cariyaṃ;)

The young quail, a twice-born, whose wings and feet were undeveloped, lying within a very tiny nest, by the power of truth, in a space of sixteen karīsas, caused the forest fire to be extinguished, to remain so firmly for the rest of the aeon.

36.

36.

Yo gijjhakākabakabāṇakabhakkhabhuta-

Bandhu nidāgharavitāpaparikkhayā’pe,

Ritte saramhi parimocayi maccharājā

Saccena’kālajaladāgamapaccayena; () (Maccharāja cariyaṃ;)

When the lake was empty, its water wasted away by the heat of the summer sun, and his kin had become food for vultures, crows, herons, and hawks, the fish king, by an act of truth that caused unseasonal rain clouds to appear, released his relatives.

37. [O 0.0105]

37.

Duṭṭhāhidaṭṭhavisavegavimucchitaṃ yo

Maṇḍabbatāpasavaro’rasayaññadattaṃ,

Katvāna saccakiriyaṃ karuṇāya kaṇha-

Dīpāyano muni mumoca tamāpadamhā; () (Kaṇhādīpāyana cariyaṃ;)

The sage Kaṇha-Dīpāyana, having performed an act of truth with compassion, released from that peril Maṇḍabba, the chief ascetic, his own son given as a sacrifice, who was unconscious from the powerful venom of a wicked snake's bite.

38.

38.

Yo porisādavasago sutasomarājā

Rajje tiyojanasate sakajīvite’pi,

Saccaṃ rarakkha nanu saccaparo nirāso

Dinnaṃ paṭissavamubhinnamapānukubbaṃ; () (Sutasomacariyaṃ; Iti saccapāramī;)

King Sutasoma, who was under the power of the man-eater, even regarding his kingdom of three hundred yojanas and his own life, guarded the truth; devoted to truth, without craving, he did not break both given promises.

39.

39.

Nibbinnarajjavibhavo bhavabhīrūtāya

Yo mūgapakkhabadhirākati mūgapakkho,

Nīte nikhātumapaki sīvathikāvakāse

Daḷhaṃ adhiṭṭhitavataṃ vata nojahāsi; () (Temiyacariyaṃ; Iti adhiṭṭhāna pāramī;)

Disgusted with royal splendor, fearing existence, he who had the appearance of being mute, crippled, and deaf, when led to be buried in the charnel ground, did not abandon his firmly undertaken vow.

40. [O 0.0106]

40.

Mettavihāraparamo piturandhayaṭṭhi

Yo somasommayadayo’pi suvaṇṇasāmo,

Vāḷehi samparivuto pavane vihāri

Mettākhyapāramimapūrayi pāpabhīrū; () (Suvaṇṇasāmacariyaṃ;)

Dwelling supremely in loving-kindness, the walking stick of his blind father, Suvaṇṇasāma, whose heart was gentle and mild, dwelt in the forest surrounded by wild beasts, and fulfilled the perfection of loving-kindness, fearing evil.

41.

41.

Yo ekarājavisuto bhuvi kāsirājā

Mettākalattadutiyo sakajīvite’pi,

Avachinnarajjavibhāve paṭipakkharāje

Mettāya samphari samaṃ paribhāvitāya; () (Ekarājacariyaṃ; Iti mettā pāramī;)

Renowned as the sole king of Kāsi on earth, with loving-kindness as his wife and companion, even at the risk of his own life, he suffused the hostile king, who had taken his unbroken royal splendor, with impartial, fully cultivated loving-kindness.

42. [O 0.0107]

42.

Yā lomehaṃsavisuto’pi tulāsarikkho

Mānāvamānanakaresu sukhe ca dukkha,

Vāsaṃ cavaṭṭhiparikiṇṇasusānamajjhe

Veraṃ averamanupecca rarakkhu’pekkhaṃ; () (Lomahaṃsacariyaṃ; Iti upekkhāka pakāramiṃ)

Though renowned as Lomahaṃsa, he was like a balance toward those who offered honor and dishonor, and in pleasure and pain; dwelling amidst charnel grounds strewn with bones, not meeting enmity with enmity, he maintained equanimity.

43.

43.

So bodhiyā’bhiniyato paripakkañāṇo

Buddhaṅkuro’pacitapāramitābalena,

Nijjhāmataṇha’sitakañjakkhuppipāsa-

Lokantarorunirayesu na jātu jāto; ()

That Buddha-sprout, destined for enlightenment, with fully matured wisdom, strengthened by the power of his accumulated perfections, was never again born in the great inter-world hells, which are characterized by burning craving, black gruel, hunger, and thirst.

44.

44.

Nālattha paṇḍakanapuṃsakamūgapakkha-

Chaccandhajātibadhiritthijaḷattabhāvaṃ,

So makkhikāmakasakutthakipillikādi-

Jātyā napātubhavi kīṭapaṭaṅgajātyā; ()

He never attained the state of being a eunuch, an impotent person, mute, lame, blind from birth, deaf from birth, female, or idiotic. Nor was he born into species such as flies, mosquitoes, bugs, or ants, nor into the species of insects or moths.

45. [O 0.0108]

45.

Nālattha gandhagajato puthulatta bhāvaṃ

Nālattha vaṭṭasusukā sukhumanta bhāvaṃ,

Nālattha umdanamammanakatta bhāvaṃ

Nālattha evamatihīnataratta bhāvaṃ;

He never attained the state of being large like a rutting elephant, nor the subtle state of a round worm, nor the state of being swollen and festering, nor any such extremely inferior existence.

46.

46.

Nāhosi mātuvadhako pitughātako vā

Nāhosi saṅghabhiduro arahantaghāto,

Nāhosi duṭṭhahadayena tathāgatassa

Nāhosi saṃjananako rudhirassa kāye; ()

He was not a matricide or a parricide, nor was he a schismatic or a murderer of an arahant. He did not, with a malicious heart, cause blood to arise on the Tathāgata's body.

47.

47.

Kammaṃ phakhalaṃ tadubhayaṃ paṭibāhino ye

Ucchedadiṭṭhigatikā vihariṃsu tesaṃ,

Laddhiṃ kadāci naparāmasi saddahāno

Kammaṃ phalaṃ niyatabodhiparāyaṇo so; ()

He never embraced the doctrine of those who rejected both action and its fruit and who lived holding annihilationist views, for he was one who believed in action and its fruit, whose ultimate goal was fixed enlightenment.

48. [O 0.0109]

48.

Yasmiṃ bhave bhavati nāmacatukkamattaṃ

Tatrā’pi puññakaraṇattha masaññasatte,

Aṭṭhānato napaṭisandhimagaṇhi suddhā-

Vāsesu pañcasu kadāci papañcabhīrū; ()

In whatever existence he dwelt, even in the state of the mere four mental aggregates, there too he made merit; but he was not born among the mindless beings. He never took rebirth in the impossible states, nor, fearing proliferation, did he ever take rebirth in the five Pure Abodes.

49.

49.

Buddhaṅkuro niyatabodhipado kadāci

Dīghāyukesu’pibhavesu sukhānapekho,

Katvā’dhimuttivacanaṃ idha jīvaloke

Nibbatti so tidasapāramipūraṇatthaṃ; ()

The Buddha-sprout, whose path to enlightenment was fixed, not seeking happiness even in the long-lived existences, having made a declaration of firm resolve in this world of living beings, was reborn to complete the thirty perfections.

50.

50.

Iccevaṃ so purisanisabho duppavesassa bodhi-

Pāsādassā’vataraṇasamattiṃsatisseṇirūpaṃ,

Nipphādento parahitarato pāramīdhammajātaṃ

Saṃsāre saṃsari cirataraṃ ghoradukkhaṃ titikkhaṃ; ()

Thus, that bull among men, delighting in the welfare of others, accomplishing the collection of perfection-qualities—which are like the thirty flights of stairs for entering the Bodhi-palace, difficult to access—wandered in saṃsāra for a very long time, enduring terrible suffering.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānanda dānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe durenidāne pāramidhammābhisaṅkharaṇa pavatti paridīpo catuttho saggo.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, 'The Exposition of the Course of Accumulating the Perfection-Qualities,' from the Distant Origin section of the Jinavaṃsadīpa, a source of delight for the hearts of all poets, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda.

1. [O 0.0110]

1.

Atthavattapadaṃ nānāvaṇṇamaṇṇavajānvitaṃ,

Patthyāvattamivāhosi jetuttarapuraṃ pure; () (Silesa bandhanaṃ;)

In former times, the city of Jetuttara was a place of wealth and meaning, endowed with various colored ocean-born jewels; it was like a well-wrought necklace. (A play on words)

2.

2.

Parikhāmekhalādāma baddhapākārasoṇinī,

Rarāja rājadhānī sā vadhūva patimaṇḍitā; ()

That royal city shone, adorned like a bride, with its moat as a girdle-band and its ramparts as hips.

3. [O 0.0111]

3.

Maṇisiṅgaṃsumālābhi bālaṃsumālivibbhamaṃ,

Sasaṅkamaṇḍalaṃ tasmiṃ palamhesā’bhīsārikā; ()

Therein, the disk of the moon, with garlands of rays from jewel-peaks and the splendor of the rising sun, was like a woman hastening to a tryst.

4.

4.

Indirāmandirā’mandamaṇimandirasālinī,

Hemaddhajāvali tasmiṃ kiḷāpayi kalāpino; ()

Endowed with great jewel-palaces like the mansion of Indra, therein rows of golden flags caused the peacocks to sport.

5.

5.

Rarāja nāgarājānaṃ kappitābharaṇehi ca,

Dāṭhāhi dānadhārāhi meghavacchantā’va sā purī; ()

That city shone with its kings of elephants; equipped with ornaments, with their tusks and streams of ichor, they were like raining clouds.

6.

6.

Turaṅganikaroṇḍutadhulidhūsaritambaraṃ,

Nivāritātapaṃraṅgavitānassirimāhari; ()

The sky, made grey by the dust stirred up by the multitude of horses, assumed the splendor of a stage-canopy, warding off the sun's heat.

7. [O 0.0112]

7.

Nīlasevāladhammillā samphullakamalā’nanā,

Tahimuppalalola’kkhī haṃsapīnapayodharā; ()

There, with tresses like blue-black algae, faces like full-blown lotuses, eyes restless as water-lilies, and breasts plump like swans,

8.

8.

Kiñjakkharājirasānāruddharodhanitambinī,

Bhiṅgālimaṇimañjirā nārī’vā’suṃ sarojinī; () (Silesa bandhanaṃ;)

with banks for hips bound by girdles of lotus filaments, and swarms of bees for jeweled anklets, the lotus ponds were like women. (A play on words)

9.

9.

Kevakalaṃ kapparukkhehi vinā sā rājadhānya’hu,

Visāṇārājadhānī’va sabbasampattisālinī; ()

Lacking only the wish-fulfilling trees, that royal city was like the royal city of Visāṇā, endowed with all prosperity.

10.

10.

Kadāci purisājañño rājā’hosi pure tahiṃ,

Vessantaro’tināmena vissuto bhuvanattaye; ()

Once upon a time, in that city, there was a king, a noble man, known by the name Vessantara, famed throughout the three worlds.

11. [O 0.0113]

11.

Kumāro’va samāno so dānakīḷāparāyaṇo,

Kāyūpagāni dhātīnaṃ ratanābharaṇāni’pi; ()

Though still a prince, he was devoted to the sport of giving; even the jewel-ornaments worn on the bodies of his nurses,

12.

12.

Khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ karitvāna navakkhantuṃ kapariccaji,

Evaṃ bāhiravatthūnidadanto aṭṭhavassiko; ()

he gave away nine times, having broken them into pieces. Thus, giving away external things, he was eight years of age.

13.

13.

Pāsādamabhirīhitvā sonisajjā’bhiyācanaṃ,

Dassāmī’ti vicintesi sisakkhimaṃsalohitaṃ; ()

Having ascended the palace and seated himself, he thought, 'To one who asks, I will give my head, eyes, flesh, and blood.'

14.

14.

Sukhedhito mahāsatto sukkapakkhe’va candimā,

Pālesi dasadhammena patvā rajjasiriṃ pajaṃ; ()

The Great Being, nurtured in happiness, like the moon in the bright fortnight, having attained the glory of kingship, ruled the people with the ten royal virtues.

15.

15.

Nisajjo paripāsāde so rājā ekadā raho,

Kāmānaṃ saṅkilesañca vokārādīnavaṃ sari; ()

That king, seated alone in the palace one day, recollected the defilement of sensual pleasures and the danger of the aggregates.

16. [O 0.0114]

16.

Pabbajjāhirato rājā nibbinto vibhavebhave,

Sampattisāramādāya hitvā rajjasiriṃ varaṃ; ()

The king, delighting in the going forth, disenchanted with all existence, having taken the essence of his attainments and abandoned the excellent glory of kingship,

17.

17.

Mattamātaṅgarājā’va aggipajjalakānanā,

Rudato ñātisaṅghassa agārasmā’bhi nikkhamī; ()

like a rutting elephant king from a blazing forest, went forth from the household life while his assembly of kinsmen wept.

18.

18.

Campakāsokavakulatarusaṇḍasumaṇḍitaṃ,

Sikhaṇḍimaṇḍalākhaṇḍakīḷaṃ kokilakūjanaṃ; ()

Adorned with groves of campaka, asoka, and vakula trees, where many flocks of peacocks sported, and which resounded with the cooing of cuckoos;

19.

19.

Anekamigapakkhīnamāsayaṃ salilāsayaṃ,

Vīkāsakusumāmodappavāsitasamīraṇaṃ; ()

a resort for many beasts and birds, a place of reservoirs, with breezes perfumed by the fragrance of blooming flowers;

20.

20.

Madhumattā’liṅdhaṅkāranibbhara’mburuhākaraṃ,

Sampātanijjharā’rāvagambhīrabhuribhūdharaṃ; ()

an abundance of lotuses filled with the humming of bees intoxicated with honey, and with great mountains made profound by the sound of cascading waterfalls;

21. [O 0.0115]

21.

Pavavekakkhamaṃ vaṅkapabbhāraṃ girigabbharaṃ,

Duppavesapakathaṃ vaṅkagirināmatapovanaṃ; ()

a place suitable for solitude, with winding slopes and mountain caves, difficult to enter—an ascetic grove named Vaṅkagiri.

22.

22.

Patvā laddhe’sipabbajjā kavilāso so mahībhujo,

Caranto brahmacariyaṃ cirassaṃ vītināmayi; ()

Having reached that place and obtained the going-forth of a seer, that king spent a long time practicing the holy life.

23.

23.

Tassarañño mahesipi maddīnāma sukhedhitā,

Puttadhītūbhisaddhiṃ taṃ tapovanamupāvisi; ()

That king's chief queen, Maddī by name, who was nurtured in happiness, also entered that ascetic grove together with her son and daughter.

24.

24.

Mahiccho pūjakovippo tadā bīgacchadassano,

Yena vessantarosattasāro tenupasaṅkami; ()

Then a greedy brahmin, a seeker of gain, approached the place where Vessantara, the essence of virtue, was.

25. [O 0.0116]

25.

Attho kammakarehī’ti jarājajjaritassa me,

Puttañcadhītaraṃ yācī dhīraṃ patvā dayāparaṃ; ()

Having approached the wise and compassionate one, he begged for his son and daughter, saying, 'I, who am worn out by old age, have need of servants.'

26.

26.

Ubho kaṇhājinaṃ jāliṃ sasenahabhārabhājanaṃ,

Sammāsambodhikāmo so taṇhādāsabyamuttiyā; ()

He, desiring perfect enlightenment and freedom from the slavery of craving, for both Jāli and Kaṇhājinā, who were the vessels bearing the weight of his affection,

27.

27.

Dakkhiṇodakasamputajūjaka’ñjalibhājane,

Samappayittha bandhitvā agamā’dāya niddayo; ()

poured dedication water into the vessel of Jūjaka's cupped hands and entrusted them to him; and that merciless one, having tied them up and taken them, departed.

28.

28.

Dānādhimuttīvīmaṃsī vippākappenu’pāgato,

Saṃyāci devarājā’tha maddideviṃ patibbataṃ; ()

Then the king of the devas, wishing to test his resolve for giving, approached in the guise of a brahmin and begged for Queen Maddī, the devoted wife.

29.

29.

Dakkhiṇodakaniddhotahattho so dakkhiṇodakaṃ,

Katvā devesavippassa deviṃ devo pariccaji; ()

With hands washed by the dedication water, having poured the water of dedication, that king relinquished the queen to the brahmin who was the lord of the devas.

30. [O 0.0117]

30.

Sattakkhattuṃ pakampittha tassa pāramitejasā,

Sādhusādhūti pattānumodantī’va mahīvadhū; ()

By the power of his perfection, the earth trembled seven times, as if the earth-goddess, rejoicing in his attainment, were crying, 'Well done! Well done!'

31.

31.

Iccevaṃ purisārañño paripācinapāramī,

Maṇiraṃsismujjota pāsādasatalaṅkate; ()

Thus indeed, the perfections of that king of men, having matured, were resplendent like the surface of a palace adorned with the light of jewels.

32.

32.

Mandamandāniloṇḍūta pañcavaṇṇaddhajālīnaṃ,

Maṇikiṃkiṇijālānurāvasotarasāyane; ()

In the delightful sound for the ear from the nets of jewel-bells, and in the rows of five-colored banners swayed by a very gentle breeze;

33.

33.

Dibbehi naccagītehi vāditehi manorame,

Kandappamaṇḍapākāra raṅgamaṇḍapamaṇḍite; ()

Adorned with pleasure pavilions, walls, and stage pavilions, with divine dances, songs, and delightful music;

34.

34.

Dibbantadibbarājūnaṃ indacāpasatehi’va,

Cūḷāmaṇīmarīcihī sambādhīkaḷita’mbare; ()

In the sky, made crowded by the rays of the crest-jewels of the divine and most divine kings, as if by hundreds of rainbows;

35. [O 0.0118]

35.

Accharāhi kucañcandanamitaṅgīhi dūrato,

Vidhūtacandikārāji cārucāmara mārute; ()

In the breeze from beautiful chowries, waved from afar like rows of moonlight by celestial nymphs whose limbs were anointed with sandalwood upon their breasts;

36.

36.

Suttappabuddhaposo’va tusite tidasālaye,

Tato cavitvā nibbatti hutvā santusita’vhayo; ()

Like a person awakened from sleep, having passed away from that life, he was reborn in Tusita, the abode of the gods, and came to be named Santusita.

37.

37.

Dibbesu pañcakāmesu vasanto tusitālaye,

Pañcindriyāni lokekalocano paricārayi; ()

Dwelling in the Tusita abode, amidst the five divine sensual pleasures, he, the sole eye of the world, attended to the five faculties.

38.

38.

Tadā dasasahassesu cakkavāḷesu devatā,

Ekattha sannipatitā sutvā buddhahaḷāhaḷaṃ; ()

Then, having heard the 'Buddha-uproar,' the deities in the ten thousand world-systems gathered together in one place.

39.

39.

Teno’pasaṅkamitvāna yenā’si purisuttamo,

Katvā tabbadanambhojaṃ nayanālikulālayaṃ; ()

Having approached him, the supreme among men, they made his lotus-like face an abode for the swarms of bees that were their eyes.

40. [O 0.0119]

40.

Cūḷāmaṇimayukhambutiddhotacaraṇāsane,

Baddhañjalipuṭambhojamakulāti samappayuṃ; ()

On the foot-stool, washed by the water of the rays from his crest-jewel, they placed their cupped hands, joined in reverence, like lotus buds.

41.

41.

Cakkavattipadaṃ sakkamārabrahmapadatayā,

Nakho mārisa patthetvā pāramī paripācitā; ()

O venerable sir, it was not by aspiring to the state of a Wheel-Turning Monarch, or to the state of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, that your perfections were brought to maturity.

42.

42.

Veneyyabandhubhutena sammāsambodhimicchatā,

Tayā mārisa kicchena pūritā dasapāramī; ()

O venerable sir, by you, who became a kinsman to those to be guided and who wished for perfect enlightenment, the ten perfections were fulfilled with difficulty.

43.

43.

Sadevakassa lokassa hitāya mātukucchiyaṃ,

Uppajjatūti yāciṃsu taṃdhīraṃ karuṇāparaṃ; ()

For the welfare of the world with its gods, they entreated that wise one, who was intent on compassion, saying, 'May you arise in a mother's womb!'

44.

44.

Satavassāyuheṭṭhāpi uddhaṃ sahasahassato,

Yasmā akālo buddhānaṃ tasmā kālaṃ vipassi so; ()

Since it is an unsuitable time for Buddhas when the human lifespan is below a hundred years or above a hundred thousand, he therefore discerned the proper time.

45. [O 0.0120]

45.

Yasmā aññesu dīpesu sambuddhā nopapajjare,

Jāyanti jambudīpasmiṃ tasmā dīpaṃ vipassi so; ()

Since Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise in the other continents but are born in Jambudīpa, he therefore discerned the continent.

46.

46.

Yasmā milakkhadesesu nūppajjanti tathāgatā,

Jāyare majjhime dese tasmādesaṃ vipassi so; ()

Since Tathāgatas do not arise in barbarian lands but are born in the Middle Country, he therefore discerned the region.

47.

47.

Yasmā najāyare vessasuddatvayesu jāyare,

Khantiye brāhmaṇe buddhā kulaṃ tasmā vipassi so; ()

Since Buddhas are not born into the two castes of merchants or servants, but are born as warriors or brahmins, he therefore discerned the lineage.

48.

48.

Yasmā anaññavisayā kucchi sambuddhamātuyā,

Tasmā āyuparicchedavasena passi mātaraṃ; ()

Since the womb of a Buddha's mother is not a domain for any other being, he therefore discerned the mother by means of the limit of her lifespan.

49.

49.

Lokekalocano evaṃ katvā pañcāvalokanaṃ,

Tāsaṃ paṭiññaṃ pādāsi karuṇāpuṇṇamānaso; ()

Thus the Sole Eye of the world, having made the fivefold survey, gave his assent to them, his mind filled with compassion.

50. [O 0.0121]

50.

Tappādatāmarasacumbita moḷimālā

Sampattadevaparisā’ntaradhāyi tāva,

Ogayha nandanavanaṃ tusitādhirājā

Tamhā cavī matidayādayināsabhāyo; ()

Then the assembled host of devas, whose garlands on their crowns were kissed by his lotus-like feet, disappeared. Having entered the Nandana Grove, the supreme king of Tusita, that leader endowed with wisdom and compassion, passed away from there.

Iti medhānandābhidhānenayatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānandadānatidāne jinavaṃsadīpe durenidāne vessantaracariyappabhutidevārādhanā pavatti paridīpo pañcamo saggo.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, which illuminates the account of the Vessantara story and the entreaty of the devas, and so forth, in the Jinavaṃsadīpa, in the section on the Distant Origin, composed by the sage named Medhānanda, a work that bestows supreme joy upon the hearts of all poets.

Jinavaṃsadīpe dūrenidāna bhāgo paṭhamo.

Here ends the first part of the Jinavaṃsadīpa: the section on the Distant Origin.

1. [O 0.0122]

1.

Yā sattasārapabhavā sirijambudīpe

Phītā’marāvatipurī’va purīvataṃsā,

Ādiccavaṃsikanarindapaveṇi bhūmi

Lakkhyālayā kapilavatthupurī pure’si; ()

In glorious Jambudīpa, the source of the seven essences, there was formerly the city of Kapilavatthu, the crest-jewel of cities, splendid like the city of Amarāvatī, the abode of prosperity, the land of the lineage of kings of the Solar Dynasty.

2.

2.

Vaṇṇehi kaṇṇasukhasaddarasehi jāta-

Rūpehi atthavisarehi yatīhi yuttā,

Yā rājadhāni puthupāṇagaṇappadehi

Āsī (vasantatilakā) racanā yatheva; () (Silesa bandhanaṃ;)

That royal capital, endowed with fine complexions, sounds pleasing to the ear, and tastes, with golden forms and abundant wealth, frequented by ascetics, and with places teeming with multitudes of beings, was just like a poetic composition.

3. [O 0.0123]

3.

Pācīdisābhujalatāya mahīyuvatyā

Sannaddhasaṅkhavalayassirimāvahantaṃ,

Yassā sudhāsuparikammakataṃ rarāja

Pākāracakkamacalaṃ makuṭānukāraṃ; ()

Its immovable, wheel-like wall, well-finished with plaster, shone like a crown, bearing the splendor of a conch-shell bracelet fastened to the arm-creeper of the youthful earth in the eastern direction.

4.

4.

Yassā rarāja parikhā nagarindirāya

Kiñjakkhiñjaritatīradasābhirāmā,

Saṃsibbitālivittīmaṇitantupantī

Pākārasoṇibharato galitambaraṃ’va; ()

Its moat shone, delightful with its banks yellowed with the pollen of filaments, interwoven with rows of gem-like threads of bee swarms, appearing like a garment of the city-goddess fallen from the heavy hip that was the city wall.

5.

5.

Kandappadappamadirāmadamattadhuttā

Mandānileritasunīlalatāvitānaṃ,

Yasmiṃ vilolanayanañjalipiyamānaṃ

Āpānabhuminibhamopavanaṃbhajiṃsu; ()

In that city, rogues intoxicated with the intoxicating wine of Cupid's pride resorted to the grove, which resembled a tavern, its canopy of beautiful dark vines stirred by gentle breezes, being drunk by the cupped hands of their restless eyes.

6. [O 0.0124]

6.

Mattaṅganāya navayobbanagabbitāya

Raṅgālayaggamaṇidappaṇabimbitehi,

Yā rājadhāni ghanapīnapayodharehi

Sommānanehi bhaji mānasavāpisobhaṃ; ()

That royal capital attained the beauty of the Mānasa lake through the gentle faces and full, firm breasts of intoxicated women proud of their fresh youth, reflected in the chief gem-mirrors of the theater.

7.

7.

Saṅkappitābharaṇaraṃsi sateratālī

Dāṭhābalākavisarā madavuṭṭhidhārā,

Yasmiṃ pure gharamayūrakulaṃ akāle

Kīḷāpayiṃsu varavāraṇavārivāhā; ()

In that city, the best elephants, who were like rain-clouds, made the flocks of domestic peacocks dance out of season, for the rays of their willed ornaments were like a hundred flashes of lightning, their tusks were like a flock of cranes, and the streams of their ichor were like showers of rain.

8.

8.

Pākāracakkabahiniggata muggarāgaṃ

Yasmiṃ turaṅganikaruddhaṭadhūlijālaṃ,

Racchāvatārajanatāya khaṇaṃ janesi

Bhītiṃ padittapalayānalajālasobhaṃ; ()

In that city, a mass of dust, dark red in color, raised by a multitude of horses and issuing forth from outside the wheel-like wall, for a moment generated fear in the people descending into the streets, for its splendor was like the blazing flames of the fire of destruction.

9. [O 0.0125]

9.

Yasmiṃ vimānamaṇisiṅgajutippabandha-

Sañcumbitaṃ jitaraviṃ hariṇḍakabimbaṃ,

Nārījanānanasarojakatāvamānaṃ

Kodhābhibhutamiva vaṇṇavikāramāpa; ()

In which city, the disk of the sun, surpassed and kissed by the stream of rays from the gem-pinnacles of the mansions, put the lotus-like faces of the women to shame, undergoing a change of color as if overcome by anger.

10.

10.

Yatthissarehi samadhiggahitāni tuṅga-

Kelāsakuṭadhavalāti manoharāti,

Niccaṃ sudhāsuparikammakatāni cā’suṃ

Lakkhīniketananibhāni niketanāni; ()

Where the residences, possessed by the wealthy, were lofty, charming, and white as the peaks of Kailāsa; constantly well-finished with plaster, they resembled the abodes of Lakkhī.

11.

11.

Yatthindanilamaṇimāpitamaṇḍapagge

Hemaddhajāvaliparibbhamaṇaṃka puramhi,

Jīmūtakūṭapamukhe satavijjumālā-

Līlāvahaṃ virahinīnamaghaṃ janesi; ()

Where in the city, upon the tops of pavilions made of sapphire, the fluttering of rows of golden banners, bearing the grace of a hundred garlands of lightning upon a cloud summit, generated sorrow for the lovelorn women.

12. [O 0.0126]

12.

Sañjhānurāgamaṇitoraṇadīdhitīhi

Bhinnandhakāranikarā’khilanāgarānaṃ,

Yā rājadhāni janayantipi tuṅgatuṭṭhiṃ

Pītyā navāsi rajanīsma bhisārikānaṃ; ()

That royal capital, which, with the rays from its gem-gateways glowing like the twilight, dispelled the mass of darkness for all citizens, generating great delight; yet for the women going to their trysts, it was not a night for their pleasure.

13.

13.

Sevālakesarasamākulatīrabhāgā

Samphullarattapadumuppalakallahārā,

Haṃsālisārasasamosaraṇābhirāmā

Yasmiṃ sunimmalajalā kamalākarāsuṃ; ()

In which city there were lotus ponds with perfectly clear water, their banks dense with moss and kesara flowers, adorned with full-blown red lotuses, blue water lilies, and white water lilies, and made delightful by the gathering of flocks of swans and cranes.

14.

14.

Yasmiṃpure kulavadhūvadanambujānaṃ

Laddhuṃ nirūpamasiriṃ bhusamussahantā,

Yāvajja setasarasiruhasītaraṃsī

Aññoññabaddhapaṭighā’va vajanti nāsaṃ; ()

In that city, the white lotus and the cool-rayed moon, striving mightily to attain the unsurpassed splendor of the noblewomen's lotus-faces, went to destruction as if bound by mutual enmity.

15. [O 0.0127]

15.

Yasmiṃ suvaṇṇamakaṇirūpiyavaṃsavaṇṇa-

Muttāpavāḷacajirehi mahārahehi,

Nānāpaṇā sukhumakāsikasāṇahaṅga-

Koseyyakhomavasanehi’bhavuṃ papuṇṇā; ()

In which city, various shops were filled with gold, gems, silver, bamboo-hued gold, pearls, coral, and other precious things, and with fine fabrics of Kāsika cotton, hemp, Koseyya silk, and Khoma linen.

16.

16.

Cakkāsisattidhanukuntagadādibhatthā

Sannaddhahemakavacā vijitārivaggā,

Saṅgāmasāgarasamuttaraṇātisurā

Yodhā yahiṃ puravare akariṃsu rakkhaṃ; ()

In that noble city, warriors performed its protection: they were armed with discus, swords, spears, bows, lances, and clubs; clad in golden armor; victorious over the host of enemies; and exceedingly brave in crossing the ocean of battle.

17.

17.

Phūṭṭhā ka vāṭanikaṭe maṇimandirānaṃ

Kappāsapaṭṭadhavalā saradabbharājī,

Yasmiṃ khaṇaṃ javanikāsirimādadhānā

Thīnaṃ jugopa madhupehi mukhambujāni; ()

In which city, a line of autumn clouds, white as cotton cloth, spreading near the windows of the jeweled mansions, for a moment assumed the splendor of a curtain and guarded the women's lotus-faces from the bees.

18. [O 0.0128]

18.

Nibbiddhavīthivisarehi susajjitehi

Niccussavāya puramussitatorasehi,

Bhogindabhoganikarehi rasātalaṃ’va

Yaṃ sampasāritaphaṇehi babhuva rammaṃ; ()

Which city was made delightful by its well-adorned, extensive streets, its constant festivities, and its lofty archways, just as the netherworld is made delightful by the coiled bodies of the serpent lords with their hoods spread wide.

19.

19.

Yasmiṃpure vivaṭamandirajālakānaṃ

Uddhūtadhulimalinīkaḷitālakānaṃ,

Nārinamindurucīrānana dappaṇesu

Lokassa locanamaṇi paṭibimbitā’suṃ; ()

In which city, the eye-jewels of the people were reflected in the mirrors of the women's moon-like faces, whose locks of hair were soiled by dust raised from the open lattices of the mansions.

20.

20.

Gambhīrasaṅkhapaṭabhaddhanibhūrighosaṃ

Kelāsakūṭadhavalālayapheṇapiṇḍaṃ,

Yaṃ puṇṇasattaratanaṃ purakhīrasindhuṃ

Lakkhī alaṅkari turaṅgataraṅgavegaṃ; ()

Lakkhī adorned that city, which was like the milk ocean: its deep and mighty sound was like that of conches and drums; its mansions, white as the peaks of Kailāsa, were its masses of foam; it was filled with the seven gems; and its horses possessed the speed of waves.

21. [O 0.0129]

21.

Reṇuppabandhamalinaṃ kavanarājinīlaṃ

Madhavātimattamadhupaṃ padumābhirāmaṃ,

Yaṃ rājahaṃsabhajitaṃ avatiṇṇalokaṃ

Āsi puraṃ vikacakañjavanaṃ yatheva; () (Silesabandhanaṃ;)

That city was like a blooming lotus grove: soiled by clouds of dust or pollen; dark with rows of crows or blue lotuses; with bees exceedingly drunk on wine or nectar; lovely with its lotus-faced women or lotus flowers; frequented by noble men like royal swans; and a resort for the populace or for living creatures.

22.

22.

Yasmiṃpuramhi ratanujjalanīlakaṇṭhā

Rāgāvamadditadharā’vivaṭadvijāli,

Āsuṃpayodharabharā’viraḷappadesā

Sampattavuṭṭhidivasāviyamātugāmā; () (Silesabandhanaṃ;)

In which city the women resembled a day of heavy rain: their throats dark and shining with jewels, like the sky dark with clouds and lit by lightning; their lips reddened by passion, like the earth colored by red insects; their rows of teeth revealed, like flocks of birds appearing; bearing the weight of their breasts, like the day heavy with rain clouds; and with their nether regions sparsely covered, like the land sparsely populated.

23. [O 0.0130]

23.

Dhammānudhammapaṭipatti parāyaṇassa

Saṃsārabhīrukajanassa tapovanābhā,

Yā rājadhāni pacurandhaputhujjanānaṃ

Āpānabhumiva babhūvu’bhayappakārā; ()

That royal capital was of a dual nature: for the people who feared saṃsāra and were devoted to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, it was like an ascetic's grove; but for the numerous unenlightened worldlings, it was like a tavern.

24.

24.

Buddhaṅkurassa ravivaṃsapabhaṅkarassa

Sammā sukhānubhāvanāya subhumibhutā,

Bho yādisi kapilavatthupuri pure’si

Dhammassabhāvamadhunā paridīpaye sā; ()

O, such was the city of Kapilavatthu in former times, a fertile ground for the perfect experience of bliss for the Buddha-to-be, the light-maker of the solar dynasty. May that city now illuminate the true nature of the Dhamma.

25.

25.

Tasmiṃ babhūva nagare nagarādhirāje

Rājā sunīticaturo catusaṅgahehi,

Dhammena sabbajanarañjanako kadāci

Suddhodanavhavisuto ravivaṃsaketu; ()

In that king of cities, there was a king renowned by the name of Suddhodana, the banner of the solar dynasty. He was skilled in just policy, employed the four means of conciliation, and righteously delighted all people at all times.

26. [O 0.0131]

26.

Disvā’vatārakalusikatamattabhāvaṃ

Ukkaṇṭhite’va kamalā kamalāpatissa,

Bhūpālipālibhajitaṃ caraṇāravindaṃ

Saṃsevi yassa ravivaṃsadhajassa rañño; ()

As if distressed upon seeing the form of her lord, the Master of Lotuses, slightly sullied by his incarnation, Kamalā served the lotus feet of that king, the banner of the solar dynasty—feet that were honored by rows of monarchs.

27.

27.

Yassā’vanīsakavino kavikaṇṭhabhusā

Vāṇivadhū madhurakomakalakattavāṇī,

Patvā catummukhamukhambujakānanamhā

Haṃsīva mānasataḷākamalaṅkarittha; ()

Like a female swan journeying from the lotus-forest of the four-faced Brahmā's mouth to the Mānasa lake, so the goddess Vāṇī—an ornament for the necks of poets, her voice sweet, gentle, and melodious—graced the mind-lake of that poet-king, lord of the earth.

28.

28.

Sabbāridappamathanopari ekadhatvā

Ajjhattikāriparājiyamappasayhaṃ,

Saṃsuddhacittanikase nisitena tāva

Paññāyudhena avadhittha mahībhujo yo; ()

That king, after crushing the pride of all his external enemies at once, then slew the irresistible, internal foe with the sharp weapon of wisdom upon the touchstone of his perfectly purified mind.

29. [O 0.0132]

29.

Yasmā mahīpatimahīdharato upekkhā-

Veḷātalāvadhi dayāsalilena puṇṇā,

Mettāsavanti pabhavā muditumimālā

Ajjhottharittha bhuvanattayagaṃjanoghaṃ; ()

From that king, who was a great mountain, arose a river of loving-kindness, filled with the water of compassion, its waves a garland of joy, and its banks the shores of equanimity; this river inundated the multitudes of beings throughout the three worlds.

30.

30.

Sampannadānasadanambudharehi yassa

Dānādhimuttiparamassa manodahesu,

Taṇhātaṭāni kapaṇaddhikayācakānaṃ

Hinnāni sattaratanambunipātanena; ()

From the clouds of perfect giving of that king, whose highest resolve was generosity, a shower of the water of the seven gems fell, washing away the banks of craving for the poor, the needy, and the supplicant.

31.

31.

Yassindanīlanayanaṃ rajatāvadāta-

Dantaṃ suvaṇṇavadanañca pavāḷasīsaṃ,

Muttāmayaṅgavayavaṃ ratanehi nānā

Dehaṃ sumāpitamivāsi pitāmahena; () (Sīlesabandhanaṃ)

His body seemed as if perfectly fashioned by the Grandsire Brahmā from various gems: his eyes were sapphires, his teeth were white as silver, his face was gold, his head was coral, and his limbs were made of pearl.

32. [O 0.0133]

32.

Yassātipaṇḍarayasovisaro’sadhīso

Saṅekkācitānanasaro’rinarādhipānaṃ,

Sokandhakārabhiduro ripurājinīnaṃ

Āsāgarantapathaviṃ paridhikarittha; ()

His far-spreading, exceedingly white fame, like the moon, encompassed the earth to the ocean's shores. It dispelled the darkness of sorrow for the queens of his enemies and was a lake wherein the lotus-faces of hostile kings would close.

33.

33.

Rājaññachappadakulaṃ sakalaṃ padesa-

Rajjādhipaccamakarandarasābhilāsaṃ,

Yassattabhāvakamalākaraphullitāni

Saṃsevi cārucaraṇambūruhāni bhatyā; ()

The entire host of royal clans, like bees desiring the nectar-like essence of sovereignty over their own regions, served with devotion his beautiful lotus-feet, which blossomed in the lotus-pond of his being.

34. [O 0.0134]

34.

Setātapattamiva vissutakittipuñjaṃ

Katvā’sipattamiva pāvakabhīmatejaṃ,

Yasmiṃ sarajjamanusāsati sesabhūpā

Chattāsibhūsitakarā sakakiṅkarā’va; ()

While he ruled his kingdom, having made his mass of fame into a white parasol and his fire-like, awesome majesty into a sword-blade, the other kings, though their hands were adorned with their own parasols and swords, were like his very own servants.

35.

35.

Dvārāni’nekakapaṇḍikayācakānaṃ

Ugghāṭitopya’virataṃ ratanālayesu,

Saddhādisattadhanarakkhaṇatapparo saṃ

Dvārattayaṃ pidahi yo kapilādhinātho; ()

Though the doors of his treasure-houses were constantly open for numerous poor and needy supplicants, that lord of Kapila, intent on guarding the sevenfold wealth of faith and so on, kept the triple doors of action firmly closed.

36.

36.

Yassussitaddhanueṇo pabalārivaggaṃ

Vissaṭṭhābāṇavisarabbisamubbahanto,

Bhasmikari karikarāyatapīnabāhu-

Sappo suphoṭhitajiyāpariphandajivho; ()

His serpent-like arm, long and stout as an elephant's trunk, reduced the mighty host of his enemies to ash; its hood was his upraised bow, its flickering tongue was his vibrating bowstring, and it bore a shower of discharged arrows.

37. [O 0.0135]

37.

Lakkhīnidhānanagaraṇṇavapātubhūto

Mantindakūṭasikharīvalayāvuto yo,

Vālaggamattampi rājasiṇerurājā

Kodhānilena ripuraññamakampiyo’si; ()

That king, a veritable King Sineru, who had emerged from the ocean that was his city, a treasury of fortune, and who was encircled by the mountain peaks of his chief counselors, was not shaken even a hair's breadth by the winds of anger from enemy kings.

38.

38.

Bhasmikatākhīlavipakkhanarindakaṭṭho

Kodhānalo sarasamīraṇabhāvitopi,

Nibbāyi paggharitabappajalehi yassa

Lolabbilocanaghaṭehi vipakkhathīnaṃ; ()

His fire of anger, which reduced to ashes the firewood of all enemy kings, though fanned by the wind of his arrows, was extinguished by the trickling tears from the water-pots of the trembling eyes of his enemies' women.

39.

39.

Sannītimaggajalituggamatippadīpo

Kittippabandhadhavalīkatajivaloko,

Rājindamoḷimaṇilaṅkatapādapīṭho

Dhammena rajjamanusāsi ciraṃ sarājā; ()

That king—a lamp of lofty wisdom lighting the path of good policy, whose continuous fame whitened the world of the living, and whose footstool was adorned with the crest-jewels of kings—long ruled the realm righteously.

40. [O 0.0136]

40.

Tassatipīvarapayodharabhaddakumbha-

Dvandātibhāraviraḷīkatamajjhabhāgā,

Niddosabālaravimaṇḍalacārugaṇḍā

Dibbaccharājitavirājitarūpasobhā; ()

Her middle part was made slender by the excessive weight of her very full breasts, a pair of auspicious jars; her flawless, charming cheeks were like the orb of the morning sun; and the beauty of her form shone, surpassing the celestial nymphs.

41.

41.

Samphullanīlakamalāmalanīlanettā

Olambamānamaṇikuṇḍalalambakaṇṇā,

Muttāvalivadasanāvali haṃsadhenu-

Helāpahāsagamanā muducāruvāṇī; ()

With eyes pure and dark blue like a blooming blue lotus; with long ears adorned with dangling gem-studded earrings; with a row of teeth like a string of pearls; with a gait that playfully mocked the grace of a female swan; and with a soft, beautiful voice;

42.

42.

Bimbādharā jaladharāyatakesapāsā

Sovaṇṇadappaṇanibhānanacandabimbā,

Sannīrapupphamakuḷopamacārujaṅghā

Kandappa maṅgalasilātalasoṇibhāgā; ()

With lips like bimba fruit; with a mass of hair as long as a rain cloud; with a face like a golden mirror or the orb of the moon; with beautiful shanks like unopened water lily buds; and with hips like an auspicious stone platform for the god of love;

43. [O 0.0137]

43.

Nābhālavāḷaruhanīlatamālavallī-

Līlāvinaddhanavakomalaromarājī,

Lāvaṇṇavāridhitaraṅgabhujā’bhinīla-

Subbhulatāmakaraketanacāparūpā; ()

With a fresh, soft line of hair playfully entwined like a dark tamāla creeper growing from the basin of the navel; with arms like waves on the ocean of beauty; and with beautiful, very dark blue eyebrows shaped like the bow of the Makara-bannered one;

44.

44.

Bhupālavaṃsakamalākararājabhaṃsi

Māyāvadhu iva sujampatino sujātā,

Candassakomudi’va vijjuriva’mbudassa

Rañño’ticārucaritāsi piyā mahesi; ()

Like a royal swan in the lotus pond of the royal lineage, like the lady Māyā, a well-born wife to a noble husband, like moonlight to the moon, and like lightning to a cloud, she was the king's beloved chief consort, of exceedingly beautiful conduct.

45. [O 0.0138]

45.

Tasmiṃ nagopamaghare nagare tadāsi

Āsāḷhimaṅgalamaho divasānisatta,

Milāsugandhaparamaṃ vigatāsavaṃ taṃ

Nakkhattakīḷamakarittha mahesi māyā; ()

In that city, in a palace like a mountain, the auspicious festival of Āsāḷha was then held for seven days. Queen Māyā, supremely adorned with garlands and perfumes and free from intoxicants, celebrated that star festival.

46.

46.

Vuṭṭhāya sattamadināgatapuṇṇamāya

Pāto sugandhaparivāsitavārinā sā,

Katvā sinānamatulaṃ kapaṇḍikānaṃ

Dānaṃ adāsi catulakkhadhanabbayena; ()

Having risen in the morning on the full moon, the seventh day, she performed an incomparable bath with water scented with fragrance and gave alms to the destitute, expending four hundred thousand in wealth.

47.

47.

Vatthāhatehi sunivatthasupārutā sā

Bhutvā’ggabhojanamadhiṭṭhituposatha’ṅgā,

Niddāturā supinamovarakaṃ pavissa

Kalyāṇamaddasa sirīsayane nipannā; ()

Well-dressed and fully covered with new cloths, having eaten choice food and undertaken the Uposatha vows, she, overcome by sleep, entered her private chamber. Lying on her royal couch, she saw a beautiful dream.

48. [O 0.0139]

48.

Netvā nipannasayanaṃ himavantapasse

Heṭṭhā visālatarasāḷamahīruhassa,

Naṃ saṭṭhiyojanakacārumanosilāyaṃ

Āropayiṃsu caturo kira devarājā; ()

It is said that four divine kings took her, lying on her bed, to the slopes of the Himalayas, and beneath a very broad great sāl tree, they placed her upon a beautiful, sixty-league-wide slab of red arsenic.

49.

49.

Netvā manussamalasaṃharaṇāya tamhā’

Notattanāmarahadaṃ sunahāpayitvā,

Devitthiyo sapadi dibbamayehi nesaṃ

Vatthehi gandhakusumehi alaṅkaritvā; ()

Leading her from there to the lake named Anotatta to remove any human stain, and having bathed her well, the goddesses quickly adorned her with divine clothes, perfumes, and flowers.

50.

50.

Tatthubbhavo lasati rūpiyapakabbato yo

Tassodare’tirucire kanakabbimāne,

Pācīnasīsavati dibbamayamhi sammā

Paññāpitaggasayanamhi sayāpayiṃsu; ()

There, a shining silver mountain arose, and in its interior, in an exceedingly beautiful golden palace, they laid her down on a divine, excellent, well-prepared bed with its head to the east.

51.

51.

Oruyha setavaravāraṇarājaveso

Buddhaṅkuro rucirakañcanapabbatamhā,

Āruyha sajjhudharaṇidharamuttarāya

Soṇḍāya setasarasiruhamubbahanto; ()

The Bodhisatta, in the guise of a noble white elephant king, having descended from a beautiful golden mountain, ascended the silver mountain, bearing aloft a white lotus with his excellent trunk;

52. [O 0.0140]

52.

Patvā vimānavathakuñcanadaṃ naditvā

Katvā padakkhiṇamalaṅkatamātuseyyaṃ,

Bhetvāna tāyapana dakkhiṇapassamanto

Kucchiṃ paviṭṭhasadiso supinena diṭṭho; ()

Having reached the excellent palace and trumpeted, and having circumambulated the adorned mother's couch, he was seen in the dream as if entering the womb by piercing her right side.

53.

53.

Māyāya rājavadhuyā rucirānanāya

Āsāḷhipuṇṇamiyamuttara’sāḷhabhena,

Buddhaṅkurassa paṭhamena mahāvipāka-

Cittena sampati ahū paṭisandhigabbhe; ()

On the Āsāḷha full moon, under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation, the Bodhisatta's conception in the womb of Queen Māyā, she of lovely face, occurred with the first great resultant consciousness.

54.

54.

Buddhaṅkurassa paṭisandhigatassa gabbhe

Māyāya cārucaritāya ca khaggahatthā,

Nissesupaddavanirākaraṇāya rakkhaṃ

Gaṇhiṃsu tāva caturo surarājaputtā; ()

While the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of Māyā of beautiful conduct, four sons of divine kings, swords in hand, took up guard for the complete removal of all dangers.

55. [O 0.0141]

55.

Māyāya bhattuparamāya tatoppabhuti

Nūppajji kiñci purisesu sarāgacittaṃ,

Sā pañcakāmasukhinī akilantakāyā

Lābhenuḷārayasasāpyabhivaḍḍhitāsi; ()

From that time onwards, no lustful thought toward Māyā, who was devoted to her husband, arose in any man. She, enjoying the five sensual pleasures, with unwearied body, grew in gain and widespread fame.

56.

56.

Paññāyi dhotaratane janikāya anto

Kucchiṃ gato yatharivāvutapaṇḍusuttaṃ,

Taṃ kucchinā pariharī dasamāsamattaṃ

Pattena telamiva rājini appamattā; ()

The Wise One, having entered the mother's womb, was visible within, like a pale yellow thread enclosed in a clear gem. The queen, ever mindful, carried him in her womb for ten full months, like oil in a bowl.

57.

57.

Pāto’va pāṭipadage divase pabuddhā

Rañño kathesi supinaṃ atha so narindo,

Vedaṅgavedacature catusaṭṭhamatte

Pakkosayī dvijavare dvijavaṃsaketū; ()

Having awakened at dawn on the first day of the lunar fortnight, she told the king her dream. Then that lord of men summoned sixty-four excellent brahmins, experts in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, the crests of the brahmin lineage.

58. [O 0.0142]

58.

Lājuttarāya paribhaṇḍakatāya bhumyā

Paññāpitesu sukhumattharaṇatthatesu,

Bhaddāsanesu bhavanamhinisinnakānaṃ

Nemittikānamavanīpati bhusurānaṃ; ()

For those brahmin diviners, seated in the palace on splendid seats spread with fine coverings, on ground prepared and strewn with excellent parched grain, the lord of the earth...

59.

59.

Pakkhittasappimadhusakkhirakhīramissa-

Pāyāsapuṇṇaharirūpiyabhājanehi,

Vatthāhatāni dhanadhaññacayañca dhenū

Datvāna diṭṭhasupinassa phakhalaṃ apucchi; ()

Having given golden and silver bowls filled with rice porridge mixed with ghee, honey, sugar, and milk, and having given new cloths, heaps of wealth and grain, and cows, he inquired about the result of the dream that had been seen.

60.

60.

Mācintayittha tava rājiniyā janinda

Kucchimhi tampati patiṭṭhahi puttagabbho,

Ajjhāvasissati sañcepana cakkavatti

Rājā bhavissati agāramasaṃsayaṃ so; ()

"O king, do not worry. In your queen's womb, a son has now been conceived. If he remains a householder, he will, without a doubt, become a universal monarch.

61. [O 0.0143]

61.

Hitvā sasattaratanaṃ catudīparajjaṃ

So pabbajissati sace bhavanā’bhigantvā,

Buddho bhavissati dhuvaṃ catusaccabuddho

Iccabruviṃsu supinatthavidū vidū te; ()

"But if, having abandoned his kingdom of the four continents with its seven treasures, he goes forth from the household life, he will surely become a Buddha, one awakened to the Four Truths." Thus spoke those wise interpreters of dreams.

62.

62.

Sā gabbhabhāravaṭharikatamajjhabhāgā

Gantuṃ sakaṃ kulagharaṃ kulakañjahaṃsi,

Icchāmahanti paṭivedayi devi rañño

So sampaṭicchi vacanaṃ karavīkavāṇyā; ()

She, whose middle was weighed down by the burden of her womb, a swan in the lotus of her clan, announced to the king, "I wish to go to my family's home." He consented to the words of she who had a voice like a karavīka bird.

63.

63.

Tamhā mahānagarato nagaraṅgapuṇṇaṃ

So yāva devadahanāmikarājadhānī,

Muttā’vadātapuḷinattharaṇehi rājā

Lājopahāravidhinā kamaluppalehi; ()

From that great city, complete in all its aspects, all the way to the royal capital named Devadaha, the king had the road prepared with white sand strewn like pearls, with offerings of parched grain, and with lotuses and water lilies.

64. [O 0.0144]

64.

Santīrapupphakalasehi samappitehi

Mandātileritapaṭāka dhajāvalīhi,

Kārāpayī kanakarūpiyatoraṇehi

Addhānamaggasamalaṅkaraṇaṃ’takhippaṃ; ()

With placed vases of scattered flowers, with rows of banners and flags waving in the gentle breeze, he swiftly caused the entire length of the road to be adorned with arches of gold and silver.

65.

65.

Vandī’bhigītathutimaṅgalagītikāhi

Pañcaṅgikehi turiyehi katupahāraṃ,

Tasmiṃ sumaṇḍitapasādhitamañjasamhi

Dibbavcarāsiriviḍambanarūpasobhaṃ; ()

With praises sung by bards and auspicious songs, an offering was made with the five kinds of musical instruments. In that well-decorated and adorned palanquin, her beautiful form shone, rivaling the splendor of a celestial nymph.

66.

66.

Deviṃ suvaṇṇasivikāya susajjitāya

Āropayitva khacitāya maṇīhi nānā,

Pesesi bhupati purakkhatañātisaṅghaṃ

Saddhiṃ sahassasacivehi sukhedhitaṃ so; ()

Having placed the queen in a well-decorated golden palanquin, studded with various jewels, the king, well-pleased, sent her forth, preceded by a retinue of relatives and accompanied by a thousand ministers.

67. [O 0.0145]

67.

Samthullapupphaphalapallavavattabhāra-

Rukkhākulaṃ ghanasunīlalatāvitānaṃ,

Hintālatālanaḷakīcakanāḷikera-

Sannīrapūgatiṇapādapapantisāliṃ; ()

Crowded with trees burdened with an abundance of flowers, fruits, and shoots; with a dense, dark canopy of vines; adorned with rows of hintāla palms, palmyra palms, reeds, bamboos, coconut palms, nipa palms, betel palms, grasses, and trees;

68.

68.

Sevālanīlasalilānilasītalehi

Otiṇṇakahaṃsavisarehi samullasattaṃ,

Jhaṅkārarāvamukharālikulākarāla-

Kiñjakkhajālabharitamburuhākarehi; ()

Shining with flocks of descended swans, cooled by the wind and by waters as blue as sevāla moss, with lotus ponds filled with masses of filaments and made resonant by the humming of swarms of bees;

69.

69.

Pupphābhigandhasurabhīkatagandhavāhaṃ

Addakkhisabbajanalocanapīyamānaṃ,

Nindantanandanavanaṃ vanajāyatakkhī

Sā lumbinīvanamanaṅgavimānabhūtiṃ; ()

The lotus-petal-eyed queen saw that Lumbini grove, whose breezes were made fragrant by the abundant scent of flowers, pleasing to the eyes of all people, scorning the Nandana grove, and which was like the splendor of the god of love's palace.

70. [O 0.0146]

70.

Sā rājinī navadalaṅgulipantīcāru-

Sākhābhujopahitamañjaricāmarehi,

Sannaddhakomalalatāvanitānamagge

Attupahārakaraṇāya katāvakāsā; ()

That queen made way on the path for the creeper-women, adorned with tender vines, to make their offerings with charming rows of fingers like fresh leaves and branch-like arms holding whisks of flower clusters.

71.

71.

Senāya cārucaraṇamburuhoddhaṭehi

Reṇūhi dhūsaritamaggamanakkamanti,

Saddhiṃ sakāya parisāya tatotaritvā

Taṃ lumbinīvanamupāvisi rāmaṇeyyaṃ;()

Without treading upon the path, which was made dusty by the dust stirred up by the lovely lotus-like feet of the army, she then descended from there with her own retinue and entered that delightful Lumbini grove.

72.

72.

Taṃ rājiniṃ vanavadhu jitahaṃsagāmiṃ

Āmodamandamalayānilahatthagehi,

Sambhāvayittha mukharālikulābhikiṇṇa-

Reṇuppabandhaharisaṅkhasatehi magge; ()

The spirit of the forest honored on the path that queen, whose gait surpassed that of a swan, with gentle, fragrant Malayan breezes as if with hands, and with hundreds of golden conches like swarms of buzzing bees thick with streams of pollen.

73. [O 0.0147]

73.

Gacchantiyā caraṇanūpuranādapāsa-

Baddhānamunnatasiromigapotakānaṃ,

Ummīlitāyatavilocanapantipakkhe

Dassesi nīlanalinīvanarājisobhaṃ; ()

As she walked, the splendor of a line of blue lotus ponds revealed itself in the wide rows of the opened eyes of the young deer, whose heads were raised, bound by the snare of the sound of her anklets.

74.

74.

Uddhaṃ samaggasikharehi katāvakāsa-

Maggantarehi kalikākusumākulehi,

Nānālatākulamahiruhatoraṇehi

Uyyānabhumi upahārarate’va bhuya; ()

Above, with paths formed in the spaces between the uniform treetops, crowded with buds and blossoms, and with arches of diverse trees tangled with vines, the parkland seemed as if eager to offer gifts.

75.

75.

Ukkhittapiñchabharamantasikhaṇḍimālā-

Kīḷāhi kokilakulaṅanikāhaḷehi,

Uyyānabhumi makaraṅajaraṅgabhumi-

Līlaṃ bhajittha bhamaraddhanivallakīhi; ()

With the playful displays of rows of peacocks raising the burden of their plumage, and with the resounding calls of flocks of cuckoos, the parkland assumed the graceful air of a stage for the god of love, with the humming of bees as if it were the music of lutes.

76. [O 0.0148]

76.

Niccaṃ vasantasamayassirimubbahantaṃ

Taṃkhovanaṃ vanavadhūhadayānutāpī,

Patto nidāghasamayopi janesi tuṭṭhiṃ

Tassā sirisakusumālikulāvataṃso; ()

That grove, always bearing the splendor of the spring season and sympathetic to the heart of the forest nymph, generated joy for her, even when the summer season—itself adorned with a crest-garland of sirisa blossoms—had arrived.

77.

77.

Tasmiṃ nidāghasūriyātapatāpitāmbhaṃ

Rittālavāḷamivakālamakālamegho,

Cintāturaṃ hadayamattasakhījanopi

Pīṇesi gabbhaparipākabharaṃ vāhantyā; ()

Like an untimely cloud in that summer, it soothed her anxious heart—a heart like an empty water basin heated by the sun's rays—as she carried the burden of her maturing womb, even though she was surrounded by her dear friends.

78.

78.

Kaṭṭhāvasiṭṭhataravo parihīnapattā

Tassādharakkhidasanajjutisaṅgamena,

Āsuṃ navaṅkurapalāsavikāsapuppha-

Saṃvellitā’va ramaṇīyavanappa dese; ()

In that delightful woodland region, the trees, which were mere stumps devoid of leaves, by contact with the radiance of her lips, eyes, and teeth, became as if entwined with new shoots, leaves, and blossoming flowers.

79. [O 0.0149]

79.

Gimhābhītāpaparipīḷitaṅdhallikānaṃ

Gambhīrarāvamukharīkatadāyarāji,

Dukkhāturabbirahinīpamadājanassa

Āsi vilāpabadhirīkaḷite’va sāḷā; ()

The rows of groves were made resonant with the deep cries of creatures afflicted by the summer's heat, and the sal trees were as if deafened by the lamentations of women tormented by the sorrow of separation.

80.

80.

Tasmiṃ vikāsakalikāvalihārihārā

Kiñcāpi pakkaphakhalavallarikaṇṭhabhusā,

Nāsakkhi pūgatarupanti sumaṇḍitāya

Māyāya tāya sirimābharituṃ ghaṭantī; ()

Though the rows of betel nut trees had charming garlands of blooming buds and were adorned with vines of ripe fruit, striving, they could not bear the splendor of that beautifully adorned Māyā.

81.

81.

Uyyānamubbhamitamattamadhubbatehi

Campeyyapupphamakulehi samākulaṃtaṃ,

Uddhutadhumapaṭalehi manobhavassa

Dīpehi vāsabhavakanaṃ’va lasantamāsi; ()
