As the Bodhisatta was going, the deities, remembering that the time had come for his awakening to enlightenment, created and showed him a decrepit and ugly form, like a dilapidated cart, capable of bringing about cessation from existence.

3. [O 0.0225]

3.

Kimidamitihapuṭṭho jiṇṇarūpaṃ vipassa

Vimatiparavaso so sārathiṃ rūpasāro,

Nijahadayanidhāne devatācoditassa

Nidahi dhanamivagghaṃ tassadhammopadesaṃ; ()

Seeing the aged form, the essence of beauty, the Bodhisatta, asked the charioteer, 'What is this?' He then took to heart the Dhamma teaching of that charioteer—who was prompted by the deities and whose will was controlled by another—placing it in the treasury of his heart like a priceless jewel.

4.

4.

Haritanaḷakalāpaṃ maṅgaluyyānamagge

Yathariva’himukhaṭṭhā kuñjari bhañjamānā,

Tathariva’bhibhavantī sabbayobbaññadappaṃ

Kharatarajaratā sā attapaccakkhabhūtā; ()

Just as an elephant, standing on the path of the auspicious garden, demolishes a bundle of green reeds, so that very harsh old age, having become directly experienced, overcame all the pride of youth.

5.

5.

Mukhakukavalayagabbhā bhaṭṭhakiñjakkhasobhā

Bhavi kaṭhinajarārikhaṇḍadantaṭṭhipanti,

Kuṭilapalitajātaṃ tañjarāyā’bhiseke

Sirasi racitasetacchattasobhaṃ babandha; ()

His mouth was like the hollow of a gourd, its beauty like faded flower filaments; he became a row of bones and teeth, broken by the harsh enemy, old age. The mass of crooked grey hair on his head, at the consecration of that old age, assumed the splendor of a fashioned white parasol.

6. [O 0.0226]

6.

Aviraḷavaliyo tā jiṇṇarūpassa camme

Pabhavabalavatejodhātuveguṭṭhitā’suṃ,

Taralasalilapiṭṭhe seyyathāpo’dadhissa

Taralasalilapiṭṭhe seyyathāpo’dadhissa

Palayapavanavegu’ttuṅgakallolamālā ()

The dense wrinkles on the skin of that aged form arose, stirred by the force of his powerful vital heat, like rows of high waves on the surface of the trembling ocean, agitated by the wind of dissolution.

7.

7.

Ṭhitamupavanapanthe vaṅkagopāṇasi’va

Anujukamujubhutaṃ daṇḍamolubbha bhumyā,

Nijataruṇavilāsaṃ lakkhamāpādayantaṃ

Dhanumiva saguṇaṃ taṃ rūpamaddakkhi dhīro; ()

The wise one saw that form: standing on the path near the grove, bent like a curved roof-rafter and leaning on a staff on the ground; crooked and stooped, it was like a strung bow, making his own youthful charm seem but a distant mark.

8. [O 0.0227]

8.

Jiniajagarabhoge jiṇṇanimmokabhāraṃ

Tilakavibatacammaṃ tantirojattabhāve,

Apagataghanamaṃso phāsukaṭṭhippandho

Ajinitiravalepaṃ kuḍḍadāruppabandhaṃ; ()

He saw that form, like the coils of an old python, burdened with the slough of decay; with skin spread with spots and a body that was a web of sinews; devoid of solid flesh, a mere framework of ribs; like a wooden frame for a wall, with its plaster worn away.

9.

9.

Vigatabalamadādiṃ vissavantaṃ sarīre

Navhi vaṇamukhehi guthamuttādya’sūviṃ,

Valivisamakapolaṃ kampamānuttamaṅgaṃ

Suvisadamatino taṃ passato jiṇṇarūpaṃ; ()

The one of exceedingly clear mind beheld that aged form, from which strength, pride, and the like had departed; its body oozing impurities such as excrement and urine from nine wound-like openings; with uneven, wrinkled cheeks and a trembling head.

10.

10.

Bhuvanamanavasesaṃ tassu’paṭṭhāsi sampa-

Jjalitamatha jarāyā’dittagehattayaṃ’va,

Ahamapaki anatīto dhammametanti vatvā

Bhavanavanamagañchi jātiyu’kkaṇṭhitatto; ()

Then the entire world appeared to him as utterly blazing, like the three realms on fire with old age. Thinking, 'I too am not beyond this nature,' he, his mind distressed by birth, returned to his palace.

11. [O 0.0228]

11.

Punarupavanamaggaṃ ogahantassa rañño

Sukhamanubhavanatthaṃ devatāmāpayitvā,

Parapariharanīyaṃ ghorarogāvatiṇṇaṃ

Aparamapi virūpaṃ dassayuṃ vyādhirūpaṃ; ()

Again, as the king was entering the path to the grove for the purpose of experiencing pleasure, the deities created and showed him another ugly form: a diseased form, afflicted with a terrible illness, to be avoided by others.

12.

12.

Visadamati vimatyā sakyavaṃsekaketu

Kimimivapalipannaṃ vaccapassāvapaṅke,

Pabhavabalavadukkhaṃ taṃ parādhīnavuttiṃ

Kimidamiti padisvā pājitāraṃ apucchi; ()

With clear and discerning mind, the banner of the Sākya clan, seeing him fallen like a worm in a mire of excrement and urine, a source of powerful suffering, living dependently on others, asked his charioteer, 'What is this?'

13.

13.

Varamati varadhammaṃ tena sūtena vuttaṃ

Amatamiva pibanto sotadhātvañjalīhi,

Agamapi anatito byādhidhammanti tamhā

Nijabhavanavanaṃ sopā’ga saṃviggarūpo; ()

He of excellent wisdom drank the excellent Dhamma spoken by that charioteer as if it were nectar, with the cupped hands of his ears. And realizing, 'I too have not transcended the nature of disease,' he, deeply shaken, returned to his own palace-grove.

14. [O 0.0229]

14.

Tadupavanavimānaṃ vājiyānena nāthe

Vajati sati kadāci māpayuṃ devatāyo,

Suṇakhakulalagijjhādīhīvā khajjamānaṃ

Narakuṇapasarīraṃ uddhumātaṃ paṭhamhi; ()

On another occasion, as the lord was going by chariot to that palace-like grove, the deities created and placed on the path a human corpse, swollen and being devoured by dogs, hawks, vultures, and the like.

15.

15.

Pabhavakimikulānaṃ cālayaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ

Vaṇavivaramukhehi lohitaṃ paggharantaṃ,

Sakuṇagaṇvitacchiṃ makkhikāmakkhitaṅgaṃ

Sumati matasarīraṃ addasā sārahīnaṃ; ()

He of good wisdom saw that lifeless body, devoid of essence: blue-colored, a dwelling for swarms of emergent worms, oozing blood from the openings of its wounds, its eyes pecked out by flocks of birds, its limbs smeared with flies.

16.

16.

Abhigami gamayanto bhāratiṃ sārathissa

Nijasavaṇayugasmiṃ hematāḍaṅkasobhaṃ,

Ahampi maraṇaṃ bho nātivattoti vatvā

Vanamiva migarājā sakyarājā vimānaṃ; ()

Listening intently with his ears, which had the splendor of golden earrings, to the speech of the charioteer, and saying, 'Sir, I too am not beyond death,' the Sākyan king returned to the palace, like a lion king to the forest.

17. [O 0.0230]

17.

Punapi sapariso so yānamāruyha bhadraṃ

Katipayadivasānaṃ accayenā’dhirājā,

Kapilapuravaramhā’naṅgaraṅgālayābhaṃ

Tadupavanamagañchi pañcabāṇābhirūpo; ()

Once again, after a few days had passed, that great king, beautiful as the Five-Arrowed God of Love, with his retinue, mounting his splendid chariot, went from the excellent city of Kapilapura—which resembled the abode of the God of Love—to that pleasure grove.

18.

18.

Guṇamaṇi maṇivaṇṇaṃ pattamādāya patthe

Panasasarasarāgaṃ vīvaraṃpārupitvā,

Ṭhitamavikalacakkhuṃ nimmitaṃ devatāhi

Sumati samaṇarūpaṃ buddharūpaṃ’va passi; ()

Sumati saw the form of a recluse, which was like the form of a Buddha: created by the deities, standing with unwavering eyes, wearing an outer robe the color of ripe jackfruit, and holding in his hand a bowl the color of a jewel.

19.

19.

Tadahani vibudhā’dhiṭṭhānato bhāvanīyo

Yatipatiriva sūto atthadhammānusāsi,

Samaṇaguṇamanekādīnavaṃ pañcakāme

Tamavadi gamanasmiṃ ānisaṃsañca gehā; ()

On that very day, due to the inspiration of the deities, the charioteer, like a master of ascetics, instructed him in the meaning and the Dhamma, speaking of the virtues of a recluse, the many dangers in the five sensual pleasures, and the benefits of going forth from the household life.

20. [O 0.0231]

20.

Kuhanalapanamicchājīvamohāya kucchi-

Paraharaṇasamatthaṃ mattikāpattamassa,

Kara kamakalagataṃ so pāramīcoditatto

Visadamati padisvā sampasādaṃ janesi; ()

Seeing his earthen bowl, held in his lotus-like hand and capable of sustaining his body—not for the purpose of deceit, chatter, wrong livelihood, or delusion—he of clear wisdom, impelled by the perfections, generated serene faith.

21.

21.

Vikasitakalikālaṅkāramuddālasāla-

Miva samaṇavilāsaṃ cīvarobhāsamagge,

Nayanamadhukarānaṃ bhāramādhāya dhīro

Nijamanasi janesi cīvare sampasādaṃ; ()

The wise one, drawing his eyes like a swarm of bees to the splendor of the recluse in the radiance of his robe—which was like a sāla tree adorned with blossoming buds—generated serene faith in the robe within his mind.

22.

22.

Khaṇikamaraṇadukkhāvaṭṭamābādharāsi-

Makaranikarabhimaṃ taṃ jarāvīcivegaṃ,

Bhavajaladhimagādhaṃ jātivelāvadhiṃ so

Ayamiva paṭipannā nittareyyuntya’vedi; ()

He understood that those who enter upon this path will cross over the unfathomable ocean of existence—which has birth as its shore, the crushing waves of old age, made frightful by hosts of Makaras, a mass of diseases, and the whirlpool of the suffering of momentary death.

23. [O 0.0232]

23.

Samaṇavadanapīnaccandabimbodayena

Vikasitamanakundo nandanuyyānasobhaṃ,

Upavanamabhīgantuṃ sandanaṃ cāraye’ti

Tadahani manujindo sandanācārimāha; ()

His mind, like a kunda flower, having blossomed at the rising of the full moon of the recluse's face, the lord of men, desiring to go to the pleasure grove which had the splendor of Nandana grove, on that day said to his charioteer, 'Drive the chariot!'

24.

24.

Valayitanaḷatāḷītālahintālapantiṃ

Malayajatarujāyāsītalaṃ nimmalāpaṃ,

Upavanamavatiṇṇo nandanaṃ vāsavo’va

Akari divasabhāgaṃ sādhukīḷaṃ sarājā; ()

That king, having entered the grove—encircled by rows of reeds, palmyra palms, fan palms, and hintāla palms, cooled by the shade of trees from Mount Malaya, and having pure water—like Vāsava entering Nandana, spent part of the day in joyful play.

25.

25.

Dasasatakiraṇasmiṃ yassa kittippabandha-

Saradajaladarājichāditasmiṃ nabhasmiṃ,

Uparisirasi setacchattasobhaṃ bhajante

Tadiyacaraṇalakkhyā’laṅkari vāpitīraṃ; ()

While the thousand-rayed sun shone in a sky veiled by the stream of his fame—like a line of autumn clouds—and while the splendor of a white parasol was held over his head, his footprints adorned the bank of the pond.

26. [O 0.0233]

26.

Sarasijavadanehi haṃsapīnatthanehi

Kuvalayanayanehī nīlikākuntalehi,

Madhumadamuditālīnūpurebhā’varodha-

Janamiva ramaṇīyaṃ otari so taḷākaṃ; () (Silesabandhanaṃ)

He descended into that lovely lake, which was like the women of the harem: with faces of lotuses, breasts of full-breasted swans, eyes of blue lilies, dark tresses of hair, and the sound of anklets like bees joyful with the intoxication of honey.

27.

27.

Varayuvatijanānaṃ kumbhagambhīranābhi-

Vivaragahitavāri vāpi sā rittarūpā,

Ghanathanajaghanānaṃ saṅgamene’tarāsaṃ

Punarabhavi kapapuṇṇā pītivipphārinīva; ()

That lake, being empty, took water from the deep, pitcher-like navels of the excellent young women; then, by the meeting of their full breasts and hips, it became full of water again, as if suffused with joy.

28.

28.

Abhinavaramaṇinaṃ jātulajjāturānaṃ

Vimukhanayanamīne mīnaketupamena,

Upavadhitumīvagge khittajālabbilāsaṃ

Khaṇamavahari raññā viddhahatthambudhārā; ()

As if to mock the school of fish in the averted eyes of the new, beautiful women afflicted with sudden shyness, the king, who was like the god of love, with a stream of water from his skilled hand, in an instant displayed the charm of a cast net.

29. [O 0.0234]

29.

Navajalakaṇikālaṅkāravattāravindā

Ghanakucakalahaṃsā kesasevālanīlā,

Patimathitataraṅgākiṇṇasussoṇivelā

Sarasi sarasi’vā’si tatra kīḷāture’kā; ()

With her lotus-face adorned with droplets of fresh water, her full breasts like Kalahamsa swans, her hair dark-blue like seaweed, and her beautiful hip-shore strewn with waves churned by her lover—there, a certain woman, agitated by sport, was in the lake like a lake herself.

30.

30.

Sasirūciramukhīnaṃ khomavatthantarīye

Sanikamapanayante vicīhatthehi raññā,

Racitanayanakantī byanta gambhīranābhī-

Sarasijapariyantā nāḷapantīri’vā’si; ()

As the king with his wave-like hands slowly removed the linen undergarments of the women with faces lovely as the moon, one, with the beauty of her eyes displayed and her deep navel manifest, appeared like a row of lotus stems around the edge of a lotus.

29. [O 0.0234]

29.

Navajalakaṇikālaṅkāravattāravindā

Ghanakucakalahaṃsā kesasevālanīlā,

Patimathitataraṅgākiṇṇasussoṇivelā

Sarasi sarasi’vā’si tatra kīḷāture’kā; ()

With her lotus-face adorned with droplets of fresh water, her full breasts like Kalahamsa swans, her hair dark-blue like seaweed, and her beautiful hip-shore strewn with waves churned by her lover—there, a certain woman, agitated by sport, was in the lake like a lake herself.

30.

30.

Sasiruciramukhīnaṃ khomavatthantarīye

Sanikamapanayante vivibhaṇthehi raññā,

Racitanayanakantī byanta gamhīranāhī

Sarasijapariyantā nāḷapantiri’vā’si; ()

As the king with his wave-like hands slowly removed the linen undergarments of the women with faces lovely as the moon, one, with the beauty of her eyes displayed and her deep navel manifest, appeared like a row of lotus stems around the edge of a lotus.

31. [O 0.0235]

31.

Punarapi kucakumbhañcandahārenivā’pe

Nijagaḷaparimāṇe sannimuggaṅganānaṃ,

Malinakamalinī sā locanehā’nanehi

Abhavi bhamarabhāra’mbhojasaṇḍā’kule’ca; ()

Again, with the women submerged up to their necks, their pitcher-like breasts adorned with moon-like necklaces, that lotus pond, darkened by their eyes and faces, became like a lotus grove agitated by a swarm of bees.

32.

32.

Madhumadamadhupehi gīyamānehi vici-

Bhujasatapahaṭāhi soṇibherīhi thinaṃ,

Lalitakamalasīse naccamānindirāya

Ajini jalajinī sā dibbasaṅgītasālaṃ; ()

With songs sung by bees intoxicated with honey, and with hip-drums beaten powerfully by hundreds of wave-like arms, that lotus pond, where Indirā danced gracefully upon a lotus-head, surpassed the divine music hall.

33.

33.

Tuhinakaramukhīnaṃ tantaḷāka’ntalikkhe

Sulalitabhujavallī vijjulekhābhirāmā,

Kuvalayavanarāji nīlajīmutarāji

Patinayanamayūre kīḷayantī rarāja; ()

In that sky which was a lake, a woman with a moon-like face shone; her very graceful, vine-like arms were lovely as streaks of lightning, the rows of her eyes were a forest of blue lotuses, and her hair a line of dark clouds, delighting the peacock of her husband's eyes.

34. [O 0.0236]

34.

Phuṭakuvalayahatthaṃ rājabhaṃsehi khittaṃ

Vividhamadhupabhuttaṃ dhammavelātivattaṃ,

Yathariva gaṇikaṃ taṃ kañjaniṃ so janindo

Tadahani paribhutvā’mandamānanvdamāpa; () (Silesabandhanaṃ)

That lord of men, having enjoyed that lotus pond that day, gained immense joy, as if enjoying a courtesan: its lotuses, with hands of blossoming blue petals, were tossed by royal swans and enjoyed by various bees, having passed their time in the water; just as she is passed among kings, enjoyed by various lovers, and has transgressed the bounds of righteousness.

35.

35.

Caraṇa’nuvajamānabbīcisaṅkhobhatīraṃ

Jahati sati taḷākaṃ sāvarodhe narinde,

Sarasivirahinīsaṃruddhanissāsarūpo

Mudusurabhisamīro mandamandaṃ pavāyi; ()

When the king, with his harem, was leaving the lake, whose shore was agitated by waves following his footsteps, a soft, fragrant breeze blew gently, like the stifled sigh of the lake-nymph, now separated from her beloved.

36. [O 0.0237]

36.

Paribhavi ravibimbaṃ taṅkhaṇatthācalaṭṭhaṃ

Tahimupalatalaṭṭho bhānuvaṃsekabhānu,

Atha sarasivadhūnaṃ kiñcisaṅkovitāni

Sarasijavadanāti sokadīnānivā’suṃ; ()

Standing there on the stone surface, the king, the sole sun of the Solar Dynasty, outshone the sun's orb, which at that moment stood upon the setting mountain. Then the lotus-faces of the lake-nymphs contracted slightly, as if they were wretched with sorrow.

37.

37.

Asitanabhasi sañjhāmeghamālāvilāsaṃ

Abhibhaviya nisinne tatra sakyādhināthe,

Tuvaṭamupagatā taṃ kappakā’nekavatthā-

Bharaṇavikatihatthā bhūpatiṃ bhūsaṇatthaṃ; ()

While the Lord of the Sakyans sat there, surpassing the splendor of a garland of evening clouds in the dark sky, attendants, with hands skilled in arranging various garments and ornaments, quickly approached to adorn the king.

38.

38.

Ravikularavino kho dhammatejābhibhūto

Surapati suraputtaṃ vissakammābhidhānaṃ,

Sapadi pahiṇi sammā dibbavatthādinā bho

Tibhuvanasaraṇaṃ taṃ bhūsayassū’ti vatvā; ()

Indeed, the Lord of the Gods, overcome by the majesty of the Dhamma of that sun of the Solar clan, at once sent the divine being named Vissakamma, saying: 'Go, sir, and properly adorn that refuge of the three worlds with divine garments and other adornments.'

39. [O 0.0238]

39.

Gahitamanujaveso so’pasaṅkamma sīse

Sukhumapaṭasatehī veṭhanañcā’pi datvā,

Maṇikanakamayehi bhūsayi bhūsaṇehi

Tadahani bhavi sakko devarājā’va rājā; ()

He, having assumed a human guise, approached and, having placed on his head a turban made of a hundred fine cloths, adorned him with ornaments of jewels and gold. On that day, the king became like Sakka, the king of the gods.

40.

40.

Timirahamarabhāra’kkantapācīnapassaṃ

Mukulitasatasañjhāmeghapattāvalīnaṃ,

Gaganatalataḷākādhāramandāranāḷaṃ

Kamalamakulasobhaṃ bhānubimbaṃ babandha; ()

The sun's orb, beautiful as a lotus bud, shone forth, its eastern side overcome by the weight of darkness. With rows of evening clouds like hundreds of unfolding petals, it appeared as the stalk of a Mandara flower in the lake of the sky.

41.

41.

Pahiṇi pitunarindo sāsanaṃ tāva tassa

Nijatanujakumāru’ppattimārocayitvā,

Pamuditabhadayo so lekhaṇālokanena

Avaditi mama jātaṃ bandhanaṃ rāhujāto; ()

Then his father, the king, sent him a message announcing the birth of his own son. He, upon seeing the letter, declared: 'A bond is born to me, an impediment has arisen.'

42. [O 0.0239]

42.

Tadahanipituraññā vuttavākyānurūpaṃ

Tahimakhilapadatthaṃ saddasatthakkamena,

Karahacī manujindo ayyako saṅgahetvā

Avaditi mamatattā rāhulonāmahotaṃ; ()

On that day, the grandfather, the lord of men, in accordance with the words spoken by the father-king, and following the meaning of that utterance, declared: 'Let his name be Rāhula.'

43.

43.

Vanasuravanitānaṃ locanindīvarehi

Mahitasirisariro bhadramāruyha yānaṃ,

Sabhavanamabhigantuṃ osari nāgarānaṃ

Suvimalanayanālītoraṇākiṇṇavīthiṃ; ()

His glorious body honored by the blue-lotus eyes of the forest goddesses, he mounted a splendid vehicle and proceeded towards his palace, along a street crowded with archways formed by the rows of the citizens' pure eyes.

44.

44.

Vivaṭamaṇikavāṭo’pantikaṭṭhā vimāne

Jitasuravanitā’si yā pitucchāya dhītā,

Nayanakarapuṭehi rūpasāraṃ nipīya

Samitaratipipāsā sā kisāgotamī thī; ()

In a nearby mansion with its jeweled gates standing open was the daughter of his paternal aunt, a woman who surpassed the celestial nymphs. That woman, Kisāgotamī, drank the essence of his beauty with the cupped hands of her eyes, and her thirst for passion was quelled.

45. [O 0.0240]

45.

Jitamanasijarūpaṃ īdisaṃ yesamatthi

Tanujaratanamaddhā nibbutā sā’pi mātā,

Pitujagatipatī so nibbuto sītibhūto

Nijapiyabhariyā’pi nibbutā’tye’vamāha; ()

She spoke thus: 'Indeed, the mother who has such a jewel of a son, whose form conquers the god of love, is surely at peace. The father, a lord of the world, is at peace, become cool. His own beloved wife is also at peace.'

46.

46.

Hadayagatakilese nibbute vūpasante

Yatipatiriva diṭṭho nibbuto so’hamasmi,

Iti varamati sutvā tāya gāthaṃ sugītaṃ

Vividhanayavibhattaṃ tappadatthaṃ avedi; ()

He of excellent wisdom, having heard that well-sung verse from her, distinguished by its various meanings, understood the meaning of that word, thinking: 'One is truly at peace when the defilements residing in the heart are extinguished and calmed.'

47.

47.

Ahamitipadamassā nibbutiṃ sāvito’smi

Sumariya garubhatyā tāya lakkhagghamaggaṃ,

Dhavalakiraṇabhāraṃ bhāsuraṃ hārihāraṃ

Pahiṇiya bhavanaṃ so pāvisi sāvarodho; ()

Thinking, 'I have been taught about Nibbāna by her,' and regarding her with great respect, he sent a captivating, radiant necklace worth one hundred thousand, with a mass of white rays, and then entered his palace with his retinue.

48. [O 0.0241]

48.

Mayamiva varabodhiṃ bujjhamānassa jātu

Manasi vupasame’ti tuyhamekādasaggi,

Upagamumupasantiṃ vyākarontī’va tāva

Aparadisi vinaddhā’nekasañjhāghanālī; ()

'Just as for one awakening to supreme enlightenment, may the eleven fires in your mind certainly be calmed.' As if predicting this attainment of peace, a line of many dense evening clouds then gathered in the western sky.

49.

49.

Atuladhavajachattaṃ dhotamuttāvalīhi

Valayitamiva rañño tassa sihāsanasmiṃ,

Udayasikharisīse tāvatārāvalīhi

Parivutamatisobhaṃ candabimbaṃ bahāsa; ()

The incomparable white parasol over that king's lion throne, seeming as if encircled by strings of pure pearls, shone as exceedingly beautiful as the moon's orb on the peak of the sunrise mountain, surrounded by a host of stars.

50.

50.

Ghanataratimirehā’vattharattehi loke

Masimalinavilāsaṃ taṅkhaṇe dassayanti,

Rajanikarakarehi vipphurattehi phītā

Katanavaparikamme’vā’si sā rājadhāni; ()

At that moment, while the world, shrouded in dense darkness, displayed a tarnished appearance like black ink, that capital, flourishing with the spreading rays of the moon, seemed as if newly renovated.

51. [O 0.0242]

51.

Himakarakarabhārakkattarattandhakāra-

Galitatimiralekhākāramāvī karonti,

Phuṭakumuda vanesu cāsikundāṭavīsu

Sumadhura madhumattā bhiṅgamālā pamattā; ()

The mass of the moon's rays, overcoming the darkness of the night, makes manifest the appearance of lines of melting shadows. Meanwhile, in the forests of blooming water-lilies and in the groves of kunda flowers, a swarm of bees, intoxicated with sweet honey, roams in delight.

52.

52.

Jitasurapativeso dhammacintāparo so

Jalita maṇipadīpālokabhinnandhakāre,

Nijasiribhavanasmiṃ hemasīhāsanasmiṃ

Nacira mabhinisajjī pañcakāme viratto; ()

He, who had surpassed the lord of the gods in splendor, devoted to reflection on the Dhamma and detached from the five sensual pleasures, sat for a short while on his golden lion throne in his own glorious dwelling, where the darkness was dispelled by the light of a jeweled lamp.

53.

53.

Sapadi turiyahatthā nīlajimutakesā

Kuvalayadalanettā candalekhālalāṭā,

Vikacakamalavattā mekhalābhārasoṇī

Kucaharaviraḷaṅgī cāruvāmorujaṅghā; ()

At once, women appeared with musical instruments in hand, hair like dark clouds, eyes like blue lotus petals, foreheads like the crescent moon, faces like blossoming lotuses, hips heavy with girdles, slender waists, and lovely, beautiful thighs and shanks.

54. [O 0.0243]

54.

Kumudamudakapolā kuṇḍalolambakaṇṇā

Avivaradasanālimālatīdāmalilā,

Kanakaratanamālābhāragīvā, bhirāmā,

Abhinavavanitāyo naccagītesu chekā; ()

With cheeks soft as water-lilies, ears with dangling earrings, a row of teeth like an unbroken garland of jasmine, and necks burdened with necklaces of gold and jewels—these lovely young women were skilled in dance and song.

55.

55.

Rahadamivapasannaṃ niccalāsinaminaṃ

Sumatimupanisinnaṃ saṃvutadvārupetaṃ,

Tamabhiratinirāsaṃ buddhabhāvābhilāsaṃ

Abhiramayitukāmā otaruṃ raṅgabhūmiṃ; ()

Desiring to delight him—who was like a clear and serene pool, ever calm and composed, seated in wisdom, with senses well-restrained, free from sensual pleasures, and aspiring to Buddhahood—they descended to the stage.

56. [O 0.0244]

56.

Maṇimayavasumatyā pādasaṅghaṭṭanena

Kanakavakalayaghosaṃ kāci nicchārayantī,

Calakisalayalīlā aṅguli cālayanti

Anulayamabhinaccuṃ hemavallīvilāsā; ()

With their feet striking the jeweled ground, some women produced the sound of golden anklets. Moving their fingers playfully like tender shoots, they danced in rhythm, with the grace of golden vines.

57.

57.

Narapatimukhabimbaṃka lakkhamāpādayantī

Nayanakharasarānaṃ raṅgasaṅgāmabhūmyā,

Jitakalaravavāṇī kāci rāmā bhirāmā

Savaṇasubhagagītaṃ gāyamānā vibhāsuṃ; ()

Making the king's face their target, with their sharp eyes as arrows on the battlefield of the stage, some lovely, delightful women, whose voices surpassed sweet sounds, shone brightly while singing songs pleasing to the ear.

58.

58.

Jitasuralalanāyokāvi pañcaṅgikāni

Tadahani turiyāni vādayuṃ lolapāṅgā,

Savaṇamadhuravīṇā bherinādehi tāsaṃ

Gaganatala mivā,si pāvuse raṅgabhūmi; ()

That day, with darting glances, they played the fivefold instruments, which surpassed those of celestial women. With the sweet sound of lutes and the roar of drums, the stage was like the sky in the rainy season.

59. [O 0.0245]

59.

Varamati ramaṇīnaṃ taṃ mahābhūtarūpa-

Ppabhavamivavikāraṃ naccamaddakkhi tāsaṃ,

Visamabhavakuṭīre rājarogāturānaṃ

Asunituriyarāvaṃ gītamaṭṭassaraṃ,va; ()

The one of excellent wisdom saw their dance as a transformation as if born from the great elements, and like the harsh sound of song and instruments to those afflicted by the king of diseases in the perilous hut of existence.

60.

60.

Bhusamanahirato so naccagītesu tāsaṃ

Sirisayanavarasmiṃ sīhaseyyaṃ akāsi,

Itigahitavihesā laddhaniddāvakāsā

Sapadi madanapāsā tā nipajjiṃsunārī; ()

Not delighting at all in their dances and songs, he assumed the lion's posture on the best of splendid beds. Thus, seized by weariness and finding an opportunity for sleep, those women, caught in the snare of passion, at once lay down.

61.

61.

Sahakumudiniyā so suttamattappabuddho

Nijasirisayanasmiṃ sannisinno rajanyā,

Gahitaturiyabhaṇḍe tatthatattho, ttharitvā

Yuvatijanamapassi daḷhaniddābhibhūtaṃ; ()

He, awakened from a light sleep in the night like a water lily, sat upon his own splendid couch. He saw the young women, with their musical instruments strewn about here and there, overcome by deep slumber.

62. [O 0.0246]

62.

Anilacalakapo lā kāci lālaṃ gilante

Galitabahaḷakhe ḷā kāci khādanti dante,

Bhagamapagataco ḷā kāci saṃdassaya nne

Khalitavacanamā lā kāci yaṃyaṃ lapante; ()

Some, with cheeks moving with their breath, were swallowing saliva; some, with thick saliva dripping, were grinding their teeth; some, with their garments fallen away, were exposing their private parts; some were muttering whatever faltering words came to them.

63.

63.

Khipitamapi karontī kāci kāsantikāci

Iti pacuravikāraṃ nissirikaṃ asāraṃ,

Bhavanamanavasesaṃ tassu, paṭṭhāsi daḷhaṃ

Narakuṇapavikiṇṇaṃ āmakāḷāhaṇaṃva; ()

Some were sneezing, some were coughing. Thus that entire abode, full of many deformities, unlovely and worthless, appeared vividly to him like a charnel ground strewn with human corpses.

64.

64.

Tadahani tibhavaṃ cā,dittagehattayaṃ,va

Sumariya vatabho, passaṭṭhamopaddutaṃ bho,

Iti paramamudānaṃ kavattayaṃ tabbimutyā

Manasi purisasūro sūrabhāvaṃ janesi; ()

On that day, recollecting the triple existence to be like a burning house, and seeing the great affliction and peril, the heroic man generated heroic courage in his mind for the sake of liberation, uttering a supreme, inspired utterance.

65. [O 0.0247]

65.

Suratacaturarāmārakkhasivāsabhūte

Siribhavanavanasmiṃ mohayantamhi bāle,

Alamiti mama vāso handa nikkhamma tamhā

Tibhavabhayavimuttiṃ esayissāmahaṃ,ti; ()

In the splendid palace grove, a dwelling place for delightful, skillful women and demonesses, which deludes the foolish, he declared: 'Enough of this dwelling for me! Now, having departed from here, I shall seek liberation from the fear of the three realms!'

66.

66.

Upakamiya vimānadvāramummārupante

Sayanupari nipannaṃ channamuṭṭhāpayitvā,

Tamavadi abhigantuṃ kappayitvaṃ, nayeti

Pabalajavabalaggaṃ vājirājaṃ sarājā, ()

Approaching the palace gate, he roused Channa, who lay asleep on a couch nearby. The king said to him: 'Saddle and bring the royal steed, foremost in power, speed, and strength!'

67.

67.

Gatasati hayasāḷaṃ taṅkhaṇe channamacce

Sakapatigamanatthaṃ esamaṃ kappanattho,

Agamiti sahajāto katthako vājirājā

Akari vipulahesārāvamānandabhāro; ()

At that moment, the minister Channa, being mindful, went to the horse stable to saddle the steed for his master's departure. The royal steed Kanthaka, born at the same time, filled with joy, made a loud neigh.

68. [O 0.0248]

68.

Pavisiya sirigabbhaṃ teladīpujjalantaṃ

Ratanakhacitamañce gandhapupphābhikiṇṇe,

Dharaṇipatinipannaṃ hemabimbopamānaṃ

Nijatanujakumāraṃ passibimbāyasaddhiṃ; ()

Entering the splendid inner chamber, lit by oil lamps, on a couch inlaid with jewels and strewn with fragrant flowers, the king saw his own son, the prince, resembling a golden image, lying with Bimbā.

69.

69.

Yadi ahamapanetvā deviyā hatthapāsaṃ

Mama tanujakumāraṃ aṅkamāropayāmi,

Vadanajitasarojā rājinī vuṭṭhahitvā

Vanamahīgamanaṃ me vāraye dunnivāraṃ; ()

If I were to remove the queen’s embracing hand and take my son, the prince, onto my lap, the queen, whose face surpasses the lotus, would awaken and would surely prevent my journey to the great forest.

70.

70.

Tanujamukhasarojaṃ buddhabhūto samāno

Nayanamadhukarānaṃ jātu kāhāmibhāraṃ,

Sumariya caraṇaṃ so uddharanto,va meruṃ

Avatari bhavanamhā ukkhipitvā pavīro; ()

Thinking, 'When I have become a Buddha, I shall surely make my son's lotus-face a feast for the bees of my eyes,' the great hero, reflecting thus, descended from the palace, lifting his foot as though he were uprooting Mount Meru.

71. [O 0.0249]

71.

Kuvalayadalanettañcandamamhojavattaṃ

Madanaratharathaṅgākārasussoṇibhāraṃ,

Kathamavatari bimbānāmadeviṃ pahāya

Narapati bhavanamhā hemabimbābhirāmaṃ; ()

How could the king descend from the palace, abandoning the queen named Bimbā—she who was lovely as a golden image, with eyes like blue lotus petals, a face that outshone the moon, and beautiful, heavy hips shaped like the wheels of the chariot of the god of love?

72.

72.

Marakatapaṭimābhaṃ sambhavaṃ sakyavaṃse

Samupacitasupuññaṃ lakkhaṇākiṇṇagattaṃ,

Pajahiya sukumāraṃ rāhulākhyaṃ kumāraṃ

Kathamavatari pādamandamukkhippa dhīro; ()

How could the steadfast one, having abandoned the tender prince named Rāhula—he who was born in the Sākya clan, resembling an emerald image, of well-accumulated merit, his body endowed with auspicious marks—how could he deliberately lift his foot and depart?

73.

73.

Ripugajamigarājaṃ jambudīpaggarājaṃ

Tadahani piturājaṃ puttasokaṇṇavamhi,

Kathamamitadayo so niddayo pakkhipitvā

Avatari bhavanamhāka uddharitvāna pāde; ()

How could he—a lion to enemy elephants, the foremost king of Jambudīpa, one of boundless compassion—how could he, as if merciless, descend from the palace, lifting his feet, having on that day cast his father, the king, into an ocean of sorrow for his son?

74. [O 0.0250]

74.

Sakalapathavicakkaṃ cakkavāḷāvadhiṃ so

Abhivijiya asattho sattame vāsaramhi,

Narahari katapuñño cakkavatti ahutvā

Kathamavatari tamhā ukkhipitvāna pāde; ()

How could he, the lion among men, the maker of merit, descend from there, lifting his feet, without becoming a universal monarch, who on the seventh day, unarmed, would have conquered the entire circle of the earth up to the Cakkavāḷa mountains?

75.

75.

Avatariya vimānā ajja maṃ tārayatvaṃ

Tvamapitibhavato)haṃ uttareyya’nti vatvā,

Tamabhiruhi janindo vājirājinda’maṭṭhā-

Rasaratanapamāṇaṃ dhotasaṅkhāvadātaṃ; ()

Having descended from the palace, the lord of men said, 'Today, you carry me across; I, in turn, shall help you cross over from the three realms of existence.' So saying, he mounted that chief of royal steeds, which was eighteen cubits in height and pure white like a washed conch.

76.

76.

Pavanaturitavego kanthako vājirājā

Yadahani padasaddaṃ cā’pi hesaṃ kareyya,

Nanu sakalapuraṃ so yāti ajjhottharitvā

Tadahani katasaddaṃ vārayuṃ devatāyo; ()

If Kanthaka, the king of horses, swift as the wind, had on that day made the sound of his hoofs or even neighed, surely the entire city would have been awakened. Therefore, on that day, the deities prevented him from making any sound.

77. [O 0.0251]

77.

Karakamalatalesu devatānimmitesu

Panihitapadavāraṃ assa māruyha dhīro,

Lahumupagami channaṃ vāladhiṃ gāhayitvā

Thirapihitakavāṭadvārapākārupantaṃ; ()

The steadfast one, mounted on the horse whose excellent hooves were placed upon the lotus-like palms created by the deities, swiftly approached the vicinity of the city rampart, with Channa holding the horse's tail, to the gate whose doors were firmly shut.

78.

78.

Yadi pihitakavāṭugghāṭanaṃ nā’bhavissā

Hayavaramapi channāmaccamādāya sohaṃ,

Asari purisasiho uppateyyanti aṭṭhā-

Rasaratatapamāṇu’ttuṅgapākāracakkaṃ; ()

He thought, 'If the firmly shut gates do not open, then I, a lion among men, taking the noble steed and the minister Channa, shall leap over the towering circle of ramparts, eighteen cubits high.'

79.

79.

Tathariva hayarājā channanāmo ca mantī

Vīriyabalasamaṅgī cīntayuṃ tāvadeva,

Vivari tadadhivatthā devatā coditattā

Purisadasasatenu’gghāṭiyaṃ dvārabāhaṃ; ()

Just as he thought, so too the noble horse and the minister named Channa, endowed with energy and strength, were of the same mind. Then, urged on by the deity dwelling there, the gate-bolt, which would have required a thousand men to open, opened.

80. [O 0.0252]

80.

Mama visayamasesaṃ esasiddhatthanāmo

Abhibhaviya subodhiṃ jātu bujjhissatīti,

Atha sumariya māro pāpimā’tīvakuddho

Paṭipathamupagañchi nikkhamitvā vimānā; ()

Thinking, 'This one named Siddhartha will surely overcome my entire domain and awaken to perfect enlightenment,' Māra the Evil One became exceedingly angry, and departing from his abode, he went to stand in the path.

81.

81.

Turitamahivajante māraverimhi māro

Asitanabhasi ṭhatvā itthamārocayittha,

Varapurisa ito kho sattame vāsaramhi

Tvamahivijiya lokaṃ hessase cakkavattī; ()

As the Foe of Māra swiftly advanced, Māra, standing in the dark sky, proclaimed thus: 'O excellent man, indeed, on the seventh day from now, you shall conquer the world and become a universal monarch.'

82.

82.

Sukhamanubhavamāno cakkavattī bhavitvā

Gharamadhivasa cakkaṃ vattayaṃ yāvajīvaṃ,

Amitamati tuvaṃ mā nikkhamassū’ti māro

Abhigamananisedhaṃ kātumiccānusāsi; ()

‘Enjoying happiness as a universal monarch, dwell at home, turning the wheel of sovereignty as long as you live. O you of boundless wisdom, do not go forth!’ Thus Māra exhorted him, wishing to prevent his departure.

83. [O 0.0253]

83.

Namuvilapitavācaṃ sotadhātvañjalīhi

Savisamiva pibanto taṃ tuvaṃ ko’si pucchi,

Pavanapathaṭhito’haṃ issaro devatānaṃ

Naravara vasavattī pāpimā’tye’va māha; ()

Hearing the words of Namuci as if drinking poison with the cupped hands of his ears, he asked him, ‘Who are you?’ Standing in the path of the wind, Māra declared, ‘I am Vasavattī, the lord of deities, the Evil One, O best of men.’

84.

84.

Suranarasaraṇo so nibbhayo dibbacadda-

Ratanajananamaddhā mārajānāmaha’nti,

Paṭivacanamadāsi mādiso duppasayho

Bhavati dasasahassehā’pi tumhādisehi; ()

He, the fearless refuge of gods and men, replied, ‘I know you, Māra. One like me is difficult to subdue, even by ten thousand like you.’

85.

85.

Yadi manasi siyā te kāmadosabbihiṃsā-

Pabhutiparivitakko tāvajānāma’hanti,

Paṭighaparavaso so kiñciotārapekho

Anupadamanubandhi tassa chāyāyatheva; ()

‘If thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, harm, and the like arise in your mind, then I shall know it.’ Overcome by aversion, seeking some opportunity, he followed him step by step, just like a shadow.

86. [O 0.0254]

86.

Punarabhivajatovā’sāḷhiyā puṇṇamāya

Kapilapuravibhūtiṃ daṭṭhukāmamhi jāte,

Vasumati parivattī dassayi assarañño

Puravarabhimukhaṭṭho cetiyaṭṭhānabhumiṃ; ()

Again, on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, as I was proceeding, when the desire arose in me to see the glory of Kapilavatthu, the earth turned, showing the king of horses the ground for the future shrine, facing the best of cities.

87.

87.

Sapadi dasasahassicakkavāḷesu devā

Tibhuvanasaraṇassā’rakkhaṇe vyāvaṭāsuṃ,

Maṇikanakamayehi daṇḍadīpādikehi

Animisatanaye’ke maggamālokayiṃsu; ()

Instantly, in the ten-thousandfold world-system, the gods were engaged in protecting the refuge of the three worlds. Some of the gods illuminated the path with staffs, lamps, and the like, made of jewels and gold.

88.

88.

Surabhikusumadāmolambamānabbitāna-

Kanakakalasasetacchattaketuddhajehi,

Tadahigamanamaggaṃ devatā’laṅkariṃsu

Bhuvanakuharamāsi pupphapūjābhirāmaṃ; ()

The deities adorned the path of his coming with fragrant flower garlands hanging from canopies, golden pitchers, white parasols, banners, and flags. The hollow of the world became delightful with floral offerings.

89. [O 0.0255]

89.

Gaganamasanighosacchantamevaṭṭhasaṭṭhi-

Turiyasatasahassāravavipphāramāsi,

Mahitasurabhipupphākiṇṇamaggāvatiṇṇo

Aturitamabhigantvā yojanantiṃsamattaṃ; ()

The sky was filled with a sound like thunder, and the widespread clamor of sixty-eight hundred thousand instruments. Having descended upon the path strewn with honored, fragrant flowers, unhurried, he went for thirty yojanas.

90.

90.

Vimalasalilapuṇṇaṃ pheṇamālābhikiṇṇaṃ

Vikacakamalarājiṃ tuṅgakallolarājiṃ,

Sasiratarasamīraṃ vāḷukākiṇṇatiraṃ

Samupagami anomānāmagaṅgaṃ savīro; ()

The hero approached the river named Anomā, full of pure water, strewn with garlands of foam, adorned with rows of blooming lotuses and high waves, its banks strewn with sand and cooled by swift breezes.

91.

91.

Asitamaṇitalābhā channa kā nāmikā’yaṃ

Iti varamati pucchi so anomānadīti,

Tamavadi yadi tīre ettha’haṃ pabbajeyyaṃ

Ativiya saphakhalā me sā anomāsiyā’ti; ()

‘Channa, what is this river called, which has the sheen of a dark blue jewel?’ Thus the one of excellent intellect inquired. He replied, ‘This is the Anomā River.’ He then thought, ‘If I were to go forth here on its bank, my renunciation would be truly “not inferior” (anomā) and exceedingly fruitful.’

92. [O 0.0256]

92.

Ravikulatilako so paṇhiyā vājirājaṃ

Sajavamadadi saññaṃ tāya aṭṭhosabhāya,

Suvimalasalilāyā’nomagaṅgāya tīre

Taraṇiriva ṭhito’si uppatitvā turaṅgo; ()

He, the ornament of the solar dynasty, with his heel gave a swift signal to the king of steeds for that leap of eight usabhas. Having leaped across, the horse stood on the bank of the Anomā River with its perfectly pure water, like the sun.

93.

93.

Sitapulinatalaṭṭho tiṇhadhārā’sihattho

Visadamati samoḷiṃ cūḷamādāya daḷhaṃ,

Aluni sirasi sesā dvaṅgulā nīlakesā

Na tadupari parūḷhā dakkhiṇāvattayiṃsu; ()

Standing on the white sandy shore, sword with sharp-edged blade in hand, the one of clear intellect firmly grasped his topknot together with its diadem. He cut the hair on his head; the remaining two finger-breadths of dark blue hair grew no longer, but curled to the right.

94.

94.

Abhavi tadanurūpaṃ dāṭhikā massucā’pi

Ayamupari sacā’haṃ ṭhātu buddho bhaveyyaṃ,

Nabhasi khipi sikhaṃ taṃ iccadhiṭṭhāya dhīro

Paribhaviya ṭhitā sā meghamālāvilāsaṃ; ()

His beard and mustache were also of a corresponding length. With the resolution, ‘If I am to become a Buddha, let this remain in the air,’ the steadfast one cast that topknot into the sky. It remained there, surpassing the splendor of a garland of clouds.

95. [O 0.0257]

95.

Sapadi surapuramhā devarājābhi’gantvā

Tamabhihariya cūḷaṃ cāricaṅgoṭakena,

Ratanamayamuḷāraṃ cetiyaṃ māpayittha

Suragaṇamahanīyaṃ tatra cūḷāmaṇinti; ()

Instantly, from the city of the gods, the king of devas approached, and taking that topknot in a beautiful casket, he had a magnificent jeweled shrine built there, revered by the hosts of gods and named the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya.

96.

96.

Vidhirabhavi sahāyo yo ghaṭikāranāmo

Adadi samaṇakappaṃka so kaparikkhāramassa,

Gahitasamaṇaveso pubbabuddhā’va nātho

Nabhasi khipi nivatthaṃ sāṭakaṃ saṃharitvā; ()

The Brahmā named Ghaṭikāra, who was his friend, gave him the requisites of an ascetic. Having adopted the ascetic's guise, the Lord, like the Buddhas of the past, gathered the garment he had worn and cast it into the sky.

97.

97.

Tamabhihariya dussaṃ pakkhipitvā samugge

Ratanamayamatulyaṃ yojanadvādasuccaṃ,

Akari parahitatthaṃ brahmalokeka vidhātā

Makuṭamaṇimaricīcumbiyaṃ cetiyaṃso; ()

Taking that cloth and placing it in a casket, the sole creator of the Brahma-world, for the welfare of others, made an incomparable jeweled shrine, twelve yojanas high, which was kissed by the rays of its crest-jewel.

98. [O 0.0258]

98.

Pitunarapatino tvaṃ bhusaṇādīni datvā

Iti mama vacanenā’rogyamārocayassu,

Sacivamanupalabbhā’ dāni pabbajjituṃ te

Pahiṇi hayasahāyaṃ ovaditvāna channaṃ; ()

‘Give these ornaments and the like to my father the king, and in my name, announce my well-being.’ Having thus advised Channa, he sent him away with his companion the horse, as he himself was now to live the life of renunciation without an attendant.

99.

99.

Paṭipathamavatiṇṇo gantukāmo saraṭṭhaṃ

Dharaṇipativiyogā sokanibbiddhagatto,

Turagapati cavitvā kanthako devaputto

Bhavi kanakavimāne taṅkhaṇetāvatiṃse; ()

Having set out on the return path, desiring to go to his own country, his body pierced with sorrow from separation from the lord of the earth, the lord of horses, Kanthaka, passed away and at that very moment became a devaputta in a golden mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

100.

100.

Sakalavanasurānaṃ añjalimañjarihi

Mahitañcaraṇapīṭho yena pabbajjito so,

Tadavasarianomānāmanajjā samīpe

Vanamanupiyanāmaṃ ambarukkhābhirāmaṃ; ()

He who had thus gone forth, his feet honored with the cupped hands of all the forest deities, arrived at the grove named Anupiya, delightful with mango trees, near the river named Anomā.

101. [O 0.0259]

101.

So nikkhamma abhinnakhattiyakulā nekkhamma dhammālayo

Bhogakkhandhamuḷāracakkaratanaṃ uccārabhāraṃ viya,

Ohāyā’nupiyambanāmavipine sattāhamajjhāvasaṃ

Pabbajjāpaṭilābhasambhavasukhaṃ vedesi buddhaṅkuro; ()

Having gone forth from the renowned warrior clan, he, whose abode was the Dhamma of renunciation, abandoning the mass of enjoyments and the great wheel-treasure as one would a burdensome load of filth, the Buddha-to-be dwelt for seven days in the Anupiya Mango Grove and experienced the bliss arising from the attainment of renunciation.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakala kavijana hadayānanda dānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe avidūre nidāne mahābhinikkhamana pavattiparidīpo dasamo saggo.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, entitled ‘The Illumination of the Account of the Great Renunciation,’ in the Proximate Section of the Jinavaṃsadīpa, a treasure that bestows delight upon the hearts of all poets, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda.

1. [O 0.0260]

1.

Mandānileritatarusaṇḍamaṇḍite

Tasmiṃ tapovanagahaṇe tapodhano,

Bhutvā (pabhāvati) vanadevatā yathā

Dibbaṃ sukhaṃ sukhamanagāriyaṃ tato; ()

In that dense hermitage, adorned with groves of trees stirred by gentle breezes, the one rich in austerity, having enjoyed the bliss of homelessness, a divine bliss like that of a forest deity, thereafter...

2.

2.

Yo seniyo narapati māgadho tadā

Yasmiṃ pure vasati puraṅgabhāsure,

Rājaggahaṃ tamahipavesanatthiko

Addhānamosari samatiṃsayojanaṃ; ()

Desiring to enter Rājagaha, the city where the Magadhan king Seniya then dwelt, a city radiant with fine mansions, he traveled a road of thirty yojanas.

3.

3.

Cakkaṅkitassiricāraṇo susaññamo

Dīghañjasaṃ vasi tadahena khepayaṃ,

Rājaggahaṃ kapuravaramindirālayaṃ

Sampāvisi jitagajarājagāmi so; ()

He whose auspicious feet were marked with wheels, well-restrained, spent that day traversing the long road. With the gait of a conquered elephant king, he entered Rājagaha, the best of cities, an abode like Indra's.

4. [O 0.0261]

4.

Indāsudhāvalivalayikato mahā-

Maggamhi jaṅgammaṇipabbatoriva,

Khattiṃsalakkhaṇasamalaṅkato mahā-

Vīro taponidhi yugamattadassano; ()

On the great road, like a moving mountain of jewels, as if encircled by a divine white rampart, the great Hero, a treasure-store of austerity, adorned with the thirty-two marks, gazed only a yoke's length ahead.

5.

5.

Bodhāpayaṃ budhajanamānasambuje

Avhāpayaṃ pathikajana’kkhipakkhino,

Vimhāpayaṃ nijasiriyā sadevake

Tasmiṃ pure cari sapadānacārikaṃ; ()

Causing the lotuses of the minds of the wise to blossom, summoning the birds that were the eyes of the people on the path, and astonishing the world with its gods by his own splendor, he wandered on his alms-round in that city.

6.

6.

Piṇḍāya gacchatisati rūpadassana-

Pabyāvaṭā’khilajanatāya gotame,

Saṅghobhitā’suramisarehi sā puri

Patte yatheva’surapuri purindade; ()

When Gotama went for alms, and all the people were engaged in gazing upon his form, that city was agitated, just as the city of the Asuras is when Purindada arrives.

7. [O 0.0262]

7.

Khattiṃsalakkhaṇasuracāpabhāsure

Rūpambare varapurisassa gacchato,

Lokassa locanasakuṇāvalitadā

Antaṃ napāpuṇi parisaṅkamantīpi; ()

As the best of men proceeded, his form radiant with the thirty-two marks and shining like a divine rainbow, the flocks of birds that were the eyes of the world, though circling about, could not reach the limit of his beauty.

8.

8.

Mañjīrapiñjarakara kandharāmaṇi-

Keyūrabhāsuracaraṇā sirimato,

Sīmantinī paramasiriṃ vipassituṃ

Dhāviṃsu nijjitakalahaṃsakāminī; ()

To behold the supreme glory of the Fortunate One, the women ran, surpassing the grace of female swans, their feet shining with anklets, their hands golden, their necks with jewels, and their arms with bracelets.

9.

9.

Nārijanā mahitumivā’bhigacchato

Rūpindirāya’ nimisalocanuppale,

Dhammillavellitabhujacampakāvalī

Dhāviṃsu pīvarakucahārapīḷitā; ()

The women ran, as if to worship the approaching Lord of Beauty with their unblinking, lotus-like eyes; their braided hair, swaying arms, and garlands of champaka flowers trembled, and they were burdened by their full breasts and necklaces.

10. [O 0.0263]

10.

Nissāsinī samajalabinducumbita-

Vattambujā sithilitakāsikambarā,

Kācitthiyo samaṇamudikkhituṃ pathe

Dhāvantiyo kimupatisaṅkiyā’bhavuṃ; ()

Some women, breathing heavily, their lotus-like faces kissed by drops of sweat, their Benares silk garments loosened, running on the path to see the ascetic—what apprehension could they have had?

11.

11.

Ugghāṭitā’sitamaṇisihapañjarā

Rāmāpasāritavadanambujāka vasiṃ,

Daṭṭhuṃ pabhujanabhavanesu taṅkhaṇe

Mandākinisarasivilāsamāharuṃ; ()

The dark-jeweled lion-windows were opened, and the lovely women, putting forth their lotus-like faces to see him, at that moment brought to the mansions of the nobles the splendor of the Mandākinī lake.

12.

12.

Ucchaṅgatopatitasutā’bhirūpino

Rūpappalamhitahadayāka pūrīvadhū,

Passantiyo pathikajanassahatthage

Nākaṃsu kiṃ adhikaraṇā’dhiropaṇaṃ; ()

The city women, their hearts captivated by the form of the beautiful one, let their children fall from their laps as they gazed. Why did they not raise quarrels with the people on the path?

13. [O 0.0264]

13.

Eke janā yatipatirūpadassana-

Kotuhaḷā sakapaṭibhānamabravuṃ,

Sīmantinī manakumudāni bodhayaṃ

Patto’tya’yaṃ pakatinisāpatīnukho; ()

Some people, eager to see the form of the lord of ascetics, spoke from their own wit: ‘This one, awakening the water-lilies of the minds of women, is he not indeed the natural lord of the night?’

14.

14.

Sutvāna taṃ sakalakalāntaropagaṃ

Bimbaṃ tadaṅkitahariṇaṅkamambare,

Tumhe napassatha himaraṃsino iti

Gabbābhijappitavacanā’parejanā; ()

Having heard that, other people spoke with words muttered in pride: ‘Do you not see in the sky the orb of the cool-rayed one, which encompasses all arts and is marked with the sign of a deer?’

15.

15.

Accherapaṅkajavisarāni cintiya

Sañcumbituṃ puralalanānana’mbuje;

Verocano idhupagamā virūpimā

Iccabravuṃ punaranisammakārino; ()

Thus spoke the unreflecting ones again: ‘Thinking of wondrous lotus-clusters, and desiring to kiss the lotus-faces of the city women, Verocana, the deformed one, has come here!’

16.

16.

Sutvāna taṃ gaganatalaṅgane’dhunā

Verocanassa’bhicarato napassatha,

Caṇḍātapaṃ thiraparivesamambuja-

Pāṇinti gajjitavacanā’parejanā; ()

Having heard that, other people with voices like thunder spoke: ‘Do you not see Verocana now traversing the courtyard of the sky—the one of fierce heat, with a steady halo, the lotus-handed one?’

17. [O 0.0265]

17.

Uttuṅgamandiramaṇicandikātale

Dibbaccharānibharamaṇihi vañcito,

Eyā’marāvatinagariti cintiya

Sakko care nanu sakavādamapakpayuṃ; ()

Thus they put forth their own argument: ‘Deceived by the beautiful women on the high, moonstone-jeweled terraces, who are like a host of celestial nymphs, might not Sakka wander here, thinking this is the city of Amarāvatī?’

18.

18.

Sakkassa dānavavijayā’bhilāsino

Pāṇimhi dissati vajirāyudhaṃ kharaṃ,

Saṃvijjare dasasatalocanāni’pi

Notādiso ayamiti tabbipakkhino; ()

His opponents replied: ‘In the hand of Sakka, who desires victory over the Dānavas, a fierce thunderbolt weapon is seen, and a thousand eyes are also found. This one is not like that.’

19.

19.

Yā sālavatya’dhivacanā’bhirūpinī

Sañcodito jitagirijāya tāya ho,

Kelāsapabbatanibhapaṇḍavācala-

Ñattaṃ vajaṃ ayamitiissaro’bravuṃ; ()

They declared him to be Īśvara, saying: ‘Urged on by the conquered Girijā, and by the beautiful city named Sālavatī, this one is proceeding to the Paṇḍava mountain, which resembles Mount Kailāsa.’

20. [O 0.0266]

20.

Tumhe napassatha paramissarassa kiṃ

Naggattanaṃ pasusayano’pavesanaṃ,

Pāṇiṃ kapālakamadhikakkhimaṇḍalaṃ

Itthaṃ paveditavacanā’parejanā; ()

Thus other people declared: ‘Do you not see the Supreme Lord’s nakedness, his lying and sitting like an animal, the skull in his hand, and the prominent eye on his forehead?’

21.

21.

Esā’valambitapurakhīranīradhiṃ

Lakkhiṃ samekkhiya nijalakkhisaṃsayo,

Pītambaraṃ paridahiya’ñjase caraṃ

Nārāyano iti matimappayuṃ sakaṃ; ()

They put forth their own idea: ‘This is Nārāyaṇa, who, seeing a beauty that outshines the milk ocean, and doubting his own auspicious mark, has donned a yellow robe and now walks here with ease.’

22.

22.

Nārāyano kuvalayanīlaviggaho

Kopantaro’ragasayanindirādhano,

Cakkāyudho’llasitakaro’tivāmano

Tabbādamaddanacature’tare janā; ()

Other people, skilled in refuting that argument, said: ‘Nārāyaṇa has a body blue as a water lily, is wrathful within, has the serpent for his couch and Indirā for his wealth, wields the discus, has a radiant hand, and is a great dwarf.’

23. [O 0.0267]

23.

Vedattayaṃ vibudhajanānamānane

Sva’jjhāyataṃ vasatinukho sarassatī,

Sañjātasaṃsaya jaṭito pitāmaho

Tassāgavesanapasuto’tyu’dīrayuṃ; ()

Thus they proclaimed: ‘With the three Vedas being well-recited in the mouths of the wise, does Sarasvatī truly dwell there? With this doubt arisen, the matted-haired Grandfather, Brahmā, must be intent on searching for her.’

24.

24.

Sutvāna taṃ sarasijayonino sadā

Pāṇimhi vijjati varamattapotthakaṃ,

Cattāricānanapadumāni dissare

Gacchaṃ ayaṃpana puriso natādiso; ()

Having heard that, others replied: ‘In the hand of the lotus-born one there is always a fine palm-leaf book, and his four lotus-faces are seen; but this man who is going forth is not like that.’

25.

25.

Suddhodanavhayavasudhādhipa’trajo

Buddho bhavissati iti vedakovidā,

Koṇḍaññabhusurapamukhā dvijā tadā

Pabyākaruṃ tanu bahubhāsaṇena kiṃ; ()

‘The son of the lord of the earth named Suddhodana will become a Buddha.’ Thus did the twice-born skilled in the Vedas, headed by the brāhmaṇa Koṇḍañña, then prophesy. What need is there for much speaking?

26. [O 0.0268]

26.

Ukkaṇṭhito sakabhavanā mahāmatī

Nikkhamma sattamadivasoti vissuto,

Āpāthagaṃ nijasavaṇañjalihi bho

Taṃ byappathaṃ napivatha kiṃ yathāmataṃ; ()

The great-minded one, distressed by his own home, went forth and became renowned on the seventh day. O sirs, with your own ears as cupped hands, why do you not drink in that declaration to your fill?

27.

27.

Vedāgataṃ varapurisaṅgalakkhaṇaṃ

Dehamhi vijjati samaṇassa gacchato,

Andhā’va bho apagatarūpadassanā

Tumhe’pi kiṃ talahatha rūpadassanaṃ; ()

The marks of an excellent man, as transmitted in the Vedas, are present on the body of the wandering ascetic. O sirs, you are like the blind, devoid of the sight of true form! Why then do you still seek for the sight of mere appearances?

28.

28.

Nikkhamma chaḍḍitavibhavo mahākulā

Suddhāsayo sugahiya pattacīvaraṃ,

Pabbajjiyā’nahiramito bhavattaye

Atthācaraṃ anugharamañjase’dhunā; ()

Having gone forth from a great family, renouncing his wealth, with pure intent, having rightly taken up the bowl and robe, he lives unattached to the threefold existence. Now, for the welfare of others, he wanders truly from house to house.

29. [O 0.0269]

29.

Suddhodanāvanipatino varoraso

Eso samujjalasatapuññalakkhaṇo,

Vyāpārito kusalabalena bodhiyā

Hote’va gotamasamaṇo nasaṃsayo; ()

This noble son of King Suddhodana, radiant with a hundred marks of merit, impelled by the power of his wholesome deeds toward awakening, will without a doubt become the ascetic Gotama.

30.

30.

Disvā tapodhanamahiyantamañjase

Ye mānavā sakasakavādamappayuṃ,

Tabbādabandhanaviniveṭhanā paraṃ

Iccāhu paṇḍitapurisā yathāvato; ()

After those young men, upon seeing the truly honored ascetic, had put forth their respective arguments, the wise men, now disentangled from the bonds of that debate, spoke rightly thus:

31.

31.

Dutā tadā surasi samappitañjalī

Rañño tamacchariyapavattimāharuṃ,

Addakkhi bhupati caramānamañjase

Piṇḍāya’thabbivariya sihapañjaraṃ; ()

Then the messengers, with hands respectfully joined, brought that wondrous news to the king. The lord of the earth, having opened the lion-window, then saw him wandering truly for alms.

32.

32.

Nā go siyā paṭhaminimujjanaṃ ka re

Yakkho siyā sahayamadassanaṃ ka re,

De vo siyā gaganatalaṅgaṇañca re

Poso siyā yadi paṭiladdhamāha re; ()

‘Could he be a Nāga, who sinks into the earth? Could he be a Yakkha, who suddenly vanishes? Could he be a Deva, who traverses the courtyard of the sky? If he is a man, then tell me what you have ascertained!’

33. [O 0.0270]

33.

Dūtenu’sāsiya magadhādhipo iti

Vīmaṃsituṃ pakatimanaṅgahaṅgino,

Pāhesi te padamanugammu’pāgamuṃ

Saddhiṃ mahāsamaṇavarena paṇḍavaṃ; ()

Thus instructed by the messenger, the king of Magadha sent them to investigate the nature of that one who was free from pride. They followed his tracks and arrived at Paṇḍava mountain along with the great and noble ascetic.

34.

34.

Vikkhālayaṃ mukhakamalaṃ kule kule

Bhikkhāṭanena’ bhihaṭamissabhojanaṃ,

Laddhā jigucchiya vasi paṇḍavācala-

Cchāyāya mārabhi sunisajja bhuñjituṃ; ()

Having obtained by his alms-round from house to house the mixed food that was brought to him, the ascetic, feeling revulsion, went to dwell in the shade of Paṇḍava mountain. Having sat down properly, he began to eat.

35.

35.

Bhattamhī kukkuravamathūpame muhuṃ

Antodaraṃ pavisati dhīmato sati,

Antāni bāhirakaraṇāni’vā’bhavuṃ

Taṃkho sahī vasisanisampajaññavā; ()

As the food, which was like dog's vomit, repeatedly entered the belly of the wise one, his entrails felt as if they were coming out. Yet that ascetic, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, endured it.

36. [O 0.0271]

36.

Pabbajjitaṃ sugahitapattacīvaraṃ

Disvā ratiṃ pajahiya rājabhojane,

Siddhattha no tvamabhigamittha attanā

Attānamovadiya pabhuñji bhojanaṃ; ()

‘O Siddhattha, having seen yourself gone forth with well-grasped bowl and robe, having abandoned delight in royal feasts, you have indeed come to this on your own. Admonish yourself, and then partake of this food.’

37.

37.

Dūtehi coditahadayo dayādhano

So māgadho narapati tena pāvisi,

Yenā’si paṇḍavagiri bhadravāhanaṃ

Āruyha dassanarasaghedhalocano; ()

That king of Magadha, rich in compassion, his heart urged by the messengers, ascended a fine vehicle and proceeded to where Paṇḍava mountain was, his eyes greedy for the taste of that sight.

38.

38.

Aññāya sākiyakulasambhavaṃ vasiṃ

Rājā pasidiya ariye’riyāpathe,

Mā kāhase sakha iti dukkaraṃ kharaṃ

Rajjena taṃnarapavaraṃ pavārayi; ()

The king, having understood that the ascetic was of Sakyan lineage and being pleased with his noble deportment, made an offer to that excellent man with his kingdom, saying: ‘Friend, do not undertake this! It is difficult and harsh.’

39. [O 0.0272]

39.

Rajjena kiṃ tava caturaṇṇavāvadhiṃ

Rajjaṃ nijaṃ pajahiya āgatassa me,

Bodhiṃ pabujjhiya paṭhamaṃ tathāsati

Āgacchataṃ mama vijitantya’voca naṃ; ()

He replied to him: ‘What use is your kingdom, bounded by the four oceans, to me, who have come here having renounced my own? First, after I have awakened to enlightenment, you should then come to my conquered realm.’

40.

40.

Datvā paṭissavamatha bhumibhattuno

Lokassa locanamaṇitoraṇākule,

Dīghañjase vasi ṭhapitaṅghipaṅkajo

Āḷārākaṃ isipavaraṃ upāvisi; ()

Then, having given his promise to the lord of the earth, the ascetic set his lotus-feet upon the long, straight path. Amidst the jeweled arches that were the eyes of the world, he approached the eminent sage Āḷāra.

41.

41.

Patvāna kiṃ kusalagavesi so vasi

Āḷārakaṃ virajamuḷārajhāyinaṃ,

Icchāmahanti’si tava santike’dhunā

Dhammaṃ samācaritumidhāgato bruvi; ()

That ascetic, a seeker of the good, approached Āḷāra, the dust-free and profound meditator, and said: ‘O sage, I wish to practice the doctrine in your presence; it is for this that I have now come here.’

42. [O 0.0273]

42.

Sutvāna taṃ tatiyamarūpikaṃ vasi

Jhānaṃ viyākari paṭiladdhamattanā,

Khippaṃ taponidhipaguṇaṃ akāsi taṃ

Dhammaṃ sakācariyanayā’valambiya; ()

Hearing this, the ascetic Āḷāra explained the third immaterial absorption, which he himself had attained. Relying on his teacher's method, that treasure of austerity quickly mastered that teaching.

43.

43.

Nā’yaṃ vasi tanutarasaddhayā mamaṃ

Dhammaṃ sayaṃ samadhigataṃ viyākare,

Gosāmiko yathariva pañcagorasaṃ

Addhāphalaṃ anubhavatīti tintiya; ()

“This ascetic would not, with slight faith, declare the Dhamma I have myself attained. Just as a master of cows enjoys the five products of a cow, so too does he truly experience the fruit,” thus thinking.

44.

44.

Kālāma dve adhigatajhānasambhavaṃ

Tvaṃ yāvatāsukha manubhosi maṃ vada,

Puṭṭhassa tassi’ti nacakiñci bhāviyaṃ

Ākiñcanaṃ avaca akiñcanālayo; ()

“Kālāma, tell me how much bliss you experience from the jhāna you have attained.” When asked thus, he whose abode was nothingness spoke of the base of nothingness, thinking, “There is nothing.”

45. [O 0.0274]

45.

Saṃvijjare mamapaki imassi’ve’sino

Saddhāsatīvīriyasamādhibuddhiyo,

Evaṃ vitakkiya naciraṃ katussaho

Jhānaṃ labhī tatīyamarūpikaṃ vasī;

“Faith, mindfulness, energy, concentration, and wisdom are found in me, just as in this sage.” Thus reflecting, and making an effort, the ascetic before long attained the third formless jhāna.

46.

46.

Yaṃ kho tuvaṃ viharasi jhātamapakpito

Sampajja sampati viharāmahanti taṃ,

Āḷāri’si varapurisena sāvito

Lābhā’vusotyavaca suladdhamāvuso;

“That jhāna in which you dwell, having meditated and being unshaken—I too now dwell in it, having fully attained it.” The sage Āḷāra, addressed by the excellent man, said: “It is a gain for us, friend! It is well gained, friend!”

47.

47.

Jānāmi pāvacanamahaṃ yathā tuvaṃ

Jānāsi pāvacanamahaṃ yathā tuvaṃ,

Tvaṃ tādiso ahamapi yādiso bhave

Tvaṃ yādiso ahamapaki tādiso bhave;

“I know the teaching just as you do; you know the teaching just as I do. As I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.”

48. [O 0.0275]

48.

Ehā’vuso samaṇa mayaṃ ubho janā

Kāhāmi’to pariharaṇaṃ gaṇassi’daṃ,

Vatvāna ācariyasamānako sakaṃ

Sissaṃ akā tamasamamattanā samaṃ; ()

“Come, friend ascetic, let us both lead this group.” Having spoken thus, the teacher made his own disciple, that peerless one, equal to himself.

49.

49.

Dhammopya’yaṃ nabhavati nibbidāya vā

Bodhāyavā navupasamāya kevalaṃ,

Āruppabhumiyamupapattiyā siyā

Iccānalaṅkariya tato apakkami; ()

“This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, nor to awakening, nor only to peace; it is for rebirth in the formless realm.” Thus, not being satisfied, he departed from there.

50.

50.

Kālamato uparivisesamuddako

Jaññā’tya’yaṃ sumariya rāmaputtako,

Patvā’ssamaṃ samadhigataṃ tvayā’pa’haṃ

Dhammaṃ samācaritumidhāgato’bruvi; ()

Recalling, “Uddaka Rāmaputta may know a higher distinction than Kālāma,” he reached his hermitage and said: “I have come here to practice the Dhamma that you have attained.”

51. [O 0.0276]

51.

Ñatvā sakācariyamatañhi buddhimā

Dhammañcare mama samayo ca tādiso,

Vatve’vamuddakavasi khippamattano

Sikkhesi pāvacanapathe tapodhanaṃ; ()

“A wise man, having known his own teacher’s doctrine, should practice the Dhamma; and my tradition is such.” Having spoken thus, Uddaka the ascetic quickly trained the ascetic in the path of his teaching.

52.

52.

Saddhāya maṃ sakasamayā’nusāsako

Addhā samādhijaphalamāhare’tya’yaṃ,

Cintāparo varapuriso arūpikaṃ

Jhānaṃ valañjasi katamantya’pucchi naṃ; ()

Thinking, “This instructor of his own doctrine will surely, with faith, lead me to the fruit born of concentration,” the excellent man, devoted to thought, asked him: “You practice the formless jhāna—how far is the end?”

53.

53.

Sutvā tamuddakavasi santamānaso

Santaṃhi’daṃ paramamidanti bhāviyaṃ,

Sāmaṃ valañjanakamarūpabhumikaṃ

Jhānaṃ catutthakamavikampamāharī; ()

Hearing this, Uddaka the ascetic, with a peaceful mind, thinking, “This indeed is peace, this is the highest,” declared the fourth, unwavering, formless jhāna, which he himself practiced.

54. [O 0.0277]

54.

Saṃvijjare mamapi manoniketane

Saddhādisagguṇaratanāni’massi’va,

Evaṃsaraṃ naciramarūpikaṃ vasi

Jhānaṃ labhī vīriyabalenavā’ntamaṃ; ()

“In my own abode of the mind, the jewels of good qualities beginning with faith are found, just as in his.” Thus recollecting, the ascetic, by the power of his energy, before long attained the final formless jhāna.

55.

55.

Laddhaṃ tayā yamadhigatanti tammayā

Ārocite samaṇa vare’sipuṅgavo,

Amhe gaṇaṃ supariharāmu’bho’timaṃ

Vatvā tamācariyadhurena mānayi; ()

“O noble ascetic, bull among sages, since you have declared what you have gained and attained, let us both lead this group together.” Having spoken thus, he honored him with the burden of a teacher.

56.

56.

Nā’yaṃ patho bhavaparimuttiyā siyā

Addhābhave mamapaki bhavaggapattiyā,

Evaṃ vavatthitahadayo mahādayo

Nibbijjaso tadapagato’nalaṃiti; ()

“This is not the path for release from becoming; indeed, it is for the attainment of the peak of becoming.” Thus resolved in heart, the greatly compassionate one, being disenchanted, departed from there, thinking, “This is not enough.”

57. [O 0.0278]

57.

Mokkhesako jitavaravāraṇakkamo

Ekocaraṃ vasi magadhesu cārikaṃ,

Senānivissunnigamo yahiṃsiyā

Taṃ tāpasālayamuruvelamosari; ()

Seeking liberation, with the gait of a conquered, noble elephant, the ascetic wandered alone on tour in Magadha. He approached the hermitage at Uruvelā, where the market town of Senāni was located.

58.

58.

Addakkhi so hariṇavihaṅgamākulaṃ

Mandānileritatarusaṇḍamaṇḍitaṃ,

Nerañjarāsalilapavāhasitalaṃ

Pāsādikaṃ paramatapovanaṃ tahiṃ; ()

There he saw a supreme and delightful hermitage, thronged with deer and birds, adorned with groves of trees stirred by a gentle breeze, and cooled by the flowing waters of the Nerañjarā.

59.

59.

Antojaṭaṃ jaṭilajaṭā’livumbita-

Pādambujo vijaṭayituṃ ghaṭaṃ vasī,

Attāhitāpanapaṭipattiyā tahiṃ

Vijjādhare jaṭilavare pasādayī; ()

The ascetic, whose lotus feet were surrounded by the swarms of matted locks of the matted-haired ascetics, strove to disentangle the inner tangle. There, by the practice of self-mortification, he inspired confidence in the excellent matted-haired ascetics, the holders of lore.

60. [O 0.0279] Sañcārito janapadacārikaṃ tadā

60. Then, having wandered through the country,

Patvā tapovanamatha pañcavaggiyā,

and having reached the hermitage, the group of five bhikkhus

Bhikkhu mahāpurisamupaṭṭhahiṃsu taṃ

attended to that great man,

Āraddhadukkarakiriyaṃ yathābalaṃ. ()

who was undertaking arduous practices, according to their ability.

61. Dhīro’tidukkarapaṭipattipūrako

61. The wise one, fulfilling the exceedingly difficult practice,

Dantāni vīsatidasanehi vīsati,

pressing teeth against teeth,

Tāluṃ nirumhiya rasanāya cetasā

and pressing his tongue against his palate, with his mind

Cittaṃ nipīḷayi paritāpayi tahiṃ. ()

he crushed and tormented his mind.

62. Paggayha muddhani balavā’tidubbalaṃ

62. Just as a strong man, having seized a very weak man by the head,

Nipphīḷaye yathariva dhīmato tathā,

Attāhitāpanapasutassa paggharuṃ

Kacchādinā’dhīkatarasedabindavo; ()

might crush him, so it was for the wise one; for him, devoted to self-mortification, excessive drops of sweat flowed from his armpits.

63. [O 0.0280] Maggobhavatya’yamiti bodhisiddhiyā

63. Thinking, “This is the path for the attainment of awakening,”

Appāṇakaṃ paṭipada mācaraṃ ciraṃ,

Vāsaṃ akā vasi mukhato ca nāsato

Assāsamappaṭipaṭimo’parundhiya; ()

the peerless ascetic for a long time practiced the path of non-breathing, restraining the in- and out-breaths from his mouth and nose.

64.

64.

Ruddhesu tesva’ pihitasotarandhato

Vāto’bhinikkhami adhimattanissano,

Kammāragaggarimukhato ravo bhusaṃ

Niggacchate abhidhamanena seyyathā; ()

From those blocked and covered ear-orifices, wind burst forth with an exceedingly loud sound, just as a loud sound issues forcefully from the mouth of a blacksmith's bellows when it is blown.

65.

65.

Yāvedanā kharasikharena jāyare

Sīsassa vijjhanasamaye sukhatthino,

Evaṃ tadā kaṭhinasirorujā’bhavuṃ

Ruddhānilassa hi mukhakaṇṇanāsato; ()

As are the pains from a sharp point piercing the head of one who seeks pleasure, so then did severe head-pains arise from the wind blocked in the mouth, ears, and nose.

66. [O 0.0281]

66.

Vātābhighātanasamaye sudhimato

Sīse’bhavuṃ punarapisisavedanā,

Daḷhena yo sirasi varattakena yaṃ

Daḷhaṃ dade yathariva sisaveṭhanaṃ; ()

At the time of the striking of the winds, for the wise one, pains arose again in his head, just as a strong man would apply a tight head-binding with a strong strap.

67.

67.

Sammā nirumhitamukhakaṇṇanāsato

Dhīro samīraṇamuparundhicu’ttariṃ,

Gabbhantaraṃ kharataravedanā’turaṃ

Vātā’bhimanthiya parikantayuṃ tato; ()

With mouth, ears, and nose well restrained, the steadfast one further stopped the wind; then the winds, churning within his belly, cut through and around, afflicting him with extremely harsh pains.

68.

68.

Goghātako caturataro vikattaye

Kucchiṃ gavaṃ tikhiṇavikantanena ce,

Ruddhātileha’nariyamaggagāmino

Jātā tathā kharatara kucchivedanā; ()

Just as a very skilled butcher would slice open a cow's belly with a sharp knife, so too arose extremely harsh belly pains for him who was blocking the ignoble path of excessive craving.

69. [O 0.0282]

69.

Appānakaṃ punarapi jhānamācaraṃ

Vīro samīraṇa muparundhi sabbathā,

Cīntubbhavaṃ sakamukhakaṇṇanāsagaṃ

Tenā’si kāyikadaratho dhitīmato; ()

Again, the hero, practicing the breathless jhāna, completely stopped the wind. From this, a sensation arose in his own mouth, ears, and nose, and thereby there was bodily torment for the resolute one.

70.

70.

Daḷhaṃ ubho carapurisā mahabbalā

Bāhāsu gaṇhiya purisaṃ’tidubbalaṃ,

Aṅgārakāsuyamahitāpayantice

So tādisiṃ anubhavi dukkhavedanaṃ; ()

Just as if two strong men of great strength, having seized a very feeble man by the arms, were to roast him over a pit of embers, even so did he experience such a painful feeling.

71.

71.

Khittaṃ kaliṅgaramivakāvidevatā

Ruddhānilubbhavakharavedanāturaṃ,

Vīraṃ vilokiya patitaṃ tapovane

Pabyākaruṃka varapuriso mato iti; ()

Seeing the hero fallen in the ascetic grove—afflicted by the harsh pain arising from the blocked wind—like a discarded log, some deities declared: 'This excellent man is dead.'

72. [O 0.0283]

72.

Kālaṃkarotya’yamiti kāci devatā

Nocāhukiṃ taditara devatā vataṃ,

Asse’va gotamasamaṇassa mārisā

Ārocayuṃ viharaṇamīdisaṃiti; ()

Some deities exclaimed, 'This one is dying!' But other deities said, 'Not so, sirs; such is the state of this ascetic Gotama,' they announced.

73.

73.

Yaṃnūna’haṃ paṭipadaheyyamāyatiṃ

Āhārayāpanaharaṇāya sabbaso,

Evaṃ sacintayi karuṇāya coditā

Tā devatā tuvaṭumupecca gotamaṃ; ()

Those deities, urged by compassion, swiftly approached Gotama, reflecting thus: 'What if we were to provide him with a means for completely removing his need for sustenance?'

74.

74.

Ārocayuṃ yadipana niccabhojano-

Pacchedanaṃ samaṇatuvaṃ karissasi,

Kāhāma te mayamitilomakupato

Dibbojamokiriya sariratappaṇaṃ; ()

They said: 'Ascetic, if you are going to undertake the cutting off of all food, then we shall infuse you through the pores of your skin with divine essence that will nourish your body.'

75.

75.

Ghāsassachedanavīriyaṃ karomi ce

Yāpenti tā madhura sudhārasena maṃ,

Tenā’bhiyāpanavidhimicchato sato

Taṃkhotapaṃ nabhavati kiṃ musā mamaṃ; ()

If I exert effort to cut off food, and they sustain me with sweet nectar-juice, then for me, being sustained by that method, would not that austerity of mine be a falsehood?

76. [O 0.0284]

76.

Nālanti so kuhanavasena devatā-

Vimhāpaneti’ha nijadehatappaṇaṃ,

Evaṃ anussariya’nuvāsaraṃ vasī

Āhāramāhari virasaṃ parittakaṃ; ()

He thought: 'It is not proper to deceive the deities by means of trickery and to nourish my own body here.' Thus reflecting, the master dwelt day after day, taking only tasteless and meager food.

77.

77.

Svācelako vicarikarāpalekhaṇo

Ācāramuttya’bhavi nacehitiṭṭhiko,

Uddissakaṃ abhihaṭakaṃ nimantanaṃ

Nāsādayi piṭakakalopikumbhikaṃ; ()

He wandered as a naked ascetic, licking his hands; he was one who had abandoned conventions, not responding to 'Come, stand.' He did not accept food specifically intended for him, brought to him, or offered by invitation, nor from a basket, pot, or jar.

78. [O 0.0285]

78.

So daṇḍamuggaramusale’ḷakantaraṃ

Pāyantigabbhinipanitīhi cā’haṭaṃ,

Sāmakkhikāvisaya muhinnamekikaṃ

Saṅkittinodanamapi nābhisādayī; ()

He did not accept food taken from between a stick, mallet, or pestle, nor from a sheep pen; nor what was brought by a nursing, pregnant, or cohabiting woman; nor from a place infested with flies, nor from a place of ill repute.

79.

79.

Sovīrakaṃ napivi suraṃ namerayaṃ

Sukkhāmakaṃ yadapi tikovisuddhikaṃ,

So macchamaṃsakavikatiṃ paṭikkhipi

Appekadā tapasi nirāmagandhiko; ()

He drank no sour gruel, nor liquor, nor mead. He rejected preparations of fish and meat, even that which was thrice-purified. At times, the ascetic was free from the smell of raw flesh.

80. [O 0.0286]

80.

So sattatoppabhuti kamena hāpayaṃ

Yāvekamāhari kabalaṃ balatthiko,

So sattatoppabhuti kamena hāpayaṃ

Ekaṃ kulaṃ upagami yāva bhikkhituṃ; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

Gradually reducing from seven mouthfuls, he, desiring strength, came to take but a single one. Gradually reducing from seven families, he came to approach but a single one for alms.

81.

81.

Ekāya dīhipi ticatūhi pañcahi

Dinnaṃ paṭiggahi chahi dattisattahi,

Ekāhikappabhutikamaddhamāsikaṃ

Mūlaṃ sayaṃ patitaphalaṃ pabhuñji so; ()

He accepted what was given in one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven portions. He ate at intervals ranging from once a day up to once every half-month. He partook of roots and fruits that had fallen by themselves.

82.

82.

Sāmākataṇḍulamathasākamaddakaṃ

Nīvārakuṇḍakahaṭadaddulādikaṃ,

Piññākagomayatiṇa jhāmakodanaṃ

Vīro mahāvikaṭamapānubhuñji so; ()

He ate grains of wild millet, herbs, wild rice, rice-bran, rice-scum, water-plants, and the like; oil-cake, cow-dung, grass, and burnt rice. The hero partook of such extremely foul food.

83. [O 0.0287]

83.

Thokaṃ pivi pakasatamitaṃ hareṇuka-

Yūsaṃ tathā canaka kulatthamuggajaṃ,

So appabhojanaparamo sajīvitaṃ

Ekena yāpayi tilataṇḍulena’pi; ()

He drank little, just a handful of lentil soup, and likewise the juice of chickpeas, horse gram, or mung beans. Devoted to minimal food, he sustained his life even with a single sesame seed or a grain of rice.

84.

84.

Sāṇammasāṇa?Jina’jinakkhipacchava-

Dussaṃ tirīṭakakusavākacīrakaṃ,

So kesakambalamapivāḷakambala

Moḷukapakkhikaphalakānya’dhārayi; ()

He wore garments of hemp, of coarse cloth, of hides, of rags, of bark, of kusa grass, and of wood-shavings. He wore a blanket of human hair, a blanket of horse-tail hair, a garment of owl's feathers, and wooden planks.

85. [O 0.0288]

85.

Dubbaṇṇanattakamayamaggapuggalo

Appekadā paridahi paṃsukūlakaṃ,

Attantapovaraṇa parāyaṇo bhavi

So massukuntalatanulomalocako; ()

The foremost person became of poor complexion; sometimes he wore rag-robes. He became devoted to the practice of self-mortification, one who plucked out his beard, head-hair, and body-hair.

86.

86.

Ubbhaṭṭhako’bhavi parivajjitāsano

Ukkaṭṭhamukkuṭikavataṃ adhiṭṭhahī,

Uddhaggakaṇṭakavīsame apassaye

Seyyaṃ akā tadupariṭhānacaṅkamaṃ; ()

He became one who stood upright, avoiding seats. He undertook the extreme practice of squatting. In a shelterless place, thorny and uneven, he made his bed, and there he stood and walked.

87.

87.

So sāyatatiyakamudakāvarohaṇa-

Yutto pavāhayitumaghaṃ samussa hī,

Ātāpayaṃ iti paritāpayaṃ sakaṃ

Dehaṃ ciraṃ parihari pāpabhīruko; ()

He was engaged in descending into the water up to three times a day, striving to wash away evil. Thus heating and tormenting his own body, he, fearing evil, carried on this practice for a long time.

88. [O 0.0289]

88.

Yo nekahāyanagaṇiko’tthi’tinduka-

Rukkhassa kho papaṭikajātakhāṇuko,

Evaṃ tathā papaṭikajātamattano

Gattañca sannivitarajomalaṃ bhavi; ()

Just as the stump of a tinduka tree, standing for many years, becomes covered with bark-scales, so too his own body became scaly, and was covered with accumulated dust and dirt.

89.

89.

Sovā paro natu parivajjayī rajo-

Jallāni kajjalamalināni pāṇinā,

Dehaṃ subhojanajahanena jajjaraṃ

Telaṃ vilepiya rajasā’bhithūlayī; ()

He did not wipe away with his hands the soot-stained dust and grime. His body, worn out from abandoning good food, he first anointed with oil and then caked with dust.

90.

90.

So dve’kapassayikavataṃ papūrayī

Āpānako’ bhavi phalake’pi thaṇḍile,

Seyyaṃ akāka vihari vivekakāmavā

Ajjhogahaṃ adutiyako mahāvanaṃ; ()

He fulfilled the vow of sleeping on one side; he made his bed on a plank or on the bare ground. He practiced the breathless state. Desiring seclusion, he dwelt alone, plunging into the great forest without a companion.

91. [O 0.0290]

91.

Pāṇe ime visamagate’tikhuddake

Nā’haṃ vadhissamiti paṭicca’nuddayaṃ,

Ussāvamaddanahirabhīrutāya so

Nātho abhikkami ca sato paṭikkami; ()

Out of compassion for these very tiny creatures moving about, he resolved, 'I will not kill them.' The Lord, careful not to harm or crush them, stepped forward mindfully and stepped back mindfully.

92.

92.

Ninnatthalā vanagahanā vanāsayo

Ninnatthalaṃ vanagahanaṃ migo yathā,

Hīto vipassiya vipinopage jane

Tāsābhibhū papanati evamevakho; ()

Just as a deer in a low-lying, dense forest, upon seeing people approaching the woods, flees, overcome by dread; even so, the forest-dweller, shy and seeing people approach, would flee, overcome by dread.

93.

93.

Disvāna luddakavanakammikādayo

Gopālake tiṇanaḷakaṭṭhahārake,

Mācaddasaṃ ahamapi tetya’yaṃjano

Mā maṃ vipassatu samadhiṭṭhahaṃ vataṃ; ()

When he saw hunters, forest workers, cowherds, and gatherers of grass, reeds, and firewood, he resolved in his vow: 'May I not see these people, and may these people not see me.'

94.

94.

Ekovasaṅgaṇikavihārabhītiyā

Ninnatthalā vanagahanā taponidhī,

Ninnatthalaṃ vanagahanaṃ papāta so

Tassāsi tādisi pavivittatā tadā; ()

From fear of dwelling in company, he, a treasury of asceticism, plunged into the low-lying, dense forest. He plunged into that low-lying, dense forest. Such was his solitude at that time.

95. [O 0.0291]

95.

Yasmiṃvane caratamavītarāgīnaṃ

Romuggamo caraṇatalāni kampare,

Disvāna bhiṃsaṇakavanaṃ tathāvidhaṃ

Ajjhogahaṃ vasi pavivekakāmavā; ()

In that forest where, for those wandering who were not free from passion, their hair stood on end and the soles of their feet trembled; having seen such a terrifying forest, I plunged into it and dwelt, desiring seclusion.

96.

96.

Ussāvapātatasamaye’ntaraṭṭhake

Hemantike sisiratarāya rattiyā,

Abbhāvakāsika mabhipūrayi vataṃ

Kicchaṃ vasi vasi vanasaṇḍago divā; ()

At the time of heavy dewfall, during the eight days of winter, on a very cold night, he fulfilled the vow of dwelling in the open air. He dwelt with difficulty, residing in a forest grove by day.

97.

97.

Gimhotu pacchimadivasantare divā

Abbhāvakāsikadhutadhammapūrako,

Rattiṃ vane vihari javaṭṭhikānyu’pa

Nissāya so asayi susānabhūmiyaṃ; ()

In the last days of the summer season, by day fulfilling the ascetic practice of dwelling in the open air, at night he dwelt in the forest; relying on a jawbone, he lay down in the charnel ground.

98. [O 0.0292]

98.

Buddhaṅkuraṃ upagamiyo’ṭhubhanti’pi

Omuttayantipi rajaso’kiranti’pi,

Gomaṇḍalā savaṇakhilesu daṇḍakaṃ

Datvā vadāpayitumupakkamanti’pi; ()

Approaching the Buddha-sprout, they spat upon him, they urinated on him, and they scattered dust on him. In cattle-pens and on threshing-floors, giving him a stick, they also tried to make him speak.

99.

99.

Sovādhivāsayi satimā upekkhako

Taṃvedanaṃ kaṭukaka manaññavediyaṃ,

Dukkhe sukhe sumati tulāsarikkhako

Bālesu tesva’pi navikopayimanaṃ; ()

Mindful and equanimous, he endured that bitter pain, which was unbearable for others. Wise, like a balance in the face of pain and pleasure, even among those fools he did not allow his mind to be agitated.

100.

100.

Āhāratappaṇavidhinā visuddhi’ti

Eke vadanti’ha samaṇāññatitthiyā,

Kolādibhojanavikatiṃ tathāvidhaṃ

Appicchatāya’nubhavi suddhikāmavā; ()

Some ascetics and other sectarians here say, 'Purity is by the method of satisfaction through food.' He, however, desiring purity, partook of such food preparations as jujube fruits and the like out of his desire for fewness of wishes.

101. [O 0.0293]

101.

Appojabhojanavikatiṃ pabhuñjato

Khattiṃsalakkhaṇasiriyā samujjalaṃ,

Kāyo suraddumaruciro’dhimattaka-

Sīmānamaṭṭhikataca māpadhīmato; ()

Pabbānivā asitalanāsva’sitika-

Vallisu unnata’vanatāni seyyathā,

Āsuṃ tathā karacaraṇādikāni’pi

Tassu’nnatonata’vayavāti viggahe; ()

As he partook of food preparations with little essence, the body of the wise one, though shining with the glory of the thirty-two marks and as lovely as a celestial tree, reached the utmost limit of becoming skin and bones. Just as the joints on a black snake or a black creeper are raised and lowered, so too were his hands, feet, and other limbs raised and lowered on his body.

103.

103.

Mokkhesino karabhapadaṃva nissiriṃ

Nimmaṃsa mānisada mahū sirimato;

Tassu’ntatāvanatakapiṭṭhikaṇṭako

Āsi yathāvalayitavaṭṭanāvali; ()

For that glorious seeker of liberation, his feet became like a camel's footprint, devoid of splendor, without flesh and blood. His spine, with its protruding and receding vertebrae, was like a string of threaded beads.

104. [O 0.0294]

104.

Gopāṇasi sithilitabandhanā jara-

Sāḷāya heṭṭhupariṭhite’va dhīmato,

Nimmaṃsalohitakakalebare pya’va-

Bhaggā bhavuṃ pavisamaphāsukāvalī; ()

Just as the rafters of an old hall with loosened bindings stick out unevenly, so for that wise one, in his body devoid of flesh and blood, his row of ribs was broken and protruding.

105.

105.

Appaṃ kubhojanavikatiṃ pabhuñjano

Tassa’kkhikūpagayugalakkhitārakā,

Okkāyikā abhavu magādhagā tadā

Gambhīrakupagadakatārakāka viya; ()

As he ate little, partaking of poor food preparations, the pupils of his eyes, situated in their sockets, became sunken and deep-set, like stars seen at the bottom of a deep well.

106.

106.

Vātātapena’ bhiphusito yathā’maka-

Cchinno’bhisamphuṭani alābu tittako,

Sīsacchavī sukhumachavissa bhojano-

Pacchedanena’bhiphuṭitā ṭhitaṃ tathā; ()

Just as a bitter gourd, cut while raw and scorched by wind and sun, becomes shriveled, so too the skin of his head, of him with delicate skin, stood shriveled due to the cutting off of food.

107. [O 0.0295]

107.

Tassodaracchavi pana piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ

Alliyi so muni malamuttamocako,

Okujjito paripati pūtimūlaka-

Lomāni tabbapugalitāni bhūmiyaṃ; ()

The skin of his belly clung to his very spine. When that sage went to relieve himself, he would fall down headlong. The hairs of his body, their roots decayed, fell out onto the ground.

108.
