108.

So piṭṭhikaṇṭakamavasaṅgapāṇinā

Kucchicchaviṃ phusitumito parāmasi,

So piṭṭhikaṇṭakamavasaṅgapāṇinā

Kucchicchaviṃ phusitumito parāmasi; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

When with his hand he went to touch the skin of his belly, he grasped his spine. When with his hand he went to touch his spine, he grasped the skin of his belly.

109.

109.

Kālonukho varapuriso’ti no tathā

Sāmonukho napi nanumaṅguracchavi,

Āsuṃ tadā kavimatikathāparā narā

Disvā malaggahitamasobhanacchaviṃ; ()

Seeing his unlovely skin covered with dirt, men given to poetic speculation would say: 'Is this excellent person black? No, not so. Is he dark? No, nor is he golden-skinned.'

110. [O 0.0296]

110.

Ye santī sampatī samaṇā’bhavuṃ pure

Attantapā tapasi anāgate siyuṃ,

Te vedanaṃ kaṭukamitodhikaṃ kimu

Vedenti vedayu mabhivedayissare; ()

Whatever ascetics in the past, present, or future have been, are, or will be self-tormentors engaged in austerity—surely they have not felt, do not feel, nor will they feel a pain more bitter than this.

111.

111.

Īhāya dukkarakiriyāyi’māya’pi

Neva’jjhagā yamariyañāṇadassanaṃ,

Attūpatāpanakasirassa kevalaṃ

Bhāgī bhavi anariyamaggagāmiso; ()

Even with this striving and difficult practice, he did not attain that which is noble knowledge and vision. He became merely a partaker of the misery of self-torment, a traveler on the ignoble path.

112.

112.

Saṃsāre sātisāre barataradarathe saṃsaraṃ saccasandho

Khedevedesi devāsiranarasaraṇoesayaṃsattasantiṃ,

Dhīrovīrovaroyopabhavabhavabhayopāpatāpabbipatto

Āyogaṃ yogiyogī parihari hirimāevamevacchavassaṃ; () (Muttāhāra bandhanaṃ)

Wandering in perilous saṃsāra with its great and terrible fears, he, true to his word, experienced misery. A refuge for devas, asuras, and humans, he sought peace for beings. That wise, heroic, and supreme one, free from the fear of becoming and non-becoming, devoid of calamity and affliction, a conscientious yogi devoted to the practice, thus abandoned this vile body.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakala kavijana hakayānandadānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe avidurenidāne mahābodhisattassa mahā padhānānuyogappavattiparidīpo ekādasamosaggo.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, entitled 'A Lamp Illuminating the Course of the Great Bodhisattva's Practice of the Great Exertion,' in the section on the Not-Distant Origin of the Jinavaṃsadīpa, a source of joy for the hearts of all poets, composed by the monk named Medhānanda.

1. [O 0.0298]

1.

Kāmaṃ kāmasukhallikā’nuyogo

Hīno’natthakaro’tya’ne(’karūpaṃ),

Cintetvāna tapovanaṃ vimānā

Tvaṃ siddhatthu’pagamma kāhase kiṃ; ()

Having reflected, 'Indeed, the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasure is low and unbeneficial,' you, Siddhartha, left the palace and approached the ascetic grove—what will you do?

2. [O 0.0299]

2.

Konāma’ntu’patāpanā’nuyutto

Patto hoti sukhappadaṃ kadāci,

Tasmā attu’patāpanā’nuyogo

Hīno’natthakaro’ti cintayassu; ()

What person devoted to self-torment has ever attained a state that gives happiness? Therefore, you should consider: 'The practice of self-torment is low and unbeneficial.'

3.

3.

Attānaṃ sayamevamovaditvā

Piṇḍāyā’nugharaṃ caritva laddhaṃ,

Bhattaṃ bhuttavato sakamhi kāye

Āsuṃ pākatikāni lakkhaṇāni, ()

Having admonished himself in this way, he wandered from house to house for alms. When he had eaten the food he received, the natural marks reappeared on his own body.

4.

4.

Hīnantadvayavajjanena jātu

Ñāṇukkaṃsagatamhi tamhi vīre,

Bodhāyū’pasamāya nibbidāya

Ukkaṭṭhaṃ paṭipattimācarante; ()

That hero, having avoided the two low extremes and reached the height of knowledge, then practiced the supreme path for the sake of awakening, peace, and disenchantment.

5. [O 0.0300]

5.

Chabbassānya’nidukkaraṃ karitvā

Bodhiṃ nājjhagato subhojanāni,

Bhuñjanto kimu kubbate’ padhānā

Vibbhanto iti pañcavaggiyāyaṃ; ()

'For six years he performed extreme austerities and did not attain awakening. Now that he is eating fine food, how will he achieve the goal?' Thinking thus, the group of five monks lost faith in him.

6.

6.

Madaditvā sikataṃ sinehaladdhā

Kevā’suṃ samaṇaṃ hi’maṃ upecca,

Ko mūḷho’dhigamādhigantumicche

Cintetvā migadāyamotariṃsu; ()

Thinking, 'Who would try to get oil by pressing sand? Who now would follow this ascetic? What fool would hope to achieve realization through him?' they departed for the Deer Park.

7.

7.

Senānīnigame tadāni seṭṭhi-

Dhītā sāmikulaṃ alaṅkatā’si,

Bhārenā’vanataṅginī kucānaṃ

Haṃsivā’lasagāminī sujātā; ()

At that time, in the market town of Senānī, the merchant's daughter, Sujātā, was adorned for her husband's family. Her limbs were bowed by the weight of her breasts, and her languid gait was like that of a swan.

8. [O 0.0301]

8.

Jāte patthitapatthanāsamiddhe

Rukkhā’dhiggahitāya devatāya,

Kātuṃ sābalikammaka mānayitvā

Dhenū laṭṭhivanopagā sahassaṃ; ()

Her prayer for a son having been fulfilled by the deity dwelling in the tree, she, in order to make an offering in gratitude, brought a thousand cows to the Laṭṭhivana grove.

9.

9.

Tāsaṃ pañcasatāni duddhakhīraṃ

Pāyetvā katapuna yāvatā’ḍhadhenū,

Khīrānaṃ parivattanaṃ vidhāya

Paccūsamhi dudoha tā’ḍhadhenū; ()

Having fed the milk of five hundred of those cows to another group, and so on in succession, arranging this transfer of milk, at dawn she milked the final choice cows.

10.

10.

Missetvā sayamevava duddhakhīraṃ

Pāyāsaṃ pacituṃ samārabhittha,

Devā tattha sudhārasaṃ khipitvā

Ārakkhādimakaṃsu uddhanasmiṃ; ()

She herself took that milk and began to cook milk-rice. The devas, casting divine nectar therein, placed a guard over the hearth.

11.

11.

Tassā’si himāvācalo’padhānaṃ

Pallaṅko pathavitalaṃ ahū ce,

Hatthā pacchimapubbasāgaresu

Pādā dakkhiṇasāgare bhaviṃsū; ()

For him, the Himālaya mountain was his pillow, and the surface of the earth was his couch. His hands lay in the western and eastern oceans, and his feet in the southern ocean.

12. [O 0.0302]

12.

Uggantvā tiṇajāti nāhirandhā

Tassā’hacca ṭhitā nabhaṃ asesaṃ,

Chādesuṃ caraṇuṭṭhitā’ssa kaṇha-

Sīsā’jānuyugā’pya’kaṇhakīṭā; ()

A species of grass, growing from his navel, stood reaching to the very sky. And white worms with black heads, arising from his feet, crept up and covered him to his knees.

13.

13.

Cattāro sakuṇā catuddisāhi

Patvā tappadapañjaraṃ vivaṇṇā,

Setā’suṃ puthumīḷhapabbatassa

Sīse caṅkami so alimpamāno; ()

Four birds of various colors from the four directions, having approached his feet, became white. He walked upon the summit of a vast mountain of filth without being soiled.

14.

14.

Iccevaṃ sumati’ṭṭhapākadāni

Passitvā supināni pañca niṭṭhaṃ,

Patto ajja bhavāmahanti buddho

Nigrodhaṃ samupecca sannisīdi; ()

Thus the wise one, having seen these five dreams and reached a firm conclusion, thinking, 'Today I shall surely become a Buddha!', approached the Banyan tree and sat down.

15. [O 0.0303]

15.

Sodhetaṃ sahitā tu puṇṇadāsī

Paccūse vaṭamūlapubbasele,

Taṃ lokekaraviṃ virājamānaṃ

Disvā’voca sujātametamatthaṃ; ()

At dawn, at the foot of the banyan tree on the eastern hill, Sujātā, together with the maid Puṇṇā, saw him shining brightly, the one sun of the world, and spoke these words:

16.

16.

Lakkhagghaṃ haripātimāharitvā

Sā āvajjayi pakkabhājanaṃ so,

Pāyāso vinivaṭṭito ṭhito’si

Tāyaṃ pokkharapattatova’toyaṃ; ()

Having brought a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, she presented the cooked food to him. The milk-rice, when poured out, stood firm, just like water on a lotus leaf.

17.

17.

Sā aññāya suvaṇṇapātiyā taṃ

Chādetvā muditā pasantacittā

Gantvā maṇḍana maṇḍitā sasīse

Katvā pūjayi bhojanaṃ sujātā; ()

She, understanding, joyful and with a serene mind, having covered the meal with the golden bowl, went forth. Adorned with ornaments, and having placed it upon her head, Sujātā respectfully offered the food.

18.

18.

Kālaṃ ettakamevabodhisattaṃ

Nātikkamma vidhātudinnapatto,

Sampatto’si adassanaṃ tato taṃ

Pātiṃ soṇṇamayaṃ paṭiggahetvā; ()

The Bodhisatta did not transgress that very moment in time; the bowl given by the Creator vanished, and thereupon he accepted that golden bowl.

19. [O 0.0304]

19.

Haṃsālimalinīkatāravinda-

Reṇucchannasunīlanīrapurā,

Yā nerañjaravissutā’si tāya

Najjātīramagañji sattasāro; ()

The hero of beings went to the bank of that river famed as the Nerañjarā, which was full of deep blue water, with lotuses covered in pollen and frequented by swans and bees.

20.

20.

Pāyāsāmisapuṇṇasoṇṇapātiṃ

Kāsāvāni jinaṅkuro ṭhapetvā,

Tīre tāya savantiyā nahātuṃ

Titthaṃ gandhagajorivo’tarittha; ()

The future Buddha, having set aside the golden bowl filled with milk-rice and his saffron robes on the bank of that flowing river, descended to the bathing-place to bathe, like a fragrant elephant.

21.

21.

Rolambākulanīlanīrajehi

Sevālehi nadījalaṃ sunilaṃ,

Nikkhantajjutisañcayehi dehā

Otiṇṇassa jagāma piñjarattaṃ; ()

The river's water, deeply blue with dark blue lotuses agitated by bees and with algae, became tawny from the mass of radiance emitted from his body as he descended into it.

22. [O 0.0305]

22.

Gaṅgākāmini kañjareṇugandha-

Cuṇṇaṃ tuṅgataraṅgabāhunā taṃ,

Bhattāraṃ salilena sītalena

Makkhetvāsunahāpayantī’vā’si; ()

The river maiden, with her arms of towering waves, anointed that Lord with the fragrant powder of lotus pollen and with cool water, as if bathing him well.

23.

23.

Tulyaṃ tabbadanambujena laddhuṃ

Āyantaṃ raviraṃsisaṅgamena,

Haṃsasseṇi sarojakosarāsiṃ

Saṃdūsesi āvāriyo hi pāko; ()

The flock of swans disturbed the mass of lotus buds, which sought to become equal to his lotus-face by receiving the union of the approaching sun's rays; for their budding state was indeed an obstruction.

24.

24.

Tīre sārasacakkavākapakkhī

Sosāya’ssavisāritaṃ’sapakkhā,

Gambhīrambhasi mattamāhariṃsu

Maññe nikkaruṇāya ettakantī; ()

On the shore, cranes, ruddy geese, and other birds, with wings spread wide to dry, drank their fill from the deep water, as if, I think, to diminish his compassion.

25. [O 0.0306]

25.

Tuṇḍe maṇḍitapuṇḍarīkadaṇḍo

Pakkhe keravapaṇḍare pasārī,

Nāthassu’bbahi mattahaṃsarājā

Setacchattavibhutimuttamaṅge; ()

With the stalk of an adorned white lotus in its beak, and having spread its wings, white like water-lilies, the king of intoxicated swans held aloft the glory of a white parasol over the Lord's supreme head.

26.

26.

Vattamhojapalobhitālicakkaṃ

Cakkhavāpāthagataṃ jinaṅkurassa,

Saṃdassesi padhānabhuṭhitassa

Nilasmiṃ kasiṇamhi bhūtibhāraṃ; ()

A swarm of bees, enticed by a round lotus, entered the future Buddha's field of vision. To him, who had arisen for the great exertion, it appeared as a heap of ashes upon a blue kasiṇa.

27.

27.

Veyyāvaccakarārivāpagāyaṃ

Sevālādimalāpanena mīnā,

Pādañcandagamīnalakkhaṇassa

Tassa’gge vimalikariṃsu vāriṃ; ()

The fish in the river, as if performing a service, by removing the dirt of moss and the like, purified the water before his foot, which bore the auspicious marks of the moon and the fish.

28. [O 0.0307]

28.

Uttiṇṇassa visālasāḷasākhī-

Sākhāhatthapuṭehi puñknāya,

Gattaṃ mandasugandhagandhavāha-

Vatthaṃ sāḷavanaṅganā adāsi; ()

To him who had emerged from the water, the nymphs of the Sāla forest, with their cupped hands of branches from the broad Sāla trees, gave a garment wafted by a gentle, fragrant breeze to wipe his limbs.

29.

29.

Lokindo parimaṇḍalaṃ nivattho

Chādetvāna timaṇḍala’ntariyaṃ,

Bandhitvopari kāyabandhanampi

Kāsāvaṃ paridhāyi paṃsukūlaṃ; ()

The Lord of the World, dressing in a perfectly even manner, having covered the three circles with the under-robe, and having also tied the waistband above, donned the ochre robe, a cast-off cloth.

30.

30.

Pāyāsassa nirūdakassa ūna-

Paññāsappamite vidhāya piṇḍe,

Pācīnābhimukho nisajja najjā

Tīre tāya akāsi bhattakiccaṃ; ()

Having made forty-nine morsels of the milk-rice which was prepared without water, he sat facing the east on the bank of that river and partook of his meal.

31. [O 0.0308]

31.

Pāyāso madhuro’yamassa satta-

Sattāhaṃ paṭividdhabodhino hi,

Ojāsamapharaṇāya ṭhānamāsi

Tasmā so pavihāsi nibbihesaṃ; ()

Indeed, this sweet milk-rice was the basis for the spreading of vigor for him who was to penetrate enlightenment, sustaining him for seven weeks. Therefore, he dwelt without needing anything further.

32.

32.

Bujjheyyaṃ yadi bodhimajja sohaṃ

Uddhaṃsotamayaṃ suvaṇṇapāti,

Gaṅgāyaṃ khipaki gacchatūti vatvā

Dhīmā dakkhiṇahatthagaṃ tamagghaṃ; ()

The wise one, having said, 'If I am to awaken to enlightenment today, let this golden bowl go upstream!', cast that precious bowl, held in his right hand, into the river.

33.

33.

Sotaṃ bhindiya sā savantimajjhe

Ṭhatvā pāti yato asītihatthaṃ,

Uddhaṃsotamupecca sannimujji

Tasmā so’pi nimujji pītinajjaṃ; ()

That bowl, having split the current, stood in the middle of the river. From there, having gone eighty cubits upstream, it sank completely. Therefore, he too sank into the river of joy.

34.

34.

Nāgānaṃ bhavanaṃ upecca tiṇṇaṃ

Buddhānaṃ panimamhi bhaddakappe,

Sāpātiparibhuttasoṇṇapāti

Ghaṭṭetvāna ṭhitā katānurāvā; ()

Having reached the abode of the Nāgas, that bowl struck the golden bowls used by the three previous Buddhas of this fortunate eon, and came to rest, making a reverberating sound.

35.

35.

Taṃ dīghāyukakālanāgarājā

Sutvā saddamathajjape’kabuddho,

Uppannoti jinaṃ abhitthavanto

Aṭṭhāsi thutigītikāsatehi; ()

Hearing that sound, the long-lived Kāla, king of the Nāgas, praised the Victor, saying, 'Today another Buddha has arisen!', and stood extolling him with hundreds of songs of praise.

36.

36.

Chāyābaddhavisālasāḷasālaṃ

Patvāsāḷavanaṃ nadīsamīpe,

Ājīvaṭṭhamasīlasaṃvarena

Ādoyeva visuddhakāyavāco; ()

Having reached the Sāla grove near the river, a place of broad Sāla trees providing deep shade, he, who from the very beginning was pure in body and speech through the restraint of the morality ending in right livelihood, spent the day there.

37.

37.

Katvāṭṭhārasapiṭṭhikaṇṭakānaṃ

Koṭīnaṃpaṭipādanaṃ kamena,

Pallaṅkassanisajjabandhanena

Kammaṭṭhānasatiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā; ()

Having step by step subdued eighteen crores of thorny hindrances, and having established mindfulness on the meditation subject by binding himself in the cross-legged posture,

38. [O 0.0310]

38.

Ānāpānasatiṃpariggahetvā

Nibbattesimalaggahītapubbe,

Rūpārūpasamādhayo’ṭṭhapañcā-

Bhiññāyo vasitāca so vasīso ()

he, the master, having taken up mindfulness of breathing, brought into being what had not been grasped before: the eight form and formless absorptions, the five higher knowledges, and the masteries.

39.

39.

Jhānassādarato divāvihāraṃ

Katvā sāḷavane surāsurehi,

Dhīro maggamalaṅkataṃ karīva

Gantuṃ otariyatrabodhimūlaṃ; ()

Delighting in jhāna, having thus spent the day in the Sāla forest honored by devas and asuras, the steadfast one set out for the foot of the Bodhi tree, like an elephant adorned for the path.

40.

40.

Lājādīkusumehivippakiṇṇo

Muttāpaṇḍaravāḷukātthato so,

Maggo tuṅgataraṅga bhaṅgahāri

Lakkhīvāsapayodadhīri’vā’si; ()

That path, strewn with roasted grain and other flowers, and spread with pearls and white sand, was like the ocean, the abode of Lakkhī, charming with the breaking of its high waves.

41. [O 0.0311]

41.

Majjhā’ropitapaṅkajābhirāmaṃ

Muttādāmasamākulaṃ samantā,

Kaṇṇolambasuvaṇṇaghaṇṭamassa

Deṭā dibbavitāna mukkhipiṃsu; ()

The deities raised a divine canopy for him, beautiful with lotuses placed in its center, adorned all around with pearl garlands, and with golden bells hanging from its corners.

42.

42.

Lokatthaṃ karaṇāya coditasmiṃ

Tasmiṃ lokadivākare’kavīre,

Gacchante sahajātabodhimūlaṃ

Āloko udapādi sabbaloke; ()

As that sun of the world, the unequalled hero, urged to act for the welfare of the world, proceeded toward the foot of the co-nascent Bodhi tree, a light arose throughout all the worlds.

43.

43.

Āyantaṃ tiṇhārako pathamhi

Disvā sotthiyanāmabhūsuro taṃ,

Pādāsi tiṇamuṭṭhiyo’ṭṭhamattā

Nātho tāni tiṇāni sampaṭicchi; ()

Seeing him coming on the path, the grass-carrier, a brahmin named Sotthiya, offered him eight handfuls of grass. The Lord accepted those grasses.

44. [O 0.0312]

44.

Vattatte varapāṭihāriyamhi

Magge gandhagajo’ca jamhamāno,

Sampatto karuṇākalattabhattā

Sambodhādhigamāya bodhimūlaṃ; ()

While the excellent miracle was proceeding on the path, the fragrant elephant, as it were, stretching, he whose spouse is compassion, arrived at the foot of the Bodhi tree to attain supreme enlightenment.

45.

45.

Tassosīdaṭhitaṃ’va cakkavāḷaṃ

Heṭṭhā dakkhiṇato’ttarānanassa,

Paññāyu’ttaracakkavāḷamuddhaṃ

Laṅghitvānaṭhitaṃ’va ābhavaggaṃ; ()

When he stood on the southern side, facing north, the world-sphere below sank down. Then, on the northern side, the world-sphere above rose up, as if leaping to the very peak of existence.

46.

46.

Evaṃ pacchimamuttaraṃ disampi

Aṭṭhānanti padakkhiṇaṃ karonto,

Gantvā ṭhānavaraṃ puratthimasmiṃ

Aṭṭhāsi vasi pacchimānano so; ()

Thus, considering the western and northern directions also as unsuitable places, he circumambulated them. Then, having gone to the excellent spot in the east, he stood there, facing west.

47. [O 0.0313]

47.

Dhīmā dakkhiṇapāṇipallavena

Agge tāni tiṇāni sattharī so,

Tamhā cuddasahatthamuppatitvā

Pallaṅko samalaṅkarī dumindaṃ; ()

The wise one, with his right hand, tender as a shoot, scattered those grasses by their tips. Thereupon, a throne fourteen cubits high arose and adorned the lord of trees.

48.

48.

Dakkho kārupavīṇacittakāro

Kātuṃ vā’likhituṃ yathānasakkā,

Aṭṭhaṃsu haritāni santhatāni

Evaṃ tāni tiṇāni uppatitvā; ()

Those grasses, having sprung up, were so green and well-spread that not even a skilled craftsman or painter would be able to create or depict them.

49.

49.

Maṃsādī upasussare nahārū

Aṭṭhīcepyavasissare sarīre;

Muñceyyaṃ caturāsavehi yāva

Bhindissāmi natāvimaṃ ahanti; ()

‘Let my flesh and sinews dry up, and let only bones remain in my body; until I am freed from the four taints, I shall not break this posture.’

50. [O 0.0314]

50.

Daḷhaṃ cintiya daḷhamānaso so

Pācīnābhimukho dumindabandhaṃ;

Katvā piṭṭhigataṃ nisīdi bodhi-

Pallaṅkamhi yugandhare ravī’va; ()

Having resolved firmly, steadfast in mind, he sat facing east, with the trunk of the lord of trees at his back, upon the seat of enlightenment, like the sun upon the Yugandhara mountain.

51.

51.

Lokeso sasimaṇḍalāvabhāsaṃ

Setacchattamadhārayī tadaññe,

Suddhāvāsatalaṭṭhadevatā taṃ

Pūjesuṃ makuṭappitañjalīhi; ()

A world-lord held a white parasol, radiant as the orb of the moon. Then other deities, standing on the Suddhāvāsa plane, worshipped him with hands joined in reverence upon their crowns.

52.

52.

Ye rūpāvacare vasanti devā

Te ca’ññatra asaññasattadeve,

Sampatvā vajirāsane nisinnaṃ

Pūjesuṃ kusumākulañjalīhi ()

Those gods who dwell in the Form Realm, except for the non-percipient beings, having arrived, worshipped him seated on the adamantine seat with their hands full of flowers.

53. [O 0.0315]

53.

Ekacce paranimmitādilokā

Patvā bhattibharā’marā mahiṃsu,

Pūjābhaṇḍasamābhikiṇṇahatthā

Mārāriṃ tahimāpa pāpimā kiṃ; ()

Some gods from the Paranimmita and other realms, their hands laden with articles of worship, arrived and, filled with devotion, honored the Foe of Māra. The Evil One also arrived there. What then?

54.

54.

Ye nimmāṇaratimhi nijjarā te;

Patvā gandhakaraṇḍamaṇḍalehi,

Sampūjesumalaṅkataṅghipīṭhaṃ

Naṃ seṭṭhaṃ vijayāsanopaviṭṭhaṃ; ()

Those gods who delight in creation, the ageless ones, arrived with circles of fragrant caskets and worshipped the supreme One, seated on the seat of victory, and his well-adorned footstool.

55.

55.

Aṭṭhāsi tusitālayā saseno

Patvā santusitavhadevarājā,

Vijento harimora piñchapuñja-

Sobhaṃ kañcanatālavaṇṭapantiṃ; ()

Santusita, the king of gods, having come from the Tusita abode with his army, stood waving a row of golden palm-leaf fans, splendid as a mass of green peacock feathers.

56.

56.

Patvā yāmasurālayā saseno

Saṃvijesi suyāma devarājā,

Dhīraṃ soṇṇapaṇāḷikānipāta-

Dhārāsannibhacārucāmarehi; ()

Suyāma, the king of gods, having come from the abode of the Yāma gods with his army, fanned the steadfast One with beautiful yak-tail whisks that resembled streams of water pouring from golden gutters.

57. [O 0.0316]

57.

Devindo vijayuttarākhyasaṅkhaṃ

Vīsaṃ hatthasataṃ dhamītadaññe,

Pūjesuṃ tamupecca koviḷāra-

Pupphādīhi ca tāvatiṃsadevā; ()

Devinda blew the conch named Vijayuttara, two thousand hands in measure. Then other Tāvatiṃsa gods, having approached, worshipped him with Koviḷāra flowers and so forth.

58.

58.

Yakkhādīhi purakkhatā’pi deva-

Rājāno caturo catuddisāsu,

Rakkhaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu devalokā

Taṃ patvāna vinaṭṭhalomahaṭṭhaṃ; ()

The four great kings in the four directions, though attended by yakkhas and others, and the gods from the heavenly worlds, having approached him with their hair standing on end in awe, arranged for his protection.

59.

59.

Vādento saramaṇḍalaṃ vidhāya

Vīṇaṃ pañcasikho’pi beḷuvākhyaṃ,

Taṃ sampūjayi kālanāgarājā

Thomento thutigītikāsatehi; ()

Pañcasikha also, playing the lute named Beḷuvapandavī, having arranged the full range of tones, and the Nāga king Kāla, worshipped him, praising him with hundreds of hymns and songs.

60. [O 0.0317]

60.

Evaṃ kāhaḷabherisaṅkhavīṇā-

Ghaṇṭāvījanichattacāmarehi,

Naccādīhicalājapañcamehi

Dīpaddhupadhajehi mānayuṃ taṃ; ()

Thus they honored him with trumpets, drums, conches, lutes, and bells; with fans, parasols, and whisks; with dances and other performances, with offerings of which roasted grain is the fifth, and with lamps, incense, and banners.

61.

61.

Siddhattho paṭisiddhamāradheyyo

Kattuṃ attavase sadevalokaṃ,

Sutvā vāyamatīti bodhimaṇḍe

Māro tatra samārabhitthagantuṃ; ()

Māra, hearing that Siddhattha—he who had overcome Māra's dominion—was striving at the Bodhi-maṇḍa to bring the world with its gods under his control, resolved to go there.

62.

62.

Tasmiṃ kho samaye bhayāvahāni

Mārasso’taraṇāya kāraṇāni,

Cakkhacāpāthagatāni dunnimitta-

Rūpādīni tilokalocanassa; ()

At that very moment, terrifying portents giving Māra his opportunity—ill-omened sights and the like—came into the range of vision of the Eye of the Three Worlds.

63. [O 0.0318]

63.

Sukkha’mhodhararāvabherirāva-

Vipphārābadhirīkatambarampi,

Bhīmaṃ vijjulatā’sighaṭṭaṇehi

Mārassā’havambḍalābhamāha; ()

The sky itself was deafened by the widespread roar of war-drums and the thunder of dry clouds; with the fierce clashing of lightning-swords, it proclaimed the coming of Māra's battle.

64.

64.

Mārassā’gamanañjase rajova

Vājīnaṃ khuraghaṭṭaṇena jāto,

Ukkāpātasataṃ janesi tassa

Cakkhavāniṭṭhaphakhalaṃ disāsu ḍāho; ()

Dust, born from the striking of horses' hooves, was like Māra's direct approach. A hundred meteors fell, and a burning in all directions was produced—an unwelcome sight for his eye.

65.

65.

Vehāse vicaruṃ kabandharūpā

Kākolā balipuṭṭhavāyasārī,

Unnādiṃsu kharānilo pavāyī

Abbhuṭṭhāsi rajo disāsu dhūmo; ()

Headless forms roamed in the sky. Crows, ravens, and vultures shrieked. A harsh wind blew. Dust and smoke arose in all directions.

66.

66.

Āloko vigato ghaṇandhakāro

Otiṇṇo mahikāsamābhikiṇṇo,

Ākāso pathavi bhūsaṃ pakampi

Meghacchannadinaṃ dinaṃ babhūva; ()

Light vanished; a thick darkness, overspread with mist, descended. The sky and the earth quaked violently. The day became as if covered by clouds.

67. [O 0.0319]

67.

Siddhatthañhi asiddhamatthametaṃ

Kātuṃ assavamārakiṅkarāme,

Vatve’thā’ti pajāpatī saseno

Tattheva’ntaradhāyi tāvadeva; ()

Then the great god Pajāpati, with his army, vanished at that very moment, as Māra and his tainted minions came to render Siddhattha's purpose unachieved.

68.

68.

Sā setā purato pajāpatissa

Āsī bārasayojanaṃ vinaddhā,

Evaṃ dakkhiṇavāmano ca loka-

Dhātvantāvadhīmāsi pacchato’pi; ()

That army of Pajāpati Māra extended twelve yojanas before him. Likewise, to his right and left, and also behind him, it stretched to the very edge of the world-sphere.

69.

69.

Uddhaṃ sā navayojanappamāṇā

Saddo bhūmividāraṇori’vā si,

So’paḍḍhaṃ satayojanaṃ babhūva

Uccaṃ so girimekhalo gajindo; ()

In height, the army was nine yojanas. Its sound was like the earth splitting apart. And the elephant-king Girimekhala was one hundred and fifty yojanas high.

70. [O 0.0320]

70.

Nāhesuṃ parisāsu nimmitāsuṃ

Dveyodhā sadisāyudhādadhānā,

Tabyāsena alañhi lomahaṃso

Yassā’nussaraṇena ce siyā me; ()

In those magically created assemblies, no two warriors bore similar weapons. The terror was such that the mere recollection of it would be enough to make one's hair stand on end.

71.

71.

Māpetvā sahasā sahassabāhuṃ

Gaṇhitvā vividhāyudhāni tehi,

Ārūḷho girimekhalaṃ saseno

Māro pāturahosi baddhavero; ()

Having instantly created a thousand arms and seizing various weapons with them, Māra, harboring intense animosity, mounted Girimekhala with his army and appeared.

72.

72.

Deveso yasasā samaṃ sakena

Setacchatta magañchi saṃharitvā,

Deveso yasasā samaṃ sakena

Saṅakkhaṃ piṭṭhigataṃ vidhāya dhāvī; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

The lord of gods, his glory departing with him, folded his white parasol and went away. The other lord of gods, his glory departing with him, placed the conch upon his back and fled.

73. [O 0.0321]

73.

Saṅkocā’nanakāhalo jagāma

Pātālaṃ khalu kālanāgarājā,

Vīṇādoṇisakho sakhānapekho

Tamhā pañcasikho kalahuṃ palāyi; ()

Indeed, King Kālanāga, with his hood withdrawn and without clamor, went to Pātāla. Pañcasikha, with his lute as his companion, heedless of his friends, fled from that quarrel.

74.

74.

Disvā mārabalaṃ samosarantaṃ

Sampattā janatā palāyi bhītā,

Sosīho’va vihāsi sakyasīho

Eko kamārakarindakumhabhedī; ()

Seeing Māra’s army advancing, the assembled people fled in terror, but the Sakyan Lion remained alone, like a lion, breaking the forehead of the elephant of craving.

75.

75.

Passitvā’dharakantibhāramassa

Vattamhoruha mindirāvihāraṃ,

Siddhatthena samo nacatthi loke

Iccevaṃ kalimā’ha mārasenaṃ; ()

Beholding the abundant radiance of his lower lip and his lotus-like face, the abode of splendor, Kali Māra thus spoke to his army: 'In this world, there is none equal to Siddhattha.'

76. [O 0.0322]

76.

Etasasā’bhimukhā mayaṃ kadāci

Nosakkoma’bhiyujjhitunti tātā,

Vatvā uttarapassato samāro

Khandhāvāramabandhi baddhavero;

'My dears, we are by no means able to stand face to face against such a one, nor to engage him in battle.' Having spoken thus, Māra, harboring animosity, established his camp on the northern side.

77.

77.

Disvā’jjhottharamānamārasenaṃ

Ārakkhāvaraṇaṃ thiraṃ vidhāya,

Khandhāvāramabandhi sopi vīro

Jetuṃ taṃ dasapāramī bhaṭehi; ()

Seeing Māra’s army surging forward, that hero, establishing a firm protective defense, also arrayed his camp to conquer him with the warriors of the ten perfections.

78.

78.

Māro bhudharamerucakkavāḷe

Rukkhādīni vicuṇṇituṃ samatthaṃ,

Khobhetvā bhuvanattayaṃ disāsu

Uṭṭhāpesi samīraṇaṃ sughoraṃ; ()

Māra, capable of crushing mountains, Meru, the world-systems, trees, and so forth, stirred up the three worlds, raising a most dreadful wind in all directions.

79.

79.

Vāto pāramidhāmavārito so

Nittejaṃ palayānilassamopi,

Patto cāmaramandamārutova

Tandehotuparissamaṃ jahāsi; ()

But that wind, warded off by the power of the perfections, though it was like the wind of destruction, lost its fierceness and, having become like a gentle breeze from a fan, dispelled the body's weariness.

80. [O 0.0323]

80.

Dhārāvegavihinnabhūmibhāgaṃ

Gambhīrā’sanirāvanibbharā’ghaṃ,

Māro māpayi tuṅgavīcabhaṅgaṃ

Vassoghaṃ paripātarukkhaselaṃ; ()

Māra caused a torrential downpour with a stream-force that shattered parts of the earth, filling the deep abyss with the roar of thunder, with high waves, felling trees and rocks.

81.

81.

Vīro pāramipāḷibandhanena

Rakkhaṃ bandhi nijantabhāvakhette,

Teno’gho vipathaṅgamo vipakkha-

Senāyā’si pavāhaṇe nidānaṃ; ()

The hero, by the binding of the array of perfections, bound protection in his inner realm; thereby that flood, going astray, became the cause for the hostile army's being swept away.

82.

82.

Tejokhaṇḍasamānamattano so

Tattaṃ pajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ,

Māpetvo’palavassamappasayhaṃ

Jhāpetuṃ tamupakkamittha māro; ()

Māra, himself like a blazing mass of fire, hot, burning, full of light, having created an irresistible rain of stones, attempted to scorch him.

83. [O 0.0324]

83.

Mārasseva patantamuttamaṅge

Ghoraṃ pāramivāyuvegaruddhaṃ,

Taṃvassaṃ vajirāsanūpacāre

Pūjāpupphaguḷattanaṃ jagāma; ()

That fierce rain, as if falling on Māra's own supreme head, stemmed by the force of the wind of perfections, in the vicinity of the adamantine seat, became a heap of offering flowers.

84.

84.

Assaddho visadiddhatiṇhadhāraṃ

Ādittaṃ pihitambaro’daraṃ so,

Māpesi asisattitomarādi-

Vassaṃ sabbadisānipātamānaṃ; ()

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakala kavakijana hadayānandadānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe avidūre nidāne devaputta mārabala viddhaṃsana pavattiparidīpo dvādasamo saggo.

Thus, in the Jinavaṃsadīpa, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which is a source of delight for the hearts of all poets, in the introductory section, the twelfth chapter, called 'The Lamp illuminating the Story of the Destruction of the Army of Māra, the Son of a God,' is completed.

42.

Karatalamburuhoparicakkhumā

Yathārivā’malakībadarīphalaṃ,

Cutupapattigatepi tathāgate

Tibhuvanamhi yathicchita maddasa; ()

Just as one with eyes sees an emblic myrobalan or a jujube fruit upon the lotus of his palm, so he saw, as he wished, those beings thus-gone to death and rebirth in the three worlds.

43.

43.

Navupapātakhaṇeca cutikkhaṇe

Visayabhāvamupenti tathāgatā,

Tadupacāravaseni’hadassanaṃ

Khamati aṭṭhakathācariyāsabho; ()

At the moment of new arising and at the moment of death, beings come into the state of being an object. The bull among commentary teachers approves of the seeing here by means of proximity to that.

44. [O 0.0345]

44.

Upadhihīna’dhihanīnatathāgate

Anapanītapaṇīta tathāgate,

Anabhirūpa’bhirūpatathāgate

Sugati duggati dugga mupāgate; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ;)

He saw beings inferior due to clinging, and beings superior and inferior; beings base and excellent; beings ugly and beautiful; beings who had gone to good destinations, bad destinations, and difficult places.

45.

45.

Tiriyamuddhamadhopatitīya so

Matipahaṃ abhipassi yathārahaṃ,

Nicitakammapatheca tathāgate

Upari pādakajhānasamuṭṭhito; ()

Having arisen from the jhāna based upon the soles of the feet, he, with extensive wisdom, clearly saw as it truly is—across, upwards, and downwards—beings on the path of their accumulated kamma.

46.

46.

Akusalāni kariṃsu ime tidhā

Sucaritāni kariṃsu tidhā ime,

Ariyamaggaphalehika samaṅgino

Nasamaṇā’tipi antimavatthunā; ()

‘These have done unwholesome deeds in three ways; these have done good conduct in three ways. These are endowed with the fruits of the Noble Path; and these, by their final state, are not true recluses.’

47.

47.

Guṇanirākaraṇena asādhavo

Upavadiṃsu nasanti guṇā’ti’me,

Apicasappurisā’riyapuggale

Tadanurūpaguṇehi pasaṃsayuṃ; ()

By rejecting virtue, the ignoble reviled them, saying, ‘These virtues do not exist.’ Moreover, the good people praised the noble individuals with virtues befitting them.

48.

48.

Vitathaladdhiparāmasanā ime

Paramaladdhiparāmasanā ime,

Gahitaladdhivasena tahiṃtahiṃ

Nicitakammapathā janatā ayaṃ; ()

These are attached to false views; these are attached to the supreme view. By the power of the views they have grasped, this populace proceeds here and there on the path of accumulated kamma.

49.

49.

Caturapāyamapāyamapāyatiṃ

Upagatā sugati sugatiṃiti,

Yati samāhitavāhitavā’ ddasa

Animisakkhisamakkhisamanvito; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

‘The four woeful states, the woeful state, the future woeful state; having gone to a good destination, to a good destination’—thus the ascetic, composed and acting for others' welfare, saw, endowed with an unblinking eye that sees directly.

50. [O 0.0347]

50.

Sammāsammasatosato satimato kammādihetubbhavaṃ

Rūpārūpamanāgataṅni mahā mohandhakāro dhiyā,

Abbhatthaṅgami yāya soḷasavidhā kaṅkhācatekālikā

Sākaṅkhātaraṇabbisuddhu dutiyeyāme pavattā mati; ()

For him who was rightly considering, being mindful, the arising from causes such as kamma concerning the form, formless, and future realms, the great darkness of delusion was dispelled by wisdom. By this wisdom the sixteen kinds of doubt pertaining to the three times were overcome. That wisdom, the Purification of Overcoming Doubt, arose in the second watch.

Iti medhānandābhidhānenayatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānandadānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe avidure nidāne pubbenivāsañāṇadibbacakkhuñāṇādhigama pavattiparidīpo terasamo saggo.

Thus, in the Jinavaṃsa Dīpa, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, which is a source of giving joy to the hearts of all poets, this is the thirteenth chapter, 'A Light on the Account of the Attainment of the Knowledge of Previous Lives and the Divine Eye,' in the section on the near-past.

1. [O 0.0348]

1.

Sudhākare vikasitakeravākare

Kamenu’ pāsati sati pacchimaṃ disaṃ,

Vihāvarī sasirucirānanaṃ jinaṃ

Bhajanti pacchimamathayāma motari; ()

While the moon, a mine of blossomed white water lilies, was gradually approaching the western direction, then the final watch descended. They attended upon the Victor, whose face was as beautiful as the moon.

2.

2.

Khaṇaṃ nisāpati virahātureva’yaṃ

Nisāvadhū malinapayodharambarā,

Catuddisāyatanayanehi sampati

Mumoca sīkaranikarassubindavo; ()

For a moment, this night-bride, as if distressed by separation from the lord of the night, her cloud-garment grown dark, now released from her eyes, the spheres of the four directions, tear-drops that were a mass of fine dew.

3.

3.

Kilesanāsanapasuto samādhinā

Puthujjano tadanusayaṃ yathubbahe,

Tathaṃ’sunā bhuvanakalaṅkasodhano

Nahe kalānidhi sakalaṅka mubbahī; ()

Just as an ordinary person, devoted through concentration to the destruction of defilements, might remove their underlying tendencies, so the moon—the treasure of digits, the purifier of the world's stain with its rays—did not, indeed, remove its own stain.

4. [O 0.0349]

4.

Puratthime nabhasi vikiṇṇa tārakā-

Pabandhanibbharatimiraṃ viyākarī

Nisāvadhu valayitahārabhāsura-

Sunīlakomalanavakuntalassiriṃ; ()

In the eastern sky, the dawn made manifest the beauty of the night-bride's soft, new, dark-blue tresses, radiant with encircling garlands—a beauty that was the dense darkness interspersed with a sequence of scattered stars.

5.

5.

Vipassanābalavimalīkatantaro

Jinaṅkuro duritamalaṃva candimā,

Maricisañcayadhavalīkatambaro

Tamocayaṃ tamanucaraṃ nirākarī; ()

The scion of the Conqueror, his inner nature purified by the power of insight, dispelled the mass of darkness and its followers, just as the moon, whose garment is whitened by a collection of its rays, dispels the stain of darkness.

6.

6.

Pavāyi sītalamalayānilo bhusaṃ

Disaṅganā sisiratusārabindavo,

Mumoca sā vicari nisā nisākara-

Marīcimañjariparicumbite bhuvi; ()

The cool Malaya breeze blew strongly. The maidens of the directions released cool dewdrops. That night wandered upon the earth, kissed by the clusters of rays from the moon.

7. [O 0.0350]

7.

Niraṅgaṇe nirupakilesa niccale

Mudumhi kammaniyavisuddhibhāvage,

Samāhite manasi vipassanāmanaṃ

Athāsavakkhayamatiyā’ bhīnīhari; ()

Then, when his mind was concentrated—stainless, undefiled, unmoving, pliant, and having reached the state of workable purity—he directed his insight-mind towards the wisdom of the destruction of the taints.

8.

8.

Sabārasaṅgikabhavacakka majjhagā

Anukkamena’pi paṭilomato sudhī

Vavatthayaṃ yamariyañāṇadassanaṃ

Visuddhiyā visaddhiyā taduccate; ()

That noble knowledge and vision, whereby the wise one thoroughly comprehended the twelve-linked wheel of existence in its forward and reverse order, is declared for the sake of purity and confidence.

9.

9.

Khaṇena yo sarati sahassalocano

Yathāvato dasasatamattha massapi,

Vidhātuno nijacaraṇaṅgulippabhā-

Vibhusitā’khilabhuvanodarassa’pi; ()

He who in a moment remembers, as it truly is, a thousand matters concerning the thousand-eyed one, and even concerning the Creator, by the radiance of whose own toe-nails the entire interior of the world is adorned.

10. [O 0.0351]

10.

Asesanīvaraṇatusārasosino

Samādhisambhava’ khilajhānalābhino,

Jagattayaṃ karabadaraṃ’va dassino

Nayassa kassaci visayatta māgataṃ; ()

Of him who dries up the frost of all hindrances, who attains all jhānas born of concentration, who sees the triple world like a myrobalan fruit on his palm—his path has not come into the domain of anyone.

11.

11.

Adiṭṭha mappaṭi viditaṃ sayaṃpurā

Anuttaraṃtamariyañāṇadassanaṃ,

Imassa gotamasamaṇassa sijjhate

Garūpasevanavirahassa abbhūtaṃ; ()

Unseen, unpenetrated, and never before realized, that unsurpassed noble knowledge and vision is accomplished for this ascetic Gotama—a marvel, for one without the service of a teacher.

12.

12.

Bhavebhave parivitadānapārami-

Balena’hū vijaṭitalobhabandhano,

Samettikhantyanugatasīlapāramī-

Jalena nibbutapaṭighādipāvako; ()

In existence after existence, by the strength of the perfection of generosity thoroughly practiced, he became one who had disentangled the bonds of greed; by the water of the perfection of virtue, accompanied by loving-kindness and patience, he extinguished the fire of aversion and the like.

13. [O 0.0352]

13.

Bhavebhave bhavi thirañāṇapāramī-

Padhaṃsitā’khilaviparītadassano,

Vināyakappabhuti garūpasevana-

Vasena pucchiya hatamohasaṃsayo; ()

In existence after existence, by the firm perfection of wisdom, he destroyed all wrong views; through the service of teachers, beginning with the Leader, he questioned and destroyed delusion and doubt.

14.

14.

Bhavebhave budhajanapujanādinā

Garūbhivādanabahumānanādinā,

Janāpacāyanavidhinā vinodayi

Sadappa munnati mabhimāna muddhaṭaṃ; ()

In existence after existence, by honoring the wise and so on, by revering teachers with homage and great esteem, and by the practice of deference, he dispelled pride, haughtiness, conceit, and arrogance.

15.

15.

Bhavebhave vibhavaratiṃ ratiṃbhave

Anaṅgasaṅgamarati maṅganāratiṃ,

Gharā’bhinikkhamiya’nagāriyaṃrato

Apānudī paṭilabhi jhāna mattanā; ()

In existence after existence, having gone forth from home and delighting in the homeless life, he drove away delight in non-existence, delight in existence, delight in sensual union, and delight in women; and by himself, he attained jhāna.

16. [O 0.0353]

16.

Bhavebhave sa’vīriya saccapāramī-

Parāyaṇo adhikusalesu cāratiṃ,

Jahaṃ vacīduritamalaṃ catubbidhaṃ

Visodhayī nijahadayañca paggahī; ()

In existence after existence, being energetic and devoted to the perfection of truth, delighting in higher wholesome states, and abandoning the fourfold stain of verbal misconduct, he purified his own heart and exerted it.

17.

17.

Bhave bhave iti samatiṃsapāramī-

Visujjhitā’ kusalamanomalimaso,

Kamena indriya paripākataṃ gato

Nacaññasampada mahipatthayī sudhī; ()

Thus, in existence after existence, purified by the thirty perfections and cleansed of the stain of the unwholesome mind, he gradually attained the maturity of the faculties, and the wise one did not long for any other accomplishment.

18.

18.

Bhave bhave agaṇitameva bodhiyā

Dayāya coditahadayo’hi kapatthanaṃ,

Akā catubbidhaphalasampadā tato

Padissare niravasarā riva’ntani; ()

In countless existences, his heart urged by compassion, he indeed made the aspiration for awakening. Therefore, the accomplishment of the fourfold fruit shone forth, as dense as the stars in the sky.

19. [O 0.0354]

19.

Bhave bhave sakapaṇidhānasattiyā

Tidhā’hisaṅkhatakusalaṃ imassa bho,

Nasādhaye kimariyañāṇadassanaṃ

Anaññapuggalavisayaṃ nasaṃsayo; ()

In existence after existence, by the power of his own resolve, he performed wholesome actions conditioned in three ways. What noble knowledge and vision could he not accomplish? Without doubt, this is the domain of no other person.

20.

20.

Aniccato’dayavayatāya dukkhato

Sadukkhatāyapi avidheyatādinā,

Anattato varamati khandhapañcakaṃ

Punappunaṃ samupaparikkha mussahī; ()

As impermanent, due to arising and passing away; as suffering, due to its painful nature and being uncontrollable, and so on; and as not-self—with excellent wisdom, he strove to investigate the five aggregates thoroughly again and again.

21.

21.

Kalāpasammasanamukhena bārasa-

Vidhe anādikabhavacakkanissite,

Kamena sattasu anupassanāsu so

Jinaṅkuro tadavayave’bhinīhari; ()

Through the entrance of contemplation on aggregates, based on the twelve-fold beginningless wheel of existence, the scion of the Conqueror gradually directed his mind to its parts in the seven contemplations.

22. [O 0.0355]

22.

Aniccatobhusamanupassamuddhari

Asesasaṅkhatagataniccasaññitaṃ,

Anattato samanuvipassa dukkhato

Sasaṅkhatepajahi sukhattasaññitaṃ; ()

Constantly contemplating impermanence, one completely removes the perception of permanence concerning all conditioned things. Contemplating not-self and suffering in conditioned things, one abandons the perception of happiness and self.

23.

23.

Vinodayī sumati virāganibbidā-

Vasena saṅkhatagatarāganandiyo,

Nirodhanissajanavasā’nupassiya

Tathodayādiyanamasesaṅghate; ()

By means of dispassion and disenchantment, the wise person dispels delight and attachment concerning conditioned things. Contemplating by means of cessation and relinquishment, one thus perceives the arising and passing away of all conditioned things.

24.

24.

Vidhāyadubbidhamanupassato kasato

Asesasaṅkhatamapi nāmarūpato,

Nidānato punakhaṇato’dayabbayaṃ

Upaṭṭhahi dviguṇitapañcavisadhā; ()

For one cultivating and contemplating the twofold division of all conditioned things into name-and-form, their arising and passing away—from their cause and from moment to moment—appeared in fifty ways.

25. [O 0.0356]

25.

Sudhīmato taruṇavipassanāyi’me

Vipassakassi’ti dasupakkilesakā,

Bhavuṃpabhāsatimatipītinicchayo

Sukhī’hanāsamathanikantyupekkhanā; ()

For the wise meditator with nascent insight, these ten corruptions of insight arose: brilliance, knowledge, rapture, serenity, bliss, resolution, exertion, mindfulness, equanimity, and attachment.

26. [O 0.0357]

26.

Pasannalohita paripuṇṇaviggahā

Viniggatā niravadhilokadhātusu,

Vipassanābalapabhavā’bhipatthari

Sudhantakañcanarasapiñjarappabhā; ()

From him of clear blood and perfected body, a radiance born from the power of insight emerged and spread forth into the limitless world-systems, glowing with the tawny hue of refined molten gold.

27.

27.

Ayaṃpatho nabhavati tappabhādayo

Visattikāpabhutikilesavatthukā,

Punodayabbaya manupassato tato

Patho samubbhavi dasupakkilesagaṃ; ()

This is not the path: that brilliance and so on, which are the basis for defilements such as attachment. But for one contemplating arising and passing away, from that the true path arose, which overcomes the ten corruptions of insight.

28.

28.

Pathāpathaṃ samupaparikkhatoiti

Sudhīmato taruṇavipassakassayā,

Samuṭṭhitā nisitavipassanāmati

Pathāpathikkhaṇakavisuddhi vuccate; ()

For the wise meditator with nascent insight who thus thoroughly examines the path and the non-path, a sharp insight-wisdom arises; this is called the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of What Is and Is Not the Path.

29. [O 0.0358]

29.

Narāsabho adhigatañātatīraṇa-

Pariññavā uparipahāṇasaṅkhayā,

Pariññayā ubhaya visuddhisiddhiyā

Tisaccadassanapasuto samārabhī; ()

The Bull among men, possessing the full understanding of the known and of discernment, by means of the higher full understanding of abandonment and destruction, and by the accomplishment of both purifications, being intent on seeing the three truths, began his striving.

30.

30.

Aniccalakkhaṇamapaki dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ

Anattalakkhaṇamatha sabbasaṅkhate,

Yathāvato nasamanupassi santati-

Riyāpathehica pihitaṃghaṇenaso; ()

He did not truly see the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, and the characteristic of not-self in all conditioned things, as they were concealed by continuity, by the postures, and by compactness.

31.

31.

Visodhayaṃ matimudayabbaye tato

Lahuṃ tilakkhaṇavisadattago bhusaṃ,

Vipassanāpathapaṭipanna mattanā

Alatthabhaṅgadhibhayañāṇamādikaṃ; ()

Purifying his mind by observing arising and passing away, he swiftly and greatly attained clarity concerning the three characteristics. Having entered the path of insight by himself, he attained the knowledge of dissolution, the knowledge of fear, and the knowledges that follow.

32. [O 0.0359]

32.

Sayambhuno uparinavānupassanā-

Vibhāvanā navaguṇavaṇṇanāyidha,

Vidhīyate navavidhañṇabhāvanā

Pavuccate sapakaṭipadāvisuddhiti; ()

Herein is set forth the analysis of the nine higher contemplations of the Self-Awakened One, with a description of their nine qualities. This is called the ninefold development of knowledge, and it is the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of the Way of Practice.

33.

33.

Matīhitihipi catusaccachādaka-

Tamovidhaṃsana samanantaraṃ thiraṃ,

Nirodhagocaramalabhittha gotrabhu-

Matiṃ sudhī anariyagottabāhiraṃ; ()

Immediately after firmly dispelling with wisdom the darkness that conceals the four truths, the wise one attained the change-of-lineage knowledge, which has cessation as its object and is external to the lineage of the ignoble.

34. [O 0.0360]

34.

Pasatthagotrabhumatidinnasaññakaṃ

Samūlamuddhaṭakalusattayaṃ sudhī,

Vibandhaduggativinipātanādikaṃ

Athādimaṃpaṭilabhī ñāṇadassanaṃ; ()

Then the wise one attained the first knowledge and vision, which is signaled by the praised change-of-lineage knowledge, which uproots the three stains, and which fells bondage, bad destinations, and the like.

35.

35.

Yadevanantaraphaladanti paṇḍitā

Vadantitapphalamapi paccavekkhaṇaṃ,

Alattha so puna dutiyāya bhumiyā

Vipassanaṃ samadhigamāya bhāvayī; ()

He attained that which the wise declare as giving the immediate fruit—that is, the fruit itself and the reviewing knowledge. Then, for the attainment of the second stage, he again developed insight.

36.

36.

Bhusovisosita bhavadukkhakaddamaṃ

Akālikaṃ tanukatakibbisattayaṃ,

Anuttaraṃ dutiyamalattha tapphalaṃ

Sapaccavekkhaṇamatha ñāṇadassanaṃ; ()

He attained the unsurpassed second knowledge and vision—which thoroughly dries up the mud of the suffering of existence, is immediate, and attenuates the three defilements—together with its fruit and reviewing knowledge.

37. [O 0.0361]

37.

Vipassanaṃpunarapibhāvayaṃ sayaṃ

Samuddhaṭālayapaṭighaṃ bhavāpahaṃ,

Sapaccavekkhaṇaphalañāṇamajjhagā

Anuttaraṃ tatiyaka ñāṇadassanaṃ; ()

Again developing insight by himself, he attained the unsurpassed third knowledge and vision—which uproots craving and aversion and diminishes becoming—together with its fruit and reviewing knowledge.

38.

38.

Tilakkhaṇaṃ thiramatimā’bhipattiyā

Subhāvayika upari catutthabhumiyā,

Avāriyāsaniriva tālamatthake

Kilesamuddhaniranihaccacārinaṃ; ()

With steadfast understanding, through the attainment of the three characteristics, having well cultivated them beyond the fourth plane, like an unimpeded thunderbolt upon a palm's crown, he wanders, having utterly struck down the head of the defilements.

39.

39.

Nivāritākhila bhavacakkavibbhamaṃ

Savāsanāparimita pakāpanāsanaṃ,

Anaññagocara varañāṇadassanaṃ

Alattha tapphalamapipaccavekkhaṇaṃ; ()

Having warded off all the delusions of the wheel of existence, having destroyed the limitless agitations together with their latent tendencies, he attained the supreme knowledge and vision whose domain is not elsewhere, and also the retrospection of its fruit.

40. [O 0.0362]

40.

Tadāsavakkhayamatigñāṇadassana-

Visuddhivuccati arahattapattiyā,

Sahevacuddasavidha buddhabuddhiyo

Jino catubbidha paṭisambhidālabhī; ()

Then, the purity of knowledge and vision concerning the understanding of the destruction of the taints is called the attainment of Arahantship. Together with this, the Victor attained the fourteen kinds of Buddha-knowledges and the fourfold analytical knowledge.

41.

41.

Asādhāraṇaṃ ñāṇachakkaṃbalāni

Dasa’ṭṭhārasāveṇikā buddhadhammā,

Catuddhāvisārajjamiddhānubhāvā

Samiddhāsahecārahattena tassa; ()

The six kinds of uncommon knowledge, the ten powers, the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities, the four kinds of intrepidity, and the majestic power of psychic abilities were fully accomplished by him together with Arahantship.

42.

42.

Abhiññeyyadhamme abhiññāya sāmaṃ

Pariññeyya dhamme pariññāya sāmaṃ,

Pahātabba dhamme pahantvāna sāmaṃ

Sanibbānamaggapphalaṃ sacchikatvā; ()

Having directly known by himself the things to be directly known, having fully comprehended by himself the things to be fully comprehended, having abandoned by himself the things to be abandoned, and having realized by himself the path and fruit of Nibbāna;

43. [O 0.0363]

43.

Siyāyāvatāñeyya dhammappavatti

Siyātāvatā tassa ñāṇappavatti,

Abhiññāya sabbaññutāñāṇa māsi

Sahevārahattena sabbaññu buddho; ()

To whatever extent there is an occurrence of knowable phenomena, to that extent for him there is an occurrence of knowledge. Having directly known, the knowledge of omniscience arose; together with Arahantship, he was the All-Knowing Buddha.

44.

44.

Mahāmohaniddāpagomaggañāṇa-

Ppabuddho’hisambodhiyā sobhamāno,

Munindo dinindaṃ’ susandohahāsi-

’Ndirāmandirindivarābhaṃahāsi; ()

Awakened from the great sleep of delusion by the path-knowledge that removes it, shining with supreme enlightenment, the Lord of Sages, the Lord of the Day, possessed a brilliant, radiant splendor, a radiance like a blue lotus in the abode of Indirā.

45.

45.

Subuddhābhisambodhipubbācalambhā

Sahevāruṇo buddhasūrodayena,

Samuṭṭhāsi veneyya bandhūhisaddhiṃ

Pabujjhiṃsu abbhuggatamhojakosā; ()

With the rising of the Buddha-sun, together with the dawn from the eastern mountain of supreme, perfect enlightenment, he arose along with his kinsmen who were to be trained. They awoke, their lotus-buds having opened.

46. [O 0.0364]

46.

Uḷārāvabhāso tadā jātikhette

Bhusaṃpātubhuto mahīsampavedhi,

Siḷāsāḷaseḷāvataṃsā subhāni

Nimattāni battiṃsajātātiloke; ()

Then a great radiance powerfully manifested in the birthplace, and the earth trembled greatly. Thirty-two beautiful signs, crests of rock, Sāla trees, and mountains, arose in the three worlds.

47.

47.

Tamojālaviddhaṃsanādīni loke

Karontova cattārikiccāni’māni,

Samuṭṭhāsi tasmiṃkhaṇe raṃsimāli

Rivādiccavaṃsubbhavo buddhasūro; ()

While performing in the world these four tasks, beginning with the destruction of the net of darkness, at that moment the Buddha-sun, born of the solar lineage, arose like the radiant sun.

48.

48.

Mahīlājavuṭṭhīhi sañchannabhutā

Nabhaṃ kanibbharaṃ gandhadhupaddhajehi,

Chaṇhokulā kevalaṃ lokadhātu

Mahāmaṅgalāvāsa kalīlāvalambiṃ ()

The earth was covered with showers of celestial parched rice; the sky was filled to capacity with fragrances, incense, and banners. The entire world-system, abounding in festivity, was suffused with the charm of a great and auspicious abode.

49. [O 0.0365]

49.

Tadātappadambhoja pūjāgatānaṃ

Siro bhattibhārañjalīnaṃ surānaṃ,

Nirālambamākāsa randhaṃ babhāsa

Pabhāsāra cūḷāmaṇihakā’karāḷaṃ; ()

Then the unsupported expanse of the sky shone, dazzling like a mine of radiant crest-jewels, with the heads of the gods who had come to worship his lotus feet, their hands clasped in reverence, bowed by the weight of devotion.

50.

50.

Guṇonāma sakkhandhasantāna suddhi

Sakosuddhakhanvdhappabandhohi buddho,

Namobuddhabhutassa nipphantañāṇa-

Ppahāṇānubhāvāhirūpassatassa; ()

Virtue, by name, is the purity of the continuity of one's own aggregates. Indeed, the Buddha is one whose own succession of aggregates is pure. Homage to him who has become the Buddha, whose form is manifested by the power of perfected knowledge and abandonment.

Iti medhānandābhidhānenayatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānandadānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe avidure nidāne mahā bodhisattassa ariyamaggañāṇābhisambodhi samadhigama pavattiparidīpo cuddasamo saggo.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, entitled 'The Illumination of the Great Bodhisatta's Attainment of Noble Path Knowledge and Supreme Enlightenment,' in the Jinavaṃsadīpa—a source of joy for the hearts of all poets—composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda, in the introductory section, the 'Avidūre Nidāna'.

Jinavaṃsadīpe avidure nidānabhāgo dutiyo.

The second part of the 'Avidūre Nidāna' section in the Jinavaṃsadīpa.

1. [O 0.0367]

1.

Asseva pakallaṅkavarassakāraṇā

Sīsakkhimaṃsāni ca dārasunavo,

Datvā cirassaṃ akarinti dukkaraṃ

So (indavaṃsā’)bhidhajo vicintayī; ()

For the sake of this excellent seat, having for a long time given his head, eyes, flesh, wife, and sons, he did not consider it a difficult deed. Thus he, the banner of the Inda lineage, reflected.

2.

2.

Pallaṅkato tāva navuṭṭhahaṃ tahiṃ

Pallaṅkamādhāya nisajja sattahaṃ,

Saṅkappapuṇṇo’dhisamādhayo muni

Sammā samāpajji anekakoṭiyo; ()

Having sat there for seven days in the cross-legged posture, thinking 'I will not rise from this seat,' the sage, his resolve fulfilled and his meditative attainments supreme, rightly entered into many crores of concentrations.

3.

3.

Nā’yaṃ jahāte vijayāsanā’layaṃ

Yaṃkiñcikiccaṃ karaṇiyamassahi,

Saṃvijjate dānipi kāci devatā

Saṅkābhighā’tābhivitakkayuṃ iti; ()

'He does not abandon this seat, the abode of victory. For whatever task was to be done by him is already accomplished.' Thus, even now, some deities, assailed by doubt, pondered.

4. [O 0.0368]

4.

Tāsaṃ viditvāna vitakkamāsanā

Abbhuṭṭhito so gaganaṅgaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ,

Saṃdassayanto yamapāṭihāriyaṃ

Nissaṃsayo saṃsayasallamuddharī; ()

Having known their thought, he rose from his seat into the courtyard of the sky for a moment. Displaying the Twin Miracle, he, being free from doubt, extracted their dart of doubt.

5.

5.

Nissāya pallaṅkamimaṃ mahīruhaṃ

Sampattasambodhipado’smi cintiya,

Oruyha pakallaṅkaṭhitappadesato

Pubbuttarānañhi disāna mantarā; ()

Thinking, 'Relying on this seat and this great tree, I have attained the state of perfect enlightenment,' he descended from the place where the seat was established, to a spot between the eastern and northern directions.

6.

6.

Sattāha mindivaracārulocana-

Pañcappabhāsāranisecanena so,

Samapūjayanto jayabodhimāsanaṃ

Aṭṭhāsi lokekavilocano jino; ()

For seven days, the Victor, the one eye of the world, stood honoring the seat of victorious enlightenment, sprinkling it with the stream of five-colored radiance from his beautiful lotus-like eyes.

7. [O 0.0369]

7.

Gantvā ṭhītaṭṭhānajayāsanantarā

Pubbāparassaṃ disi sattavāsaraṃ,

Nikkhittacakkaṅkitapādapaṅkajo

So caṅkamī nimmitaratanacaṅkame; ()

Having gone to a place between where he had stood and the victory seat, he whose lotus-feet are marked with wheels paced for seven days in an east-west direction on a jeweled promenade created by the gods.

8.

8.

So bodhito uttarapacchimantarā

Devehi nānāratanehi nimmite,

Sattāhamattaṃ maṇimandire muni

Sammābhidhammaṃ pavihāsi sammasaṃ; ()

To the northwest of the Bodhi tree, the sage dwelt for seven days in a jeweled mansion created by the gods with various jewels, contemplating the supreme Abhidhamma.

9.

9.

Manthācale’nambunidhiṃ’va kesavo

Viññāṇakaṇḍādiṭasā catubbidhaṃ,

Tasmiṃ nisinno muni dhammasaṅgaṇi-

Mālolayī ñāṇabalena duddasaṃ; ()

Like Kesava churning the ocean at Mount Manthara, the sage, seated there, with the power of his knowledge stirred up the Dhammasaṅgaṇī—which is difficult to perceive and deals with the fourfold section on consciousness and so forth.

10. [O 0.0370]

10.

Vebhaṅgiyaṃ khandhavibhaṅgamādikaṃ

Gambhīramaṭṭhārasadhā sudubbudhaṃ,

So mārabhaṅgo’tha vibhaṅgasāgaraṃ

Saṃkhobhayī ñāṇayugantavāyunā; ()

Then that destroyer of Māra stirred the ocean of the Vibhaṅga—which begins with the analysis of the aggregates, is profound, eighteenfold, and very difficult to understand—with the epoch-ending wind of his knowledge.

11.

11.

So dhātusuññattapajānano jino

Nissattanijjivasabhāvadhātuyo,

Vitthārayanto tadanantaraṃ varaṃ

Nānānayaṃ dhātukathaṃ vavatthayī; ()

Then the Victor, who understands the emptiness of the elements, analyzed the excellent Dhātukathā with its various methods, elaborating on the elements whose nature is without a being and without a soul.

12.

12.

Khandhādipaññattivasena chabbidhā

Paññattiyo’ti suvibhattamātikaṃ,

Paññāya sabbaññujino’tha puggala-

Paññatti mālolayi aggapuggalo; ()

Then the all-knowing Victor, the foremost person, with his wisdom examined the Puggalapaññatti, with its well-analyzed matrix of the six kinds of concepts, such as the concept of the aggregates.

13. [O 0.0371]

13.

Vādībhasīho sakavādamaṇḍalaṃ

Oruyha sammā paravādamaṇḍalaṃ,

Suttāni saṅgayha sahassamaṭṭhadhā

Saṃkhitta mādo mukhavādayuttikaṃ; ()

The lion among debaters, having descended from the circle of his own doctrine to rightly enter the circle of others' doctrines, summarized the suttas in eight thousand ways, abandoning pride, endowed with skillful arguments.

14.

14.

Ñāṇena vitthāriyamāna mattano

Kiñcāpya’nantāpariyanta muttamaṃ,

Takkīhi nakkāvacaraṃ nakehici

Nātho kathāvatthu mathā’bhisammasi; ()

Although his own knowledge, being expanded, was endless, limitless, and supreme, and not the domain of any logicians whatsoever, the Protector then thoroughly contemplated the Kathāvatthu.

15.

15.

Yaṃ mūlakhandhādivasā dasabbidhaṃ

Uddesaniddesapadā’nurūpato,

Niṭṭhānato saṃsayato vibhāgiyaṃ

Gambhīrañāṇena’tha sāgarūpamaṃ; ()

Which is tenfold, by way of the pairs beginning with the Roots and the Aggregates; which proceeds according to the terms of summary and exposition, conclusion, and question; which is to be analyzed with profound knowledge, and which is ocean-like;

16. [O 0.0372]

16.

Santaṃ paṇitaṃ nipuṇaṃ sududdasaṃ

Guḷhaṃ atakkāvacaraṃ acintiyaṃ,

Nānānayaṃ taṃ yamakaṃ susaññamo

Dhammassaro sammasi nippadesato; ()

Peaceful, sublime, subtle, very hard to see, hidden, beyond the sphere of logic, inconceivable—that Yamaka, with its various methods, the essence of the Dhamma, the well-restrained one comprehended completely, without remainder.

17.

17.

Nānānayu’ttuṅgataraṅganibbharaṃ

Neyyatthanītatthamaṇihi maṇḍitaṃ,

Dhammantarāvaṭṭasataṃ athāparaṃ

Saddhammakhandhodakakhandhapūritaṃ; ()

Filled with towering waves of various methods, adorned with gems of implicit and explicit meanings; and further, with a hundred whirlpools within the Dhamma, and filled with the water-mass of the aggregates of the Good Dhamma;

18.

18.

Satthā catubbisa timattapaccaya-

Velaṃ paricchedavisālapaṭṭanaṃ,

Gambhīrapaṭṭhāna mahaṇṇavaṃ kathaṃ

Ālolayaṃ sammasi ñāṇamerunā; ()

How did the Teacher, with the Mount Meru of his wisdom, stirring up the great ocean of the profound Paṭṭhāna—which has the twenty-four conditions as its shore, and vast ports of delimitation—comprehend it?

19. [O 0.0373]

19.

Nissaṅgañāṇo muni hetupaccayo

Iccādinā’ropitamātikārahaṃ,

Niddiṭṭhanidedasapadaṃ papañcita-

Ñeyyaṃ catubbīsavidhaṃ sudubbudhaṃ; ()

The worthy sage, with non-clinging knowledge, comprehended the knowable—twenty-fourfold and very difficult to understand—which is expanded with specified and illustrative terms, its matrix established with 'cause-condition' and so forth.

20.

20.

Nissāya bāvīsavidhe tike tika-

Paṭṭhāna mantogadhanāmarūpike

Nissāya nissesake tathā duka-

Paṭṭhāna mantogadhanāmarūpike ()

Based on the twenty-twofold triplets, the Triplet-Paṭṭhāna wherein name-and-form are included; and likewise, based on the exhaustive dyads, the Dyad-Paṭṭhāna wherein name-and-form are included.

21.

21.

Bāvisamattā tikamātikā duke

Pakkhippa paṭṭhānavidaṃ dukantikaṃ,

Bāvīsamattāya tike sataṃduke

Pakkhippa paṭṭhānamidaṃka tikaddukaṃ; ()

Having inserted the twenty-two triple matrices into the dyads, this Paṭṭhāna of the wise ends in dyads; having inserted the twenty-two triplets into the hundred dyads, this Paṭṭhāna is of triplets and dyads.

22. [O 0.0374]

22.

Katvā tikesve’va tike duvīsati

Paṭṭhāna mantogatike tikattikaṃ,

Katvā dukesve’va tathā sataṃduke

Paṭṭhāna mantāgetike dukaddukaṃ; ()

Having applied the twenty-two triplets to the triplets themselves, the Paṭṭhāna containing triplets becomes the Triplet-Triplet section; likewise, having applied the hundred dyads to the dyads themselves, the Paṭṭhāna containing dyads becomes the Dyad-Dyad section.

23.

23.

Iccānulome janayāni pakkhipaṃ

Cha ppaccanīye’pi nayāni pakkhipaṃ,

Evaṃ khipitvā anulomapaccani-

Yecā’pi cha ppaccaniyā’nulomake; ()

Thus, inserting the methods in the forward order, and also inserting the six methods in the reverse order; having thus inserted the forward-reverse methods, and also the six reverse-forward methods;

24.

24.

Gambhīrapaṭṭhānamahodadhiṃ iti

Saṅkhobhayaṃ sammasi ñāṇamerunā,

Taṃ sammasantassa savatthukaṃ chavi-

Vaṇṇo pasanto’si pasīdi lohitaṃ; ()

Thus, stirring up the great ocean of the profound Paṭṭhāna with the Mount Meru of his wisdom, he comprehended it. As he was comprehending it with its entire substance, the color of his skin became serene, and his blood was purified.

25. [O 0.0375]

25.

Tasmiṃkhaṇe cattajavaṇṇadhātuyo

Aṭṭhaṃsu ṭhānamhi asitihatthake,

Aññatra’dhiṭṭhānabalaṃ sarīrato

Chabbaṇṇaraṃsī visarā’hiniccharuṃ; ()

At that moment, the properties of his complexion extended over a space of eighty cubits. Apart from the power of his resolution, six-colored rays streamed forth intensely from his body.

26.

26.

Sevālakālindinadi’ndirāpati-

Nilambari’ndivaravaṇṇasantibhā,

Kesa’kkhimassūhika viniggatā bhusaṃ

Nīlappabhā’sesadisā alaṅkaruṃ; ()

Resembling the hue of moss, the Kāliṇdī river, sapphire, a blue garment, or the blue lotus, blue rays, having streamed forth copiously from his hair, eyes, and beard, adorned all directions.

27.

27.

Tāsaṃ vasā’ sesadisāvilāsinī

Āsuṃ yathā pārutanīlakambalā,

Tā cakkavāḷāti papūrayantiyo

Dhāviṃsu nilopalacuṇṇasannibhā; ()

By their power, all directions became resplendent, as if covered with blue blankets. Those rays, resembling the powder of blue gems, rushed forth, filling the entire world-system.

28. [O 0.0376]

28.

Nissesalokaṃ haritālakuṅkuma-

Cuṇṇehi sovaṇṇarasehi missakaṃ,

Ālepayantīviya pītaraṃsiyo

Yā niggatā kañcanasannibhattacā; ()

The yellow rays, which emerged from his skin of golden hue, were as if anointing the entire world with a mixture of powders of yellow orpiment and saffron, and with golden liquid.

29.

29.

Tāsaṃ vasenā’si siṇerupabbata-

Rājā vilino’va mahaṇṇave jalaṃ,

Saṃkappitā’va’ṭṭha disāgajā’bhavuṃ

Niddhantacāmīkarakappanādinā; ()

By their power, Sineru, the king of mountains, was as if dissolved like salt in the great ocean; the elephants of the eight directions appeared as if fashioned from refined gold and so forth.

30.

30.

Lākhārasānaṃ parisecanaṃ viya

Nindūracuṇṇo’kiraṇaṃ’va yādisi,

Sañjhāpabhārattasurattaraṃsiyo

Nikkhamma dhāviṃsu samaṃsalohitā; ()

Like a sprinkling of lac juice or a scattering of vermilion powder, rays redder than the twilight glow, exceedingly red, emerged from his flesh and blood and rushed forth.

31.

31.

Tāsaṃ vasenā’khilabhūmikāminī

Āsī nimuggāriva uttaraṇṇave,

Ambhojarāgehi sunimmitāni’va

Sabbāni dabbānya’bhavuṃ jagattaye;()

By their power, the lady that is the entire earth was as if submerged in the northern ocean; all things in the triple world became as if perfectly fashioned with the hues of the lotus.

32. [O 0.0377]

32.

Yākundasogandhikacandacandikā-

Kappūrakhīrodadhivīcipaṇḍarā,

Aṭṭhīhi dāṭhāhī vitassaṭā bhusaṃ

Odātaraṃsī dhavalīkaruṃ disā; ()

The white rays—white like kunda flowers, white water-lilies, the moon and its light, camphor, and the waves of the milk-ocean—spreading out greatly from his bones and eye-teeth, whitened the directions.

33.

33.

Tāsaṃ vasenā’si yathā mahīvadhu

Odātavatthehi nivatthapārutā,

Tā khīradhārāparisekabandhurā

Dhāviṃsu buddhassa yasonibhāpabhā; ()

By their power, the earth-bride was as if clothed and covered in white garments. Those rays, lovely as a sprinkling with streams of milk, rushed forth, a radiance like the glory of the Buddha.

34.

34.

Sabbādisāyo’khilalokadhātuyo

Mañjiṭṭhapaṅkehi vilepayanti’ca,

Nikkhamma mañjiṭṭhapabhā tatotato

Dhāviṃsu sañcuṇṇapavāḷasantibhā ()

Rays of madder hue, resembling crushed coral, having emerged from here and there, rushed forth, as if anointing all directions and the entire world-sphere with madder paste.

35. [O 0.0378]

35.

Nīlādidhātussarasehi pañcahi

Vaṇṇehi pupphehi maṇīhisattahi,

Sampūrayantī’va pabhā pabhassarā

Nikkhamma lokaṃ sakalaṃ alaṅkaruṃ; ()

The radiant light, shining brilliantly, emerged and adorned the entire world, as if filling it with five colors—blue and the others—with flowers, and with the seven kinds of gems.

36.

36.

Tā raṃsiyo byāpiya mediniṃ mahī-

Sandhārakaṃ vāri matho samīraṇaṃ,

Heṭṭhā’jaṭākāsatalaṃ tathūpari

Gaṇhiṃsu lokaṃ tiriyaṃ nirāvadhiṃ; ()

Those rays, having pervaded the earth, the water that supports the earth, and then the wind, seized the open space below and likewise above, and the world across without limit.

37.

37.

Devaddumu’yyānavimānabhusaṇa-

Canda’kkatārānikarā’marā tato,

Saṇṭhānamattehi vijāniyā’bhavuṃ

Tā niggatā ajjatanā’pi dhāvare; ()

Thereafter, the celestial trees, gardens, mansions, ornaments, the moon, sun, hosts of stars, and the deathless ones became discernible by their mere forms. Those rays, having gone forth, endure even to this day.

38. [O 0.0379]

38.

Tamhā’bhīgantvā ghananīlasākhino

Nigrodhasākhissa’japālasaññino,

Mūle nisajjā’dhisukhaṃ vimuttijaṃ

Satthā’nubhonto pavihāsi sattahaṃ; ()

From there, having approached the banyan tree known as the Goatherd's, with its dense, dark-blue branches, the Teacher, having sat at its root, dwelt for seven days, experiencing the supreme bliss born of liberation.

39.

39.

Oruyha tasmiṃsamaye vimānato

Dānādayo pāramiyo bhavābhavaṃ,

Dhāvaṃ asādhāraṇañāṇasiddhiyā

Eso’va nā’haṃ abhisaṅkhariṃ iti; ()

At that time, descending from his mansion, Māra reflected thus: 'This one, by attaining unique knowledge, running through existence after existence fulfilling the perfections of generosity and so on—it was not I who fashioned him!'

40.

40.

Otārapekho navipassa ettakaṃ

Kālaṃ kalaṅkaṃ akalaṅkarūpino,

Sokā’kulo acchi chamāya soḷasa-

Lekhā vilekhaṃ kalimā avammukho; ()

Looking for an opening, he saw no blemish for any length of time in that one of stainless form. Overwhelmed by sorrow, the wicked one sat on the ground with face downcast, drawing sixteen lines.

41. [O 0.0380]

41.

Kasmā napaññāyati’dāni nopitā

Olokayanti kva gato’ti dukkhitaṃ,

Sokena lekhā likhamāna mañjase

Disvā nisinnaṃ pitaraṃ sudummukhaṃ; ()

Grieving, they looked about, saying, 'Why does our father not appear now? Where has he gone?' Then, on the path, they saw their father seated, very downcast, drawing lines in sorrow.

42.

42.

Tatro pagantvā vasavattidhītaro

Pucchiṃsu taṇhā aratī ragā lahuṃ,

Kiṃ tāta kiṃ tāta kimettha jhāyasi

Ko te paro kena parājito tuvaṃ; ()

Then the daughters of Vasavattī—Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā—swiftly approached and asked: 'Why, father, why, father, do you grieve here? Who is your enemy? By whom have you been defeated?'

43.

43.

Suddhodanassā’vanipassa oraso

Patvā’hisambodhipadaṃka mukhe masiṃ,

Makkhesi me chinditamārabandhano

Tasmā’nusocāmi kathesi pāpimā; ()

'The legitimate son of King Suddhodana, having attained the state of perfect enlightenment and having cut the bonds of Māra, has smeared soot on my face. Therefore, I grieve,' said the Evil One.

44. [O 0.0381]

44.

Ānīya taṃ mattagajaṃ’va mārajiṃ

Rāgādipāsehi mayaṃ subandhiya,

Dassāma vo passatha tāta no balaṃ

Māsoci mājhāyi’ti dhītaro’bravuṃ; ()

'Having brought that conqueror of Māra, like a maddened elephant, and having bound him well with the snares of lust and so on, we will show you. Father, behold our power! Do not grieve, do not be anxious!' Thus spoke the daughters.

45.

45.

Siṅgārasaṅgāmadharā’vatārinī

Bhubhaṅgabāṇāsanamattadhārinī,

Āropitā’pāṅgasarā’pya’nissarā

Kāmārimārārisaravyadāraṇe; ()

Descending, bearing the panoply of the battle of love; wielding the great bow of a moving brow, with the arrow of a sidelong glance fitted but not yet released, for piercing the enemy of Māra, the foe of desire.

46.

46.

Sevālanīlāmalakuntalākulā

Bālindulekhe’valalāṭamaṇḍalā

Niluppalakkhī calahemakuṇḍalā-

Laṅkārakaṇṇā’likalāpabhā’lakā ()

Her hair, tangled and abundant, was dark and pure like blue water-plants; her forehead was like a crescent moon; her eyes were like blue water lilies; her ears were adorned with swinging golden earrings; and her forehead shone with the splendor of a swarm of bees.

47. [O 0.0382]

47.

Vāṇilatāvellitaphullamālatī-

Dantāvalī pallavapāṭalādharā,

Kandappakīḷālayahemakāhaḷa-

Saṅkāsanāsā kamalāmalānanā; ()

Her row of teeth was like blossoming jasmine entwined with reed-creepers; her lips were pale red like tender shoots; her nose resembled a golden trumpet in the playground of the god of love; her face was like a spotless lotus.

48.

48.

Vijjullatā cārubhujā calācala-

Līlāvalambatthanahaṃsamaṇḍalā,

Cāmīkarāliṅgavilāsakandharā

Lāvaṇṇa vallidalakomalaṅgulī; ()

Her arms were graceful like creepers of lightning; her pair of breasts, like swans, hung down with playful movement; her neck was lovely, adorned with embracing gold; her fingers were lovely and tender like the shoots of a vine.

49.

49.

Nimmekhalālinavilaggabhāginī

Kīḷānadīkulavisālasoṇinī,

Kandappadappānaladhūmakajjala-

Romāvalivellitanābhimaṇḍala; ()

She possessed a slender waist; her hips were broad like the banks of a play-river; the circle of her navel was entwined with a line of fine hair, dark as the soot from the smoke of the fire of Kāma's pride.

50. [O 0.0383]

50.

Pīnorujaṅghā kalikānakhāvalī

Tā’naṅakgaraṅgaṅajahāriviggahā,

Māraṅganā yatra niraṅgaṇo jino

Tatrā’gamuṃ rāgasurāmadā’turā; ()

Her thighs and shanks were plump, her row of nails was like flower buds, their bodies captivating, a veritable house of love's every limb. Where the stainless Victor was, there came those women of Māra, distressed by the intoxication of the liquor of lust.

51.

51.

Aṅgīrasassā’nanasoṇṇadappaṇe

Tā sundarī bimbitalocanindirā,

Kandappakīḷākalahaṃ vidhātave

Kāloyamiccāhu tuvaṃ yadicchasi; ()

In the golden mirror of the face of Aṅgīrasa, the splendor of the eyes of those beautiful women was reflected. They said: 'This is the time to engage in the sport and strife of love, if you so wish.'

52. [O 0.0384]

52.

Vyāpāritā te paricārikā mayaṃ

Etthāgatā homa manobhunā’dhunā,

Vattambujānaṃ paricumbane ayaṃ

Kālonu bhogotama kiṃnayicchasi; ()

'We are your attendants, employed for your service; now we have come here, sent by the Mind-Born. Is this not the time for kissing lotus-like mouths? O best of enjoyers, what is it that you desire?'

53.

53.

Bho puṇṇakumbhe’va tavo’ramandire

Uddhaggalomu’ssitanīlaketane,

Kāmāhisekussavamaṅgalāya no

Sajjethi’me pīnapayodhare nakiṃ; ()

'Behold, like full pots on the temple of your chest! With hair standing on end like a raised blue banner! For the auspicious festival of our consecration in love, will you not make use of these plump breasts?'

54.

54.

Vattambuje no adharaṃ’subandhure

Nettālimālā nahivumbare tava,

Amhesuyevā’bhipatanti bhomuni

Kandappabāṇā karuṇā kuhiṃ tavaṃ ()

'On our lotus-faces, our lips are lovely, but your eyes, like a garland of bees, do not alight upon them. The arrows of the god of love fall only upon us, O sage! Where is your compassion?'

55. [O 0.0385]

55.

Tvaṃ yobbano sāmi mayañca yobbanī

Kālo vasatto vipinaṃ manoramaṃ’

Mandānilo vāyati kiṃ cirāyate

Tuyhaṃ anaṅgo’va niraṅgaṇo’si kiṃ; ()

'You are youthful, master, and we are youthful women. The season is spring, the forest is delightful, a gentle breeze is blowing. Why do you delay? Are you truly without passion, stainless?'

56.

56.

Dibbāni vatthābharaṇāni’māni’pi

Lajjāya saddhiṃka sithilibhavanti no’

Amhesvanaṅgena samaṃ anaṅgaṇaṃ

Daḷahatta māyāti manaṃ tava’bbhutaṃ; ()

'These divine garments and ornaments of ours become loose along with our shame. While we are overcome with love, O passionless one, your mind goes to firmness—how amazing!'

57.

57.

Iccānigammaṃ hadayaṅgamaṃ giraṃ

Vatvāna dibbena sarena mañjunā,

Kāmāturānanti pumānamāsayā

Uccāvacā cintiyamāradhītaro; ()

Thus having spoken heart-pleasing words with a sweet, divine voice, the daughters of Māra, distressed by lust and with their minds set upon the man, considered various things.

58. [O 0.0386]

58.

Kaññāvilāsādivasena viggahe

Nimmāya paccekasataṃ padassiya,

Pāde mayaṃ bho paricārayāma te

Vatvā tamārādhayituṃ parakkamuṃ; ()

Having created and shown a hundred bodies each, with the charm of a maiden and so forth, they said, 'Sir, we shall attend to your feet,' and thus strove to win him over.

59.

59.

Gāthā imā dhammapade mahāmuni

Saṅgāyi tāsaṃ tamanaṅgabhaṅgīnaṃ,

Vatvā nasakkoma mayaṃ pakalobhituṃ

Tā rittahatthā pitaraṃ upāgamuṃ; ()

The Great Sage recited these verses from the Dhammapada to break their lust. Saying, 'We are not able to tempt him,' they went empty-handed to their father.

60.

60.

Gantvā tato so mucalindasaññino

Rukkhassa mūle mucalindabhogino,

Bhogāvaligandhakuṭiṃka samappito

Sattāhamajjhāvasi jhānamuttamaṃ; ()

Having gone from there to the foot of the Mucalinda tree, which belonged to the Nāga king Mucalinda, he was enclosed as if in a fragrant chamber by the coils of the Nāga's body and dwelt for seven days in supreme absorption.

61. [O 0.0387]

61.

Mulamhi rājāyatanassa sākhino

Pallaṅka mādhāya nisajja sattahaṃ,

Tamhābhi’gantvā bhavabandhanacchido

Satthā valañjesi vimuttijaṃ sukhaṃ; ()

Then, the Teacher, the cutter of the bonds of existence, having gone from there to the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, sat in the cross-legged posture for seven days and enjoyed the bliss born of liberation.

62.

62.

Satthā evakaṃ vasanto parahitatirato sattasattāhamattaṃ

Yaṃkiñcāhārakiccaṃ dhuvaparihariyaṃ kiccamuccāvacampi;

Nākāsi jhānamaggapphakhalasukhamakhilaṃ samphusanto vibhāsi

Pādāsi dantapoṇodaka magada’bhayaṃ tassa devanamindo; ()

Thus the Teacher, intent on the welfare of others, dwelt for seven weeks. He did not perform any regular duties of taking food or other various tasks; experiencing the entire bliss of absorption, path, and fruition, he shone forth. To him, the fearless one, the king of the gods gave a tooth-stick, water, and medicine.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānandadānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe santikenidāne bhagavato sattasattāhavitikkamappavatti paridīpo paṇṇarasamo saggo.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Elucidation of the Passing of the Seven Weeks by the Blessed One, in the Santike Nidāna of the Jinavaṃsadīpa, a source of delight for the hearts of all poets, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda.

1. [O 0.0389]

1.

Mūle rājāyatanaviṭapacchāyāmano (hārini)

Vikkhāletvā bhagavati mukhaṃ tasmiṃ nisinne sati,

Vāṇijjatthaṃ nija janapadā dve bhātikāka vāṇijā

Gacchantā majjhimajanapadaṃ taṃṭhāna majjhotaruṃ; ()

While the Blessed One, having washed his face, was sitting at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree in the delightful shade of its branches, two merchant brothers, going from their own country to the Middle Country for the purpose of trade, came upon that place.

2.

2.

Buddhaṃ disvā nirupamasiriṃ saddhāya sañcoditā

Sampādetvā madhurivamadhuṃ manthaṃ madhūpiṇḍikaṃ,

Bhante tumhe anubhavatha no bhikkhaṃ paṭiggaṇhiya

Evaṃ vatvātadubhayajanā aṭṭhaṃsu baddhañjalī; ()

Having seen the Buddha of matchless glory, and being impelled by faith, they prepared barley-meal and honey-cakes. Saying, 'Venerable Sir, having accepted our alms, please partake of them,' those two people stood with joined palms.

3.

3.

Sabbe buddhā nahi karatalambhojesu gaṇhanti kho

Saṅkappettassi’ti bhagavatokismiṃ paṭicchāmahaṃ,

Cittācāraṃ sumariya silāpatte pamāṇupage

Pādāsuṃ sampati catumahārājā kuverādayo; ()

'All Buddhas, indeed, do not receive food in the palm of the hand.' Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: 'In what shall I receive it?' Remembering this custom, the Four Great Kings, Kuvera and the others, at that moment offered stone bowls of a suitable size.

4. [O 0.0390]

4.

Ekaṃ katvā samuti caturo patte adhiṭṭhāya te

Bhutvā’hāraṃ bhuvananayano bhuttānumodaṃ kari,

Buddhaṃ dhammaṃ saraṇamagamuṃ te tenuho’vāṇijā

Jātā loke sakalapaṭhamaṃ dvevāciko’ pāsakā; ()

Having resolved upon the four bowls and made them one, the Eye of the World ate the food and gave thanks for the meal. Those merchants went for refuge to the Buddha and the Dhamma, and thus became the very first lay disciples in the world with the two-fold formula.

5.

5.

Tesaṃ dvinnaṃ suparihariyaṃ dethā’ti saṃyācataṃ

Jālaṅkā’laṅkatakaratalo rupindirā mandire,

Sīsaṃ nilopalamaṇighaṭīlīlāvilāsaṃ phusaṃ

Sevāli’ndīvaradalasiriṃ so kesamuṭṭhiṃ adā; ()

When those two requested, 'Give us something to venerate,' he, a mansion of splendid form, whose palms were adorned with the mark of a net, touching his head which was graceful and charming like a pot of blue lotus gems, gave a handful of hair having the splendor of a blue water-lily petal.

6. [O 0.0391]

6.

Patvā tesaṃ janapadamubho pakkhippa tā dhātuyo

Jīvantasmiṃ bhagavati mahāthūpaṃ patiṭṭhāpayuṃ,

Vimhāpento vanasuragaṇaṃ yatrā’japālābhidho

Nigrodho’si tahimupagamī muṭṭhāya tamhā jino; ()

Having reached their country, they both enshrined those relics and established a great stūpa while the Blessed One was still alive. Then the Victor, having arisen from that place, went to where the banyan tree named Ajapāla was, astonishing the host of forest deities.

7.

7.

Svā’yaṃ dhammo sayamadhigato dubbodhanoduddaso

Iccevaṃ so samabhivivinaṃ dhammassa gambhīrataṃ,

Appo’ssukko’bhavi bhagavato cittaṃ viditvā mahā-

Brahmā’gantvā sayamadhigataṃ desetumāyācī taṃ; ()

Reflecting thus, 'This Dhamma, self-realized by me, is profound, hard to understand, difficult to see,' he became inclined to inaction. Knowing the mind of the Blessed One, the Great Brahmā approached and requested him to teach that which he had realized himself.

8.

8.

Gaṇhitvā so bhuvanasaraṇo ajjhosanaṃ brahmuno

Deseyyaṃ kho paṭhamamasamaṃ dhammaṃ imaṃ duddasaṃ,

Kassā’hanti sumariya vasī āḷārakocuddako

Abbhaññātuṃ vata paṭibalātesaṃ cutiṃ addasaṃ ()

He, the refuge of the world, having accepted the request of Brahmā, thought: 'To whom first should I teach this unequalled Dhamma, so hard to see?' Then the self-controlled one remembered Āḷāra and Uddaka: 'Indeed, they were capable of understanding.' But he saw that they had passed away.

9. [O 0.0392]

9.

Āvajjento munikatavidū te pañcavagge bhavā

Bhikkhu dhamme kataparicayā kutrā’dhunā vijjare,

Bārānasyaṃ itisipatane ñatvāna āsāḷhiyā

Māse pañcaddasiya masamo bārāṇasiṃ pāvisi; ()

The sage, knowing the practice of sages, reflected: 'Those monks of the group of five, who have some familiarity with the teaching, where do they now dwell?' Having understood that they were at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī, the Unequalled One, on the fifteenth day of the month of Āsāḷha, entered Bārāṇasī.

10.

10.

Āgacchantaṃ samuni upakaṃ ājīvakaṃ antarā-

Magge disvā gamanasamaye buddhattanaṃ attano,

Ācikkhitvā vimati matarī saññāya taṃ dūrato

Nibbinditvā katika makaruṃ vaggā samaggā vasī; ()

On the way, that sage saw the Ājīvaka Upaka coming. At that time of his journey, having declared his own Buddhahood, he dispelled Upaka's doubt. Recognizing the Buddha from afar, the group of five self-controlled monks, being displeased, made an agreement among themselves.
