11. [O 0.0393]

11.

Ñatvā tesaṃ manasi vikatiṃ odissakaṃ samphari

Mettaṃ cittaṃ narahari tato phuṭṭhāsamānā vasī,

Nāthaṃ natvā dasanakhasamodhāna’jalīhā’gataṃ

Paccuggantvā tahimahiharuṃ papphoṭhayitvā’sanaṃ; ()

The Lion of Men, having known the corruption in their minds, suffused them with a mind of specifically directed loving-kindness. Touched by it, those self-controlled ones went out to meet the Lord who had come, bowed with hands joined in reverence, took his bowl and robe, and prepared a seat.

12.

12.

Mākho tumhe pariharathamaṃ eyā’vusotyā’dinā

Saññāpetvā samuni samaṇe sabbaññutaṃ attano,

Koṭīha’ṭṭhārasahi navuto brahmehi cā’laṅkari

Bārāṇasyaṃ pani’sipatane paññattabuddhāsanaṃ; ()

That sage convinced the ascetics of his own omniscience, instructing them, 'Do not address me as "friend" and so on.' Then, at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī, the prepared Buddha-seat was adorned and praised by eighteen crores of Brahmās.

13.

13.

Saṃvattetvā parahitakaro so dhammacakkaṃ jino

Koṇḍaññākhyassamaṇapamukhe koṭīnamaṭṭhārasa,

Brahmāno te paṭhamakaphale sammā patiṭṭhāpayi

Kampitthā’yaṃka vasumativadhū suttāvasāne bhusaṃ; ()

The Victor, a benefactor to others, having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, firmly established eighteen crores of Brahmās, headed by the ascetic Koṇḍañña, in the first fruit. At the conclusion of the discourse, this lady earth, Vasumatī, shook greatly.

14. [O 0.0394]

14.

Vappatthero dutiyadivase’ tye’vaṃ dinānukkamaṃ

Sotāpannā taditaravasī ātappamanvāya te,

Sabbetherā bhaṇitasamaye vitthāritassuññate

Suttattasmiṃ vigatadarathā āsuṃ pahiṇāsvā; ()

The Elder Vappa on the second day, and so on, day by day, the others became Stream-enterers; having undertaken the ardent practice, they became masters of themselves. At the time that Sutta expounding emptiness was delivered, all those elders became free from distress, with their taints abandoned.

15.

15.

Nibbinditvā nikhilavisaye nikkhanta māvāsato

Disvā satthā yasakulasutaṃ pakkosayitvāna taṃ,

Tāyaṃ ratyaṃ paṭhamakaphalaṃ ratyāvasāne dine

Pabbājesi uparimakhilaṃ maggapphalaṃ pāpayaṃ; ()

Having become disillusioned with all sense-objects, he departed from his dwelling. The Teacher, seeing Yasa, son of a noble family, summoned him. That very night he attained the first fruit, and at the end of the night, on the following day, having ordained him, He led him to attain all the higher paths and fruits.

16. [O 0.0395]

16.

Pabbājetvā yasakulasutassambhattamitte jane

Sampāpesi adhikacaturo paññāsa maggapphalaṃ,

Evaṃ khīṇāsavavasigaṇe jāte’kasaṭṭhyā bhuvi

Vassāna’nte pahiṇi muni te bhikkhu disācārikaṃ; ()

Having ordained the intimate friends of Yasa, son of a noble family, he caused fifty-four more to attain the path and its fruit. Thus, when the community of self-controlled ones free from taints had grown to sixty-one on earth, at the end of the rains-retreat, the Sage sent those monks to wander forth.

17.

17.

Gacchanto so haririva mahāvīro’ruvelaṃ sayaṃ

Disvā kappāsikavanaghaṭe tiṃsappamāṇe jane,

Pabbājesi katavinayanā te bhaddavaggeyyakā

Bhikkhūmaggapphalarasamudā anvācaruṃ cārikaṃ; ()

That great hero, journeying like a lion, went himself to Uruvelā. Seeing thirty people in the Kappāsika cotton-tree grove, he ordained those Bhaddavaggiyas, having trained them. Those monks, delighted with the flavor of the path and its fruit, undertook the wandering life.

18.

18.

Netā jetā vijaṭitajaṭo patto’ruvelaṃ tato

Saṃdassetvā vimatiharaṇaṃ so pāṭihīraṃ varaṃ,

Pabbājetvā jaṭilapavare tebhātike’nekadhā

Chindāpetvā vinayamakā antobahiddhajaṭaṃ; ()

The leader, the conqueror, who had disentangled the tangle, reached Uruvelā from there. Displaying a supreme miracle that dispels doubt, he ordained the eminent Jaṭilas, the three brothers, in many ways. Having caused their inner and outer tangled locks to be cut, he established them in the discipline.

19. [O 0.0396]

19.

Pabbājetvā pacurajaṭile katve’tare nijjaṭe

Saddhiṃ tehī dasasatamahākhīṇāsavehā’samo,

Nicchārento disidisi bhusaṃ chabbaṇṇaraṃsiṃka subhaṃ

Rañño vācaṃ sumariya puraṃ rājaggahaṃ pāvisi; ()

Having ordained the many Jaṭilas and made them free of their matted hair, the Incomparable One, together with those thousand great Arahants, entered the city of Rājagaha, remembering the king's words and sending forth in every direction the beautiful and brilliant six-colored rays.

20.

20.

Tatrā’sante vasati sugate laṭṭhibbanuyyānage

Vuttantaṃ taṃ savaṇasubhagaṃ uyyānapāloditaṃ,

Sutvā baddhañjalisarasije pādāsane pūjayī

Bhunātho bārasahi nahutehā’gamma so māgadho ()

While the Sugata was dwelling there in the Laṭṭhivana grove, the park-keeper related that delightful news. Hearing it, the Magadhan lord, having come with twelve myriads, honored the Buddha's feet with his lotus-like hands clasped in reverence.

21. [O 0.0397]

21.

Bhetvā diṭṭhiṃ ciraparicitaṃ te kassapādī vasī

Disvā rājā bhagavati tadā dhammaṃcarante tahiṃ,

Nikkaṅkho so sumadhurataraṃ pitvāna dhammāmataṃ

Saddhiṃ ekādasahi nahutehā’dophalaṃ pāpuṇi; ()

The king, seeing the Blessed One and those self-controlled ones headed by Kassapa practicing the Dhamma there, broke his long-held view. Then, free from doubt, having drunk the sweetest nectar of the Dhamma, he, along with eleven myriads of his retinue, attained the first fruit.

22.

22.

Laddhassāso darathavigamā hutvā mahopāsako

Svemebhikkhaṃ kasugatapamukho saṅghādhivāsessatu,

Āyācitvā namiya caraṇadvandāravindadvayaṃ

Paccuṭṭhāyā’gami sapariso so bimbisārābhidho; ()

Having gained assurance and become free from distress, he became a great lay follower. He requested, 'May the Sangha headed by the Sugata accept my alms tomorrow.' Having bowed to the pair of lotus-like feet, he, called Bimbisāra, then rose and departed with his retinue.

23.

23.

Pāto rājaggahanagarato koṭīnamaṭṭhārasa

Daṭṭhuṃ buddhaṃ nirupamasiriṃ laṭṭhīvane nāgarā,

Rāsibhūtā dutiyadivase ekassa bhikkhussa’pi

Sambādhattā nahipavisanokāso’si dighañjase; ()

At dawn, from the city of Rājagaha, eighteen crores of citizens came to see the Buddha of matchless glory in the Laṭṭhivana grove. On the second day, they were so crowded together that on the long path there was no space for even a single monk to enter.

24. [O 0.0398]

24.

Āvajjetvākimanabhimataṃ sakko nisinnāsanaṃ

Uṇhākāraṃ janayi’ti tadā hutvā navo māṇavo,

Maggo’tiṇṇo abhavi purato gāthāhi vatthuttayaṃ

Saṃvaṇṇetto bhavatu bhagavā māchintabhatto iti; ()

Then Sakka, reflecting, and seeing the seated assembly growing agitated, took the form of a young man. He entered the path before them, praising three matters in verses, thinking: 'May the Blessed One's meal not be interrupted!'

25.

25.

Dānaṃ datvā sugatapamukhassaṅghassa rājaggahaṃ

Sampattassā’vanipatipuraṃ aññatravatthuttayā,

Bhante sohaṃ kathamihavase velāya’velāyapi

Ākaṅkheyyaṃ tvadupagamituṃ iccevamārocayī; ()

Having offered alms to the Sangha headed by the Sugata, the king, upon arriving at his royal city in Rājagaha, announced thus: 'Venerable sir, how may I reside here, wishing to approach you at any time, suitable or unsuitable, apart from the three formal occasions?'

26. [O 0.0399]

26.

Sandacchāyaṃ vijanapavanaṃ yaṃ veḷudāyavhayaṃ

Uyyānaṃ me jitasuravanaṃ taṃ nātidurantike,

Sampūjento jinakaratale jālāvanaddhe hari-

Bhiṅkārenā’hariyaka salilaṃ pātesi taṃ patthivo; ()

That cool-shaded, solitary, and pleasant grove called Veḷudāya, my pleasure garden, which surpasses the groves of the devas, is not too far and not too near. Honoring the Conqueror's hand, adorned with a net-like pattern, the king poured water from a golden pitcher.

27.

27.

Lokālokācalataṭakaṭī viñjhāṭavīlocanā

Gaṅakgāpāṅakgā danakasikharibāhā tikuṭatthanā,

Ugghosentī jaladhivasanā puññānumodantiva

Sādhū’tyā’yaṃ vasumativadhū saṅkampi tasmiṃkhaṇe; ()

With the edge of the Lokāloka mountain as her waist, the Viñjhā forest as her eyes, the Ganges as the corners of her eyes, the peaks of Danaka as her arms, and Trikūṭa as her breasts, this lady earth, clad in the ocean, resounded as if rejoicing in the merit, saying 'Excellent!', and trembled at that moment.

28.

28.

Āramaṃ taṃ parama ruciraṃ satthā paṭiggaṇhiya

Dhammaṃ vatvā’gami parivuto bhikkhūhi vuṭṭhā’sanā,

Tasmiṃ kāle paramamamataṃ ye daḷhamittā ubho

Taṃ taṃ gāmaṃ nigamanagaraṃ anvesamānā’caruṃ; ()

The Teacher accepted that most delightful park. Having preached the Dhamma, he rose from his seat and departed, surrounded by the monks. At that time, those two firm friends, seeking the supreme deathless, wandered through villages, market towns, and cities in search of him.

29. [O 0.0400]

29.

Āhiṇḍantaṃ tahimanugharaṃ piṇḍāya tesva’ssaji-

Ttheraṃ disvā samitadamitaṃ vippo’patissā’bhidho,

Laddho’kāso padamanuvajaṃka sutvādvi gāthāpadaṃ

Sotāpanno’ bhavi vijaṭayaṃ saṃyojanāhaṃ tayaṃ; ()

The Brahmin named Upatissa saw the Elder Assaji, calmed and tamed, wandering there from house to house for alms. Obtaining an opportunity and following in his footsteps, he heard two lines of a verse and became a Stream-enterer, severing the three fetters.

30.

30.

Gāthaṃ sutvā amatamadhuraṃ taṃ sāriputto’ditaṃ

Moggallāno kaapanuditathāsaṃyojanānaṃ tayaṃ,

Pabbajjitvā tadubhaya janā netvā paribbājake

Patvārāmaṃ amataparamā satthāramārādhayuṃ; ()

Moggallāna, having heard that verse, sweet as the deathless, spoken by Sāriputta, likewise dispelled the three fetters. Both men then went forth, and leading the other wanderers, they reached the park and attended upon the Teacher, the supreme in the deathless.

31. [O 0.0401]

31.

Sattāhene’va’dhigami mahābhute pariggaṇhiya

Moggallāno vasi taditaraṃ maggattayaṃ tapphalaṃ,

Māsassa’ddhaṃ katavīriyavā suttaṃ parasso’ditaṃ

Sutvā dhammaṃ adhigami vasī taṃ dhammasenāpatī; ()

In just seven days, Moggallāna, having comprehended the great elements, became a master and attained the other three paths and their fruits. In half a month, being energetic, the General of the Dhamma, having heard the Dhamma in a discourse spoken to another, gained mastery.

32.

32.

Dhammassāmī karahaci ubho te sāvakānaṃ mamaṃ

Aggaṃ bhaddaṃ yugamiti ime pabyākarotto munī,

Aggaṭṭhāne purimacaritaṃ ñatvā patiṭṭhāpayī

Sampinento sakalaparisaṃ cando’va kundāṭaviṃ; ()

The Lord of the Dhamma, the Sage, at a certain time declared: 'These two disciples of mine are the foremost, excellent pair.' Knowing their past conduct, he established them in the highest rank, delighting the whole assembly as the moon delights a jasmine grove.

33.

33.

Sutvā suddhodananarapati putto mamaṃ sampati

Buddho hutvā padahiya ciraṃ nissāya rājaggahaṃ,

Uttārento sakalajanataṃ saṃsārakantārato

Saṃvattetto vasati sivadaṃ saddhammacakkaṃiti; ()

King Suddhodana heard: 'My son, having striven for a long time, has now become a Buddha and is dwelling near Rājagaha. He is leading all people across the wilderness of saṃsāra, turning the Wheel of the True Dhamma which bestows security.'

34. [O 0.0402]

34.

Jiṇṇovuddho pariṇatavayappatto’ hamasmyā dhunā

Jīvantoyevahi mamasutaṃ icchāmi daṭṭhuṃ bhaṇe,

Evaṃvatvā’dhikadasasataṃ ekaṃ amaccaṃ tahiṃ

Uyyojesi nayanavisayaṃka puttaṃ karohīti me; ()

'I am now aged, old, and have reached the end of my years. While still alive, I wish to see my son,' he said. So saying, he dispatched a minister with a retinue of a thousand, saying: 'Bring my son into my range of sight.'

35.

35.

Gantvā’macco catuparisatiṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇantaṃjinaṃ

Disvā baddhañjali sapariso tatre’kamantaṃ ṭhito,

Sutvādhammaṃ paramamadhuraṃ patvā’ggamaggapphalaṃ

Pabbajjitvā hadayakamalaṃ kasaṅkocayī rājino; ()

The minister went and saw the Victor preaching the Dhamma to the fourfold assembly. With his retinue, he stood to one side with hands clasped in reverence. Having heard the supremely sweet Dhamma and attained the highest path and fruit, he went forth, causing the lotus-heart of the king to contract.

36.

36.

Aṭṭhakkhattuṃ puna saparise pāhesi rājāpare

Aṭṭhā’macce tathariva gatā’maccā napaccā’gatā,

Pabbajjitvā adhigataphalā tecā’pi raññomanaṃ

Nā’rādhesuṃ sunisitadhiyā sañchintasaṃyojanā; ()

Eight more times the king sent eight other ministers with their retinues. The ministers who went likewise did not return. They too, having gone forth and attained the fruit, with their fetters severed by sharp wisdom, did not fulfill the king’s wish.

37. [O 0.0403]

37.

Dujjāno me maraṇasamayo jiṇṇo’smi tātā’dhunā

Tasmā puttaṃ nayanavisayaṃ kātuṃ samattho’sikiṃ,

Evaṃ vatvā kapuna saparisaṃ sokāphadāyiṃ tahiṃ

Dinnokāsaṃ pahiṇi sacivaṃ pabbajjituṃ bhubhujo; ()

'The time of my death is hard to know; I am now aged, dear one. Therefore, are you able to bring my son into my sight?' So saying, the grief-stricken king sent his minister with a retinue, having given him permission to go forth.

38.

38.

Patvā’rāmaṃ parivutajano saccaddaseno’ditaṃ

Sutvā’macco thiramati catussaccā’nupubbikathaṃ,

Pabbajjitvā hatabhavabhayo hutvāna khīṇāsavo

Aggaṭṭhānaṃ paṭilabhi kulappāsādikānaṃ idha; ()

Arriving at the park with his retinue, the firm-minded minister heard the gradual exposition on the Four Noble Truths spoken by the Seer of Truth. Having gone forth, with the fear of existence destroyed, he became an Arahant and attained here the foremost place among those who inspire confidence in their families.

39. [O 0.0404]

39.

Bārāṇasyaṃ kesipatanato pattassa rājaggahaṃ

Sambuddhassā’dhikadinakatī pañcevamāsā’ bhavuṃ,

Hemantā’tusamayavigamā sante vasante maṇi-

Bhusākārā upavanavadhū cūtaṅkurā’ laṅkaruṃ; ()

For the Sambuddha who had come to Rājagaha from Isipatana in Bārāṇasī, five months and some days had passed. With the passing of the winter season, in the gentle spring, the mango shoots, like jewel ornaments, adorned the lady of the grove.

40.

40.

Kālaṃ ñatvā kapilanagaraṃ kālaññuno satthuno

Gantuṃ kālo’yamiti adhunā so kāludāyi vasī,

Saṃvaṇṇento gamanasamayaṃ kātuṃ alaṃ saṅgahaṃ

Ñātinantī sumadhurasaro gāthābhigāyī puthu; ()

That ascetic Kāludāyi, knowing that now was the time for the Teacher, the knower of time, to go to Kapilapura, describing the season for the journey, able to render service to his kinsmen, and delighting them with a very sweet voice, sang many verses.

41.

41.

Mandaṃmandaṃ surabhipavano sito’dhunā vāyati

Pupphākiṇṇā vipinaviṭapī mattālimālākulā,

Gaṅgāvāpī vimalasalīlā samphullakañjuppalā

Sāyaṃka pāto ahani vivaṭā sabbādisā pākaṭā; ()

Slowly, slowly the fragrant, cool breeze now blows. The forest trees, strewn with flowers, are teeming with swarms of intoxicated bees. The river pools, with their clear water, are blooming with lotuses and water lilies. In the evening and the morning, all directions are open and clear.

42. [O 0.0405]

42.

Bhante magge navadalasikhā jālo’jjalā mañjarī-

Bhasmacchannā bhamaravisaraddhumandhakārā bhusaṃ,

Jhāpennā’pe’tarahi virahī samphullacūtāṭavi-

Dāvaggī te lavamapi manotāpāya vattanti kiṃ; ()

Venerable sir, on the road, the tips of new leaves blaze like flames; the flower clusters, covered with pollen-ash, are greatly darkened by swarms of bees like smoke. Even now, do the forest fires of the blooming mango groves, which burn those who are separated, cause even a little mental affliction to you?

43.

43.

Kāmandhānaṃ bhadayamadhunā socāpayattā bhusaṃ

Sākhacchinnā vigalitadalā magge asokaddumā,

Aññatrā’pī vanacaravadhū pādappahārā’turaṃ

Tatvante te karakisalayassobhaṃka virūḷhaṅkurā; ()

Now greatly causing sorrow to the hearts of those blinded by lust, the asoka trees on the road have their branches broken and their leaves fallen. Elsewhere too, though afflicted by the foot-strikes of forest-dwelling women, at their tips fresh shoots have sprouted, beautiful with tender leaves like hands.

44. [O 0.0406]

44.

Pitvā cutaddūmaphalarasaṃ sammattapuṅkokilā

Saṃkujante sarasamadhuraṃ vetāḷikā’va’ñjase,

Seṇībhutā janapadavadhū te pādapīṭhe muni

Sampūjetuṃ navasarasije hiyyo’vinante dhunā; ()

Having drunk the juice of the fruit of the mango and other trees, the intoxicated male cuckoos sing sweetly and melodiously, truly like bards. The village women, arrayed in rows to worship you, O Sage, at your footstool with fresh lotuses, who yesterday did not pay homage, now do so.

45.

45.

Āmulaggā dalitaviṭapi pupphañjalihakā’dhunā

Āgacchantaṃ tvamahimahituṃ saṃdissare’vo’natā,

Vātoddhutā bhamaramukharā kiñjakkhapuñjā’ñjase

Ātatvante tavaparimukhe sovaṇṇasaṅkhassiriṃ; ()

From root to tip, the trees with their bursting branches now appear as if with hands full of floral offerings, bowed down to honor you, the great one, as you approach. Shaken by the wind and noisy with bees, masses of pollen truly spread around your face the splendor of a golden conch.

46. [O 0.0407]

46.

Bhante antokalalasalilāvāsena kālaṃ ciraṃ

Ambhojānaṃ mukulavikatī siteti’vā’kuñcitā,

Esantī’ve’tarahi saraṇaṃ te pādabhaddāsane

Uggacchante pajahiya manotāpaṃ vasantātapaṃ; ()

Venerable Sir, from dwelling for a long time within the muddy water, the lotus buds, though white, are contracted and unbloomed. Now, as if seeking refuge at your blessed foot-seat, they rise up, having abandoned their mental affliction and the heat of spring.

47.

47.

Pātheyya’mbhoruhakuvalayā’laṅkāratuṇḍā kalaṃ

Saṅkujantī pavanapadaviṃ uḍḍīyamānā’dhunā,

Haṃsasseṇika sirasi vajato te bhuyate kiṅkiṇi-

Ghosākiṇṇaṃ kusumavikaticchannaṃ vitānaṃ yathā; ()

Now, a line of swans, flying along the path of the wind, carrying in their beaks lotuses and water-lilies as provisions for the journey, and singing sweetly, becomes for you, as you go, a canopy above your head, as if covered with blooming flowers and filled with the sound of tinkling bells.

48.

48.

Sampūjenti ratanakanakālaṅkārabhārañjalī

Maggo’tiṇṇā vanasuravadhū te lājavuṭṭhīhi’va,

Kiñjakkhehi caraṇayugalaṃ kamandātilandolitā

Vallī bhiṅgāvalikisalayā’laṅkārasākhāvalī; ()

The forest goddesses, having descended onto the path, honor you with hands full of the weight of jewel and gold ornaments, as if with showers of parched grain. The greatly swaying vines, adorned with rows of bees, tender shoots, and branches, worship your pair of feet with pollen.

49. [O 0.0408]

49.

Sammārūḷho pavanaturagaṃ kāmākaro mañjari-

Tuṇiresū madhukarasare sandhānayanto’dhunā,

Campeyyādīkusumakalikāsannāhasambhāsuro

Naṭṭho loko bahujanamanosaṅakgāma mogāhati;()

Kāma, the maker of desire, having well mounted the horse of the wind, now fitting arrows of bees from quivers of flower-clusters, resplendent with armor made of Champaka and other flower buds, plunges the lost world into the battle of the minds of many people.

50.

50.

Yasmā suddhodananarapabhu ādiccavaṃsaddhajo

Jiṇṇo vuddho mamihapahiṇi tvaṃ daṭṭhukāmo pitā,

Tasmā bhante kapilanagaraṃ veneyyasattākaraṃ

Kantvā rañño hadayamakulaṃ bodhetu sokākulaṃ; ()

Since King Suddhodana, the banner of the solar lineage, old and aged, my father, longing to see you, sent me here, therefore, Venerable Sir, having gone to the city of Kapilavatthu, a mine of beings to be trained, awaken the king's heart-bud, which is afflicted with sorrow.

51. [O 0.0409]

51.

Sādhu’dāyi savisayamahaṃ patvā narādhissaraṃ

Uttāreyyaṃ pitaramitare bandhū’pi dukkhaṇṇavā,

Evaṃvatvā radanakira ṇālaṅkārabimbādharo

Dhammassāmiparivutavasīrājaggahānikkhami; ()

“Good, Udāyi. Having reached my own realm and the lord of men, I shall lead my father and other relatives across from the ocean of suffering.” Having spoken thus, he whose bimba-like lips were adorned with the rays from his teeth, the Master, surrounded by those with self-mastery, departed from Rājagaha.

52.

52.

Patvā rañño uparibhavanaṃ sokāludāyi’ddhiyā

Bhuttā’hāro tadupagamanaṃ atvāha mārocayaṃ,

Sambuddhatthaṃ pituru’pahaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃka pakaṭiggaṇhiya

Assāsento vajati nabhasā sokākulaṃtaṃ kulaṃ; ()

That Kāludāyi, having reached the king's upper palace by psychic power and eaten the meal, announced his approach. The Buddha, having openly accepted the alms brought by his father, went through the sky, comforting that family afflicted with sorrow.

53.

53.

Taṃ bhuñjanto divasadivase so yojanaṃ yojanaṃ

Saṅkhepento paramakaruṇārāmāya sañcodito,

Netvā khīṇāsavayativare vīsaṃ sahassaṃ jino

Lakkhīvāsaṃ kapilanagaraṃ māsehidvīho’tari; ()

Eating that food day by day, shortening his journey league by league, urged on by his delight in supreme compassion, the Victor, leading twenty thousand excellent ascetics whose cankers were destroyed, arrived at Kapilapura, the abode of fortune, in two months.

54. [O 0.0410]

54.

Nānuppatte bhagavati puraṃ no ñātiseṭṭhaṃ kuhiṃ

Passissāmā’tya’jahitamanokotuhaḷā sākiyā,

Ārāmoyanaṃ vijanapavano nigrodhasakkassa taṃ-

Sāruppoti tahimabhinave senāsane māpayuṃ; ()

When the Blessed One had not yet arrived in the city, the Sakyans, their mental curiosity unabated, wondered, “Where shall we see our foremost kinsman?” Thinking, “This Nigrodha park of the Sakyans, with its secluded breezes, is suitable for him,” they had a new dwelling prepared there.

55.

55.

Paccuggantvā surabhikusumākiṇṇañjaliha’ñjase

Āgacchantaṃ sumahakiya jinaṃ rājiddhiyā’laṅkate,

Ketuggāhe daharadahare katvā kumāre pure

Rājā’maccā paramaruciraṃ ārāma motārayuṃ; ()

Having gone forth to meet the approaching Victor, with hands clasped and filled with fragrant flowers, the king and his ministers, adorned with great royal splendor, having made the very young princes into banner-bearers in the city, conducted the supremely radiant one to the park.

56. [O 0.0411]

56.

Pallaṅkeno’dayagirisire cando’va tārāvuto

Nānākhiṇāsavaparivuto paññattabuddhāsane,

Āsino’yaṃ manakumuduniṃ sakyānamunniddayaṃ

Nissoko so muni parihari sokandhakāraṃ pitu; ()

Seated cross-legged on the prepared Buddha-seat, like the moon surrounded by stars on the peak of the sunrise mountain, surrounded by various ones whose cankers were destroyed, this one sat, causing the water-lilies of the Sakyans' minds to open. That sorrowless Sage dispelled the darkness of his father's sorrow.

57.

57.

Siddhattho’yaṃ paramadaharo amhehi vuddhā mayaṃ

Jāmātā’yaṃbhavati tanujo nattānujo no iti,

Mānatthaddhā daharadahare sakyā kumāre’bravuṃ

Tumhegantvā paṇamatha jinaṃ vo piṭṭhitāhomै no; ()

“This Siddhattha is very young, while we are elders. He is our son-in-law, our son, our grandson, our younger brother.” Thus, stiff with pride, the Sakyans spoke to the very young princes, “You go and pay homage to the Victor; we will be behind you.”

58.

58.

Āvajjetvā sakalaparisaṃ ñatvā tadajjhāsayaṃ

Mānummattā vibhavamadirāmattā ime khattiyā,

Muddhābaddhañjalikisalayā yasmā navandanti maṃ

Vandāpetuṃ alamiti tato jhānaṃ samāpajjiya; ()

Having adverted to the entire assembly and known their disposition, he thought: “These Khattiyas, maddened by pride, drunk with the wine of power, do not worship me, though their tender-shoot-like hands are clasped on their heads. It is fitting to make them worship me.” Thereupon, having entered meditative absorption, he performed the miracle.

59. [O 0.0412]

59.

Pattā’bhiñño nijapadarajoraṃsihi sañcumbite

Tesaṃ cūḷāmaṇigirisire sambuddhasuro lasaṃ,

Saṃdassento yamakamasamaṃ mānandhakāraṃ haraṃ

Bodhāpesi vadanakamale gaṇḍambamūle yathā; ()

Having attained higher knowledge, while their mountain-peak-like crest-jewels were being kissed by the rays from the dust of his own feet, the shining Perfectly Enlightened One, like a god, displaying the unequalled Twin Miracle and dispelling the darkness of pride, caused the lotuses of their faces to bloom, as he had done at the foot of the Gaṇḍamba tree.

60.

60.

Disvā suddhodananaravaro taṃ pāṭihīraṃ varaṃ

Pādambhoje paṇami sirasā ānandabhāronato,

Cakkaṅkālaṅkatapadarajo samphuṭṭhamuddhāñjali

Rājaññānaṃ kamalakalikāsaṇḍassiriṃ vyākaruṃ; ()

Seeing that supreme marvel, the excellent man, King Suddhodana, bent low by the weight of joy, bowed his head to the lotus feet. His clasped hands on his head were touched by the dust from the feet adorned with the wheel-mark. The kinsmen then manifested the splendor of a cluster of lotus buds.

61. [O 0.0413]

61.

Sañjhāmeghāvaliparivuto suroriva’tthācalaṃ

Khamhā bhaddāsanamavatarī sovaṇṇavaṇṇo jino,

Subabhujiñche nayanabarihī keḷāyanaṃ pokkhara-

Vassaṃ vassi nijanakharuciṃ tesaṃ samāje sati; ()

Like the sun on the western mountain surrounded by a line of evening clouds, the golden-hued Victor descended from the sky onto the auspicious seat. Then, in their assembly, he playfully rained a lotus-rain, a shower having the radiance of his own fingernails.

62.

62.

Sutvā vuttaṃ purimacaritaṃ vessantarākhyaṃ tato

Pakkantānaṃ phusiya sirasā tappādacūḷāmaṇiṃ,

Bhante bhikkhaṃ sugatapamukho saṅghodhivāsetu no

Icce’kopi paṭhamadivase nākāsi ajjhesanaṃ; ()

Then, having heard the discourse on his former conduct, the Vessantara Jātaka, of those who departed after touching the crest-jewel of his feet with their heads, not even one made this request on the first day: “Venerable Sir, may the Sangha with the Sugata at its head accept our alms.”

63.

63.

Nānākhīṇāsavaparivuto lokānukampāparo

Lokādhiso dutiyadivase āciṇṇakappārahaṃ,

Sambuddhānaṃ kapilanagare pāto’va lakhyākare

Hīnukkaṭṭhaṃ kulamavijahaṃ piṇḍāya sampāvisi; ()

Surrounded by various ones whose cankers were destroyed, intent on compassion for the world, the Lord of the World, on the second day, in the morning, in Kapilapura, the mine of fortune, entered for alms-food in keeping with the custom of the Buddhas, not avoiding any family, whether low or high.

64. [O 0.0414]

64.

Āhiṇḍattaṃ tahimanugharaṃ piṇḍāya santindriyaṃ

Satthāraṃ taṃ nirupamasiriṃ chabbaṇṇaraṃsujjalaṃ,

Pāsādaṭṭhā’nimisanayanambhojehi sampūjayuṃ

Ugghāṭetvā harimaṇimayaṃ jālāvaliṃ nāgarā; ()

The citizens, standing on their palace terraces, having opened their rows of lattices made of emeralds, worshipped with unblinking lotus-eyes that Teacher as he wandered there from house to house for alms—he of tranquil senses, of incomparable splendor, blazing with six-colored rays.

65.

65.

Ohāretvā kusumasurabhīsaṅkhārasambhāvite

Kese massuṃ rajanamalinaṃ kāsāvavatthaṃ kharaṃ,

Acchādetvā kapaṇapuriso’va’yyo gahetvā sīḷā

Pattaṃ patto kapilanagaraṃ pakiṇḍāya āhiṇḍati; ()

This noble one, having cast off his hair and beard that were once honored with fragrant preparations, and having put on a rough saffron robe soiled with dust, now, like a wretched man, has taken up a stone bowl and wanders through Kapilapura for alms.

66. [O 0.0415]

66.

Vuttantaṃ taṃ savaṇakaṭukaṃ sutvāna bimbādharā

Bimbādevī marakatasiḷājālantarā vithiyaṃ,

Āhiṇḍantaṃ parivutagaṇaṃ mattebhagāmiṃ jitaṃ

Olokentī nayanamaṇike assūhi sampūrayi; ()

Having heard that news, harsh to the ear, Bimbādevī, her lips like bimba fruit, from behind an emerald stone lattice, looked upon the Victor wandering in the street, surrounded by his retinue, with the gait of a lordly elephant in rut, and filled her jewel-like eyes with tears.

67.

67.

Cumbanti sātanujaratanaṃ tandassanabyāvaṭā’-

Sityā’nubyañjanavilasitaṃ byāmappabhālaṅkataṃ,

Rūpaṃ rūpassiri nirupamaṃ saṅgāyi gāthaṭṭhakaṃ

Saṃvaṇṇetvā caraṇatalato yāva’ssa uṇhisato; ()

Kissing her jewel of a son, she, being occupied with seeing him—his form shining with the major and minor marks, adorned with a fathom-wide halo, an incomparable splendor of beauty—sang a set of eight verses, describing him from the soles of his feet up to his cranial protuberance.

68.

68.

Īsaṃ kālaṃ alasagamanaṃ sā kālahaṃsopakari

Oropenti abhinavakucandā’tibhārāturā,

Gantvā sīghaṃ khaḷitavacatā putto mahārāja te

Piṇḍāya’smiṃ carati nagare rājānamiccabruvi; ()

For a short while, she, like a royal swan, delayed her slow departure, distressed by the great weight of her newly developed breasts. Having gone quickly, with faltering speech, she said to the king: “Great king, your son wanders for alms in this city.”

69. [O 0.0416]

69.

Rājā senāparivutasamo tejonubhāvādinā

Taṃ sutvāṃ’se sukhumavasanaṃ katvā navaṃsāṭakaṃ,

Acchādetvā nihitamakuṭo nikkhittakhaggo bhusaṃ

Lajjāpanno tuvaṭatuvaṭaṃ gantvā tadagge ṭhito; ()

The king, equal to his army in majesty and power, having heard that, placed a fine garment and a new shawl on his shoulder. Having covered himself, with his crown laid aside and his sword cast down, greatly ashamed, he hurried quickly and stood before him.

70.

70.

Koṭṭhagārānya’pi pitukule rittāni kimmaññasi

Kasmā lajjāpayasi pitaraṃ tvaṃ bhānuvaṃsubbhavo,

Bhante tuyhaṃ pakarivutavasīsaṅghassi’to bhojanaṃ

Mā kapiṇḍāyā’cari anudinaṃ dajjeyya miccabruvi; ()

“Do you think the storehouses in your father’s family are empty? Why do you shame your father, you who are born of the solar lineage? Venerable Sir, for the community of monks under your care, I shall provide food from here. Do not wander for alms daily,” thus he spoke.

71. [O 0.0417]

71.

Tuyhaṃ vaṃso anariyapado ādiccavaṃso siyā

Mayhaṃ vaṃso sadariyapado sambuddhavaṃso siyā,

Asmiṃvaṃse anuvicaraṇaṃ piṇḍattha manvālayaṃ

Cārittaṃ bhopurimasugatā’ciṇṇanti kavatvā jino; ()

“Your lineage, the solar dynasty, is of an ignoble path; my lineage, the lineage of the Buddhas, is of the noble path. In this lineage, wandering for alms without attachment is the conduct practiced by former Sugatas,” thus spoke the Victor.

72.

72.

Uttiṭṭhādiṃ avadi kasugamaṃ gāthaṃ ṭhito vīthiyaṃ

Sotāpanto’vanipati bhavī sotāvadhānena so,

Gāthādhammaṃ suṇiya madhuraṃ dhammaṃcare’tyā’dikaṃ

Patto maggaṃ dutiyamavīraṃ dhammānudhammaṃ caraṃ; ()

Standing in the street, the Sugata spoke a verse easy to understand, beginning with “Arise.” The king, destined to be a Stream-enterer, listened attentively. Having heard the sweet verse of the Dhamma, beginning with “Practice the Dhamma,” he attained the second path, practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma.

73.

73.

Sutvā rājā cariyamaparaṃ yo dhammapālavhayaṃ

Patto maggaṃ tatiyamakhilaṃ kāmālayaṃ cālayaṃ,

Setacchattu’llasitasayane’nuṭṭhānaseyyu’pago

Saṅkhārānaṃ visadamatiyā yo lakkhaṇaṃ sammasi; ()

Hearing of the further teaching, the king, that protector of the Dhamma, attained the third path, shaking entirely the abode of lust. Under a white umbrella on his splendid bed, he attained the posture of not rising and with clear understanding contemplated the characteristics of conditioned things.

74. [O 0.0418]

74.

Viddhaṃsetvā namuviparisaṃ saṃkelasamārādikaṃ

Suro ramhāvanamiva’sinā so aggamaggāsinā,

Tuṭṭho maggapphalasukhasudhāpānena verisame

Pañcakkhandhe vijaya malbhī nibbānarajjassiriṃ; ()

Like a hero felling a plantain grove with a sword, he, with the sword of the supreme path, destroyed the assembly of Namuci, the defilements, and Māra. Delighted by drinking the nectar of the bliss of path and fruit, he conquered the five aggregates, which are like enemies, and attained the glory of the kingdom of Nibbāna.

75.

75.

Āropetvā uparibhavanaṃ pattaṃ gahetvā tato

Rājā saṅghaṃ sugatapamukhaṃ khajjena bhojjena ca,

Santappetvā puna sapariso nīce nisajjāsane

Sārānīyaṃ kathayamavasi sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ; ()

The king, having taken the bowl and led them up to the upper chamber, then satisfied the Sangha, headed by the Sugata, with food both hard and soft. Having satisfied them, he and his retinue again sat down on low seats. The Buddha then concluded by speaking agreeable and joy-inspiring words.

76.

76.

Itthāgāraṃ hadayasarasimajjhe nimuggatthana-

Haṃsaṃ dinānanasarasijaṃ soke’ṇatāpeniva,

Buddhaṃ baddhañjaliharasirokumbhehi sampūjayī

Taṃ vātabbhāhataharilatālīlaṃ jagāmo’nataṃ; ()

The women of the inner chamber, like swans with breasts submerged in the lake of the heart, and like lotuses with faces withered by the sun-like heat of sorrow, worshipped the Buddha with reverently folded hands and with heads held high like water pots. They approached him, bowing with the grace of a tender creeper struck by the wind.

77. [O 0.0419]

77.

Antogabbhe nayanasalalaṃ samapuñchamānā jinaṃ

Bimbādevī saparijanatāvyāpāritā vandituṃ,

Appatvā me yadiguṇadhanaṃ attha’yyaputto sayaṃ

Taṃ kamaṃ daṭṭhuṃ nanupavisatī’tve’vaṃ vadantī ṭhitā; ()

In the inner chamber, wiping tears from her eyes, Bimbādevī, though urged by her retinue to pay homage to the Conqueror, stood speaking thus: “If my noble son, that treasure of virtues, does not come to me himself, will he not then enter to see this state of mine?”

78.

78.

Raññā saddhiṃ purisanisaho tāyindirāmandiraṃ

Antogabbhaṃ maṇigaṇapahābhinnandhakāraṃsadā,

Ādāya’ggaṃ yatipatiyugaṃ patvā’cchi bhaddāsane

Paññatte so’dayagirisire bālaṃsumālī yathā; ()

With the king, the bull among men reached that Indra-like abode, the inner chamber, which always dispelled darkness with the radiance of its many jewels. Taking with him the two chief disciples, he approached and sat upon the excellent seat that was prepared, like the morning sun upon the summit of the Udaya mountain.

79. [O 0.0420]

79.

Disvā pīnatthanabharanatā sā rājadhītā jinaṃ

Patvā mālā kanakaratanālaṅkārahīnā lahuṃ,

Haṃsimaññe sarasijavanaṃ pāde yathājjhāsayaṃ

Sañcumbantī paṇami sirasā ādāyagopphadvayaṃ; ()

Seeing the Conqueror, that princess, bent by the burden of her full breasts, quickly approached him, devoid of garlands and ornaments of gold and jewels. As a swan might enter a lotus grove, she kissed his feet according to her heart's inclination, bowed her head, and took hold of both his ankles.

80.

80.

Pāsāda’ntovarakasarasi dhammillasevālake

Omujjantī nijabhujalatālīlātaraṅgākule,

Nāthassa’ṅghītalanakhasikhākantippabandhāmbhasi

Laddhassāsā ciravirahajaṃ tāpaṃ vinodesi sā; ()

Immersing herself in the excellent lake within the palace, where her braided hair was like algae and which was stirred with waves like the playful movements of her creeper-like arms—that is, in the water of the continuous radiance from the tips of the nails on the Lord's feet—she found consolation and dispelled the torment born of long separation.

81.

81.

Sutvā nesā kanakaratanā’saṃdhāraṇaṃ dhāraṇaṃ

Kāsāvānaṃ tavahiridhanā’vissajjanaṃ sajjanaṃ,

Nā’jjhācāre anabhiramaṇaṃ uccāsane cā’sane

Rājā’voca tvamanukurute snehodayā’hodayā; ()

Hearing that she did not wear gold and jewels, but wore saffron-colored robes; that she did not abandon the wealth of modesty nor her association with the good; that she took no delight in misconduct, nor in high and lofty seats, the king said: “You imitate him out of the arising of love.”

82. [O 0.0421]

82.

Sutvā tassāniravadhiguṇādhārāya’nūnaṃ guṇaṃ

Āvīkatvā’gami bhavapaṭicchannāpadānaṃ jino,

Netvā gehappavisanakaraggāhā’bhisekussave

Saṃvattante dutiyadivase nandākhyarājatrajaṃ; ()

Having heard the excellent virtues of her who was a vessel of limitless virtue, the Conqueror came and revealed a hidden story of a past life. Then, on the second day, while the festival for the house-entering, marriage, and consecration of the royal prince named Nanda was taking place, the Buddha led him away.

83.

83.

Gacchanto’pī saha bhagavatā so pañcakalyāṇiyā

Sīghaṃ jālaṃ vivariya thiyā vīthiṃ vilokentiyā,

Bhaṅgāpāṅgāyatabhujalatāsaṅkaḍḍhitabbhantaro

Pattaṃ bhante haratha vacanaṃ bhatyā na taṃ vyākari; ()

Even as he went along with the Blessed One, his heart was drawn in by the woman of fivefold beauty, who quickly opened the lattice and gazed down the street with sidelong glances and long, creeper-like arms. The Blessed One gave him the bowl to carry, but he, thinking of her words, did not respond.

84. [O 0.0422]

84.

Pabbājetvā visayamadirāmattāya tassā gīraṃ

Sutvā nandāpahanahadayaṃ nandaṃ narindatrajaṃ,

Icchāpetvā kakuṭacaraṇidibbaccharāliṅgane

Ñāyenā’nuttarasukhamahārajje patiṭṭhāpayī; ()

Having ordained Nanda, the king's son, whose heart was carried away by his beloved who was intoxicated with the wine of sensual pleasure, the Buddha, by causing him to desire the embrace of divine nymphs with partridge-like feet, rightly established him in the great sovereignty of unsurpassed bliss.

85.

85.

Bimbādevi sukhaparibhataṃ kīḷāparaṃ rāhulaṃ

Āliṅgitvā tanujaratanaṃ sā sattame vāsare,

Ugghaṭetvā ratanakhacitaṃ jālaṃ vimānodare

Āgacchantaṃ purisatisabhaṃ nijjhāyamānā ṭhitā; ()

On the seventh day, Bimbādevī, embracing Rāhula, her jewel of a son, who was filled with happiness and devoted to play, opened the jewel-studded lattice in the palace chamber and stood gazing at that bull among men as he approached.

86.

86.

Nānākūṭācalavalayito devindacāpākulo

Āgacchanto kanakasikharīrājāka yathā jaṅgamo,

Tatā khīṇāsavaparivuto jabbaṇṇabhānujjalo

Eso tuyhaṃ naraharika pitā iccākaha pakassāhi naṃ; ()

Resplendent with a rainbow-like aura and encircled by his monks as by many-peaked mountains, approaching like a moving king of golden-peaked mountains; surrounded by those who have destroyed the taints, radiant with the splendor of burnished gold—'This, O lion among men, is your father,' she said. 'Go and approach him.'

87. [O 0.0423]

87.

Etassā’suṃ vividhanidhayo puññānubhāvuṭṭhitā

Nāhaṃja kapakassāma’bhigamanato paṭṭhāya tekhonidhī,

Bhūsāpetvā tanujaratanaṃ sā sattavassāyukaṃ

Yācassū’ti pahiṇi pituno ñattaṃ dhanaṃ pettikaṃ; ()

“His various treasures arose from the power of his merit. I cannot make known those treasures that have been his since his arrival.” Thinking thus, she adorned her jewel of a son, who was seven years of age, and sent him to his father, saying, “Go, ask for your paternal inheritance.”

88.

88.

Uppādetvā pitari balavaṃ pemaṃ jalevu’ppalaṃ

Puttotyā’haṃ tvamasijanako chāyā’pi teme sukhā,

Aḍhāse’vaṃ lapitavacano vuṭṭhāya bhaddāsanā

Bhuttāhāroka parivutavasi gantuṃ jinocā’rabhī; ()

Arousing strong affection in his father, like a lotus in water, he said, “I am your son, and you are my father; even your shadow is pleasant to me.” Thus addressed, the Conqueror, having finished his meal, rose from his excellent seat and, as master of his retinue, prepared to depart.

89.

89.

Dāyajjaṃ me samaṇa dadataṃ atthodhanenā’ti me

Yācaṃ yācaṃ jinamanuvajaṃ sāraṅgarājakkamaṃ,

Sīhacchāporiva bhagavato daḷhaṃ surattaṅgulī-

Mālāyālaṅkari bhujalataṃ bhogindabhogāyataṃ; ()

Begging again and again, “Give me my inheritance, ascetic; I have need of wealth,” he followed the Conqueror with the gait of a king of deer. Like a lion cub, he adorned the Blessed One's creeper-like arm, long as the coil of a serpent-king, with a garland of his firm, reddish fingers.

90. [O 0.0424]

90.

Saṃyācannaṃ vibhava kamanugaṃka vaṭṭānugaṃ rāhulaṃ

Pabbājetvā’riyadhananidhiṃdemīti cintāparo,

Patvā’rāmaṃ ajahitasuto saddhammarājā imaṃ

Pabbājehi’tya’vadi sumukhaṃ tvaṃ dhammasenāpati; ()

Regarding Rāhula, who was asking for worldly wealth and following the round of existence, the Buddha thought, 'Having ordained him, I shall give him the treasure of the noble wealth.' The King of the True Dhamma, not leaving his son behind, reached the monastery and said to the fair-faced General of the Dhamma, “You are to ordain him.”

91.

91.

Chetvā nīluppaladalamuduṃ cūḷākalāpaṃ mahā-

Moggallāno kavasi abhinavaṃ kāsāvamacchādayī,

Tasso’vādaṃ akari dhutavā thero mahākassapo

Pabbājesi tanujaratanaṃ taṃ sāriputto vasi; ()

Having cut off his topknot, soft as a dark-blue lotus petal, the great Moggallāna covered him with a new saffron robe. The elder Mahākassapa, an expert in ascetic practices, gave him instruction. Sāriputta, the master, ordained that jewel of a son.

92. [O 0.0425]

92.

Sikkhākāmo aparasamaye thero mahārāhulo-

Vādaṃ sutvā’dhikataraguṇaṃ sampāpuṇī rāhulo,

Sutvā kasuttaṃ puna taditaraṃ sikkhāgarūnaṃ garu-

Ṭṭhānaṃ patto tibhavamatari patvā’ggamaggapphalaṃ;Ka ()

Desiring training, at a later time, the elder Rāhula, having heard the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, attained even higher qualities. Having then heard the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta and other discourses, he reached the state of being a teacher to the teachers, crossed the three realms of existence, and attained the supreme path and its fruit.

93.

93.

Tasmiṃ suddhodananaravaro pabbajjite nattari

Ajjhogāḷho ravikuladhajonissīmasokaṇṇave,

Dinno’kāsaṃ kamapitanayaṃ mātāpitūhā’yatiṃ

Pabbājeyyuṃ alamitivaraṃ saṃyāci vosāvakā; ()

When his grandson was ordained, the noble king Suddhodana, the banner of the solar dynasty, was plunged into a boundless ocean of sorrow. He requested this boon from the disciples: 'In the future, may a son not be ordained without the permission of his mother and father.'

94.

94.

Rañño datvā varamati varaṃ bhuttāsano āsanā-

Vuṭṭhāya’ntobhavanavanato nikkhamma mandānilaṃ,

Rukkhacchāyāviraḷasarasītīraṃ vivekakkhamaṃ

Sītaṃ sitabbanamavasarī chaddantadantī’vaso; ()

Having granted the king that excellent boon, having eaten and risen from his seat, he departed from the inner palace. He entered the cool, sparsely-shaded shore of a lake, a place fit for seclusion, like a six-tusked elephant.

95. [O 0.0426]

95.

Tasmiṃkāle gahapatikule jāto mahāseṭṭhipi

Patto rājaggahapuravaraṃ saddho sudattābhidho,

Buddhoka hutvā yamadhivasate’tya’ssosi suddhodanī

Paccūsasmiṃ amaravivaṭadvārena tatrā’gamā; ()

At that time, a great merchant named Sudatta, faithful, born into a householder's family, had reached the excellent city of Rājagaha. He heard, 'The son of Suddhodana, having become the Buddha, is dwelling there,' and at dawn, as if through a gate opened by devas, he went there.

96.

96.

Appetvā’ṅakghīratanaphalake khittañjalīmañjariṃ

Bhatyācūḷārajatakalasaṃ cittappasādāvahanaṃ,

Dhammaṃ sutvā paṭhamadivase laddhādimaggapphalo

Dānaṃ datvā sugatapamukhe saṅghe sudattodhanī; ()

Placing his hands, folded like a cluster of blossoms, upon the jewel-slab of the Buddha's feet, with devotion that brought clarity to his mind, he heard the Dhamma on the first day and attained the fruit of the first path. Then the wealthy Sudatta gave an offering to the Sangha with the Sugata at its head.

97. [O 0.0427]

97.

Bhante lakkhīkamakalamalakā saṅkāsamatthāya no

Iddhaṃ phakhītaṃ sujanabhajitaṃ sāvatthisaṅkhaṃ puraṃ,

Dhammassāmi vajatu karuṇāchāyāsakahāyo lahuṃ

Laddhassāso savisayamagāevaṃ katajjhesano; ()

"Venerable Sir, for our welfare, may the Lord of the Dhamma, compassionate and helpful, swiftly come to this prosperous and thriving city named Sāvatthī, frequented by good people and resembling Lakkhī, Kamalā, and Alakā." Having thus made his request and found reassurance, he departed for his own region.

98.

98.

Buddhatthaṃ so gahapati mahāmagge samagge divā-

Rattiṭṭhānappabhutisubhage paccekalakkhaṃ dhanaṃ,

Vissajjetvā pacuravibhavo daṭṭhabbasārepure

Kāropesi amarabhavanākāreka vihāre vare; ()

For the sake of the Buddha, that householder of abundant wealth, having spent one hundred thousand on each auspicious place along the great, level road, such as resting places for day and night, then, in that city of notable substance, had a splendid monastery built, like unto a celestial abode.

99.

99.

Koṭīha’ṭṭhārasahī asamaṃ bhūmiṃ kiṇitvā samaṃ

Koṭīha’ṭṭhārasahi pacuraṃ māpetva senāsanaṃ,

Koṭīha’ṭṭhārasahi paramaṃ ārāmapūjāmahaṃ

Sajjetvā so gahapati navaṃkammaṃ suniṭṭhāpayi; ()

Having purchased the ground for eighteen crores and made it level, having had abundant dwellings constructed for eighteen crores, and having prepared the great ceremony for the offering of the park for eighteen crores, that householder brought the new construction to a fine completion.

100. [O 0.0428]

100.

Evaṃ jetavanaṃ vihārapavaraṃ kārāpayitvā mahā-

Vīrassā’gamanāya dūtapurise pesesi seṭṭhissaro,

Tesaṃ sīsaharañjalihi mahito sutvāna taṃ sāsanaṃ

Sambuddho jalitiddhimā sapariso rājaggahā nikkhami; ()

Thus, having had the excellent Jetavana monastery built, the lord of merchants sent messengers to announce the arrival of the Great Hero. Honored by their salutations borne upon their heads, and having heard that message, the Perfectly Enlightened One, blazing with spiritual power, departed from Rājagaha with his retinue.

Iti medhānandābhidhānena yatinā viracite sakala kavijana hadayānandadāna nidāne jinavaṃsadīpe santikeka nidāne bhagavato pakiṇṇaka caritappavatti paridīpo soḷasamo saggo.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, entitled 'The Illumination of the Account of the Blessed One's Miscellaneous Conduct,' in the Santika Nidāna of the Jinavaṃsadīpa, a source of joy for the hearts of all poets, composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda.

1. [O 0.0429]

1.

Satthu jetavananāmamindirā-

Rāma motaraṇamaṅgalussave,

Rāmalakkhaṇabhagī (rathoddhatā)

Seṭṭhiputtapamukhā sumaṇḍitā; ()

At the auspicious festival of the Teacher's entry into the Jetavana park, an abode like unto Indra's, those led by the merchant's sons, beautifully adorned, were like unto Rāma and Lakkhaṇa.

2.

2.

Pañcamattasatamāṇavā navā

Pañcavaṇṇadhajabhāsura’ñjalī,

Pañcakhāṇasiriyu’jjalā’bhavuṃ

Pañcamārajinarājino pure; ()

Five hundred young men, holding shining five-colored banners with hands clasped in reverence, their heads radiant with the splendor of five kinds of ornaments, stood before the King, the Conqueror of the five Māras.

3.

3.

Hemakumbhakucakumbhavibbhamā

Seṭhidhītupamukhā kumārikā,

Puṇṇakumbhasatanibbhara’ñjalī

Tassa satthu purato tato bhavuṃ; ()

Then, young maidens led by the merchant's daughters, possessing the charm of breasts like golden pitchers and holding a hundred full water pots in their hands, stood before that Teacher.

4. [O 0.0430]

4.

Seṭṭhipādaparicārikāsakhī

Mantharā’vajitahaṃsadhenuyo,

Pañcamattasatanāriyo’bhavuṃ

Pacchato gahitapuṇṇapātiyo; ()

Five hundred women—the merchant's chief consort, her attendants, and friends—whose graceful gait surpassed that of sheldrakes, followed behind, carrying full bowls.

5.

5.

Setavatthasunivatthapāruto

Pañcaseṭṭhisatamattasevito,

Lokanāyaka manāthapiṇḍiko

Seṭṭhi pītierito tamanvagā; ()

The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, well-clad and covered in white garments, attended by some five hundred merchants and impelled by joy, followed him, the Leader of the World.

6.

6.

Nīlapītapabhūtīhi mārajī

Deharaṃsivisarehi jotayaṃ,

Añjasaṃ sahacarācaraṃ bhuvi

Jaṅgamo kanakabhūdharoriva; ()

The Conqueror of Māra, illuminating all things moving and unmoving upon the earth with the widespread rays of his body—blue, yellow, and so forth—was like a moving mountain of gold.

7.

7.

Maggadesakajanassa piṭṭhito

Bhikkhusaṅghaparivārito yahiṃ,

Jetanāmavanamotarī tahiṃ

Lokalocananipīyamānako; ()

Following behind the one who showed the path, surrounded by the assembly of monks, he entered the grove named Jeta, while being drunk in by the eyes of the world.

8. [O 0.0431]

8.

Pucchitassa paṭipajjanakkamaṃ

Tāya jetavanapujanāya so,

Dehi buddhapamukhe tapovanaṃ

Bhikkhusaṅghavisaye’ti pabruvi; ()

When asked about the proper procedure for the offering of that Jetavana, he said: 'Give this ascetic grove to the Sangha of monks, with the Buddha at its head, to be its domain.'

9.

9.

Dammi buddhapamukhe tapovanaṃ

Bhikkhusaṅghavisaye’ti bhindiya’

Byappathaṃ thiramanāthapiṇḍiko

Seṭṭhi dhotakarapaṅkajoka sadā; ()

"I give this ascetic grove to the Sangha of monks, with the Buddha at its head, to be its domain." Thus spoke the steadfast merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, ever with hands washed and pure like lotuses, as he initiated the offering.

10.

10.

Jālalakkhaṇavicitrakomaḷa-

Pāṇipallavatalesu satthuto,

Dakkhiṇodakamadāsi kañcana-

Kuṇḍikāya surabhippavāsitaṃ; ()

He poured the water of dedication, made fragrant with perfumes from a golden vessel, onto the Teacher's soft, sprout-like palms, which were beautifully marked with the sign of the web.

11. [O 0.0432]

11.

Sitamuṇhamanilātapaṃ paṭi-

Hanti ḍaṃsamakase siriṃsape,

Svā’numodanamakā jino paṭi-

Ggayha jetavanamevamādinā; ()

"It wards off cold and heat, wind and sun, gadflies, mosquitoes, and creeping things." With these words and others, the Conqueror expressed his appreciation upon accepting the Jetavana.

12.

12.

So sudattavisuto samāpayi

Vatrabhūpamapabhūvibhūsaṇo,

Seṭṭhi jetavanapūjanāmahaṃ

Cattakoṭidhanasañcayo sadā; ()

Thus the famous merchant Sudatta, adorned with abundant wealth like unto Indra's and whose fortune ever amounted to a collection of four crores, completed the great offering of the Jetavana.

13.

13.

Indirāya suramandiropamā

Candanāgarusugandhabandhurā,

Tatra gandhakuṭi bhāti medinī-

Sundarisirasi sekharo yathā; ()

There the Fragrant Chamber, like a celestial abode for its splendor, delightful with the scent of sandalwood and aloe-wood, shone like a crest-jewel upon the head of the beautiful earth.

14.

14.

Tāya gandhakuṭiyā’dhirohiṇī

Dhammarājacaraṇindirā’dharā,

Saggamokkhabhavanappavesani-

Sseṇipaddhatirivā’ti nomati; ()

The staircase of that Fragrant Chamber, which bears the splendor of the feet of the King of Dhamma, is revered as if it were a flight of stairs for entering the abodes of heaven and liberation.

15. [O 0.0433]

15.

Tabbihāraparito sudhāmaṇi-

Baddhamāvaraṇacakka māhare,

Satthu kittisirikhīrasāgaru-

Tatuṅgavīcivalayassiriṃ sadā; ()

The enclosing wall around that monastery, set with fine jewels, ever bears a splendor like that of the encircling high waves of the milk ocean of the Teacher's fame and glory.

16.

16.

Tabbihārapariveṇamosadhi-

Tārakādhavalavāḷukākulaṃ,

Vyākaroti jinakundabandhuno

Saṅgamena saradambarassiriṃ; ()

The grounds of that monastery, strewn with white sand and filled with glowing herbs like stars, reveal the splendor of the autumn sky through their association with the Jina, who is a kinsman to the white kunda flower.

17.

17.

Tattharattamaṇiketusaṃhatī-

Raṃsibhinnatimirambare na kiṃ,

Kovidehi ravicanda tārakā

Jotiriṅgananibhā’ti vuccare; ()

There, is not the darkness in the sky dispelled by the collective rays of the red, jeweled banners? And are not the sun, moon, and stars declared by the wise to be like a swarm of fireflies in comparison?

18. [O 0.0434]

18.

Bhāti phullavanarājilakkhiyā

Rattakambalamivā’hisanthataṃ,

Caccaraṃ caraṇasampaṭicchane

Satthuno kusumareṇu nibbharaṃ; ()

The courtyard, laden with flower pollen, shines with the beauty of a line of blossoming trees, appearing like a red blanket spread out to receive the Teacher's feet.

19.

19.

Bhiṅgapantimaṇitantusibbitaṃ

Mandamārutatharussitaṃ tahiṃ,

Pupphareṇupaṭalabbitāna mā-

Bhātisatthu’pari vāritātapaṃ; ()

There, gently stirred by the soft breeze, a canopy of flower pollen, woven with lines of bees like threads of jewels, shines above the Teacher, warding off the sun's heat.

20.

20.

Rājarukkhakaṇikārasākhino

Phullitā parisamantato tahiṃ,

Satthu dhammasavaṇena dissare

Cīvarāni’va nivatthapārutā; ()

There, the Kassod and Kaṇikāra trees, blossoming all around, appear as if dressed and draped in robes from having heard the Teacher's Dhamma.

21. [O 0.0435]

21.

Uggatā’likuladhūmakajjalā

Nibbikāsakalikāsikhāvalī,

Campakadadumapadīpasākhino

Ujjalanti satavaṇṭavattikā; ()

The Campaka trees, like shining tree-lamps with hundreds of stalk-like wicks, are brilliant with rows of unopened buds like flames, and swarms of bees rising from them like smoke from lampblack.

22.

22.

Jhāyataṃ kamadhuradhammabhārati-

Nijjharehi sikharidari tahiṃ,

Sammavegaparisositā da’pi

Kiṃ navūpasamayanti sādhavo; ()

There, in the mountain caves, how could the meditating sages, even those parched by spiritual urgency, not be brought to peace by the streams of the sweet words of the Dhamma?

23.

23.

Kujitālikulakokilā tahiṃ

Phullitaggasahakārasākhino,

Tibbarāgacarite’pi mūlage

Bhāvanāsu naramāpayanti kiṃ; ()

There, how could the cooing of cuckoos and swarms of bees among the blossoming mango branches distract from meditation even those whose nature is rooted in intense passion?

24.

24.

Lājapañcamakapupphasanthataṃ

Tantapovanapavesanañjasaṃ,

Vītarāgacaraṇaṅkasajjitaṃ

Saggamaggamapahāsate sadā; ()

The direct path of entrance to the dense ascetic grove, strewn with the five kinds of parched grain and flowers, and adorned with the footprints of the passionless ones, ever illuminates the path to heaven.

25. [O 0.0436]

25.

Nārivāmacaraṇāturā’pi ye

Saṅgamena vigataṅgaṇaṅginaṃ

Lomahaṃsajanite’va pītiyā;

Tatra’sokatarurāji rājate, ()

There, a row of Asoka trees shines gloriously, as if with a joy that causes horripilation, from contact with those women whose bodies are free from blemish, even those eager to touch it with their beautiful feet.

26.

26.

Kiṃsukādikusumehi bhāsuraṃ

Taṃ tapovana manālayālayaṃ,

Tesa muggatapatejasā bhusaṃ

Aggipajjalitameva dissate; ()

Bright with Kiṃsuka and other blossoms, that ascetic grove, an abode of non-attachment, appears as if greatly ablaze with fire by the fierce radiance of those ascetics.

27.

27.

Uddhavaṇṭagaḷitehi phullase-

Phālikākuḍumalehi sālinī,

Mālakā rajatavedikā kaviya

Vidadumehi khavitā virājate; ()

The garden plot, endowed with blooming Sephālikā buds fallen from their upward stalks, shines, its silver railing adorned by monkeys with coral trees.

28. [O 0.0437]

28.

Pīta cuta makaranda bindavo

Tatra kīrakaravikasārikā,

Kiṃka haranti madhuraṃ ravantipi

Mañjubhāṇīmunibhāratissiriṃ; ()

There, parrots, cuckoos, and myna birds, having drunk drops of mango nectar, even while singing sweetly—why do they steal the splendor of the speech of the sweet-speaking Sage?

29.

29.

Hemakūṭamakuṭehi nijjhara-

Bhārabhāsurataṭo’rapīvarā,

Bhuribhuridharabhubhujā tahiṃ

Cumbare jinasuta’ṅghipaṅkaje; ()

There, many mountain kings, with crowns of golden peaks, whose excellent, stout slopes are radiant with a multitude of waterfalls, kiss the lotus feet of the Jina's son.

30.

30.

Cārucañcupuṭatuṅgacucukā

Cakkavākakucamaṇḍalā tahiṃ,

Nīlikākacakalāpasālinī

Nīlanīrajavilolalocanā; ()

There, with prominent nipples like charming beaks and breast-orbs like ruddy sheldrakes, she shines, possessing a mass of dark blue hair and restless eyes like blue lotuses.

31. [O 0.0438]

31.

Seṇibaddhakalahaṃsamekhalā-

Dāmabhārataṭapīnasoṇinī,

Bhiṅgacakkaratanaṅgadāvalī

Bhaṅgavīcikaṇahārabhāsurā; ()

With a girdle like a line of geese, with full hips and thighs weighed down by garlands, with a row of jeweled armlets like a swarm of bees, and radiant with a necklace like a wavy stream.

32.

32.

Kaṇṇikāgaḷitakañjakesara-

Piñjarambuvimalambarā subhā,

Gandhavāhasukhaphassadā siri-

Mandirā kumudamandahāsinī; ()

She is beautiful, with a pure garment made tawny like water by the fallen golden filaments of the Kaṇṇikāra flower; she bestows the pleasant touch of the fragrant breeze, is an abode of splendor, and smiles gently like a white water lily.

33.

33.

Kesarāliradanā sarojinī-

Kāminī vikacapaṅkajānanā,

Vītasabbadarathehi sevitā

Dibbapokkharaṇiyo najenatikiṃ; ()

A lovely woman like a lotus pond, with teeth like a row of filaments and a face like a blossoming lotus, served by those free from all distress—does she not surpass even the divine lotus ponds?

34. [O 0.0439]

34.

Muddikāpabhutivallivellita-

Jiṇṇacīvarakuṭīhi jhāyataṃ,

Piñchāsāritasikhaṇḍimaṇḍalā-

Khaṇḍataṇḍavasumaṇḍitaṃ vanaṃ; ()

The forest is well-adorned by the intermittent dance of circles of peacocks with their tail-feathers spread, and by the huts of meditators, made from worn-out robes and entwined with grapevines and other creepers.

35.

35.

Satthu kasāvakasatehi bhāvanā-

Sattibhinnatimisāti katthaci,

Dissare niracakāsato tahiṃ

Gabbharo’darasamosarāni’va; ()

Somewhere, the great darkness is pierced by the Teacher and hundreds of wearers of the ochre robe with the spear of meditation; there they are seen continuously, as if they were assemblies in the interior of a cave.

36.

36.

Kālakā dhutapisaṅgavāladhī

Māḷakesu kalaviṅkasāḷikā,

Bhattasitthamanubhūya nibbhayā

Dhammarāvamanukūjare tahiṃ; ()

There on the terraces, crows with tawny tails, Kalaviṅka birds, and myna birds, having eaten the leftover rice from the meal, fearlessly coo in response to the sound of the Dhamma.

37. [O 0.0440]

37.

Vitamaccubhayabhantalocanaṃ

Ālavālajalapānadohaḷaṃ,

Satthu mañjusarapāsaniccalaṃ

Dissate hariṇamaṇḍalaṃ tahiṃ; ()

There is seen a herd of deer, its eyes free from the fear of death and agitation, craving to drink water from the basins at the foot of the trees, made motionless by the snare of the Teacher's sweet voice.

38.

38.

Hatthavellitalatāhi vāraṇā

Vānarāca maṇivijanīhi’va,

Vijayanti bhavatāpabhīruke

Rukkhamūlagatajhāyino tahiṃ; ()

There, elephants, with trunks swaying like creepers, and monkeys, as if with jeweled fans, fan the meditators at the roots of trees, who are fearful of the torment of existence.

39.

39.

Meghavaṇṇavanarājirājinī

Kandamūlaphalabhojanehi sā,

Dānapāramirate’va pīṇaye

Bhikkhūsaṅghasahitaṃ tathāgataṃ; ()

The queen of the forest-expanse, dark as a rain cloud, with foods of tubers, roots, and fruits, as if delighting in the perfection of giving, gladdens the Tathāgata together with the community of monks.

40. [O 0.0441]

40.

Dhammamaṇḍapavitānamuddhati

Lambamānamaṇibubbulodare,

Niccapajjalitavijjurājiyo

Bhanti nijjitaravindutārakā; ()

On high, in the interior of the canopy of the Dhamma hall with its hanging jewel-bubbles, constantly blazing streaks of lightning shine, having surpassed the sun, moon, and stars.

41.

41.

Rukkhakoṭarakulāvakodare

Kujitehi sakuṇehi taṃvanaṃ,

Jeti saṅkhaghaṇavaṃsavallakī-

Rāvasārasuraraṅgabhusiriṃ; ()

That forest, with the cooing of birds in the interior of tree hollows and nests, surpasses the splendor of a celestial stage rich with the essential sounds of conch, drum, flute, and lute.

42.

42.

Indanīlamaṇitoraṇippabhā-

Bhinditabbatimiropamaṃ tahiṃ,

Candacaṇḍakaramaṇḍaladvayaṃ

Vindateva asurindavibbhamaṃ; ()

There, the pair of orbs, the moon and the sun, obtain as it were the splendor of the lord of the Asuras, through the radiance of the sapphire archways, which is like the splitting of deep darkness.

43. [O 0.0442]

43.

Khīrasāgarataraṅgapaṇḍarā

Nekacaṅkamanamālakā tahiṃ,

Phuṭṭhacārucaraṇindirā bhusaṃ

Bhanti jhānapasutāna massame; ()

There in the hermitage, the many walkways and terraces, white like the waves of the milky ocean, shine greatly, touched by the splendor of the beautiful feet of those devoted to meditation.

44.

44.

Bhāvanāya pavanāni pāvanā

Desanāya rasanā vibhūsanā,

Sevakā danavakā sasāvakā

Mānayantī kavikanayaṃ sukhānayaṃ; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ;)

By meditation, the winds are purifiers; by teaching, the tongue is an adornment. Servants, givers, and disciples honor the poetic method, which leads to happiness. (Yamaka composition.)

45.

45.

Kīcakā tyanilakūja kīcakā

Vācakā rivagaṇassa vā cakā,

Mocakā navaphalassa mocakā

Mecakā camaṇithambha mecakā; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ;)

The Kīcaka bamboos are wind-sounding bamboos; speakers of the enemy host, or wheels. Banana trees are releasers of new fruit; and peacocks are dark like jeweled pillars. (Yamaka composition.)

46. [O 0.0443]

46.

Kūjitā’li bhajitā’parākajitā

Rājitā’lakajitā hi pūjitā,

Gāravā’kararavāyakeravā

Keravākararavā sagāravā; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ;)

The cooing bees are resorted to, unconquered; she who shines, conquered by her hair-curls, is indeed honored. With respect, they are a mine of sounds; the white water lilies are a mine of sounds, with respect. (Yamaka composition.)

47.

47.

Ketakī kusumahantacātakī

Ambare ṇukaṇikā’valambare,

Vuñcitā utuniyāmayañjitā

Rāmabhumi paramābhirāmabhū; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ;)

The Ketakī flower, alas, is like the Cātakī bird; in the sky, tiny particles hang down. Arranged and adorned by the order of the seasons, the delightful land became supremely delightful. (Yamaka composition.)

48.

48.

Tāsadā havisadāna māsadā

Yo sadātiya sadā kama taṃ sadā,

So tamo dahatamo hi tattamo

Vītamo muhatamo hī gotamo; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ;)

He who always gives, is like a cloud, do not be attached. He who always goes, always tames that desire. He is the supreme burner of darkness, indeed the ultimate reality. Free from delusion, the foremost sage, indeed, is Gotama. (Yamaka composition.)

49. [O 0.0444]

49.

Sālakā nanavilāsapā latā

Mālakā valisubhāsamā lakā,

Māḷakā valisubhāsamā lakā

Sāḷakā nanavilāsapā lakā; () (Yamakabandhanaṃ)

The young Sāla tree is a creeper protecting beauty; the garland-maker is unequalled in radiant beauty. The terrace is unequalled in radiant beauty; the young Sāla tree is a creeper protecting beauty. (Yamaka composition.)

50.

50.

Vāneva jāto vijito vaneva

Jinova’nejo kavanajānano no,

Netā vinetā vijanānu vāte

Vanī janaṃ jetavane vinento; () (Caturakkharika citta yamakaṃ;)

Born in the forest, victorious in the forest; like the Jina, he is stainless, not one who knows worldly craft. A leader and discipliner in a secluded place, a forest-dweller disciplining the people in Jetavana. (Four-syllable complex Yamaka.)

Iti medhānandābhidhānanayatinā viracite sakalakavijana hadayānandadānanidāne jinavaṃsadīpe santike nidāne jetavana vihārālaṅkāra paridīpo sattarasamo saggo.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the Illumination of the Ornament of the Jetavana Monastery, in the Proximate Story of the Jinavaṃsadīpa—the source of the gift of joy to the hearts of all poets—composed by the ascetic named Medhānanda.

1. [O 0.0445]

1.

Bhuvika yassa jinassa tādino

Vidurānaṃ mukharaṅgamandire,

Arahādi guṇāti sundarī)

Lasate kitti vilāsa sundarī; ()

Migadāyatapovane isi-patane gotama gotta ketuso,

Narasārathi vassa mādimaṃ

Vasi bārāṇasirājadhāniyaṃ; ()

On earth, the gracefully beautiful fame of that Jina, the Such-like One, shines forth in the speech of the wise, beautiful with the virtues of Arahantship and so forth. In the ascetic grove of the Deer Park at Isipatana, he, the banner of the Gotama clan, the Charioteer of Men, dwelt for the first rains-retreat in the royal city of Bārāṇasī.

3.

3.

Puna veḷuvane vināyako

Nagare rājagahe giribbaje,

Dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ catutthakaṃ

Avasi vassamanuddayāparo; ()

Again, the Leader, devoted to compassion, dwelt for the second, third, and fourth rains-retreats in the Bamboo Grove, in the city of Rājagaha, Giribbaja.

4. [O 0.0446]

4.

Muni pañcamavassa mindirā-

Layavesāli puraṃ mahāvane,

Pavihāsi puraṅgapīvaraṃ

Upanissāya yatheva kesari; ()

The Sage, during the fifth rains-retreat, dwelt in the Great Forest near Vesālī, the abode of Indirā, relying on the Gabled Hall, just as a lion.

5.

5.

Timirāpaharo’sadhīlatā-

Jalite sītala nijjharākule,

Munichaṭṭhamanālayo sukhaṃ

Vasi vassaṃ puthumaṅkulācale; ()

The Sage, the dispeller of darkness, being without attachment, happily dwelt for the sixth rains-retreat on Maṅkula Hill, a place radiant like a medicinal creeper and abounding with cool streams.

6.

6.

Tidasālayago sudubbudhaṃ

Abhidhammaṃ kathayaṃ silāsane,

Sunisajja savītināmayī

Sugato sattamavassa manvahaṃ; ()

Having gone to the abode of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, the Well-Gone One spent the seventh rains-retreat, daily expounding the most profound Abhidhamma while well-seated upon the stone seat.

7. [O 0.0447]

7.

Haricandanagandhapāvana-

Pavane bhesakalābhidhe vane,

Sanarāmara lokanāyako

Munināgo vasi vassamaṭṭhamaṃ; ()

In the forest named Bhesakalā, in a grove made fragrant and pure by yellow sandalwood, the great Sage, the Leader of the world with its gods and humans, dwelt for the eighth rains-retreat.

8.

8.

Madhurassarabhāṇi ghosita-

Visute ghosita seṭṭhikārite,

Navamaṃ vasi vassamassame

Varakosambi pure munissaro; ()

The Lord of Sages, speaking with a sweet voice, dwelt for the ninth rains-retreat in the excellent city of Kosambī, at the widely renowned hermitage built by the merchant Ghosita.

9.

9.

Munikesari pārileyyaka-

Karinājīvitadānato bhato,

Dasamaṃ vasi pārileyyake

Vanasaṇḍe tarusaṇḍamaṇḍite; ()

The lion-like Sage, sustained by the provisions offered by the Pārileyyaka elephant, dwelt for the tenth rains-retreat in the Pārileyyaka forest grove, a place adorned with clusters of trees.

10.

10.

Varadhammasudhārasena sa-

Jjana mekādasamaṃ samaṃ jino,

Dvijagāmavare’bhipīṇayaṃ

Vasi nāḷāvidite nirālayo; ()

The Victor, delighting the virtuous with the nectarous taste of the excellent Dhamma, dwelt for the eleventh year without abode in Nāḷā, the renowned village of Brahmins.

11. [O 0.0448]

11.

Dharaṇīsuragāma māsadā

Punaverañja maniñjano jino,

Pucimandadumindamūlago

Asamo bārasamaṃ samaṃ vasī; ()

Having again approached the Brahmin village of Verañjā, the imperturbable and unequalled Victor dwelt for the twelfth year at the foot of the royal Pucimanda tree.

12.

12.

Vikacappalacārulocano

Munirājā vajirācalācalo,

Sikharākulacāliyācale

Avasī teḷasamaṃ guṇālayo; ()

The King of Sages—an abode of virtues, with eyes as beautiful as a blossoming lotus, and as unshaken as the Diamond Mountain—dwelt for the thirteenth rains-retreat on Cāliya mountain, a place abounding in peaks.

13.

13.

Salilāsayasītale mudu-

Pavane jetavane tapovane,

Vasi cuddasamaṃ samaṃ mahā-

Samaṇo assamaṇā’pasādano; ()

In Jetavana, the ascetic's grove, a place cooled by its reservoir and gentle breezes, the Great Ascetic, who refutes the non-ascetics, dwelt for the fourteenth rains-retreat.

14. [O 0.0449]

14.

Kapilavhayarājadhāniyā

Avidure nararāhaseyyake,

Pavihāsi tipañcamaṃ samaṃ

Muni nigrodhatapovane subhe; ()

Not far from the royal city named Kapilavatthu, in a secluded royal park, the Sage dwelt for the fifteenth rains-retreat in the beautiful Nigrodha ascetic grove.

15.

15.

Khara mālavakañca rakkhasaṃ

Damayaṃ bhūdhara pīvarodaraṃ,

Rucirālavirājadhāniyaṃ

Viharī soḷasamaṃ samaṃ jino; ()

Taming the fierce demon Ālavaka, whose belly was as stout as a mountain, the Victor dwelt for the sixteenth year in the radiant royal city of Ālavī.

16.

16.

Puna veḷuvanaṃ tapovanaṃ

Upanissāya giribbajaṃ puraṃ,

Dasa sattama vassa māvasī

Munisīho hatamāravāraṇo; ()

Again, the Lion of Sages, who had slain the elephant Māra, dwelt for the seventeenth rains-retreat, residing in the ascetic's grove of Veḷuvana, near the city of Giribbaja.

17.

17.

Bhavadukkharujāhi mocayaṃ

Janataṃ dhammakathā’gadena so,

Vasi cāliyapabbatālaye

Jinavejjācariyo dasaṭṭhamaṃ; ()

Freeing the people from the disease of suffering in existence with the medicine of a Dhamma discourse, he, the Teacher and Victorious Physician, dwelt for the eighteenth rains-retreat in an abode on Cāliya mountain.

18. [O 0.0450]

18.

Tadanantaravassa muggadhi

Vipule cāliyapakabbate’va so,

Vasi vīsatimaṃ giribbaje

Nagare veḷuvane tapovane; ()

In the year immediately following, the nineteenth, he dwelt on the vast Cāliya mountain; for the twentieth year, he dwelt in the city of Giribbaja, in the ascetic's grove, the Bamboo Grove.

19.

19.

Anibaddhavihārato iti

Viharanto bhagavā tahiṃtahiṃ

Maṇijotiraso’va kāmado

Sarade vīsati vītināmayī; ()

Thus, by dwelling without a fixed residence, the Blessed One, abiding here and there like a wish-fulfilling gem, passed twenty autumns.

20.

20.

Muni jetavane tapovane

Bhavane cā’pi migāramātuyā,

Mahite vasi pañcavīsati-

Mitavassāni tibaddhavāsago; ()

The Sage, maintaining a fixed residence, dwelt for twenty-five years in the revered Jetavana, the ascetic's grove, and in the mansion of Migāramātā.

21. [O 0.0451]

21.

Anibaddhanibaddhavāsato

Vasato tassa sato tahiṃ tahiṃ,

Nanu vijjati kiccapañcakaṃ

Katakiccassa kathananuvāsaraṃ; ()

For him, who has accomplished his task, dwelling mindfully here and there, both with and without a fixed residence, does not the fivefold duty surely exist for him day by day?

22.

22.

Aruṇuggamane samuṭṭhito

Tadupaṭṭhākajanassa’nuggahaṃ,

Munirānanapādadhovanaṃ

Pavidhāyā’khilakicca mattano; ()

Having arisen at the break of dawn, and having performed all his personal duties, including the washing of his face and feet, the Sage does so for the welfare of those who attend upon him.

23.

23.

Sunisajja susajjitā’sane

Sapadānācaraṇāya yāvatā,

Samayo samayaññu vindati

Naciraṃ jhānasukhaṃ rahogato; ()

Well-seated on a well-prepared seat, the knower of the proper time, having entered solitude, enjoys for a while the bliss of jhāna, until the time for the alms-round arrives.

24. [O 0.0452]

24.

Paribandhiya tāyabandhanaṃ

Sunivatthantaravāsako’pari,

Arahaddhajachāditaṅgimā

Maṇivaṇṇopalapatta mubbahaṃ; ()

Having tied the waistband, being well-clad in the inner and outer robes, his limbs covered with the banner of the Arahant, he lifts up the bowl, which is the color of a jewel and like a lotus leaf.

25.

25.

Abhisaṅkhatapuññasattiyā

Vivaṭadvāravihāragabbhato,

Girigabbharato’va kesarī

Bahinikkhamma kadāci ekako, ()

By the power of his accumulated merit, from the chamber of the monastery with its door open, he sometimes emerges alone, like a lion from a mountain cave.

26.

26.

Valayikatatārakāvalī

Navacandoriva vāridodarā,

Yatisaṅghapurakkhato tato

Bahi nikkhamma kadāci so muni; ()

And sometimes that Sage emerges, escorted by the assembly of ascetics, like a new moon from the belly of a cloud, encircled by a host of stars.

27.

27.

Pakatīgatiyā’pi bhikkhituṃ

Gatiyā sappaṭihāriyā’yapi,

Yugamattadaso samācare

Nigamaggāmapurīsu katthaci; ()

Whether going for alms with his natural gait or with a miraculous one, he conducts himself somewhere in market towns, villages, or cities, seeing only a yoke's length before him.

28. [O 0.0453]

28.

Carato varapāṭihāriyaṃ

Samadhiṭṭhāya kadāci bhikkhituṃ,

Vimalīkurute mahītalaṃ

Purato mandasugandhamāruto; ()

When he walks to beg for alms, sometimes performing an excellent miracle he has resolved upon, a gentle, fragrant breeze blows before him, purifying the surface of the earth.

29.

29.

Purato’pasamenti dhūliyo

Carato cārutarañjase sire,

Vilasanti vitāna vibbhamā

Navameghā phusitāni muñcare; ()

As he walks, dust subsides before him; on the path, canopies appear with wondrous splendor, and new clouds release gentle showers.

30.

30.

Kusumāni samīraṇā’pare

Vipinenā’hariyo’kirantipi,

Nijapādatalaṃ’va bhūtalaṃ

Samataṃ yāti pathe padappite; ()

Moreover, other breezes, having brought flowers from the forest, scatter them upon his path; and where he places his foot, the surface of the earth becomes as level as the sole of his own foot.

31. [O 0.0454]

31.

Mudukā sukhaphassadā mahī-

Vanitā tappadasaṅgame’kadā,

Kamalānipi cumbare’kadā

Pathaviṃ bhejja tadaṅghīpaṅkaje; ()

Sometimes, at the contact of his feet, the earth becomes soft and pleasant to the touch; at other times, lotuses spring up, piercing the ground at his lotus-like feet.

32.

32.

Caraṇakkamitā’ravindaja-

Makarandā’ti sugandhabandhurā,

Jinagandhagajinda māsiraṃ

Parivāsenti samokirantipi; ()

The lovely, sweet fragrances from the nectar of the lotuses born from his footsteps perfume and scatter all around, enveloping the Jina, that lordly elephant of scent.

33.

33.

Makarandapabandhavibbhamaṃ

Juti sindhūravicuṇṇabandhurā,

Abhibhūya supiñjarāyate

Carato lokamimaṃ carācaraṃ; ()

As he wanders through this world of the moving and unmoving, his radiance, lovely with hues of vermilion powder, surpasses the splendor of a stream of nectar and glows with a golden light.

34.

34.

Kalahaṃsa mayūrasārikā

Karavīkā’pi sakaṃsakaṃ ravaṃ,

Dvipadā’pi catuppadā’pare

Vajato tassa napūjayanti kiṃ; ()

Do not the geese, peacocks, starlings, and Karavīkas with their own respective songs, and other two-footed and four-footed beings, revere him as he walks?

35. [O 0.0455]

35.

Turiyāni vibhūsaṇāni’pi

Sayamevā’bhiravanti taṅkhaṇe,

Tamudikkhiya pāṭihāriyaṃ

Sugate koka hi nasampasīdati; ()

Even musical instruments and ornaments sound of their own accord at that moment. Seeing such a marvel of the Sugata, who would not be filled with joy?

36.

36.

Vividhabbhutapāṭihāriya-

Katasaññāya mahājano jino,

Janayaṃ janatāya’nuddayaṃ

Idhapiṇḍatthamupāgato iti; ()

By the sign of the diverse and wondrous miracles, the great multitude perceived thus: 'The Victor, generating compassion for the people, has come here for alms.'

37.

37.

Kusumādiyamākulañjalī

Sadaneha’ntaravithi motare,

Jinaraṃsi pabandha kambala-

Satasañchanna vivaṇṇaviggahā; ()

With hands full of flowers and other offerings, people gather in their houses and in the streets, their pale forms covered by hundreds of blankets woven from the Victor's rays.

38. [O 0.0456]

38.

Janatā nakharālidīdhiti-

Nikarākāsanadīnimujjitā,

Abhivandati vandanārahaṃ

Munino pādayugaṃ pamoditā; ()

The delighted multitude, immersed in a celestial river which was a cluster of rays from the rows of his nails, pays homage to the Sage's pair of feet, worthy of veneration.

39.

39.

Dasavisativā mahājano

Jinapāmokkhayatī satampivā,

Abhiyācati detha noiti

Bhagavantaṃ vibhavānurūpato; ()

Ten or twenty people from the great multitude, or even a hundred ascetics with the Victor as their chief, beseech the Blessed One, saying, 'Pray, allow us to give according to our means.'

40.

40.

Adhivāsanamassa jāniya

Janatā’dāya jinassa hatthato,

Tamadhiṭṭhitapatta mindirā-

Sadanaṃ dānagharaṃ pavesaye; ()

Knowing his consent, the populace, receiving from the Victor's hand the bowl he firmly held, led him to the alms hall, a dwelling splendid as a mansion.

41. [O 0.0457]

41.

Catujātikagandhabhāvite

Bhuvi paññattavarāsanopari,

Ahatāhatavatthajātite

Sunisinnaṃ sugataṃ sasāvakaṃ; ()

Upon the finest seat prepared on the ground, which was scented with four kinds of fragrances, the Well-Gone One with his disciples was well-seated, clad in robes both new and laundered.

42.

42.

Paṭiyattapaṇītabhojana-

Vikatīhe’va sahatthapaṅkajā,

Abhitappayate mahājano

Patimāneti ca cīvarādinā; ()

The great multitude, with their own lotus-like hands, satisfies them with prepared, excellent food and various delicacies, and also honors them with robes and other things.

43.

43.

Saraṇāgamane’pi pañcayu

Adhisīlesu patiṭṭhahanti ye,

Catumaggaphalesu katthavi

Tadabhiññā’nusayāsayādito; ()

There are those who, by merely taking refuge, become established in the five precepts; and others, somewhere upon the four paths and fruits, according to their direct knowledge, latent dispositions, and inclinations.

44.

44.

Bhagavā katabhattakiccavā

Anurūpāya kathāya dhammiyā,

Ravibandhu vineyya bandhunaṃ

Hadayambhojavanaṃ pabodhaye; ()

The Blessed One, the Kinsman of the Sun, having finished the business of the meal, then with a suitable Dhamma talk, having trained his kinsmen, awakens the lotus-forest of their hearts.

45. [O 0.0458]

45.

Harimerugiri’va jaṅgamo

Parinaddhindasarāsanāvalī,

Visate satapuññalakkhaṇo

Muniru’ṭṭhāya vihāramāsanā; ()

Like a moving golden Mount Meru, encircled by a row of rainbows, the Sage, adorned with the hundred marks of merit, having risen from his seat, enters the monastery.

46.

46.

Varamaṇḍalamāḷake tahiṃ

Muni paññattamahārahāsane,

Khaṇamāgamayaṃ nisidati

Yaminaṃ bhojanakiccasādhanaṃ; ()

There, in that excellent pavilion, the Sage sits upon the magnificent, prepared seat, awaiting the moment for the accomplishment of the meal-duty for the ascetics.

47.

47.

Maṇivammasuvammitā viya

Karino pārutapaṃsukūlikā,

Yatayo yatirājayūthapaṃ

Parivārenti upecca taṅkhaṇe; ()

Like elephants well-armored with jeweled mail, the ascetics, wearing their dust-heap robes, approach and surround the herd-leader, the king of ascetics, at that very moment.

48. [O 0.0459]

48.

Samayaṃ samayaññuno tato

Tadupaṭṭhākavaro nivedaye,

Jinagandhagajo suvāsitaṃ

Visate gandhakuṭiṃ sugandhinā; () (Purebhattakiccaṃ)

Then his foremost attendant, who knows the time, announces that it is time. The Victor, a veritable fragrant elephant, enters the perfumed chamber, made fragrant with sweet scents.

49.

49.

Athagandhakuṭīmukhe jino

Virajo pādarajo nacatthipi,

Paridhotapadāni nikkhipaṃ

Maṇisopāṇatale khaṇaṃ ṭhito; ()

Then at the entrance of the perfumed chamber, the dustless Victor—on whose feet there was not even any dust—stood for a moment, placing his washed feet upon the jeweled staircase.

50.

50.

Udayo’pi jinassa dullabho

Khaṇasampattisamiddhi dullabhā,

Manujesu’papatti dullabhā

Jinadhammassavaṇampi dullabhaṃ; ()

The arising of a Victor is rare; the successful attainment of a favorable moment is rare; birth among humans is rare; and hearing the Victor’s Dhamma is also rare.

51.

51.

Samaṇatta mape’ttha dullabhaṃ

Tividhaṃ sāsana mappamādato,

Yatayo’vadatā’nusāsati

Abhisampādayathā’ti bhikkhave; ()

Monkhood, too, is rare in this world. Thus he instructs and admonishes the ascetics: 'Practice the threefold teaching with diligence! Strive on and accomplish it, O bhikkhus!'

52. [O 0.0460]

52.

Abhivandiya keci bhikkhavo

Bhagavantaṃtaka paṭipattipūrakā,

Atha sampaṭipādanakkamaṃ

Paṭipucchantivipassanādisu; ()

Then some bhikkhus, who are fulfilling the practice that makes an end of suffering, having paid homage to the Blessed One, inquire about the step-by-step procedure for insight and other such meditations.

53.

53.

Padadāti vipassanādisu

Muni tesaṃ cariyānurūpikaṃ,

Paṭigaṇhiya satthusāsanaṃ

Maṇidāmaṃ viya makaṇḍanatthiko; ()

The Sage gives to them instruction in insight and other practices that is suitable for their individual conduct. They, in turn, receive the Teacher's instruction like one desiring a jeweled garland for an ornament.

54.

54.

Pavidhāya jinaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ

Atha te bhattisamappitañjalī,

Pavisanti yatī sakaṃsakaṃ

Vasatiṃ santanivātavuttino; ()

Then, having circumambulated the Victor to the right, those ascetics, with hands offered in devotion, enter their own respective dwellings, living a life of peace and humility.

55. [O 0.0461]

55.

Vatapabbatapādakandara-

Pabhūtīsva’ññataraṃka padhānikā,

Pavisanti surāsuroraga-

Garuḷānaṃ bhavanesucā’pare; ()

Some of the striving monks enter one or another place, such as a cave at the foot of Mount Vata. And others enter the abodes of gods, asuras, nāgas, and garuḍas.

56.

56.

Atha gandhakuṭiṃ yadicchati

Pavisitvā pavivekakāmavā,

Muni dakkhiṇapassato sato

Sayanaṃ kappayatī’sakaṃ divā; ()

Then the Sage, desiring seclusion, enters the perfumed chamber if he so wishes, and mindfully prepares his resting place for the day, lying down on his right side.

57.

57.

Vupasantasarirajassamo

Muniru’ṭṭhāya anekakoṭiyo,

Anubhūyaka samādhayo khaṇaṃ

Bhuvanaṃ passati buddhacakkhunā; ()

The Sage, his bodily fatigue calmed, arises from his rest. Then, for a moment, having experienced many crores of concentrations, he beholds the world with the Buddha-eye.

58. [O 0.0462]

58.

Samathamhi vipassanāyavā

Dhuranikkhepakate tathāgate,

Tahimiddhibalenu’paṭṭhito

Puna vuṭṭhāpayate dayānidhi; ()

When the burden has been laid down by the Tathāgata in serenity or insight, there the treasury of compassion, supported by psychic power, rouses him again.

59.

59.

Iti pañcasatampi sāvake

Atikhippaṃ kabhagavā’nusāsiya,

Padumāniva te pabodhayaṃ

Nabhāsā yāti vihāra mattano; ()

Thus the Blessed One, having very swiftly instructed even five hundred disciples, awakening them as if they were lotuses, travels through the sky to his own dwelling.

60.

60.

Jinasindhavapādavikkamaṃ

Jinachaddantagajindakuñcanaṃ,

Jinakesarasīhagajjanaṃ

Abhipassāma suṇoma no iti; ()

May we behold the stride of the Victor, that noble steed! May we hear the trumpeting of the Victor, that king of six-tusked elephants! May we hear the roaring of the Victor, that maned lion!

61.

61.

Vihareyya yahiṃ jino tahiṃ

Aparaṇhe kusumākulañjalī,

Sunivatthasupārutā bhusaṃ

Muditā sannipatantikho janā; ()

Wherever the Victor might be dwelling, there in the afternoon the people indeed gather, greatly joyful, with hands full of flowers, well-dressed and well-robed.

62. [O 0.0463]

62.

Atha dassitapāṭihāriyo

Pavisatvā varadhammamaṇḍapaṃ,

Sūriyova yugandharo’pari

Sunisajjā’sanamatthake jino; ()

Then the Victor, having displayed miracles and entered the excellent Dhamma pavilion, sits well upon the highest seat, like the sun above the peak of Mount Yugandhara.

63.

63.

Karavikavirāvahārinā

Madhuro’dārasarena sotunaṃ,

Caturā’riyasaccamīraye

Anupubbāya kathāya nissitaṃ; ()
